News.title: Terrifying moment ‘drunk driver’ smashes into restaurant with customers crushed & three injured in Brit holiday hotspot
News.content:
Next

THIS is the terrifying moment a drunk driver ploughed into a restaurant, crushing three people at a popular British holiday hotspot.

Terrifying footage captures the moment the car, driven by a 45-year-old foreign national, speeds into the tavern in Greece, shattering tables and injuring three patrons.



Diners were scattered as the car hit, with footage capturing the vehicle backing up after the collision while angry diners ran toward it armed with dining chairs.

A breathalyser test administered at the scene which reportedly revealed the male driver was under the influence of alcohol, according to Protothema.



Large flower pots placed around the outside area, which prevented the vehicle from ploughing further among the customers.

The store owner said: “If we didn’t have planters, we would have funerals.”



The appalling incident occurred at a local Tavern full of customers in Evosmos, Thessaloniki.

The store owner said she left the store a few minutes prior and rushed back as soon as she heard about the accident in the early hours of Sunday morning.



She said: “I saw terror and panic, it was like watching a movie.”

One witness told local reporters she felt lucky to be alive saying if it weren’t for the planters they “would all have been killed”.

The driver was arrested at the scene and the trio of injured patrons were rushed to hospital.

It comes as a person was killed and seven more were injured after a driver slammed into a crowded restaurant in New Jersey last month.

The driver, identified as a 93-year-old woman, plowed into brunch diners eating on the terrace at Meg’s Grill in Lavallette.



The vehicle went through the outdoor eating area and into the building.

A 56-year-old woman from Toms River was killed at the scene, News 12 New Jersey reported.

The driver sustained minor injuries and all other victims were taken to hospital.

In June, seven people were injured – including to children – when a car slammed into a busy terrace bar on the Costa de Sol.

The driver careened through a crowd of diners, also taking out the restaurant’s tables and umbrellas.



Witnesses were seen running to the aid of the victims.

Chairs and tables were overturned and debris was left strewn across the ground in Frigiliana.

Seven people were left injured, including two children aged five and 14.

The adult victims included three women aged 48, 79, and 45, and two men aged 44 and 77.

News.title: Haunting bodycam footage shows mom refusing to let cops into home to check on kids weeks before 2 baby girls found dead
News.content:
Next

THIS is the chilling moment officers attempted a welfare check on two children and were refused entry by their mom weeks before they were found dead.

Justine May, 31, was arrested on murder charges for the deaths of her daughters, Emory Deacon, 2, and 15-month-old Harlow Deacon, on September 29.



The pair were still alive when officers turned up at their home in Ladson, South Carolina, on August 30.

Just weeks later, they would both be dead from starvation and dehydration as a result of neglect, as ruled by the coroner.



This was despite at least 13 welfare checks taking place at the property in the weeks leading up to their deaths where police “observed no signs of concern,” per the Sheriff’s Office.

Now-haunting footage released by the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office, shows checks from August 30 and September 12.

read more on crime 'UNIMANINABLE' HORROR Pregnant mum killed in mass shooting was days away from giving birth



On September 12, tensions were high when May answered the door and immediately became confrontational.

“How can I help you? No one can come in,” she said.

The deputy pointed her to two women from a crisis centre wanting to speak to her after they got a call raising concerns about her mental health.

“I’m not doing this,” she said, accusing their father of placing the phone call and venting her frustrations about the “near daily” visits she got from officers.



“I’m perfectly fine,” she told the caseworkers without allowing them inside.

During the August 30 visit, officers did gain entry to the home after she said, “I’d really rather not have you come in at all.”

They informed May that they, and a caseworker, were visiting “because after she and the kids’ father separated, her mental health has apparently declined, and no one has seen these kids in over a week.”

The social services case worker added that their father Zack Deacon had made attempts to see his daughters, and that May’s mother had also raised concerns.

May immediately clapped back accusing her ex of making up her mental health issues, and calling him and her mom “crazy.”



She then accused the girls’ father of having “erratic behavior” when he came by the home.

She denied hearing voices and having thoughts of harming anyone when questioned by deputies as she held one child and the second crawled around her feet.

One caseworker noticed a rash on one of her daughters, to which May said, “Yes, she had a diaper rash, like a normal baby does.”

Once inside, the home appeared well looked after and May’s children followed her around.

None of the visits showed alarm bells to caseworkers or deputies, the Sheriffs Office previously said.



On September 22, a week before the girls died, the sheriff’s office decided to discontinue welfare checks.

CCSO said this was “based on the totality of the information available at the time including the previous contacts, the involvement of DSS and Mobile Crisis, and the absence of new actionable information indicating an immediate threat to Ms. May or her children.”

On the day officers found the children’s bodies, May was “speaking incoherently” and told them she had been in a “blur” for two weeks, the cops said.



They added that she said she could not remember how long she had not fed her two children.

She has been charged with two counts of homicide by child abuse and is being held at the Al Cannon Detention Center.

Meanwhile, the children’s father has asked for a review of police conduct in their handling of the case..

“Emory and Harlow deserve the truth,” his lawyer said.

“Their father deserves to see the file, not to learn about the case on the news.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

If you or someone you know is affected by any of the issues raised in this story, call or text the Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline at 800-422-4453 or live chat at childhelphotline.org.

If a child or other person is in immediate danger, contact 911 immediately.

News.title: Maintenance worker left paralysed after 30ft plunge from electricity pylon caused by ‘loose nut’ wins £10m payout
News.content:
Next

A WORKER who was left paralysed after falling 30ft from an electricity pylon caused by a “loose nut” has won £10million in compensation.

Power lines maintenance guy Gavin Pugh, from Bangor, North Wales, was working to dismantle a pylon in East Staffordshire in April 2022.



He unknowingly clipped his safety line onto a section of the structure which had already been worked on by other workers, leaving it only secure at one end.

The strut spun into a vertical position when he put his weight on it, causing his safety rope to slip loose, plunging him more than 30 feet to the ground, and causing catastrophic and life-changing injuries.



Mr Pugh, who was 33 at the time, was left paraplegic and reliant on a wheelchair for life, having also suffered injuries to his brain, neck, shoulder, ribs and internal organs.

Following the fall, his Cheshire-based employer Wood Transmission and Distribution Ltd was criticised by the Health and Safety Executive, which said “adequate safety arrangements” had not been in place.



Another team had already done some work on the pylon, but Mr Pugh had not been aware that the section he clipped onto was no longer secure.

The firm was fined £240,000.

Mr Pugh sued the company at London’s High Court for compensation and after out-of-court negotiations has agreed a care and compensation package, said by his lawyers, Stewarts, to be worth “eight figures.”

The money is to compensate him for his injuries and lost future earnings, as well as to fund 24-hour live-in carers and the £1m-plus rehabilitation costs associated with his disability.



In a statement post-settlement, Mr Pugh’s lawyers said that, before the fall, he had been an “active and sociable person” who enjoyed his job and had his own fishing boat.

But his injuries had affected “every part of his life,” they said, leaving him unable to walk again and suffering with “life-changing physical limitations” and “significant psychological consequences.”

Mr Pugh’s employer agreed to pay compensation, with interim payments secured by his lawyers to fund his vital private rehab and care, and a final eight-figure settlement then agreed between the parties.

In a statement after the settlement, he said: “The fall turned my life upside down. I wasn’t able to work or go out with my friends. My life fell apart.

“The interim payments helped massively. I wouldn’t have been able to do anything without them.



“They made sure I was able to pay for any treatment or rehabilitation that I needed. They also helped in securing my new bungalow.

“The settlement ensures I’m comfortable for the rest of my life and that I’ll be looked after. Without it I would have been in a very difficult position, so I am so grateful for it.

“I’ve been able to get back into some of my past hobbies. I’m fishing and I’m able to get out and about. I’m able to go out with my friends again and enjoy myself, albeit not to the same extent, but I’m still happy.”

Following a magistrates court hearing in 2024 at which the company was fined £240,000 for breaching Regulation 4(1) of the Work at Height Regulation 2005, HSE inspector Robert Gidman said the “tragic incident” could have been prevented if the company had “put in place adequate arrangements to protect its workers from harm.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Proper assessment of the risks and consideration of work methods, adequate staffing and clear procedures for transferring towers between teams could have enabled this work to go ahead without incident,” he said.



“Instead, because of the company’s shortcomings, a worker has sadly and unnecessarily been left paralysed.”

News.title: I took tiger maul victim’s photo seconds before he leapt into enclosure, reveals shocked eyewitness to zoo horror
News.content:
Next

A MAN who was mauled to death by a tiger asked a fellow zoo visitor to take his photo before leaping into the enclosure.

Del Taylor was app­r­oached while watching 30st Altai from a viewing platform overlooking the pen on Saturday.



The man, in his early 20s, asked her: “Can you grab a shot of myself with the tiger?”

Del, who was there with her boyfriend, took the man’s phone and he posed with the five-year-old Siberian tiger in the background.



In video footage taken by her partner, the man can be heard laughing as he excitedly pleads: “One more, one more, one more.”

He then says: “Thank you, lady.”



The couple left and moments later the man climbed over a metre-high viewing barrier before dropping into the enclosure.

Ms Taylor told The Sun: “He was completely alone.

“At first he was dancing on the bridge overlooking the enclosure. He ended up standing next to me.

“My partner was recording the tiger and you can hear me having this interaction.



“You can hear him asking for a photo. I took a couple of him with his back towards the enclosure.

“I positioned the camera so I could get Altai in it with him.”

The man landed on the grass a few feet from Altai at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, in Doncaster.

Video footage captured him yelling, “No, no, no” and “Stop, stop, stop, stop, stop” as the tiger circled him before lunging for his neck.



Rangers arrived to fire warning shots and the tiger retreated to its pen.

The man died at the scene.

Some reports claimed he was using Makaton hand gestures used by people with learning difficulties as the animal struck.



Police continued to investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident.

News.title: Trump looks at renaming Atlantic and Pacific as ‘Trump Ocean’ as he reveals the one landmark he won’t touch
News.content:
Next

PRESIDENT Donald Trump has suggested renaming the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean the Trump Ocean or Ocean of the Americans.

Trump made the comments at his latest Midterm campaign rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, on Saturday.



The President, who has already announced intentions to rename the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America, said the country would “need a river.”

“We’ve got the Gulf, we’ve got a beautiful lake, and now someone said ‘you need a river,’ so, I don’t wanna change the name of the Hudson River,” he said.



“We need a river. We need an ocean. We’ll call it ‘Trump Ocean’ or ‘Ocean of the Americans’, something like that.

“Before I get out, I think we should have an ocean. And we need a great river.”

Trump’s previous executive order to rename Lake Ontario does not force Ottawa to accept the change.

However, Google made waves when it renamed the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America on its maps app.

Trump has attempted to rename the Kennedy Center after himself.

The courts later told Trump’s administration to give 30 days’ notice before making major changes to the facility.



He’s floated the idea of changing the state of New Mexico to New America and the Strait of Hormuz to the Trump Strait.

So far, he has not followed through on either idea.

News.title: Tourist ‘chases woman through hotel with knife before locking himself in room with child’ on holiday in Costa del Sol
News.content:
'WILD ATTACK' Tourist ‘chases woman through hotel with knife before locking himself in room with child’ on holiday in Costa del Sol







Next

A TOURIST has been arrested after allegedly attacking a woman with a knife and barricading himself in his hotel room with a young child.

Costa del Sol cops said the man chased his partner through a hotel in Manilva, Malaga.



The suspect allegedly became violent after a heated argument with the woman on the final day of a family holiday in Spain.

Police said his partner then grabbed two of their three kids and fled the hotel room in fear.



The man allegedly chased her through the hotel, armed with a knife.

A hero security guard then stepped in and reportedly tackled him to the ground.

But the suspect reportedly then returned to his room, locking himself inside with the couple’s third child while still armed.

Police called to a report of suspected domestic violence at the hotel rushed to the scene.

They were able to get into the hotel room with a master key and overpower the suspect.

He was then detained on suspicion of gender-based violence.



The family were reportedly due to return home the next day.

Sources told Diario Sur that cops had been called to the hotel on at least one previous occasion after reports of suspected domestic abuse linked to the couple.

It comes after the shooting of a celebrity supercharged BBL surgeon shook the Costa del Sol this week.

Brit-trained Dr Alexander Aslani, 57, was shot dead on Wednesday evening after a gunman charged into his Marbella clinic.

The plastic surgeon was shot several times in the head inside his clinic in the east of the city, which specialises in BBLs, supercharged BBLs and boob jobs.



The shooter fled the scene, sparking a huge manhunt before a Swedish teen was arrested 24 hours later.

Police probed whether the killing was a revenge attack linked to a disgruntled client who had repeatedly complained about the results of a cosmetic procedure.

The woman reportedly sent threatening messages to his Cirumed clinic the day before the murder, demanding a refund for her treatment.

Her partner had also allegedly visited the clinic and made threats against staff during an earlier confrontation.

The German surgeon, famed for his Supercharged Brazilian butt lift, had built a booming business treating British reality stars, with up to 70 per cent of his patients traveling from the UK.



The Sun revealed Aslani had been embroiled in a bitter High Court battle with an influencer who accused him of botching three operations.

Influencer Paulina Sobierajska complained she needed reconstructive surgery and warned women considering using Aslani: “DON’T DO IT.”

Aslani successfully sued her for libel after she failed to defend the case.

Mr Justice Saini awarded him £40,000 damages in 2021, saying the sum reflected the “total falsity” of the allegations.

Other court records show one customer successfully sued the Brit-trained doctor for medical malpractice after an operation from him and inadequate follow-up care left her with an infection and a fistula, a tunnel between two organs.

Her lawyers said Dr Aslani failed to cut the fistula out after it was revealed by an ultrasound.

Aslani, the hospital he worked for and its insurers were ordered to pay £19,932.66 after a Spanish court ruled they had been medically negligent in 2018.

News.title: ‘Micropenis meant I couldn’t rape’, Iranian migrant claims – as ‘predator’ is jailed for 11 years for attempted rape
News.content:
SICK EXCUSE ‘Micropenis meant I couldn’t rape’, Iranian migrant claims – as ‘predator’ is jailed for 11 years for attempted rape







Next

AN ASYLUM seeker who claimed he had a “micropenis” and was unable to have sex has been locked up for 11 years for attempted rape.

Iranian Hossein Mohmoudi, 36, came to Britain by piloting a migrant boat across the Channel.

In December 2024, he followed a 43-year-old woman for 55 minutes, including on to the same bus, as she went home after a Christmas party.



He tried to rape her in an alleyway but stopped when he was confronted by a passerby who intervened.



Mohmoudi has now been jailed for 11 years.

Judge Sarah-Jane Griffiths described him as a “dangerous sexual predator” at his trial at Snaresbrook Crown Court.

Mohmoudi had claimed he couldn’t have committed the crime because he had a “micropenis”.



Having made the claim, two doctors visited him in his cell to ascertain the size of his penis.

He also claimed at the trial that he couldn’t have committed the crime due to his obesity, smoking habit and depression which meant he had no ability or desire to have sex.

The jury heard that he had been talking on a fetish website before the attack and in his defence it was claimed it was “helpful for my English”.

Judge Griffiths said: “I do not believe for one moment that you were on that site to learn, or improve, your English.”



She added: “I also find that you were clearly able to have sexual intercourse,” concluding: “The evidence against you was overwhelming.”

The judge also said that only three months before the attack, cops had been called after Mohmoudi, who was living in an asylum hotel in east London, “terrified” a woman by following her home, waiting outside and “looking in for a considerable period of time”.

Prosecutor Christiaan Moll also told the court that Mohmoudi had previously stalked a barmaid in south-west London and harassed another woman by repeatedly emailing her at work.

Judge Griffiths said: “I have no doubt you were wandering the streets in the early hours looking to see if there was anyone around you could take advantage of.”

She added: “It is clear that this offence has caused severe psychological harm,” and saying: “You have shown no remorse at all.”



Mohmoudi’s victim, who cannot be identified due to legal protections, said: “I thought you were going to kill me that night if you hadn’t been interrupted. You still might… You completely destroyed my life.”

Due to his denials Mohmoudi could not be asked to get checked for STDs, meaning his victim had “no choice but to take medication to prevent HIV and hepatitis B”.

She said: “The side effects of the first month of taking HIV meds on my stomach, my weight and my energy were a horrific extension of what you did to me.”

The victim added: “December used to be a time I looked forward to. Now, when the Christmas lights go up and the party invitations come in, my body knows the anniversary is coming before my mind does.”

Mohmoudi as handed an 11-year prison sentence and the judge gave him an extended licence period of four years.



Judge Griffiths said he would serve two thirds of his custodial sentence before being assessed for parole and he would be liable for deportation after his custodial sentence was served.

Mohmoudi has previously notched up five criminal convictions for assault and criminal damage while living in Germany.

Having arrived in the UK, in was in prison for 10 months for piloting the small boat before being released to the asylum hostel.

In his defence, David Harounoff said Mohmoudi had fled Iran because he was being targeted for protesting against the regime and also converting to Christianity.

Det Insp Thomas Meaden, who led the Metropolitan Police’s investigation, said: “The victim has shown great strength throughout what has been an extremely hard experience.



“I hope this outcome provides some measure of justice.

“Mohmoudi is a predator who poses danger to any women and girls he may cross.

“Had he not been interrupted by a brave member of the public, he intended to commit further harm.”

News.title: Body found in search for missing woman, 60, who vanished from Morrisons petrol station – sparking urgent hunt
News.content:
TRAGIC FIND Body found in search for missing woman, 60, who vanished from Morrisons petrol station – sparking urgent hunt







Next

A BODY has tragically been found in the search for a missing woman.

Concerns were raised after Nicola, 60, vanished from a Morrisons petrol station in Brecon, Powys, yesterday evening.



She was last seen walking towards the Brynich roundabout at around 5.50pm, cops said.

An urgent appeal for information on her whereabouts was then issued in the early hours of Sunday.



However, issuing a tragic update this afternoon, Dyfed-Powys Police confirmed a body has been found in the search for Nicola.

It is not known if formal identification has taken place.



But Nicola’s next of kin have been made aware of the tragic discovery, it is understood.

The force said: “Sadly, we can confirm that a body has been found during the search for Nicola, who was reported missing from Brecon.

“Next of kin have been informed, and our thoughts are with them at this time.”

News.title: PM says it is 'clear' Russia interfered with Brexit vote
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said Russia did interfere with the Brexit referendum and warned that similar activities were taking place in France and Germany.

The prime minister told The Rest is Politics podcast, external that upon arriving in No 10, he had asked about possible Russian interference in the 2016 vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was."

"I think we've been too much on the back foot on that actually and we haven't informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas," he added.

Burnham did not provide further details about the type or extent of Moscow's activity during the Brexit referendum.

Britain Unbound, a pro-Brexit campaign group, said Burnham's comments were "another crude attempt to undermine the legitimacy of the decision that the British people made in 2016".

It said that foreign interference in UK elections was "obviously unacceptable" but added: "There is no good reason to believe that Russian intervention influenced the outcome of the referendum in 2016.

"It is also insulting to suggest that voters were so easily duped."

In his interview, due to be released on Monday, Burnham said he had discussed the problem of Russian interference with Chancellor Friedrich Merz during his visit to Germany earlier this week.

"There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics," he said.

He continued: "These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia."

It is the first time a UK prime minister has said Russia sought to sway the 2016 Brexit poll but there have long been warnings about efforts by the Kremlin to exert influence on UK politics.

In 2020, Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee published a report into Russian interventions in UK elections and referendums.

It did not provide a definitive conclusion on whether Russia had attempted to influence the results of the EU referendum but did criticise successive governments for failing to fully assess or counter the threat.

In response, the Russian foreign minister dismissed the report out of hand and called it "Russophobia".

And a Kremlin spokesman said Russia did not meddle in other countries' elections.

In the same year, however, the then-Conservative government said it was "almost certain that Russian actors sought to interfere" in the 2019 general election.

BBC Verify has tracked Russian-linked disinformation campaigns including using AI to create fake videos which impersonate journalists and news organisations reporting on Ukraine.

One fake news website falsely claimed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had bought a mansion owned by King Charles at a discounted price.

Earlier this year, Vijay Rangarajan, head of the UK Electoral Commission, told MPs that Russian deepfake videos had been "used extensively in elections around the world".

"There is no reason to assume Britain would be an exception," he added.

Last month, during his speech to the United Nations, Burnham accused Russian agencies of using "every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fears".

He announced that the UK would set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of disinformation.

A Downing Street spokesperson said: "We are focused on ensuring our citizens and our institutions are protected from foreign powers and their proxies seeking to threaten lives and undermine our democratic values.

"We are doing this by strengthening our powers through the National Security Act, strengthening the resilience of our institutions and critical national infrastructure, strengthening our borders, and strengthening our police and intelligence agencies."

News.title: Wildlife park remains closed after fatal tiger attack
News.content:
Yorkshire Wildlife Park remains closed after a man climbed into a tiger enclosure and was fatally attacked by the animal.

Emergency services were called to the park near Doncaster, South Yorkshire, at about 13:30 BST on Saturday after reports of a man climbing down into the enclosure from a walkway.

An eyewitness described seeing the man wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in and was attacked. Police said the man sadly died at the scene.

A park spokesperson said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" remain with the man's family and confirmed the Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.

The spokesperson says many people had contacted them about the tiger and he was safe and well.

Staff who were at the scene who were "deeply affected by events" would receive specialist support, they added.

South Yorkshire Police said the man's family were being supported by officers. "Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time," the force said in a statement.

It added: "We are aware of videos circulating online and we would encourage people not to share this footage."

Earlier on Saturday, in a statement posted on its website, the park said its emergency response procedures had been "immediately activated" and it was "working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened".

Sinn FÃ©in assembly member John O'Dowd rejected claims that the move to ban the parade went in favour of his party, saying "the decision went in the way of the residents" who he said have "faced an awful four weeks" since the application to walk was lodged.

News.title: Orangutans released back into Borneo forest after devastating fires
News.content:
Eight orangutans have been released back into the wild in Borneo after they were taken into captivity when their habitat was threatened by wildfires over the summer.

Three mothers, their three daughters and two adult males were freed in a reserve in the west of the island on Friday, International Animal Rescue Indonesia (Yiari) and the forestry ministry said.

Indonesian authorities rescued 46 orangutans from fires in August and September. Wildfires in the region are usual for the country's dry season but intensified this year.

The apes are critically endangered. Around 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago, according to conservation group WWF.

While Indonesia is among many countries to grapple with wildfires each summer, this year's were more intense due to the El NiÃ±o ocean warming phenomenon, which makes weather patterns more volatile and intense.

Yiari CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez said relocating the eight orangutans to the reserve was a "necessary step" when their habitats became unsafe.

Among them was Mama Nopi and her offspring Nopi, Naufal and Nopan, who had been surviving in a coconut and rubber plantation before their rescue in early September, Yiari said.

Fires had incinerated the surrounding forestry, restricting their access to food and bringing them closer to humans.

News.title: Burnham to release details of Man City meetings
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will release details of his meetings with senior figures at Manchester City following criticism of his comments in the wake of the club being found guilty of all charges related to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules.

An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than Â£830m into their football operations.

Burnham's previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester has led to questions about his relationship with City's Abu Dhabi ownership, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch demanding No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.

"I've been asked by the leader of the opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I'm happy to do and I'm going to," Burnham told the Rest is Politics podcast.

"I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester.

"None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."

The prime minister initially told the BBC he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up following the guilty verdict before later denying his reaction had "downplayed the seriousness of the findings".

However, some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by Burnham's stance that sources told BBC Sport they were "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process.

Sanctions are yet to be announced and City have lodged an appeal against the verdict.

City returned to action for the first time since the guilty verdict when they played at Liverpool on Sunday, winning 3-0.

News.title: Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central Nepal
News.content:
A flash flood has washed away houses, bridges and damaged a hydropower project along a river in central Nepal.

The army said on Sunday that it had rescued 49 people from flood affected areas, but five are still missing, the district's top official confirmed.

It is believed that the flood was caused by a landslide upstream of the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district.

Four bridges and nearly two dozen houses have been swept away, as well as a camp at a hydropower project along the river.

Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods and landslides that swept through its border towns with Tibet two months ago, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying critical energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead and missing.

More on this story.

News.title: Hamilton apologises to Ferrari as Antonelli moves to brink of title
News.content:
Hamilton did not speak to the media after the race after saying he felt unwell and being given permission to miss the interview zone, known as the media pen.

In a statement released by Ferrari, he said: "Under the virtual safety car, the team called me in but I missed the entry. After that, I decided to stay out and try to hold track position to the end but in the closing laps, I was struggling massively with tyre degradation and lost three places, finishing P6, which doesn't reflect the pace we had in the car.

"A painful lesson, but I take full responsibility for the decisions I made. Not every call will work out, and I can accept getting it wrong but I'm sorry for the team for the points we lost today. They put so much into every weekend, and I wanted to deliver more for them. I'll continue to put the work in and come back fighting at the next race."

Ferrari called both cars in to the pits during a virtual safety car that was called mid-race. Stopping under the VSC saves about 10 seconds versus stopping under racing conditions.

Hamilton said in the statement that his decision was based on his improved pace on the soft-compound tyre after he had been forced to make an earlier pit stop than planned because the medium tyre on which he started the race was not performing.

"At a track (where it's) difficult to overtake, you need to try something different and I chose to start on a new medium tyre, to go long and try to make a one-stop work," he said.

"Unfortunately the medium didn't perform as well as the soft. I had a good second stint and the pace was back, but I couldn't make the progress I needed."

His first stop was six laps before Leclerc's and when the Monegasque emerged back on to the track, Hamilton was right behind him and was initially faster.

At one stage, he pointed out to the team that he had "lost two seconds on that lap", but the team decided not to invert the cars. Hamilton followed Leclerc within two seconds for a further 10 laps before slowly starting to lose ground a couple of laps before the VSC.

Vasseur said the team decided to leave Leclerc in front because he had pitted later than Hamilton.

"The tyre advantage was for Charles, that he pitted six laps later," Vasseur said. "I think it was the right call."

However, that argument appears to be somewhat undermined by the fact that the medium tyre emerged as the worst option for the race - as Hamilton had found out in the first stint and other drivers found later on.

Leclerc was put back on the soft when he stopped under the VSC.

News.title: Riyadh airport attacks another dangerous moment in already tense conflict
News.content:
The attacks on King Khalid Airport in Riyadh mark another dangerous moment in a region that is already fraught with tension and conflict.

Saudi Arabia wasn't ready for this.

In recent weeks the Houthis have stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabian soil, but their attacks over the past few days have hit the country's critical infrastructure in the form of the capital's main airport, apparently penetrating Saudi air defences with ease.

Saturday's attack killed 12 people and hurt more than 300. On Sunday the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said an "unknown projectile" had hit a passenger hall and a cruise missile had been intercepted nearby.

The physical damage can be quickly repaired, but the country's reputation as a safe haven of stability is taking a battering.

As well as all the airport attacks, the Houthis have sought to take control of strategically significant positions along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. This further increases the risk to safe navigation along the vital maritime corridor - although the Yemeni government says it has "secured" the strait.

The civil war in Yemen between the country's government - which is internationally recognised and supported by Saudi Arabia - and the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, has been going on for more than a decade. It has left many thousands of people dead and plunged Yemen into one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

It is a complex and often confusing geopolitical conflict, and this latest escalation needs to be seen in the broader context of the tension between Iran, the United States and Israel.

News.title: Legoland Windsor evacuated over burst water main
News.content:
The Legoland Windsor attraction has closed abruptly due to a burst water main.

Customers were told to leave rides and exit the resort at about 13:00 BST on Sunday.

Thames Water said it had to shut off the damaged main near St Leonards Reservoir to prevent flooding, which affected supplies to the theme park.

It said some local residents had reportedly suffered flooded gardens and it apologised for the disruption.

One Legoland visitor, who came with her children from Cornwall, said the sudden evacuation felt "surreal".

The woman, who asked not to be named, said: "We were queuing for a ride and had got right to the front when, all of a sudden, everything stopped moving.

"Then they came out and said, 'Right, come on, everybody off.'

"Over the announcement system, they said there had been some sort of Thames Water disruption in the local area and they didn't have any water.

"We'd booked a night in the hotel and stayed there last night, so we're absolutely gutted because we've just had to drive home."

Thames Water said supplies had been restored and permanent repairs were under way. It said it would provide an update on Monday.

Legoland has been approached for comment.

News.title: UK does not support Trump's Russia diesel deal, says Streeting
News.content:
The UK does not support Donald Trump's deal with Vladimir Putin, which would see the US purchase millions of tonnes of diesel from Russia, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House, he said the agreement had been done in the context of the US president facing elections in November and at a time when politicians across the world were under pressure to ease the cost of living.

He argued that the US and other allies should focus on increasing pressure on Russia to shorten the war "and to secure Ukraine's freedom".

Trump's diesel deal is aimed at lowering fuel prices in America, which have risen following the US and Israel's conflict with Iran.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the agreement would allow Moscow to raise funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.

In response, Trump suggested Ukraine should "get a new leader" who could reach a deal with Russia to end the long-running conflict between the two countries.

Streeting said it was a matter for Ukrainians to choose their leader but added that the country was "fortunate to have someone of his calibre, his courage and his integrity leading their war effort".

He added that responsibility for the war "lies squarely and solely with President Putin and his imperialist ambitions".

The defence secretary said it was not the first time there had been public disagreements between Washington and Kyiv, adding: "In these situations we see it as our role and our responsibility to try and bring our friends back together again."

He also sought to emphasise the US's support for Ukraine, saying there was "often an understatement" of how much help they had provided.

"We're seeing US support for Ukraine in a number of ways from the provision of weapons - and we do a lot of procurement through the Americans - through to intelligence support and through the diplomatic initiative that Washington is leading."

News.title: MPs seek to overturn ruling that stops police being sued for failings
News.content:
Backbench MPs are seeking to roll back a court ruling they say will have "devastating consequences" for victims of crime by preventing them taking legal action against the police, even when there have been grave investigative failings.

The 2025 Court of Appeal judgment, which applies to England and Wales, held that police officers are immune from civil litigation both in their role as witnesses, and for conduct or statements they make when carrying out criminal investigations.

Conservative Andrew Mitchell and Labour's Jess Phillips have submitted an amendment to a bill being debated in Parliament next week seeking to counteract the ruling.

Separately, the judgment could also be overturned at a Supreme Court appeal this month.

The MPs are seeking to stop immunity applying, including in cases where police have fabricated evidence, been dishonest or negligent, and where there has been a reckless disclosure of confidential information relating to victims.

The ruling came in a case brought by a victim of serious domestic violence who fled her abuser for a secret refuge, but Sussex Police included her new address in a file sent to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) without sufficiently flagging its confidentiality.

A CPS lawyer subsequently disclosed her address in court during a bail hearing, thereby revealing it to her abuser. As a result, she had to flee again.

The woman said the disclosure of her address had meant the place she was supposed to be safe "no longer felt safe at all" and she was still living with the impact of what happened and that loss of security.

She brought claims against both the police and CPS, arguing their failure placed her in fear for her life, compelled her to leave her home, caused her to suffer loss of earnings, and resulted in her developing a psychiatric injury. Her claims were initially rejected, reinstated on appeal, then struck out again.

The key issue was who could be held legally responsible for what happened, and who would benefit from legal immunity. Witnesses and lawyers have what is known as "core immunity" for things they say in court, so that they can speak freely there.

The Court of Appeal ruling further expanded such immunity, holding that it extends to an extremely broad range of police activity, including conduct or statements which are part of an investigation leading to a potential prosecution

Most types of legal claim are thus blocked by this immunity, including cases about serious human rights abuses and data breaches, and there are no exemptions for unjustifiable conduct.

Officers can still be prosecuted in the criminal courts and held accountable by police misconduct processes.

News.title: UK launches flood taskforce to prepare for extreme winter weather
News.content:
The government has launched a new taskforce to respond to extreme weather, including the risk of flooding this winter.

After a summer of record-breaking temperatures, the group will meet this week to assess how prepared the UK is for what the Met Office described as the "heightened potential" for wet, windy, stormy weather in the coming months.

"We're facing extreme weather, with flood and drought intertwined but the government is taking decisive action," Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) Minister Emma Hardy said in a statement ahead of the meeting.

The Environment Agency has warned approximately 6.3 million homes and businesses in England remain at risk of flooding.

Defra will host the first meeting on Wednesday, bringing together the Met Office, Environment Agency and mayoral authorities as well as the farming, water and insurance industries.

Hardy said: "This will put communities and businesses at the heart of our work and will make sure the UK is ready for whatever the weather brings next."

The government has committed at least Â£10.5bn until 2036 to protect homes, businesses and critical infrastructure from the growing threat of flooding.

The Met Office has said the current seasonal outlook suggests an increased likelihood of wetter than average conditions during autumn, in part due to the El NiÃ±o weather event.

It has warned that this year's iteration of the climate phenomenon is likely to be the strongest in living memory, with the peak not expected until the end of the year.

The Environment Agency has said that while flooding is not guaranteed, the odds of repeated storms, prolonged rain and saturated catchments are higher than average this winter.

It has urged households to check their flood risk, sign up to alerts and make a flood plan to prepare for any emergencies.

The warnings follow 12 months of extreme weather across the UK, with the summer of 2026 the country's hottest on record.

Last winter brought four named storms to the UK - Bram, Goretti, Ingrid and Chandra - and several significant flooding events, with the Met Office reporting that England received 42% more rainfall than its winter average.

News.title: Swinney backs Flynn in ferry gas leak row and says 'nobody's perfect'
News.content:
First Minister John Swinney has backed Stephen Flynn in the row over whether the transport secretary had been briefed about a gas leak on a CalMac ferry.

Speaking to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg programme in an interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Swinney said emails showed Flynn had not been briefed ahead of a Holyrood committee meeting last month.

The first minister said he had confidence in his transport secretary, who "recognised that he should have been across an issue to be in front of the transport committee and he remedied that right away".

Swinney added: "Nobody's perfect, nobody's infallible".

Flynn was appearing before the transport committee on 9 September when he said he was not aware of a BBC Scotland News story published online more than nine hours earlier.

It revealed how a faulty valve led to 700kg of flammable methane gas being vented from the side of the ferry MV Glen Sannox while it was carrying passengers from Arran to Troon in June 2025.

News.title: Man, 36, arrested six years on from double murder
News.content:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder in connection with the fatal shooting of two men more than six years ago.

Junior Ajose, 36, and Cheriff Tall, 21, were shot dead at a lockdown party in the Moss Side area of Manchester in the early hours of 21 June 2020.

A Greater Manchester Police (GMP) spokesperson said a 36-year-old man was detained in Turkey and transported back to England on Saturday, where he was met at Stansted Airport by GMP officers. He remains in custody.

Det Ch Insp Neil Higginson from the force's major incident team said: "This arrest demonstrates our unwavering commitment to securing justice for Junior and Cheriff and their loved ones."

"Over the last six years, myself and my officers have been carrying out multiple warrants, analysing evidence, examining devices that have been seized during the investigation and pursuing every opportunity to identify those responsible," he added.

Ajose and Tall, who did not know each other, were both shot in the head in a car park off Caythorne Street shortly before 01:00 BST and died in hospital.

GMP said it was estimated that between 300 and 400 people were present in the car park that night.

The force issued a further appeal for information on the fifth anniversary of their deaths last year.

Higginson said they were continuing to appeal for information that could help them to establish the full circumstances of what happened that night and to identify any outstanding suspects.

A Â£50,000 reward remains available for key information that leads to the conviction of the killer.

News.title: Russo named England player of the year
News.content:
Forward Alessia Russo has been named England women's player of the year.

The 27-year-old, who also won the award two seasons ago, has been a key player in the 2025-26 campaign, featuring in all 10 games and scoring five goals.

She started nine of those games, including all six of England's 2027 World Cup qualifiers.

Last week, she scored the third goal as England beat Greece 3-1 in their 2027 World Cup play-off semi-final first leg, with the second leg at Leicester's King Power Stadium on Tuesday.

Arsenal's Russo pipped Chelsea pair Lucy Bronze and Hannah Hampton to the award, which is voted for by fans.

"To receive the award is really special, particularly as it comes directly from the fans. I am so grateful for their support," said Russo.

Russo is among 30 players who were nominated in September for the women's Ballon d'Or, with Alex Greenwood the only other English player on the shortlist.

News.title: Firefighters spend second night at scene of Glasgow scrapyard blaze
News.content:
Firefighters have spent a second night at the scene of a major blaze at a scrapyard in Glasgow.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) said the alarm was raised at the business on South Street, in the Scotstoun area of the city, at about 23:23 on Friday.

One local resident captured dramatic footage of the fire at its peak, with explosive bangs emitting from an area engulfed in flames.

Nine fire engines, two high-reach vehicles and specialist resources responded to the incident. No casualties were reported.

News.title: ‘I could have died from meningitis before my first week of university – how to tell it’s not just freshers’ flu’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

“It’s life or death if you catch it too late,” said Sofia Mattacola Westley, a university student who contracted meningitis last year. “This illness is unlike anything you’ll ever have.”

Ms Westley’s illness began during a concert, which was supposed to be the highlight of her pre-university summer when she was 18. “I never thought something like that could happen – I didn’t even know what meningitis was,” she told The Independent.

Only hours after attending, she found herself experiencing a range of symptoms: “I got a fever, and then a migraine, and then I was vomiting, and faint... it was just awful.

“We ended up going to hospital, and for five days, nobody knew what it was.”

After multiple MRIs and tests, it was almost a week after being admitted that Ms Westley was diagnosed with meningitis. “I really could have died then,” she recalled.

open image in gallery Sofia Mattacola Westley recalled the path which led to her being diagnosed with meningitis ( The Independent )

She tells her story as a new university year begins, after meningitis outbreaks were recorded at campuses in Kent, Canterbury, Oxfordshire, Dorset, and Berkshire earlier in 2026.

The outbreak in Kent in March triggered mass panic and a public response from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) after 15 cases emerged within 48 hours.

In total, 348 cases of the illness in the UK have been confirmed this year, with 26 of these resulting in death.

The illness, which can be caused by several strains of different viruses and bacteria, leads to inflammation around the brain and spinal cord, explained Daniel Turnbull, a professional standards pharmacist at Pharmacy2U. It can sometimes lead to sepsis and become fatal.

“Despite having some similar symptoms [to freshers’ flu], meningitis is a far more serious, and potentially fatal, illness,” he added.

The illness is typically transmitted through prolonged, close contact. Because of this, university students are particularly at risk, as living in close quarters, sharing items, and mingling at busy freshers’ events can spark outbreaks.

open image in gallery A year on, Ms Westley still struggles with lingering effects of the illness ( The Independent )

It is thought around 10 per cent of people carry bacteria which causes meningitis without ever showing symptoms, the UKHSA said.

But even after surviving the acute infection, the long-term reality can be debilitating.

Ms Westley’s recovery process forced her to put her plans to attend university on hold for a year. “It was really bad,” the 19-year-old explained. “After I got meningitis, I got diagnosed with something called low-pressure headaches, which is basically where any small thing you do, small activity or action, can instantly cause a headache.

“Even a year on, I’ve still got so much fatigue. Like I struggle with doing everyday things that before would have excited me, and I don’t know... I’ve lost a lot of passion for things that I loved.

“Like I’m not as adventurous. If I have to go on a long car journey, for example, all I think about before is: do I have enough caffeine with me? Am I going to get sick? Do I have everything I need medication-wise?”

open image in gallery Ms Westley has stressed the importance of raising awareness about the effects of meningitis ( The Independent )

Now, Ms Westley has urged young adults to consider how easily the illness can spread.

“I see people doing things like sharing drinks or food – all these little things that you do with your friends that seem normal, and you trust them because they’re your friends,” she said. “But it doesn’t matter how much you know that person, they could be a carrier, even if they have no symptoms.”

Her plea to new and returning students is to stay vigilant, take symptoms seriously rather than dismissing them as “freshers’ flu”, and drop the assumption that dangerous infections only happen to someone else.

“Everyone thinks ‘I’m not going to get it’ – but it’s not this rare thing,” she warned.

open image in gallery A meningitis outbreak in Canterbury earlier this year, which sparked a vaccination rollout to students in the area ( PA Wire )

In a bid to prevent outbreaks, young people in the UK can now access a free vaccination programme through the NHS.

The jab is available to anyone in the Year 13 age group, as well as those who are starting university as an undergraduate or moving into further education accommodation for the first time.

Although the NHS notes the vaccine does not eliminate the chance of contracting meningitis, it can significantly reduce the risk of hospitalisation and long-term complications.

Stressing the severity of the illness, Ms Westley said: “It’s not like you’re just coughing and you’ve got an itchy throat or your muscles are a bit tired.

“A lot of people think it’s just a worse version of freshers’ flu – it’s not.”

open image in gallery Free meningitis jabs are being offered to students across the UK ( PA )

Symptoms to be aware of include a high temperature, severe headaches, sensitivity to light, neck stiffness (not being able to touch your chin to your chest), and on some occasions, a bruise-like rash.

While rashes are often associated as a key marker of meningitis, Mr Turnbull warned: “Symptoms can occur in any order – you should never wait for a rash to appear to seek medical attention.”

For Ms Westley, awareness surrounding meningitis is the most important step to preventing its spread.

“My advice to people would just be: be proactive. Understand the symptoms and how it spreads, because I think a lot of people just don’t know.

“Don’t let being careful stop you from living your life. But know what it is, so it doesn’t take your life.”

More advice on the illness can be found through the Meningitis Now charity, or by calling its helpline on 0808 80 10 388.

News.title: Hurricane Isaias tracker latest: four dead and scores without power as storm makes landfall
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Hurricane Isaias peeled off hotel and condominium rooftops and facades along the Florida Panhandle before charging north Saturday, dishing out torrential rains and the threat of flash floods and tornadoes across the Southeast.

Two people were killed when trees fell onto homes in Florida and Alabama, and nearly 700,000 customers were without power by midday in four states. Forecasters warned that flooding could stretch into the southern Appalachians.

More than 726,000 people in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle have been left without power on Saturday after Hurricane Isaias crashed into the US Gulf Coast.

The storm made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane, then quickly moved north through Alabama as its wind speeds dropped sharply, weakening to a post-tropical cyclone, the US National Hurricane Center said in its latest advisory.

But residents are bracing for flooding and gusty winds in Isaias’ aftermath as authorities warned of the potential for tornadoes.

open image in gallery Maps show strong winds moving across Alabama ( Windy.com )

The storm is expected to continue weakening but produce gusty winds well inland as the possibility of life-threatening storm surges still looms for parts of the Florida Panhandle.

It will travel northwards across Alabama and over the Tennessee Valley later on Saturday, according to the National Weather Service.

Forecasters also warned that conditions could stir up tornadoes across parts of the Florida Panhandle and into Georgia and the Carolinas.

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season. Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white-sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars, and seafood shacks.

“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,” Florida governor Ron DeSantis said Friday.

Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola, police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways. While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.

open image in gallery The storm is expected to travel northwards across the Tennessee Valley ( Windy.com )

Some Panhandle counties temporarily suspended emergency response Friday night because of dangerous conditions.

Parts of southern Alabama also were flooded, with officials in Mobile reporting downed trees and power lines. Roads in Houston County, which is in the southeastern corner of the state, were closed because of similar conditions.

open image in gallery Kevin Hudgins helps guest Laura Gower after a power outage at the Residence Inn ( Getty )

More than 726,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.

Despite weakening, heavy rain is forecast as Isaias moves inland, with 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) or even more expected through the weekend from southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend, and southwest Georgia.

Isaias, the first hurricane to hit the eastern US since Milton tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024, is also expected to bring heavy rain and potential flooding to much of the Southeast over the weekend, then to parts of the Midwest and Northeast into Monday.

The storm also grounded most Friday flights at several panhandle airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday’s football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn’t want to disrupt emergency response efforts.

Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Simon strengthened into a Category 4 hurricane as it approached Mexico’s coast.

Tropical Storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.

— with Associated Press

News.title: Erling Haaland responds after Man City thrash Liverpool under shadow of Premier League sanction
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Manchester City striker Erling Haaland has praised the “character” of his teammates after they earned a brilliant 3-0 win over Liverpool at Anfield in their first match since the announcement of a guilty verdict for breaching the Premier League’s financial rules.

The league leaders came into the game after a whirlwind three weeks that ended with the club launching an appeal over the guilty verdict, but while their first game looked like a stern test at Anfield, they passed it with flying colours with the help of a Ryan Gravenberch red card.

After an even first half, the Dutchman was sent off just after the hour mark for a second yellow card offence and City took the lead a few minutes later, with Haaland firing an emphatic finish past Alisson.

Jeremy Doku’s stunning curled effort added a second just three minutes later, before a brilliant dummy and finish from Rayan Cherki sealed all three points in a strange, subdued atmosphere on Merseyside.

City have a three-point lead at the top of the table after six games ( PA Wire )

Speaking after the game, Haaland singled out teammate and man of the match Elliot Anderson for praise, while highlighting the “character” shown by the players.

“Every single person part of Man City, and every fan, this is a lovely moment that will stay with us for a long time,” he said after the full-time whistle.

“It was tough, it was hard but we showed amazing character from back to front. So proud of everyone. [It’s] important to stay strong mentally, stick together and do what you can do something about, and the thing we can do something about is to play good football and fight together. That's the only thing we can do.

“I spoke about the character playing with 10 men at Old Trafford, the first guy I think of is Elliot,” he explained.

“You want to win games, it's as simple as that. Perform well, play good football and win games. This was a mental battle, [it’s] never easy coming back from internationals.

“[I’m] proud that we managed to stick together, we are mentally strong,” he added.

City’s win means they maintain their 100% winning record at the summit of the league table, with 18 points from 18 and a three-point lead over nearest challengers Arsenal. Their next match comes in midweek in the Champions league against PSG, and they return to domestic action at home to Ipswich on Saturday, 17 October.

News.title: Second celebrity eliminated from Strictly Come Dancing
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Melanie Walters and Aljaž Škorjanec are the second couple to leave Strictly Come Dancing 2026.

The Gavin and Stacey star, 64, and her dance partner ended up in the dance off during Sunday night’s results show, along with Shaun Wright-Phillips and professional partner Alexis Warr.

Walters and Škorjanec had previously received a total of 17 points for their Charleston to “Ooh Ahh… Just a Little Bit” by Gina G, putting them second to last on the leaderboard.

Meanwhile Wright-Phillips and Warr took last place with a score of just 15 points for their quickstep to “I’m a Believer” by The Monkees.

The public vote didn’t save them from the unenviable fate of performing their routines a second time for the judges, and after both pairs had danced again, the judging panel shared their verdicts.

Craig Revel Horwood chose to save Wright-Phillips and Warr, as did head judge Shirley Ballas.

open image in gallery The ‘Gavin and Stacey’ star ended up in the dance off on Sunday night’s show ( BBC/Guy Levy )

Motsi Mabuse, however, chose to save Walters and Škorjanec – before Anton du Beke used his deciding vote to protect Wright-Phillips and Warr, and send the actor home.

Since last year, the deciding vote has been rotated between all four judges, rather than being placed in the hands of head judge Ballas each week.

Sunday night’s results show also featured a special performance from the professional dancers, which also featured Ballas and Du Beke.

Ballas headed up Team Latin while Du Beke was firmly Team Ballroom as the two styles went head to head in a showdown.

open image in gallery The pair received 17 points for their Charleston ( PA )

Musician Jalen Ngonda also performed his song “Burning Temptation” as pros Neil Jones and Lethabo Monametsi danced.

There are now 13 couples remaining in the competition, following the departures of Walters and celebrity hairdresser Chris Appleton, who lost out in the dance off last week.

Next week’s episode will take the theme of Icons Week, with the celebrities and their partners performing routines inspired by “some of the best-loved recording artists in history”, according to the BBC.

News.title: Andy Burnham says public execution is ‘abhorrent’ as US moves ahead with firing squad livestream
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has condemned public execution as “abhorrent” and said he would “never support” it.

Burnham’s words come as America’s plan to livestream the killing of a former army major by firing squad were questioned.

Asked about the possibility that Fort Hood gunman Nidal Malik Hasan’s execution is made public, and whether the UK should take a stand, Andy Burnham told The Rest Is Politics podcast: “I certainly would never support that.

“So, I’m happy to make my view clear.”

Hasan is due to be executed on December 3 after he was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in Texas in 2009.

Nidal Hasan who killed 13 people and wounded 31 in a November 2009 shooting spree at Fort Hood ( Reuters )

US defence secretary Pete Hegseth said it will be public, telling TV outlet Real America’s Voice: “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it.”

Vice president JD Vance has cast doubt on whether the Pentagon will livestream the execution and if it did, he said: “I’m not going to be watching it.”

Mr Burnham told the podcast, which will be released on Monday: “It’s something that I can’t say I ever want to see anywhere in the world, Alastair (Campbell, podcast host).

“It’s something that I find quite abhorrent in many ways. But, you know, I only want to speak for what we will do and why we will do it.”

Cabinet minister Bridget Phillipson previously said she found the plans “disturbing” and that she was “proud that our country did away with the death penalty a very, very long time ago”.

The equalities minister told the BBC: “The view of the Government is always that we’re repulsed to the death penalty, my personal view is that I’m opposed to the death penalty.

“And I find that rather disturbing is my honest reaction.”

She added: “It’s a matter for the US government.

“They are a close ally, does that mean that we support everything the US government does? No, but that’s not for us to involve ourselves in what are ultimately questions of US domestic policy.”

News.title: Liverpool vs Manchester City LIVE: Rayan Cherki adds third goal as City cruise to victory at Anfield
News.content:
From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging.

At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story.

The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it.

News.title: Labour voters overwhelmingly want Andy Burnham to commit to rejoining the EU, poll shows
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Nearly three-quarters of Labour voters want Andy Burnham to include talks to rejoin the European Union in the party’s next manifesto, according to a major new poll carried out as the prime minister opened the door to returning to the bloc.

Britons would also vote by nearly two to one, 57 to 30 per cent, to become part of the EU again in another referendum, the survey found.

The polling, carried out by European Movement UK in partnership with Observant, found that a majority of voters for all but one of the major parties were in favour of the inclusion of a commitment to seek membership of the EU in their next election manifesto. Reform UK was the only party whose voters were against it.

The findings come as a leading think tank has unveiled a roadmap for Britain’s return to the bloc within the next decade.

The report, drawn up by the European Movement and seen by The Independent, is backed by prominent figures from across different parties, including Conservative peer and former deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine, ex-Labour leader Neil Kinnock and the former Lib Dem business secretary Sir Vince Cable, and is being sent to the prime minister.

The plan, which aims to get the UK back into the EU by 2036 or earlier, deals with the main potential roadblocks, including strategies to overcome concerns about calls for Britain to adopt the euro or enter the Schengen free travel area.

Lord Heseltine said: “Ten years on since Brexit, this is how we solve our shared global problems.”

Lord Kinnock added: “After 10 years out, 10 years to gain full admission again is sensible. But it could be less because the immovable realities of the continuing damage to our country, of proximity to our largest markets, security needs and political influence could propel stronger awareness of the need for UK membership of the EU on both sides of the Channel.

open image in gallery Lord Heseltine has long been a critic of the decision to EU ( PA Archive )

“It is essential that, in the meantime, the significance of the unpatriotic anti-European parties is flattened so that they are no longer an impediment to trust and progress.”

It comes after the prime minister announced at the Labour conference that he would look at options on Brexit and suggested that rejoining the EU could be in the party’s next election manifesto.

Mr Burnham declared that Brexit has not worked and said it had led to “a decade of drift and division” since 2016.

A debate in parliament is set to take place on Monday on a petition supporting rejoining the EU with around 26,000 letters backing the proposal already sent to MPs.

The European Movement argues that rejoining the EU is “a prerequisite for solving many of the UK’s deep-seated problems”.

It notes: “Putting up trade barriers with our closest neighbours has left the UK between 4 per cent and 8 per cent poorer than we otherwise would have been.”

With Donald Trump in the White House it also warns that the “UK’s special relationship with the US, if it ever existed, has collapsed. China is ever more assertive. Outside the EU, the UK is less able to defend itself against unfair trade competition and punitive tariffs”.

The European Movement’s plan, which has already been shared with a number of MPs and high-profile supporters, says that a target of 2036 is required to give “a sense of urgency” while fitting within the normal time period of accession for a new member.

The shortest – around three years – was for Finland and Sweden, which joined in 1995. They were already in line with much EU law, as they were European Free Trade Association (EFTA) members and signed the European Economic Area (EEA) agreement in 1992.

The European Movement UK plan also comes after former prime minister Sir Tony Blair told Mr Burnham in a report from his think tank that he needs to include rejoining the EU in his forthcoming 10-year-plan.

The UK has a similar advantage of a high level of existing alignment, having retained a significant proportion of EU law post-Brexit.

open image in gallery Mr Burnham, pictured here with the German chancellor earlier this week, has gone far further than his predecessor when it comes to Britain’s relationship with Europe ( AFP/Getty )

But “the EU will want to see a large and resilient majority of UK voters backing ‘join’”.

In a message to Mr Burnham, it also warns that “the government of the day makes joining the EU a clear and unequivocal policy priority”.

“A clear electoral mandate” could be achieved with a manifesto commitment at the next election, expected in 2029.

But the EU would require any final deal to be ratified by another referendum before accession is granted, it notes.

Looking at the next election, though, the European Movement states: “If parties committed to EU membership achieve a majority, then the next government – single party or coalition – would have a mandate to apply.”

On the euro it points out that while EU treaties do require a commitment to join the single currency it is “at an unspecified date in the future: in other words, there is a derogation without a specified time limit”.

open image in gallery ( Getty )

The EU’s new visa system could make UK public opinion “more amenable than in the past to joining Schengen”.

But it also points out that it took many years for countries like Romania and Bulgaria to join the travel zone. There are also two major complications for the UK – that Ireland would also have to join and “the large number of… very busy maritime ports and hub airports with extensive non-EU traffic”.

Overall, it warns that when it comes to negotiations: “Unanimity among EU member states is required throughout. Any member state can singlehandedly freeze the negotiations at various points. The UK side will need to be aware of this and appoint knowledgeable and skilful negotiators.”

As part of The Independent’s Europe: The Way Back campaign, polling guru professor Sir John Curtice said that support for rejoining the EU was now at its highest level since the Brexit vote.

Former Tory chancellor George Osborne said Britain’s economy had “fallen off a cliff” since Brexit and that rejoining the EU’s customs union would be the swiftest route to recovery.

And Lord Kinnock said that those who “love their country” will want to return to the EU.
