Sports.title: Cherki cracker caps Manchester City win at Liverpool in face of Anfield taunts
Sports.content:
It is a soundtrack that Manchester City have heard before but never for such sustained spells during a match. It came from the Liverpool support, first ringing out around Anfield before kick-off and coming at regular intervals thereafter.

It was always going to be like this as City felt their way into a new reality, one conditioned by the guilty verdicts handed to them by an independent commission on virtually all of the 115 charges they have faced for breaking the Premier League’s financial rules. City maintain their innocence and have appealed.

The Kop wanted to tell City what they are. And where they were going. They wanted to tell them again and again. According to them, they are cheats, who are set to be relegated. It was not exactly a bear pit of an atmosphere; not truly intimidating. It was just an outpouring of anger and it was impossible to ignore.

City did not care. They rolled with the invective. And after a slow-burn contest turned on a second yellow card for the Liverpool midfielder, Ryan Gravenberch, in the 62nd minute, City cut loose. All that their players can do is try to blot out the noise. They did so here, running all over Liverpool’s 10 men to maintain their 100% start to the Premier League season. The key theme from them – and their fans – was defiance. City intend to keep doing what they do.

It was Erling Haaland, inevitably, who lashed them in front and Jérémy Doku, on as a game-changing substitute in the 56th minute, who curled them further ahead with a beauty. The best was still to come. Again, Doku was involved. And after Rayan Cherki dummied a pass from Elliot Anderson, he ran on to a backheel from another substitute, Josko Gvardiol. Cherki had work to do. He did it when he cut away from Jeremie Frimpong, on as a substitute, and rolled home. It was a team goal marked by individual brilliance.

Liverpool were broken and en route to a first defeat under Andoni Iraola. The manager was undermined by the absence of arguably his three best players so far this season; Dominik Szoboszlai, Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak all picked up injuries during the international window. Liverpool lacked punch.

City had reason to curse the timing of this fixture. Apart from Manchester United at Old Trafford, it could hardly have been worse than a visit here. And not only because Liverpool were one of the clubs most seriously undermined by their accountancy practices. City sneaked their team buses around the back of the stadium on the way in, avoiding the jibes from the streets, but it only postponed the inevitable. It was always going to be lively.

When the Premier League published the document that provided the first raft of detail about the decisions against City on the Tuesday before last, it hit hard. It was the weight of the language – how it dripped with contempt – as well as the sheer extent of the transgressions. Proven misconduct. Sham arrangements. Concerted attempts to frustrate the investigation. How some of the club’s witnesses gave evidence that they knew to be untrue. It served to frame this game. It will continue to frame each one that City play for the foreseeable.

View image in fullscreen Jérémy Doku doubles Manchester City’s lead with a stunning curling shot. Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty Images

The City fans came armed with scores of inflatable bananas. Some of them wore old-school replica shirts. There was a message in there somewhere. Maybe to say that their club pre-dates the Abu Dhabi takeover. It was also possible to spot banners in support of Khaldoon al-Mubarak, the club chair.

You want banners? The Kop had that boxed off. There were some that riffed off Oasis lyrics, including one with the line that “after all, you really robbed us all”. The most eyecatching was unfurled before kick-off, featuring the word ‘cheats’ and a very long sequence of pound signs.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There was very little to report in terms of first-half action. Even the melee that broke out in the 12th minute after Alexis Mac Allister tussled with Anderson was the definition of handbags. There were no big chances; the precision on the final ball was frequently absent.

Iraola gave Lewis Koumas a full league debut up front and it was the 21-year-old who had the first decent effort straight after the restart. Gianluigi Donnarumma stood tall to save. Liverpool upped the intensity and they had a spell where they pushed and the Kop felt the breakthrough was coming. Gravenberch worked Donnarumma. Mac Allister volleyed wide.

View image in fullscreen Ryan Gravenberch (right) walks off after receiving a red card from the referee Chris Kavanagh. Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty Images

Haaland blew a glorious chance from an Antoine Semenyo pass on the hour, dinking past the far post but City had otherwise created little. Then everything changed. Gravenberch caught the eye with his surging runs but he was on the wrong side when he challenged Doku, who was ready to spark a counterattack. It was clumsy from the Dutchman, the contact on Doku not exactly strong. But having been booked at the start of the second half for a foul on Anderson, Gravenberch was running an almighty risk. He did not get away with it.

City had their opening and how they piled through it. The way that they overwhelmed Liverpool was really something; a demonstration of their strength. It was not a game for the neutral. Are there any such viewers where City are concerned any more? Doku almost teed up Nico O’Reilly and City were on their way when Haaland swept home from a deflected Doku cross. A new reality? It was the same old City on the pitch.

Sports.title: Pino finishes off Nottingham Forest on Glasner’s unhappy Crystal Palace return
Sports.content:
It is fair to say Oliver Glasner has had more enjoyable afternoons. The Nottingham Forest head coach arrived in south London dressed like a bouncer from All Bar One in a black bomber jacket, as if he was anticipating trouble, but was instead given a rapturous reception by the home fans who used to worship him.

The generosity towards their former manager seemed to have extended to Palace’s players as Dan Ndoye was handed a goal in the third minute. Pierre Sage’s side were awful in the opening 40 minutes. Yet Forest could not find a way to beat Walter Benítez again as Liam Delap missed a golden chance to extend their lead and the Argentina goalkeeper’s heroics inspired a thrilling comeback that secured Sage’s first home victory in the Premier League since taking over from Glasner in the summer.

The irony that Daichi Kamada, who won the Europa League under Glasner while they were at Eintracht Frankfurt before he brought him to Selhurst Park on a free transfer, should score his first Premier League goal to equalise in his 68th appearance was surely not lost on the Austrian.

But he and the notoriously trigger-happy Evangelos Marinakis – the Forest owner who was conspicuous by his absence from the directors’ box after his public spats with his Palace counterpart, Steve Parish – will have serious concerns about how his team capitulated after conceding the equaliser. Jefferson Lerma bundled home the second from a corner just before half-time and Yéremy Pino wrapped up the points with a goal that was greeted with a chorus of: “You’re getting sacked in the morning”, directed towards Glasner.

“Call it karma or whatever but it was like I didn’t deserve to win at Selhurst Park because the players did everything,” said Glasner, who claimed not to have heard the taunts from the Palace fans. “I think this was the most dominant Nottingham Forest performance. But not the right result. So, this gives me confidence. My job is not to be influenced negatively by the result.”

There has been plenty of water under the bridge since these two sides met here 14 months ago. Marinakis is suing Palace and “persons unknown” after a banner featuring an incendiary cartoon of him was unfurled during the first half of that game, with the supporters’ group that is thought to have been behind it having since disbanded. Glasner’s decision to join Forest in the summer only added to the ill-feeling that was created by the dispute over Palace’s demotion from the Europa League last season, even if the Austrian was given a warm welcome before and after the game.

The home fans made it clear where their grievances remain as they immediately launched into the anti-Uefa and Marinakis song that was the soundtrack to their Conference League triumph under Glasner, while the Forest supporters responded with taunts of: “We’ve got Ollie Glasner”. They had more reason to celebrate after only two minutes when Anan Khalaili’s weak header presented Ndoye with the chance to run through and score. Forest could barely believe their luck.

View image in fullscreen The Nottingham Forest head coach, Oliver Glasner, responds to a generous reception from the Crystal Palace supporters. Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/Reuters

They piled on the pressure, with makeshift defender Lerma – only playing in the absence of the suspended Axel Disasi – looking particularly vulnerable. Jaydee Canvot was guilty of losing possession when Morgan Gibbs-White picked out the unmarked Ndoye and Benítez tipped over before Daniel Muñoz was inches away from scoring against his former club.

But the momentum shifted firmly towards the hosts thanks to a miraculous save from Benítez – deputising for the injured Dean Henderson – that denied Delap from three yards out after Gibbs-White’s shot rebound off the crossbar. “Walter made a save with a lot of bravery,” said Sage, who refused the opportunity to gloat about beating Glasner. “It’s not about revenge,” he insisted.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Delap spurned another golden opportunity with his head and Forest were made to pay just before the break when Kamada scrambled home inside the six-yard area after Jørgen Strand Larsen’s pass deflected straight into his path. Suddenly Palace found their belief. Tyrick Mitchell’s volley was tipped over and from the resulting corner Lerma leapt highest and the ball squirmed through the legs of Matz Sels and just over the line. Replays suggested that Lerma’s effort grazed the arm of team-mate Khalaili on its way in, but VAR let the matter go.

One characteristic Sage has inherited is his team’s difficulty in defending set pieces and Palace were lucky to escape when a header from Gibbs-White at the start of the second half was deflected on to the post by Mitchell. Forest looked at sixes and sevens at the other end when Lerma again caused chaos from a corner but they scrambled the ball away.

There was no such reprieve a few minutes later when Quinten Timber’s pass was diverted into the path of Strand Larsen and Pino made no mistake with the rebound. The Spain forward then turned provider but Strand Larsen could not find a way past Sels. That didn’t stop the Palace fans from gleefully asking Glasner what the score was. Ndoye and Neco Williams had chances to make things interesting late on but Forest – and Glasner – had been humbled by then.

Sports.title: Mohamed Belloumi grabs point for Hull in seesaw draw with Everton
Sports.content:
Hull retained their unbeaten home record since returning to the Premier League with an entertaining draw against Everton at the MKM Stadium.

Brennan Johnson found the net in the 34th minute but was denied a first Premier League goal for Everton following a video assistant referee check, leaving the sides to go in goalless at the break. The hosts wasted little time after the interval, however, as Joe Gelhardt opened the scoring in the 48th minute following an error by Ainsley Maitland-Niles.

Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall equalised for Everton seven minutes later, and Thierno Barry, who had squandered plenty of earlier chances, then put the visitors ahead midway through the second period. Hull responded swiftly, though, with the substitute Mohamed Belloumi pulling the home team level in the 74th minute.

The Tigers have returned to the top flight with an unexpected bang, tasting defeat for the first time in their final fixture before the international break at Newcastle. They were slow off the mark in the early exchanges here, but eventually produced a forward burst of play that saw both Oli McBurnie and then Lewie Coyle threaten before being thwarted.

Gelhardt caused danger with a run down the right in the 22nd minute but his shot was comfortably collected by Jordan Pickford. Matt Crooks got his head to a corner 10 minutes later, but James Tarkowski cleared and play sped to the opposite end.

Barry unleashed a shot that was gathered by Konstantinos Tzolakis, but the ball rolled from his hands and was fired in by Johnson for what appeared to be the opener 11 minutes before half-time. But, after a lengthy VAR check, the winger was ruled offside. Gelhardt and Nobel Mendy then went close to easing the nerves of home fans with near-misses before half-time.

The hosts did not have to wait long for the opener after the break though. Sorba Thomas capitalised on a mistake from Maitland-Niles and fed Gelhardt, who coolly nudged the ball beyond Pickford in the 48th minute.

The Everton response was fairly rapid, however, and Maitland-Niles atoned for his slip-up by finding Dewsbury-Hall, who headed home in the 55th minute.

View image in fullscreen Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall heads home to make it 1-1. Photograph: Lee Parker/CameraSport/Getty Images

Barry, who had much to ponder after missing two earlier chances, then redeemed himself when he pounced to lash beyond Tzolakis to put the visitors ahead for the first time in the match.

But Hull, who had made a handful of changes, were not behind for long as the substitutes Elliot Stroud and Belloumi linked up and the latter sent a left-footed shot past Pickford in the 74th minute to secure a point for the Tigers.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

David Moyes felt his Everton squad completely underperformed. Change is afoot at the club after it was announced earlier in the week they would be put up for sale, but their manager was in no mood for excuses after the draw.

He said: “I’m really disappointed that we didn’t come away with three points, I couldn’t see them getting a goal when we went 2-1 up – I thought if anything we would go on and finish it. It looked really unlike us, the way we gave the goals away today, it was very, very poor.

“Hull have had some great results here, against Manchester United and Villa, they’re not easy to beat and they weren’t [today] but I thought we should have gone on and won the game comfortably.

“The overall performance from everyone was so far below our level, way below where we should be. I’m not giving the players any room for excuses because of what’s going on, whether that be the transfer window or that be ownership.”

Sports.title: Joy for Eckert as 10-man Southampton edge out Portsmouth in feisty derby
Sports.content:
At the full-time whistle in the south coast derby, Tonda Eckert thrust his arms out wide and roared into the sky with the rest of the Southampton supporters. It had been a tense 90 minutes after a tense few months, but finally the young German coach could let it all out. At the end of a week where he found out that he will face no immediate ban for his part in the Spygate scandal that rocked the Championship last season, he helped deliver Southampton’s first home win over Portsmouth for 22 years.

Southampton played more than half of a fiercely contested game with 10 men after Cameron Bragg was sent off for a second yellow card on 44 minutes and Eckert was keen to divert credit elsewhere at full time. “I think that one today belongs to the players,” he said. “If you go a man down there’s not so much you can do as a manager outside of trying to give a structure that helps. It’s the players that dig out games like this.”

There was widespread surprise at the leniency of the punishment that allowed Eckert to take his seat in the dugout for the derby. After Southampton admitted to spying on three opponents last season, the 33-year-old was handed a six-week ban, suspended until the end of the 2027-28 campaign, and a £28,000 fine for misconduct.

An FA independent disciplinary commission noted Eckert’s “genuine contrition” at what had happened. At Southampton, there is a sense that their expulsion from the playoffs in May and subsequent four-point deduction was punishment enough, and Eckert is keen to move on from a period of uncertainty that he admitted this week had changed his life.

This win was evidence of a club sticking together. James Bree was the author of the winning goal, turning the ball home after 20 minutes, but the pattern of the game shifted with Bragg’s dismissal. Southampton, united and resolute, held on to move into the top half – they would be third without the points deduction – with Eckert now able to contemplate another promotion push.

View image in fullscreen Southampton’s James Bree coolly opens the scoring, his goal turning out to be the winner. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

Portsmouth were as usual given a pre-match police escort to St Mary’s and their full-back Jayden Meghoma, who made his professional debut for Southampton as a 17-year-old, was a magnet for Saints ire. He was a threat down the left, firing wide at the near post in a promising opening, but he lost Bree for the goal. Finn Azaz was given too much space in midfield and clipped a ball in behind a static Meghoma for Bree, forward from right-back, to guide a left-footed finish into the far corner.

Ebou Adams, who scored Portsmouth’s equaliser in a 1-1 draw in this fixture in January, was a central figure early on. He twice picked Bragg’s pocket in the Southampton half and drew yellow cards on both occasions. Bragg was consoled by his teammates after seeing red for an instinctive tug of Adams’s shirt after being caught on the ball.

The decision to start Bragg in a holding midfield role had backfired. “It will be a learning [curve] for him, but I asked him to be brave,” Eckert said. “I asked him to get on the ball and he does just that. I’ll take that on me, then.”

View image in fullscreen Cam Bragg is consoled as he walks off the pitch. Photograph: Robin Jones/Getty Images

Colby Bishop, whose header was well saved by Daniel Peretz, and Ryan Kavuma-McQueen, who drilled a shot just wide, went close to equalising before Eckert could try to plug the gaps at half-time.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The game was just as frantic after the break. Azaz was perhaps lucky not to be sent off for a wild lunge on Adams. When Bree was treated for a battle scar around his eye, Eckert held council with his remaining midfielders James Ward-Prowse and Flynn Downes as Pompey continued to knock on the door. The substitute Adrian Segecic was drifting into spaces and had fizzed a couple of low efforts wide in the minutes before, while the right-back Zak Swanson saw his cut-back cleared by Jack Stephens from under the Southampton crossbar.

View image in fullscreen Tempers fray at St Mary’s but the hosts held on for victory. Photograph: Warren Little/Getty Images

“It was a different game after the red card,” said the Portsmouth head coach, John Mousinho. “But for the amount of pressure that we had in the second half, the amount of opportunities we had, to not put the ball in the back of the net – we’re devastated.”

While Eckert gradually cut back his side’s attacking presence, Mousinho emptied his bench in an attempt to find a way through a Southampton defence marshalled by Stephens and Keven Schlotterbeck, who laid their bodies on the line more than once in front of Peretz. Their clean sheet was a priceless end to a week where their manager was given something of a clean slate.

Sports.title: European football: Lazio join Inter at top of Serie A as Roma held at Como
Sports.content:
Lazio moved level on points with Inter at the top of Serie A with a 3-1 win over Monza on Sunday as 10-man Roma played out the first goalless draw of the Italian season at Como.

Under Gennaro Gattuso, who has bounced back after his failure at the helm of the Italian national side who missed out on the 2026 World Cup, Lazio continued their strong start to the season. Still unbeaten, the Roman outfit secured a fifth victory in six matches to pull level on 16 points with Inter, who beat Parma 3-0 at San Siro on Saturday.

Nuno Tavares gave Lazio a third-minute lead and Gustav Isaksen doubled it midway through the first half. Monza had Lorenzo Lucchesi sent off on 35 minutes for hauling down Tijjani Noslin as he broke through on goal, but the 16th-placed visitors rattled Lazio after the break, pulling a goal back and coming close to equalising before conceding a third goal in the closing stages.

Roma left Como frustrated, having managed only a single point. The dismissal of league top scorer Donyell Malen for a dangerous tackle early in the second half forced them to scale back their ambitions. Neither team could find the breakthrough in a clash between two sides widely regarded as dark horses for the title, leaving Inter and Lazio two points clear of Roma after their respective wins over Parma and Monza.

“We played two-thirds of the match a man down, that is the disappointing thing,” Roma coach Gian Piero Gasperini told DAZN. “We were confident we had an excellent chance, but we were forced to defend with 10 men, and we did so with order and clarity. When you play 30 minutes with 10 men and come away with a draw, that is fine.”

Bologna picked up their first win of the season by beating Lecce 2-1. Later, Milan go to Sassuolo before surprise package Cagliari welcome Juventus to the Unipol Domus in the late kick-off.

Borussia Mönchengladbach remained rock bottom of the German Bundesliga after a 2-1 defeat to local rivals Cologne on Sunday, in a match overshadowed by ugly scenes on the terraces.

The game was suspended for several minutes and riot police surrounded the away block after Gladbach fans appeared to fire fireworks into the home sections after Said El Mala’s superb second-half winner. That maintained pointless Gladbach’s miserable start to the season as new coach Alexander Blessin failed to prevent the club falling to their fifth defeat in as many games.

Sports.title: Scottish Premiership: Celtic end losing skid and take top spot back from Rangers
Sports.content:
Jota made his long-awaited return to action as Celtic claimed a much-needed 2-0 victory at Motherwell to move top of the Premiership again and ease the sense of gloom and tension that had engulfed the club during the international break.

Five months on from a dramatic late win that helped them on their way to last season’s title, Martin O’Neill’s side enjoyed another big result at Fir Park to end a three-game losing streak and climb back ahead of Rangers, who had leapfrogged them at the summit on Saturday.

After a renewal of hostilities between supporters and the Celtic board as well as uncertainty about O’Neill’s future as manager during the three-week break since their home defeat by their bitter rivals, an early strike from Camilo Durán helped restore a semblance of calm for the Hoops.

The champions had control of proceedings thereafter and – despite an inspired display from the home goalkeeper Alex Paulsen – Celtic added to their lead through Benjamin Nygren in the 58th minute as they made it seven wins in eight league matches this term.

The huge Hoops support sporadically unfurled banners and chanted against the club’s major shareholder Dermot Desmond, who was the subject of a tennis-ball protest by a group of balaclava-clad supporters at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship at St Andrews last weekend. Long before the end of a largely one-sided encounter, however, it was Motherwell’s fans who were displaying their frustration by making for the exits as their insipid side slid to a fourth consecutive defeat.

“If we’d been beaten today, of course, that would have been four on the trot, so that doesn’t help any manager,” said O’Neill. “But we didn’t. For us to get on track again domestically was delightful.”

Derek McInnes praised his Rangers players and blamed the extended international break for some disjointed play in Saturday’s 3-1 win over Kilmarnock.

Rangers went into the break three up at Ibrox after Ryan Naderi twice headed home either side of a Kevin Kelsy strike. But Killie had chances throughout, especially after the interval, before finally getting their reward when the substitute Nicky Clescenco struck on a last-minute counterattack. The visitors ended the game with six efforts on target to Rangers’ four, but the home goalkeeper, Ivor Pandur, was seriously troubled only once before being beaten.

View image in fullscreen Ryan Naderi celebrates after opening the scoring for Rangers against Kilarnock. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

“I was really pleased with how clinical we were in the first half,” said McInnes. “We put the ball in the box, we scored goals. We just didn’t do it enough for whatever reason. But we have to be honest, for long spells we looked like a team that hadn’t been together for the last three weeks. There’s a bit of understanding for me where the players have been. Whoever came up with this idea, it’s such a long time for your players to be away. We pay their wages, we look after our players and for them to be away for nearly three weeks is too long. But we’ve got the job done and credit the players for digging deep and getting three points.”

Hearts eased to their biggest home win in the league for three-and-a-half years as they dismantled St Mirren 5-0 to remain on the coattails of Rangers and Celtic.

Third-placed Hearts dominated from the start and Laurent Mendy fired them ahead in the 20th minute. Calvin Miller scored two penalties, either side of half-time, before goals from Cláudio Braga and Josh McPake ensured a smooth afternoon for Hearts.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Hearts’ Calvin Miller scores his side’s second from the spot against St Mirren. Photograph: Zak Mauger/Getty Images

It was Hearts’ biggest league win at Tynecastle since they defeated Ross County 6-1 under Steven Naismith in April 2023 and they are now comfortably the top scorers in the league. Hearts’ manager, Wouter Vrancken, said: “We try to play a kind of football that is positive and constructive and proactive, and not a reaction. I think people come to the stadium to see nice football, to see goals from your side.”

Josh Fowler’s first-half penalty earned St Johnstone a 1-0 win over Aberdeen putting them into the top five. Fowler’s spot-kick, awarded against Jack Milne after a lengthy video assistant referee check, proved the only goal of the game as the Dons huffed and puffed to no avail in front of goal.

Ashley Hay scrambled in a stoppage-time winner to secure Dundee a 2-1 victory at Falkirk. The striker, out since early August with a ligament sprain, converted from close range after latching on to Ethan Hamilton’s free-kick in the first minute of added time. His goal completed the turnaround after Owen Bevan’s second goal for the Dark Blues had cancelled out Jacob Murrell’s first-half penalty at Falkirk Stadium.

Marink Reedijk endured a disappointing first game as Hibernian’s manager as his side suffered a 1-0 defeat against Dundee United at Tannadice. The hosts scored in the first half through winger Daniel Bennie, on loan from QPR, and the visitors finished the game with 10 men after Jacob Devaney was sent off.

Sports.title: Robbie Savage the panto villain puts scepticism aside to leave Leicester reeling
Sports.content:
It felt as though the stars had aligned when Robbie Savage’s first League One match in charge of Peterborough – his first EFL managerial role – happened to be at Leicester. He made his name here and forged a divisive and enduring reputation that has kept him a permanent fixture in English football.

Savage has long been a joker figure – an image born in his playing days, when he hurtled around midfields with long blond hair bouncing, launching into challenges that at one point made him the most booked player in Premier League history. A pantomime villain, a prankster and an eccentric who was once fined £10,000 by the Football Association – and two weeks’ wages by Leicester – for using referee Graham Poll’s toilet before a match (Savage blamed an upset stomach brought on by antibiotics.)

That persona followed him into the media after retirement and it hardly screams management material, yet Savage has quietly built a more serious reputation on the touchline in recent years.

At the phoenix club Macclesfield, he was handed his first chance in the dugout by his mate Rob Smethurst, the owner, and won promotion to the National League North with a mammoth 109 points – winning 35 of 42 games. Last season, he guided Forest Green Rovers to the National League playoffs, losing to Boreham Wood.

Perhaps because of his personality, scepticism has shadowed the 51-year-old throughout his fledgling managerial career. In a lengthy interview with the Peterborough board, he won them over with his passion and ideas for restoring confidence in a young, talented, but struggling squad. Darragh MacAnthony, the club’s chair, suggested Savage’s character and work rate were required from “top to bottom” at the club.

Even so, when Savage took the Posh job he immediately addressed “the doubters” before anyone had really expressed any doubt. He pointed out he was told he was not good enough when he was released by Manchester United – one of the forgotten members of the Class of ’92 FA Youth Cup winners – and that he had battled his way into the Leicester team.

At the King Power Stadium on Saturday, he was so animated on the touchline it bordered on parody. He approached the travelling Peterborough fans and pumped his fist towards them – a gesture most managers save for after a victory, but Savage performed before kick-off. He was equally lively when the game started, dressed in baggy dark grey trousers and jacket, if not crouching on the edge of his technical area then shouting instructions, clapping his hands, pointing his fingers. There was a lot of pointing on his way to an impressive 3-1 win away.

View image in fullscreen Robbie Savage gees up the Peterborough fans before kick-off with a few fist pumps (top left), then runs through a gamut of emotions during the match. Composite: James Holyoak/Shutterstock; Michael Zemanek/Shutterstock; Jez Tighe/Prosports/Shutterstock

His exertions were so energetic the jacket came off within 10 minutes. “I’m exhausted,” he said. “I think I’ve done 10k in the technical area, kicking every ball for my team.”

It is no surprise he was handed a two-match ban last season for yellow cards received for over-exuberant celebrations and overexuberant discussions with officials. When Lucca Mendonça crunched Bobby De Cordova-Reid, Savage leapt and punched the air with as much enthusiasm as he celebrated Owura Edwards’s opening goal.

Quick Guide League One: Plymouth on top; dream start for Savage Show Plymouth came from behind to beat Wimbledon 2-1 with a stoppage-time goal from substitute Xavier Amaechi which put them clear at the top of League One. Jayden Stockley had put the Dons ahead in the 16th minute, with Caleb Watts equalising ahead of the break. It looked like the points would be shared before Amaechi swept the ball home in the fifth minute of added time. New Peterborough manager Robbie Savage had a dream start with a 3-1 win at Leicester, to pile more pressure on Foxes’ manager Russell Martin. Posh took an early lead through Owura Edwards and Harry Leonard before an own goal from Warren O’Hora made it 3-0 just before the break. Emil Riis scored a second-half consolation for the hosts. Mark Harris and Cameron Brannagan scored as high-flying Oxford secured a 2-1 win over Notts County at Meadow Lane. Bradford were held to a goalless draw by Leyton Orient at Valley Parade, slipping two points behind Plymouth. Huddersfield missed the chance to go second after Sheffield Wednesday fought back with two late goals to snatch a 2-2 draw at the Accu Stadium after Jamal Lowe scored a penalty deep into stoppage-time. Kyle Wootton scored twice as Stockport came from behind to beat Barnsley 3-1 at Edgeley Park to sit third. Gassan Ahadme’s late goal gave fifth-placed Cambridge a 1-0 win over 10-man Blackpool at the Abbey Stadium, where there had been a 15 minute delay to kick-off because of issues affecting supporters entering the ground. Reading are sixth after a 5-1 away win at strugglers MK Dons while Luton were comprehensive victors at Wycombe with a dominant 4-1 display to spoil a day of celebration for Tom Hounsell. Efforts from Kasey Palmer, Nahki Wells, Jamie Donley and Devante Cole were more than enough against a home side who announced Hounsell as permanent head coach before the game. Leon Ayinde’s first EFL goal was enough to move Doncaster out of the bottom four with a 1-0 home win over Burton. Mansfield edged home 2-1 in their first ever game against Bromley to halt a run of four games without a victory. Wigan remain adrift at the bottom of the table after a 1-0 defeat at Stevenage. Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

As at Macclesfield and Forest Green, his football was fast and direct. A ball over the top allowed Bolu Shofowoke to round the Leicester goalkeeper before Harry Leonard tapped in.

The Posh fans started chanting Savage’s name just before half-time, then called for him to give them a wave. But he was so engrossed in the Peterborough attack that led to their third goal that he didn’t hear them.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

That marauding style does leave them exposed at the back, but Savage doesn’t care. “My philosophy is: the best players are at the top of the pitch,” he said. “If I can get it there as quick as we can, by limiting the passes, but on the floor, through the lines, you can push the full-backs out. At times we were 2-1-1-6. That’s how we play. We are open. But let’s be brave.”

Even then, Emil Riis’s back-post tap-in – Savage, held his head in his hands as though the world was ending after conceding – took only a lick of gloss off the occasion. It was a stunning result for a side that in the league had won once all season, scored four times and gone seven weeks without a victory.

View image in fullscreen Robbie Savage offers a theatrical response to Peterborough’s victory at his former club Leicester in his first game in charge. Photograph: Jez Tighe/ProSports/Shutterstock

“I’m just humble to come up against somebody like Russell Martin, who’s managed in the Premier League,” Savage said. “Two and a half years ago I was up at Hebburn and Stockton, playing in front of 200-300 people. My team have come to the King Power and put in a performance like that. I’m so proud of them.”

At the final whistle, Savage hurried around the pitch, where he must have shaken the hand or slapped the back or hugged every player, coach and staff member from both teams. The Peterborough fans stood and chanted his name long before and well after he returned to pump his fist in celebration.

Savage will be entertaining this season. And he might just surprise a few people with his football, too.

Sports.title: Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Football, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863. The Premier League is the UK’s greatest soft power export. Premier League clubs are owned by a deputy prime minister of Abu Dhabi, the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia, a billionaire based in Monaco for tax reasons and a disappointing assortment of investors and private equity funds. And what, really, could be more British than that? Football truly is the national game.

What the Manchester City case has exposed is just how difficult it is to regulate some of the richest and most powerful bodies in the world. While the wait for the verdict was frustrating, it was perhaps unavoidable given the possibility of legal objection at every turn when a leaked email from City’s in-house lawyer during Uefa’s action against the club had threatened to “spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue them for the next 10 years”. You didn’t get that with Albert Alexander Sr or Peter Swales.

Football clubs in England and Wales still represent their communities, a relationship that may be strained in certain cases by the pressures of a globalised entertainment economy, but remains broadly true. Arsenal can feel like the club of choice for the nouveau fan from across the world, but the scenes of celebration when they ended their 22-year wait for the league title last season were an undeniable expression of local pride.

The idea that there was ever an idyll when clubs were run by benevolent potentates for the good of those communities is romantic nonsense. But just because there was no golden age is not to say that the situation has always been as bleak as this.

How did we get into a situation in which clubs are flotsam on the swirling currents of geopolitics and the world economy? Chelsea alone in the past four years have had a Russian oligarch forced to sell the club after falling under UK government sanctions, while a subsequent American co-owner has been forced to sell his minority stake after his insurance business came under federal investigation in the US. It’s a curious world in which the professional gamblers feel like a welcome breath of fresh air.

View image in fullscreen Chelsea fans hold banner during a fan-led protest calling for accountability and structural change at the club in January. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images

The days of the local businessmen, the owners of mines, shipyards and factories, the hauliers and scrap-metal dealers, are gone. Some invested because they genuinely wanted to give back to their communities or liked the sport. Others did so because it was easier to fund a local football club than to improve working conditions or pay a proper wage. And some did so because, wrongly in most cases, they thought there may be money to be made.

But no one should think those were days of purity. The decrepitude of English stadiums in the 1980s should caution anyone who thinks football was uncomplicatedly better then.

The contradiction has always lain at the heart of English football. Clubs represent their communities and for fans support becomes an aspect of identity, a link to family and place and past, a role that has only become more significant as the influence of traditional institutions – the church, the workplace, the social club – has faded. Yet fans in England have almost never owned their clubs, which in part underlies the present crisis.

That is not to say fan ownership is a panacea. There is much to be admired about the German 50+1 model which, to oversimplify, ensures outside investors can never own a majority of the club. But it has not prevented Bayern Munich from winning 13 of the past 14 Bundesliga titles. Some sort of recognition that a club is not just a business, that it has a community function might, though, have prevented the free-for-all that has led to this mess.

At least when most owners were local, there was some understanding of what the club meant to its area, and a recognition that exploitation or neglect could have direct consequences. No owner wanted demonstrations at the directors’ entrance, or to be jeered as he drove the streets in his Rolls-Royce, or to have his car showroom boycotted because he put up ticket prices then sold a popular centre-forward at a knockdown price. The distant majority shareholder in his boardroom in Los Angeles, his penthouse in Monte Carlo or his luxury villa on the Gulf feels the sting less keenly.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Richard Scudamore, the former chief executive of the Premier League who did more to shape the modern competition, for good and for ill, than any other individual, always spoke of being “neutral about ownership models”. Essentially that meant taking the money without worrying too much about where it came from. The current Premier League is the consequence: a gleaming, world-leading edifice, but built on what?

Perhaps it’s not fair to be too harsh on the Premier League. This is not just modern football; it is modern Britain. As Miguel Delaney and Jack Pitt-Brooke argued on the Libero podcast this week, the Premier League is a direct outcome of Blairite economic policy, a point made clear in Oliver Bullough’s Butler to the World,. In the book he described the classic New Labour approach as “allowing something, making money from it and attempting to solve the problems it causes after they’ve occurred”.

But how do you solve those problems in football? How can football extricate itself from the clutches of the mega-rich? Regulation, up to a point, helps – and there may at least now be a sense that there can be enforcement. Whatever the flaws of the profitability and sustainability rules, or the squad cost ratio that has replaced them, it may be useful if football could accept the basic premise that the game shouldn’t just be about how rich your owner happens to be. But that can only go so far; a door open to the world has admitted a world of problems.

Short of some sort of financial crash in football, the sort of apocalyptic event that would make the sport unappealing to big finance and require the game to be built anew, with a fresh spirit that might recategorise football clubs as community assets rather than simple businesses, we’re probably stuck with it.

How, after all, could football ever escape the society that produced it?

Sports.title: Man City give Liverpool fans the slip: Enzo Maresca's side dodge baying home fans en route to Anfield before being taunted by banners and facing hostile reception after guilty verdict
Sports.content:
Manchester City avoided a hostile reception outside Anfield on Sunday afternoon by cunningly arriving to the ground via another entrance before being taunted by banners and chants inside the ground.

Swarms of Reds supporters were waiting to give Enzo Maresca's side a frosty greeting with the visitors playing for the first time since the Premier League's bombshell guilty verdict.

Liverpool supporters turned up in their droves with several red flares at the ready and multiple 'cheats' banners to try and intimidate their bitter rivals ahead of kick-off.

However, their hopes were extinguished as City came down another road, accompanied by a police escort.

Inside the ground it was a different story. The City players were booed onto the pitch and there were dozens of banners reminding the visitors of their cheating shame.

One read: 'Steven Gerrard, Premier League champion 2014.' Plenty quoted huge Man City fans Oasis, with song title 'All of your stars are fading away' seen held up in the Kop.

Noel Gallagher, incidentally, was pictured walking into Anfield accompanied by security guards.

Man City's bus avoided a hostile reception from Liverpool fans after arriving via a different way

Noel Gallagher is seen arriving at Anfield escorted by security on Sunday afternoon

There were 114 pound signs on the word 'cheat' on a banner along the bottom of the Kop

Plenty of Liverpool fans brought banners into the stadium after City's guilty charges

One of the bigger banners inside the ground referenced another Oasis song

A huge banner was unfurled in the middle of the Kop with exactly 114 pound signs in the word 'cheats', another said: 'After all you really robbed us all', referencing 'Wonderwall'.

One more read: 'A generation of supporters cheated', and some fans held up balloons reading '114' referencing the number of charges the independent commission found City guilty of.

Chants of 'cheats' and 'you're going down' echoed around the ground in the early exchanges, while City were loudly booed and whistled with every touch of the ball.

City fans, meanwhile, brought in inflatable bananas, a practice not seen for a while by the club, who first did so in 1987 when a fan tried to lift the gloom by bringing a giant one to a game against Plymouth Argyle.

It then became commonplace among City supporters and they even brought 10,000 of them to a game at one point in 1988.

Bringing them to Anfield was seen as a self-deprecating way to poke fun at their own history, given they could return to the depths of English football if their appeal fails.

City were found guilty of all serious financial rule breaches levelled against them between 2009 and 2018, a period where they saw off Liverpool to win the Premier League title in 2014-15.

The seismic findings have sent shockwaves through the football world, with potential punishments ranging from expulsion from the top flight, to points deductions and financial penalties. City have indicated their intention to appeal the verdict.

And Maresca has insisted it remains business as usual at the Etihad and he has 'complete trust' in the Abu Dhabi ownership group, while Erling Haaland called on his team-mates to 'enjoy the ride'.

City fans brought inflatable bananas to Anfield in reference to their past

Plenty of supporters made a play on words of Oasis songs, including this offering

Inflatable '114' signs were brought into the ground in reference to the number of guilty charges

The Kop was adorned by banners created especially for this much-anticipated game

‘I completely trust the club,’ Maresca said on Friday. ‘I trust the people and it’s one of the reasons I joined the club. There isn’t another club in the world where I would like to be.’

Asked if he would have accepted the job had he known what would transpire in the bitter case with the Premier League, Maresca added: ‘One hundred per cent. I know the organisation from years ago.

‘I know how serious they are and they do the right things. I want to speak about this when we win the appeal.’

Sports.title: Newcastle's new Kiwi star MAX HICKS on feeding his pet eel butter chicken, growing up on AFL and hockey, waterskiing, working on a building site with Exeter's Ethan Roots and being compared to LeBron James - is an England call next?
Sports.content:
Newcastle's new Kiwi star MAX HICKS on feeding his pet eel butter chicken, growing up on AFL and hockey, waterskiing, working on a building site with Exeter's Ethan Roots and being compared to LeBron James - is an England call next?

Newcastle Red Bull's new England-qualified arrival is full of surprises.

Let’s start with Max Hicks' childhood. He was born and raised in New Zealand. His father, James, is Maori, and his mother, Liane, comes from Cornwall.

‘I grew up in a little town called Coatesville, west of Auckland,’ explains the 27-year-old, his long limbs sprawled across a sofa at Kingston Park. ‘I had a pet eel called Scarface. We had this big creek that ran through the bottom of our property. We had agricultural day at primary school, where people would bring in sheep, calves, bunny rabbits.

'My old man was a builder and we had this old bathtub, so we went and caught one of the eels from the creek to take into school and I kept it as my pet. I put it back in the river but it would always come back. I always fed it left-over butter chicken. They don’t have good vision so it was something to do with the aromatics. It loved it. I’d pick it up and take it around the garden. I had a ram called Cookie, too. I would shout his name and he would run over to me. I was a pretty weird kid…’

His sporting journey has been equally unconventional. While the likes of Caleb Clarke and Tupou Vaa'i were nurtured through the All Blacks age grades, Hicks was often found playing hockey or Aussie Rules. A career in rugby seemed like an unlikely path.

‘My parents encouraged me to get into all sports possible,' he says. 'I played 100 games of first-team hockey at high school and played for the New Zealand Maori hockey team. I started playing AFL in my last year of high school, too, and spent some time with St Kilda (one of the AFL's most historic sides, based in Melbourne). AFL is such an athletic sport. The big men can all run, jump, kick off both feet, handle with both hands.

Newcastle Red Bull's new England-qualified arrival Max Hicks is full of surprises

While other rising stars were nurtured through the All Blacks age grades, Hicks was often found playing hockey or Aussie Rules. A career in rugby seemed like an unlikely path

‘I loved playing rugby but I was never the best. I got invited to a few of the Under 20s camps but I was built like a rake. AFL wanted me to be super fit and to be able to run forever. Rugby wanted me to bulk up. I was stuck between a rock and a hard place.

'Rugby never really hit me as a proper career path until I kind of left high school. Once I'd chosen rugby, I went on this big bulking journey to put on some weight. McDonald's, KFC, ice cream!’

Hicks became a trainee builder to fund his rugby dream. He upped his calorie intake and took on an early morning weights routine before going to work. By chance, his labouring colleague was school-mate Ethan Roots, the Auckland-born Exeter Chiefs flanker who has been capped by England.

‘We went to the same high school and we worked for the same building company, building houses around Auckland.' he says. 'We were setting out slabs, putting standing walls up, putting on cladding. You’re getting up at 4.30am and you’re in the gym at 5. I was still trying to make it in rugby but I was also planning for life if I didn't.

‘I wasn’t a young superstar who was picked up straight out of high school and straight into a rugby environment. I moved down to Tasman. They didn't offer me a full contract, but they kind of said, “Hey, if you come down here, work hard, you can earn yourself a spot on the team”.

‘The following year I joined the Highlanders. I remember going in for the first time and seeing all these guys I'd watched on TV. Guys like Aaron Smith and Shannon Frizell. Ben Smith and Tony Brown were coaching us. It was pretty surreal. I played for the Maori All Blacks, representing my dad's side, and I was really keen to have an adventure, so I shot over to France and joined Perpignan.’

Wearing the No6 jersey last season, Hicks’ turnover haul was second only to Jack Willis in the Top 14. With Europe on his doorstep, he had the opportunity to retrace his family roots.

‘My grandad was in the Royal Air Force and he got a posting in New Zealand. Mum was born in Truro and they moved over when she was around ten years old. I went to Cornwall with mum for the first time last year, that was cool. She got to show me where she grew up.

Hicks has only played two PREM games for Newcastle but he is already making a name for himself

Hicks became a trainee builder to fund his rugby dream. By chance, his labouring colleague was school-mate Ethan Roots (centre), the Auckland-born Exeter flanker capped by England

'We got an Airbnb and spent some time in St Ives. Ethan and Jimmy Roots popped over from Exeter, too. A lot of the family moved over to New Zealand but there will be a few relatives hanging around. I might have to do one of those Find My Family mouth swabs!’

Newcastle’s head of recruitment, Gavin Vaughan, learned of Hicks’ English roots last year. Vaughan previously worked for Scotland and unearthed Sione Tuipulotu and Huw Jones, scouring the rugby world for Scotland-eligible players.

In his new role with Newcastle, Vaughan has to hit targets of English-qualified players, making Hicks a particularly attractive proposition.

‘I wasn't actively looking to leave France but I was open to hearing what was out there. Red Bull approached me and my agent and it’s such an awesome project. The Red Bull influence is pretty cool. I thought, “How cool would it be to come into a new environment that's so unknown, with all this expectation, and really turn a place around?”

'You know, the Falcons had it tough for a couple years. It would be such a cool story to come here as a group of people from all around the world and fill the stadium out every week. That's what excited me. Mum was quite happy that I moved over. There’s a bit of patriotism there. I’ve represented my dad’s side and I guess now I’m representing my mum’s.’

During Newcastle’s pre-season camp at the Red Bull HQ in Austria, Hicks had another surprise for his team-mates. He wowed everyone with his wakeboarding skills out on the Wolfgang Lake – another skill he picked up living by the coast in New Zealand.

Hicks has only played two PREM games for Newcastle but he is already making a name for himself. During last weekend’s defeat by Leicester, Ireland legend Brian O’Driscoll compared his ability to hold a ball in one hand to NBA superstar LeBron James.

At 6ft 6in and 17st 9lb, Hicks resembles former Saracens flanker Theo McFarland, whose basketball background gave him an athletic point of difference. His eye-catching performances have thrown him into the mix of England’s World Cup bolters – although there has been no contact with Steve Borthwick.

During Newcastle’s pre-season camp at the Red Bull HQ in Austria, Hicks had another surprise for his team-mates. He wowed everyone with his wakeboarding skills out on the Wolfgang Lake

‘It was never my reason for coming over here but I would love to play international rugby,' he says, having represented the Maori All Blacks twice but never the full senior side.

'I'd love to represent my mum's side of the family. If that happens, it happens. If it doesn't, it doesn't. I’m here to throw all my eggs into the club. My reason for coming here was to be part of an exciting project with Red Bull.

‘I know we've had a tough start to the PREM and we've lost two, but the progress we're making as a group has been really positive. We’re still fine-tuning things, the fans are excited, and the group's gelling really well. It's just about finding those little connections with players you have never played with before.

'Some teams have been together for a few years and they know who's going to get a weak shoulder and throw an offload. We're still figuring that out with each other, but when that clicks, it's going to be exciting. We'll start getting more results come our way.’

Sports.title: Liverpool 0-3 Man City PLAYER RATINGS: Who always made the wrong decision in the big moments? Who will Andoni Iraola be demanding more from? And who could be City's main man but for pending punishments?
Sports.content:
It was a game that had so much more to it than a football match. Liverpool fans brought cheating banners, City fans brought bananas to mock their charges – but, ultimately, the Premier League leaders brought their A-game.

Underneath all the off-field chaos, there was indeed a football match taking place. And it was a good one, until Ryan Gravenberch was sent off.

Liverpool went blow-for-blow with Enzo Maresca's City, whose future remains uncertain. 'Going down,' the Liverpool fans chanted – they may well be, but, for now, they are the league's best.

Gravenberch was given his marching orders in the 62nd minute, and Liverpool couldn't cope after. City upped the tempo, and scored three goals, celebrating as if nothing was going on off the field.

Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki were all on the scoresheet as City carried on their 100 per cent record. Liverpool, meanwhile, have two wins from their six games so far, and are ninth in the standings.

Daily Mail Sport's LEWIS STEELE was at Anfield to rate the players.

Erling Haaland (centre) was on the scoresheet as Manchester City beat Liverpool 3-0 at Anfield

LIVERPOOL (4-2-3-1)

Alisson – 6

Could do nothing about any of City’s goals. Had little to do beforehand but his presence put off Haaland at 0-0.

Ronald Araujo – 5

Played fine overall but Doku and Co gave him the run-around when they started to fly forward after the red card. Booked.

Jeremy Jacquet – 6

Made some fine interventions in the first-half and has been a strong addition to Liverpool’s team.

Virgil van Dijk – 5

Slow to react at times and none of Liverpool’s defenders could cope with City when they had the man advantage. Booked.

Milos Kerkez – 5

Made some powerful runs forward but struggled defensively, which happens all too often for the Hungary international.

Milos Kerkez (right) was good going forwards but once again struggled defensively

Ryan Gravenberch was having his best game this season until an unnecessary red card

Ryan Gravenberch – 6
