World.title: Man City beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 in first game after guilty verdict
World.content:
Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki score second half goals after Ryan Gravenberch sent off.

Share Man City beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 in first game after guilty verdict on social media

Manchester City shrugged off the threat of swingeing sanctions to beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 in their first game since being found guilty on more than 100 charges of breaking Premier League financial rules.

Second half goals from Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki on Sunday extended City’s flawless start under Enzo Maresca after Ryan Gravenberch had been sent -off for two yellow cards.

Victory reestablishes City’s three-point lead at the top of the table, but the future of any title challenge rests on the outcome of the club’s appeal against widespread financial impropriety.

An independent commission found City and their Emirati owners arranged “sham” deals to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than 900 million pounds ($1.2bn) between 2009 and 2018.

No sanction has yet been handed down, but a severe points deduction or even expulsion from the English top-flight is on the table unless City overturns the decision.

There has even been speculation that there could be retrospective action to strip City’s titles.

The multiple breaches of Premier League laws came during a period in which City won three titles and a clutch of other trophies.

City’s rivals believe, however, that the illegal spending during that period also built the foundations for a golden era under former boss Pep Guardiola, who left at the end of last season.

Liverpool were one of the clubs most affected, having finished second to City three times in the past 12 years.

“There are so many moments and memories we can’t get back,” Liverpool fan Martin Reilly, 23, told the AFP news agency. “They have to throw the book at them.”



City arrived under the protection of a police escort with a hostile Anfield welcome expected, but there was no repeat of the violent scenes when their team bus was pelted with bottles ahead of a Champions League clash in 2018.

Liverpool fans lined the streets to greet the visitors with chants of “cheats” and “going down”, while merchandise stalls were littered with flags and scarves mocking City’s financial scandal.

In the iconic Kop end behind one goal, a banner read “a generation of supporters cheated”.

The battles between Guardiola’s City and Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool in recent years became the Premier League’s marquee event.

But with the eyes of the world watching today, Liverpool failed to rise to the occasion on the field.

New Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola’s options were blunted without the injured Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo as the Spaniard suffered his first defeat since taking charge of the Reds.

The home side briefly flickered into life at the start of the second half when Lewis Koumas was denied a goal on his first Premier League start by Gianluigi Donnarumma.

The Abu Dhabi-backed takeover in 2008 transformed City from mid-table mediocrity into the dominant force of the English game.

City’s economic might was on full display to help turn the game, as Maresca could turn to Jeremy Doku off the bench early in the second half.

Within minutes the Belgian winger had been chopped down by Gravenberch, who was shown a second yellow card and Liverpool never recovered.

Doku’s deflected shot was then smashed home by Haaland to break the deadlock 25 minutes from time and open the floodgates.

Three minutes later Doku curled a sensational strike into the top corner himself.

Cherki then exchanged a slick one-two with Josko Gvardiol before slotting under Alisson Becker to rub salt in Liverpool’s wounds.

City midfielder Elliot Anderson told reporters after the game that his side had shown “courage” as they got the win in a hostile atmosphere.

“We have shown togetherness and fight, this is tough place to come and we have shown courage,” he said.

“It [the noise from the Anfield crowd] was more than normal … Arriving and the first 10 minutes of the first half, but we quietened the crowd and improved in the second half.

“During the game you can feel it, and it is a game where you have to stick together and we did.”

World.title: Turkiye highway crash kills 11, injures 27 after tour bus hits truck
World.content:
Police detain tour bus driver after highway collision in western Turkiye leaves 11 dead and 27 injured.

At least 11 people have been killed and 27 injured after a tour bus and a tow truck collided in western Turkiye.

The crash happened near toll booths at Akhisar on the Gebze-Orhangazi-Izmir highway in Manisa province on Sunday morning.

According to a statement from the Manisa governor’s office, authorities received a report of the collision just after 11am local time.

The wounded were taken to local hospitals, including the bus driver, who was detained by police following his discharge.

Images from the scene showed blue body bags lined along the roadside next to the overturned bus, which sustained heavy structural damage to its rear section.

The tow truck, which appeared to be carrying wooden planks, had also overturned.

Writing on social media platform X, Turkiye’s Interior Minister, Mustafa Ciftci, referred to the victims as citizens, though authorities have not yet confirmed whether any foreign nationals were among the casualties.

The governor of Manisa, Vahdettin Ozkan, visited the crash site as emergency teams cleared the wreckage.

“Work at the scene is currently ongoing under the coordination of the Public Prosecutor’s Office,” Ozkan said. “We are experiencing, in a painful way, just how vital it is to strictly adhere to traffic rules.”

World.title: Spain’s Protesters See ‘Madness’ of Rising Rent and a ‘Martyr’ in Maricarmen
World.content:
Thousands of people marched in Madrid on Thursday in memory of María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose dramatic eviction two weeks ago shook the country and prompted Spain’s left-wing prime minister to call snap elections over a housing crisis.

Before her death on Wednesday, Ms. Abascal, popularly known as Maricarmen, became a symbol of the housing crisis. Only about 20 percent of Spaniards have to rent their homes, but that share has increased in recent years as homeownership — deeply ingrained in Spain’s culture — slides further out of reach.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has portrayed his decision to hold elections as a chance for his left-wing bloc to get a majority in Parliament that would tackle the housing crisis. But it remains far from clear whether the issue will sway enough voters, as conservative and far-right parties frame the election as a referendum on Mr. Sánchez himself.

And as the parties wrangle, many Spaniards are staying in the streets, saying they feel crushed by the problems of rising rent and stagnant wages.

World.title: Saudi capital airport hit by second Houthi strike in two days
World.content:
An international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh has been hit by a second strike in as many days, officials have said.

A Saudi military spokesman said a projectile had hit King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, causing a fire in one of its passenger halls. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said there had been injuries.

It comes a day after a strike on the same airport killed 13 people and injured 308 others, following similar strikes earlier this week.

The Houthis in Yemen said they were behind the attacks and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace.

The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones in the past 24 hours.

They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said.

He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.

The Houthis have said they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war, as well as an air strike on the airport in Sanaa.

On Sunday Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, said air defences had intercepted a missile near the airport in Riyadh, while authorities were dealing with the fire caused by an "unknown projectile" that hit Passenger Hall No 4.

US President Donald Trump has said the US would "make a decision" and "move very quickly" on whether to strike the Houthis, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting suggested the UK could "potentially" provide more support for Saudi Arabia.

World.title: Ukraine strikes Yandex data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant
World.content:
Yandex has been forced to pause its operations at a data centre near Moscow after the facility was damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike - the third attack on the Russian tech giant's sites this week.

The company - dubbed "Russia's Google" - said no one was injured at the centre in Vladimir, east of the capital, but some of its services were unavailable to users.

Earlier this week, Yandex said it was struggling to maintain its services after two of its five data centres were hit in Ukrainian strikes.

Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between them continues in its fifth year following Russia's full-scale invasion.

Kyiv said it was targeting places that provide revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the attacks could force Russia to divert its resources to repair the damage at Yandex.

Sunday's attack came hours after US President Donald Trump warned that Ukraine should "damn well stop" attacking Russia's oil refineries so Moscow could release more diesel to the global market - a deal that has drawn criticism from Europe and sparked a diplomatic row with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky.

World.title: Poland detains man suspected of planning assassination of PM Tusk
World.content:
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a man accused of plotting an assassination attack against him and his defence minister has been detained.

The interior ministry earlier reported that police had received credible information about possible attacks against Tusk and Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz.

Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about the planned attacks, with a spokesman saying officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".

Tusk thanked the police for "swift and decisive action" in arresting the suspect.

The suspect was arrested in the Lower Silesia region and was a Polish national, Jacek Dobrzynski, a spokesman for the Special Services Co-ordinator told local media.

"In this case we are talking about a strong likelihood that these threats could actually be carried out," he said.

The plan was uncovered when an email with information about the potential attack was forwarded to police by the State Protection Service, which is responsible for ministers' security, Interior Ministry spokeswoman Karolina Galecka said.

Tusk has been Polish prime minister since 2023, having previously held the office from 2007 to 2014.

He served as president of the European Council from 2014 to 2019.

World.title: Homes and bridges swept away as fresh floods hit Nepal
World.content:
A major river in Nepal has flooded, sweeping away houses, bridges and damaging a part of hydropower station, authorities have said.

Around 50 people have been rescued from along the bank of the Budhi Gandaki River in the central Gorkha district, the army confirmed. No casualties have been reported yet, however five people are missing.

A video of the flood shows the moment raging waters sweep down a valley and wash away an entire building complex.

Nepal is on high alert and still trying to recover from catastrophic floods that hit its border towns with Tibet two months ago, leaving more than 1,400 people dead and thousands missing.

Sunday's flood tore through the Gorkha district as children and communities prepared to mark the first day of the Dashain festival, a major moment in the Nepali calendar.

Families have been forced to flee their homes, with many facing uncertainty over where they will find safe shelter and access to essential supplies.

The flood swept away about a dozen houses and several suspension bridges, while a hydroelectric project was damaged, carrying some of the construction equipment away, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.

Within a couple of hours, the river's water levels at one location had risen from two metres (6ft 5in) to nearly 8.5m (27ft 9in), officials said.

Binod Parajuli, a meteorologist who works with the Nepalese government, said: "Our hydrological station was swept away and we are not getting any data from that location."

However, experts say the debris-flow is much smaller and travelled more slowly than the devastating flash floods in August.

What caused the latest flood is still unclear. Some say a landslide may have blocked the river or its tributary for some time, causing the dammed water to burst out, while others say locals upstream saw an ice-avalanche.

Save the Children is mobilising an emergency team to respond to Sunday's flood.

"Children's lives have been ripped apart in an instant yet again", the charity's director in Nepal, Tara Chettry, said.

"We are yet to see the full scale of the damage, but they may have lost their homes, schools and communities. Many children in Gorkha will still be in shock and distress after the mega floods in August, barely having a chance to get back on their feet."

The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli river, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused the previous disaster.

World.title: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says
World.content:
Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.

The attacks have left one woman dead and others injured, including children.

"These are very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity," Tusk said on Sunday, during a crisis meeting with security services.

Police have arrested 117 people across the country for possession knives or other weapons, or for threatening to attack schools or fellow students, after searching tens of thousands of schools.

A woman was arrested on Saturday after injuring three people while attacking a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw.

It came a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker.

"We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said on Sunday.

"In the past years and months, we have noted - globally and in Poland - a rise in the fascination with violence," he added.

The prime minister said the attacks were acts of "nihilistic violence" associated with the extreme right.

"Some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment," he said, adding that police had noticed a rise in online searches of Nazi content as well as of "mass killers who have become idols online".

On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.

A day later, the 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in LeszczydÃ³Å-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.

Interior Minister Marcin KierwiÅski also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".

Thousands of Polish âpolice officers visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after the stabbings sparked rumours of a "Bloody Friday" of more attacks stemming from a supposed online challenge.

Meanwhile, Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about a potential attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a spokesperson said.

A special services spokesman said officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".

World.title: Children among 139 dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says
World.content:
At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said.

The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.

IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere.

Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says.

The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered.

"This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives."

Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them.

Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change.

Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti.

World.title: Pope Leo to have surgery after lump found on lung
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated on "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check-up.

"The doctors found an early, well-localised nodule on my lung," he told the public during his weekly Sunday prayers in St Peter's Square in Rome.

The 71-year-old said his medical team "believe it would be right to intervene" and he had agreed to the operation, while reassuring pilgrims that the mass was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage".

The pontiff's admission that he would need surgery comes nearly a year-and-a-half after he succeeded the late Pope Francis, who also experienced issues with his lungs that required hospital treatment.

Leo concluded his Angelus prayer by thanking everyone for their "spiritual closeness" and said he entrusted himself to their prayers.

Holy See Press Office spokesman Matteo Bruni told the media that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of next week".

He added that the Pope is expected to take about a week to recover.

Vatican News, the Holy See's news portal, said the operation will take place at Gemelli Hospital in Rome.

The hospital set up a special Papal suite following the failed assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II's life in May 1981, which is still in use today.

Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her "personal solidarity" with the Pope as he "faces the ordeal ahead in the coming days".

Her sentiments were echoed by Italian President Sergio Mattarella, who offered his "sincerest wishes for a peaceful recovery and a speedy and full return to health".

Isaac Herzog, the president of Israel, also wished the pontiff "a full and speedy recovery".

The Pope, born Robert Francis Prevost, is the 267th occupant of the throne of St Peter â the first US citizen to do so.

He was ordained in 1982 and spent years as a missionary in Peru, where he is remembered as a figure who worked with marginalised communities.

During Sunday's service, the Pope confirmed his upcoming visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November will still go ahead.

The Archbishop of Montevideo, Daniel Sturla, said preparations for his tour will continue with "greater enthusiasm" as he called for prayers for his recovery.

A lung nodule is a small lump of tissue that is usually detected following an X-ray or CT scan of the chest, according to the NHS.

Most nodules do not cause other symptoms.

World.title: US justice department investigates TV networks over Trump pool coverage
World.content:
The US Department of Justice (DoJ) has said it is investigating several TV networks over whether they broke federal competition laws when they recently suspended pool coverage of Donald Trump.

Last month, five networks paused their presidential coverage for several days in response to the Trump administration withdrawing the credentials of reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico.

The DoJ asked ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News to hand over communications related to the pool and said the boycott could violate the Sherman Act, referring to a law that bars companies from engaging in monopolistic business practices.

Pool members usually share their material with the wider media.

A DoJ spokesperson said: "The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these ânews organisations have violated the antitrust laws."

The television networks have not yet commented.

Trump blocked CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House last month after accusing the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his team.

The White House later reinstated their access following a judge's ruling. The three outlets had sued the Trump administration, arguing the restricted access violated their First Amendment rights.

The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.

The Trump administration has taken a number of legal actions against news publications in the US, including lawsuits over coverage of the president.

In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool, which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.

The same month, the Trump administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.

World.title: TO WAZIRI ATIKU ABUBAKAR: A FINAL WORD FOR A DIMINISHING STAR (PART 1)
World.content:
I received a WhatsApp message from Waziri Atiku Abubakar on Sunday afternoon in response to my open letter to him which was published earlier that day titled ‘AND NOW YOU CALL HIM BOLA’ together with another article which I published the Sunday before titled ‘THE 7TH BID OF WAZIRI’.

For the record he wrote:

“PLEASE LEAVE ME ALONE FEMI. YOU SIMPLY DON’T HAVE THE CREDIBILITY TO CRITICISE ME”.

My response to him, inter alia, was as follows:

“IF I AM NOT CREDIBLE ENOUGH TO EXPOSE YOU THEN WHAT MAKES YOU THINK YOU ARE CREDIBLE ENOUGH TO EXPOSE OR DISRESPECT OBJ, GEJ, BAT OR KS? IF I DO NOT HAVE THE CREDIBILITY TO CRITICISE YOU OR THE RIGHT TO DO SO, WHO DOES? IF I AM NOT CREDIBLE WITH ALL I HAVE EXPERIENCED, SEEN AND BEEN THROUGH IN POLITICS OVER THE LAST 30 YEARS AND THE EVIL I HAVE SURVIVED OVER THE LAST 20 YEARS THEN WHO IS? CERTAINLY NOT YOU OR AMAECHI SIR”.

That is where our conversation ended.

Waziri, forgive me, but given this, coupled with the wild and indecorous words that you used against President Tinubu in the press conference that you gave just yesterday, I am inclined to agree with my learned friend and brother Festus Keyamo SAN, the Honorable Minister of Aviation and Aerospace, who responded by saying,

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Atiku actually needs mental health support at this critical time as he peters out into political oblivion”.

Outside of that, in the light of recent developments, I am constrained to write to you yet again.

I say this because I was told that on Sunday afternoon, at the same moment that you sent me your message on WhatsApp, your minion and most junior cheerleader, a sickly creature who looks twice his age, who is withering away from some strange disease and whose name I always forget, wrote an article in an attempt to respond to my open letter to you.

I was reliably informed that amongst much else in his “response” he wrote that my supposedly “estranged” ex-wife, who remains very close and dear to me even though we are no longer married, had said a number of ugly things about me in the past, all of which I have denied, even though we are at peace today and have put all that behind us.

The disjointed verbiage and unadulterated garbage that your dog wrote which only my press secretary found the time to read and which is below my dignity and status to respond to is, to me, like water off a duck’s back.

Lions do not respond to dogs and this is especially so when that dog only has three legs and no tail.

Simply put I do not take cognisance of anything your hired help writes: I would rather give my attention to you personally.

If you do not have the strength and courage to respond to me publicly yourself, as you have done privately, then at least send your rumbustious, owambe-loving, champagne-swirling, bon vivant and chief cheerleader whose defunct Pendulum column I used to read and who is infinitely more qualified to carry out this fool’s errand and not some unlettered village idiot or prize fool like the creature you sent.

That chief cheerleader also made reference to my ex-wife a few months ago during the course of an acrimonious debate that I had with him on X about President Tinubu and he insisted on bringing my family into the discourse.

Sadly it doesn’t stop there.

Yet another one of your cheerleaders, a former Senator with a bald head and a silver grey beard, who sometimes insists on wearing a skirt and who sleeps with cars and motorbikes in his bedroom also resorted to attacking the family of his adversaries during the course of political discourse by once threatening to “beat and impregnate” Senator Oluremi Tinubu, the First Lady, right there on the Senate floor and by insulting President Tinubu’s entire family, including his children and all of their mothers, on television just a few months ago.

In fairness to him whilst admitting that he threatened to “beat” Senator Tinubu he denied the “impregnate” part but went on to say, in the most shameless, inappropriate and indecorous manner, that she had “entered menopause”.

He also resorted to mocking the President’s age and health in the 2023 presidential election campaign by singing insulting and utterly depraved songs at campaign rallies in the presence of the godless deplorables that were on the campaign trail with him who ought to have known better and told him to stop.

My question is as follows: are you the one that encourages these troubled souls that hover around you to resort to this uncouth behaviour or is it that they are just dysfunctional and ill-mannered?

Whatever the case I hold you accountable for not being able to control them.

I am constrained to ask, is that the best your media team can do?

Talk about what wives and ex-wives say about their husbands and former husbands or rant about the personal lives and families of others?

Should they not stick to soft-sell magazines if that is the sort of rubbish they want to write about?

In any case where were these rascals when you and I sat in President Olusegun Obasanjo’s Federal Executive Council 20 years ago?

Yet since they have chosen to tread that path I pity you because what your ex-wife has said about you has now become fair game.

Ditto your family matters and the tragic misfortune that constantly stalks your closest aides each time you run for the Presidency.

If you insist that we go down this murky rabbit hole we will and we shall do so together.

Your aides forget that I am not on the ballot but you are.

There was a time when family members were regarded as being sacrosanct and kept out of political discourse and war but not anymore.

Sadly your boys have lowered the bar and your camp will regret it.

I am now constrained to go back into the records and talk about what your estranged ex-wife, Jennifer Douglas, said about you, what she did to you, what you did to her and more importantly what she allegedly did for you in the Leno Adesanya Mambilla Power Plant fraud and other questionable matters.

For example the U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations (2010) documented more than $40 million USD in suspect transfers involving your then-wife Jennifer Douglas.

I wonder what you have to say about this?

That is a real report even though, in fairness, it did not produce an indictment or a criminal conviction against you because, by that time, you had conveniently fled America.

Whatever she said about me, at least my ex-wife did not throw all my personal belongings, including my underwear, out into the streets from my Dubai home and keep everything that was there, including the furniture, the cars, the washing machine, the kitchen utensils and the house itself for herself.

Neither did she complain about the company I kept with men.

Again there are the words of Fati Muhammed, a Kannywood actress and former associate who claims she was very close to you.

Just a few days ago she said the following:

“I have been supporting Atiku in politics since 2007 and what has kept me away from him is his lies and broken promises”.

One wonders what you did to this lady to attract such ‘accolades’ from her.

I guess we shall soon find out.

Outside of that we shall also talk about precisely what you did at the airports and seaports in your younger days as a Customs officer, how you allowed 51 suitcases filled with God knows what to be smuggled through Lagos Airport and what your link with a shady Italian national called Gabriele Volpi and his son Matteo really was.

I will also mention your affiliation with NICOTES (which later became Intels) and how a Customs Officer like you went from a rather conservative salary to being a large shareholder in a multi-billion dollar corporation overnight whilst you were still in Customs.

Again what you did when you were Vice President between 1999 and 2007 which led you to be the subject of an extensive investigation by the American FBI and which caused President Obasanjo to express his deep regrets about picking you as his running mate and calling you “very corrupt” becomes relevant.

So does your link with Congressman William J. Jefferson, an American legislator who was sentenced to 13 years in 2009 after the FBI found 90,000 USD cash in his freezer which was part of a 500,000 USD bribe which had been asked for and he was planning to give to a very highly placed Nigerian Government official.

It has been alleged that the Government official in question was you but, in fairness, this is yet to be proved, you were not indicted or convicted for it and I cannot therefore confirm it as a fact and neither do I claim to do so.

Yet it is worth our attention and scrutiny and we shall find out more about this sordid case and whether you had any involvement in the malfeasance.

The easiest way for you to sort this matter out though and clear the ugly rumours that you had asked for the bribe is for you to travel to America, report to the FBI and let them ask you the relevant questions.

If you have nothing to hide or fear I suggest you do this as soon as possible so that we can finally clear the air.

Again there was the unresolved allegation of the ‘Special Purpose Vehicle’ (SPV) which was a corporate vehicle that you allegedly told your former media aide, Mr. Michael Achimugu, that you created specially for the purpose of avoiding what you allegedly described as “open corruption” and siphoning public funds in order to raise money for funding the PDP and your private usage.

In 2023 Achimugu released an audio tape of a conversation with a man whom he claimed was you making these startling and damning confessions and that voice was heard explaining to him in graphic and clear terms how a conspiracy was hatched to commit such thievery.

In fairness, you claimed that the voice was not yours and neither can I confirm or deny that it was.

However under normal circumstances this provides enough evidence to, at the very least, result in a full criminal investigation and, if found wanting, a formal prosecution but instead of thanking God that the matter was not treated with the seriousness that it deserved you still insist on running for the Presidency whilst at the same time claiming that others do not have the credibility to criticise you. What a nerve!

The truth is that the assertion that anyone that is a freeborn Nigerian lacks the credibility to criticise a man that has so many questions to answer like you is simply asinine.

Permit me to add that there are also things you allegedly did many years earlier in the 1980s and 1990s that are, to say the least, suspicious and questionable.

We shall look into all these things after which we shall all be in a position to know who has credibility and who does not.

As an opener kindly tell us why you allegedly cannot go to America freely and without your associates helping you to get a “special package visa” as they did in 2019?

If this is true and, I have no way of confirming or denying that it is, it gives cause for concern.

These things need to be looked into and discussed because you are aspiring to become our President.

You talk about credibility but I am not the one that betrayed my principal and boss and in the process privatised the whole of Nigeria!

You did that and if you had the chance you would do it all over again.

The truth is you are nowhere near me in terms of pedigree, credibility, education, upbringing or lineage.

The only thing you have is money and though your vast wealth may buy houses, cars, gold bars, private jets, political parties and the worship and adulation of your court jesters and cheerleaders it cannot buy CLASS or CHARACTER and neither can it move the finger of God or tamper with the manifest destiny of men.

(END OF PART 1)

(Chief Femi Fani-Kayode, the author of this essay, is a former Minister of Aviation, a former Minister of Culture and Tourism, Nigeria’s Ambassador to South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini, the Sadaukin Shinkafi, the Wakilin Doka Potiskum, the Aare Ajagunla of Otun Ekiti, the Otunba of Joga Orile and a Legal Practitioner)

World.title: Nigeria: Outsourcing the Presidency, One Infirmity at a Time
World.content:
Nearly 20 years ago, while stumping for his party, the Peoples’ Democratic Party, out-going president, Olusegun Obasanjo, decided to confront head-on morbid rumours about the health of his hand-picked successor. Umaru Musa Yar’Adua, then governor of Katsina State and the president’s man for the job, was said to be stricken in a hospital in Germany. From the podium, Obasanjo dialled before bellowing, “Umoru, are you dead?!” It was obviously not a question for a dead man.

Yar’Adua was mercifully alive. He returned in time to be announced winner of a presidential election in 2007 widely described as “a charade”. His tenure was dogged by concerns about ill-health until his death in May 2010.

Presidential infirmity was not unknown to Nigeria.

Ibrahim Babangida was only 46 when he was flown out of the country for medical attention in 1986. The cause, Nigerians were informed, was “Radiculopathy”, a multi-syllabic tongue-twister that sent many newsrooms consulting diagnostic standard manuals.

In November 2009, President Yar’Adua required overseas hospitalization for “Acute Pericarditis.”

In the first 46 months of his first term as civilian president from 2015 to 2019, Muhammadu Buhari spent 407 days outside Nigeria, with about 242 days or nearly 60% of that devoted to health tourism overseas. He was 72 when he was inaugurated as civilian president, an age at which infirmity is not unknown in the ordinary course of human events.

Four things emerge from these instances. First, the wellbeing of a president is a legitimate matter of public and civic concern.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Second, like all human beings, Presidents can and do from time to time take ill. Babangida and Yar’Adua were much younger than President Tinubu is today, whatever his age may be.

Third, there was a time when presidential handlers believed they owed the country the benefit of some disclosure about the wellbeing of the President or lack of it. That, it seems, is history.

Fourth, irrespective of the health status of the president, the country must always avoid a leadership vacuum.

The twin crises of power and succession that accompanied the final months of the Umaru Musa Yar’Adua presidency brought this last point home with urgency.

In response, the National Assembly enacted a constitutional amendment designed to keep the country running when a president needs to take time off for running repairs. All it requires is for the president to temporarily transfer power to his Vice and notify the National Assembly appropriately.

On-going concerns about the health status of the incumbent suggest a presidency deeply enamoured of déjà vu or, as the Punch newspaper says, invested in treating constitutional provisions as an “ornamental” inconvenience.

In office for 41 months so far, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has spent over 270 days (about 22%) outside the country, including over 100 days spent on 13 different trips of varying descriptions to France alone. The reason for the frequency of his visits to France is credibly suspected to be medical.

Rather than a temporary transfer of power as the constitution allows, it seems he may prefer instead to outsource it. To whom is not clear, but examples from other places could help.

In a study published in 1999, Herbert Abrams, writing about the United States, recounts that “Presidential infirmity, accompanied by a failure to fully inform the public, has been stamped indelibly on our history during the past two hundred years. Fourteen of the eighteen American presidents in the twentieth century had significant illnesses while in office….that were either concealed from the American people or underreported.”

Take for instance the case of Dr. Woodrow Wilson, the Nobel Prize-winning 28th president, who took the United States through the First World War and inspired the League of Nations. Returning home from Europe in July 1919 from signing the Treaty of Versailles which ended World War 1, Wilson preoccupied himself with the ultimately futile effort to persuade his country into the League.

In the middle of this effort, on October 2, 1919, President Wilson suffered a stroke. According to medical records released only in 1991, the stroke was so massive that it would have been “impossible for him ever to achieve more than a minimal state of recovery.”

Yet, as narrated by Christopher Andrew in his 1995 history of U.S. secret intelligence, For the President’s Eyes Only, Wilson’s second wife (the first died in 1914), Edith Galt, helped to “suppress accurate information about his health and to ensure that he continued as president for the remainder of his second term” until 1921.

On the other side of the Atlantic, the health of President Wilson’s contemporary and ideological adversary, Vladimir Ilich Lenin, was the subject of equally intense scheming between a shrewd wife and ruthless usurper. In 1922, Lenin elevated Josef Stalin to the position of General Secretary of the Central Committee of the Communist Party with sweeping powers over party matters. Shortly thereafter, Stalin drew Lenin’s ire when he (and another senior Central Committee member also from Georgia, Sergo Ordzonikidze) annexed Georgia.

Ill-health stayed the hand of an angry Lenin who was struck down by a massive stroke in December 1922. To preserve the life of the Party’s greatest asset, the Politburo under Stalin’s influence restricted Lenin to working for a mere 10 minutes daily. Upon learning that Lenin was doing more, Stalin accosted Lenin’s wife, Nadezhda Krupskaya, warning her rather darkly, as recounted by Stalin’s biographer, Simon Sebag Montefiore, that if she did not ensure compliance “the Central Committee would appoint someone else as Lenin’s wife.”

In France, President Georges Pompidou repeatedly denied that he had anything less worrisome than a common cold until his death in office of cancer in 1974.

In 1981, Pompidou’s successor, Valéry Gisgard d’Estaing, lost in a close election to the inscrutable Francois Mitterrand. In the same year, President Mitterrand learnt that he had prostate cancer that had metastasized to the bones. Mitterrand promptly declared this a State Secret. Hiding it even from his wife, he ran for and won a second seven-year term in 1988, promising France that he was in robust health. In his debate with Jacques Chirac in 1988, Mitterrand infamously faced a more formidable challenge from an overwrought bladder in desperate need of relief.

As the Washington Post reported in January 1996, “Mitterrand’s cancer reached such a critical state in late 1994 that he was no longer able to carry out his duties and spent most of his time resting in bed.” The week after Mitterrand’s death in January 1996, his doctor, Claude Gubler, published a book, Le Grand Secret, detailing this grand deception. French authorities promptly banned the book because it allegedly breached medical confidentiality.

Closer home, Tunisia’s founding president for 32 years, Habib Bourgiba, chose to stay in office after being diagnosed with arteriosclerosis in 1983. In November 1987, Bourgiba, already enfeebled by dementia, gave his shocked compatriots a prime-time disquisition on the state of his testicles. His once-loyal prime-minister, General Zine Abdine Ben-Ali mercifully moved to confine Bourgiba under medical detention in the appropriately-named Monastir, where he died in 2000.

When he went on trial in 1994, shortly after his overthrow at the end of 31 years as Malawi’s leader, the court ruled Dr. Hastings Banda physically and mentally unfit to attend his own trial. He had in fact been “senile for years”. Yet, for 31 years until his ouster earlier in the same year, Dr. Banda held Malawians in thrall as the all-knowing Ngwazi. Real power had been outsourced to his “Official Hostess”, Mama Cecilia Kadzamira and her uncle, John Tembo.

In Malawi also, a dead president was wilfully mis-represented as merely unwell. After he died on 5 April 2012, Malawi’s presidency contrived to export the dead remains of President Bingu wa Mutharika to South Africa to enable them buy time for an unconstitutional succession by his brother and then foreign minister, Peter Mutharika. They mis-led Malawians with the announcement that the president “had…taken ill and had been flown to South Africa for specialist treatment.”

Whatever the medical dictionaries may say, the lesson of history is quite clear: infirmity can outsource the presidency under cover of “a bodyguard of lies.” Nigeria was supposed to have made this history in 2010, but the lessons do not seem to have been learnt.

A lawyer and a teacher, Odinkalu can be reached at [email protected]

World.title: A Forecast Is Not a Verdict: Why The Economist Misreads 2027  By Kola Alapinni
World.content:
The Economist’s “Nigerians Dislike Their President, But May Re-elect Him Anyway” is a confident piece, and a narrow one. It grants the dislike, then treats it as electorally irrelevant. Incumbency, a split opposition, a Muslim-Muslim ticket, and a public that expects little will, on this reading, carry

President Bola Tinubu to a second term in January 2027. The magazine has described the machine. It has not described the country, and it has promoted a forecast to the status of a verdict.

A forecast is not a verdict. The map of 2023 will not reprint itself. Between now and polling day a week is a long time in politics, and it is not yet Uhuru for anyone who thinks the result has already been written. What follows is a reply to the claims on which the piece actually rests.

The opposition is divided. That is not a law.

The Economist builds its path to re-election on the failure of Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi to form a single ticket, and on the African Democratic Congress and the Nigeria Democratic Congress still negotiating with themselves. That split was decisive in 2023. It is not an immutable rule for 2027. The magazine records a present fact and files it as a future constant.

What has changed is the cost of vanity. A failure to unite may again hand the incumbent a plurality. That remains the opposition’s choice, and its risk. It should not be written up in London as a structural guarantee. The Economist’s error is to treat the absence of a coalition today as proof that none can be punished into existence by January. Coalitions in Nigeria have been made, and unmade, in less time than remains. It is not yet Uhuru for a divided opposition either. A week is a long time in politics, and several

months is longer.

Religion will not hold the North, and it will not hold the Middle Belt.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The piece argues that a Muslim-Muslim ticket still insulates the President where his party has traditionally done well, and that northern voters may overlook the record because they already expect little from government. Its own reporting contradicts the insulation. SBM Intelligence, which the magazine cites, finds him behind both Peter Obi and Atiku Abubakar in Borno, a state he carried with about 54 per cent in 2023. Residents of Maiduguri told the same reporters they are prepared to answer at the ballot.

Low expectations are not consent. The Economist notes the crack and then steps over it.

The larger miss is the Middle Belt, which the religious thesis cannot reach.

Plateau, Benue, and the wider belt are not the core North. In 2023 Benue was a knife-edge: 310,468 votes to Peter Obi’s 308,372. Plateau and much of the belt broke the other way. Since then, the raids have not stopped.

Farming communities in Barkin Ladi, Bokkos and Mangu have buried miners, women, pastors, and villagers through 2026. In Benue, police officers have been killed in Logo, and in early October the abduction of mourners brought protesters onto the highway. Official claims of rescues and fewer incidents in some places do not survive the burial. A magazine that explains this electorate by religion, or by cynicism, has not been there.

Where those voters can reach a polling unit, the likely reaction is punitive.

Where they have fled, the vote is suppressed. Both outcomes follow from the security failure The Economist folds into “low expectations.”

Party promises of 620,000 votes in Benue, or a million, are machine targets. They are not evidence that the villages have consented. Those pledges can still be overtaken by events. A week is a long time in politics.

Cynicism is not the shield the magazine thinks it is.

The central assertion is that disappointment will depress turnout and favour the status quo: that few will use the ballot to express it. That misreads anger as apathy. Across cities, and in rural clusters that have lost planting seasons, the mood is closer to self-defence than to resignation. SBM Intelligence counted 7,825 abductions and 1,142 deaths in captivity between July 2025 and June 2026. Around

Independence, gunmen took passengers on the Owerri–Onitsha Road, including members of the National Youth Service

Corps, while the President’s address dwelt on reform. A public living with that record is not a public that has priced disappointment in and moved on.

The same error covers power. The President asked for time on a promise that electricity would improve. Households and workshops are still on generators, or in the dark. The official residence has been given another arrangement. The Aso Rock solar mini-grid was funded with ₦10 billion in the 2025 budget and ₦7 billion in the 2026 budget, about ₦17 billion, so that

the Villa can leave the national grid. Officials have called the Villa’s annual power bill, put at about ₦47 billion, unsustainable. Seventeen billion naira has been found to buy the Presidency out of the failure. The country has been left to fend for itself. The Economist’s cynicism thesis has no room for this. A voter who can see the Villa lit, and the street dark, is not a voter who expects nothing. He is a voter who has been shown the order of priority.

I have said that if the President wants another term, he does not need to beg for it. Let the work speak. If he does not provide power, he should not be voted for. That is the test the magazine never sets.

Where The Economist is less wrong

The magazine is on firmer ground when it says incumbents win with machinery and cash, and that unpopularity alone has not been enough to remove them. Vote buying has moved off the polling unit. The INEC chairman, Joash Amupitan, has named insecurity and vote buying as the Commission’s two leading worries for 2027. A household without power, or without a harvest, is a cheaper vote. The ruling party can put money where the opposition can put a statement. Allegations around service-wide votes and gubernatorial deductions should remain allegations until proved. The asymmetry does not depend on them. It didn’t depend on them in the recent Osun State elections. That, is an argument about the field, not about affection.

The Economist slides from one to the other. Influence over logistics and security agencies is a real risk. It is not proof that INEC will write a result, and the piece should not be read as if capture were already the finding. (At least, we can presume that INEC’s computers and servers will not suffer a ‘technical glitch’ on this occasion). An election held where armed groups control the road, and where one party can fund the vote, is simply not the free test that “let the work speak” assumes. Even that advantage is not

Uhuru. Money and machinery have been overtaken before, when the week before polling rearranged the ground.

The verdict the piece withholds The Economist is wrong to treat cynicism, fragmentation, and a religious ticket as insulation. It is less wrong about the machine. Incumbency is an advantage. It is not a London consultancy’s to award, and it is not a substitute

for consent.

A forecast that the disliked incumbent may survive is a statement about cash, split votes, and unsafe roads. It is not a statement that the record has been accepted. Seventeen billion naira to take the Villa off the grid, a Middle Belt still burying its dead, and a federal highway that endangers Corp members and the general populace are already answers. If the opposition stays split, incumbency does not need public affection. The verdict still belongs to the people only to the extent that they can reach a polling unit and refuse the price of the vote. Or accept the gratification and vote the other way.

Neither camp should read this as arrival. A week is a long time in politics. It is not yet Uhuru. The magazine has written the ending before the interval.

That is the distinction it collapses. A forecast is not a verdict.

*Kola Alapinni is an international human rights lawyer and US Secretary of State Awardee on International

Religious Freedom.

World.title: TMG vs TMS: The Communication Dilemma Over Tinubu’s Future By Yushau A. Shuaib
World.content:
I was reluctant to make this disclosure. For weeks, I weighed silence against the obligation to be transparent. In the end, a video forced the matter: footage of my brotherly friend, Omoyele Sowore, leading a “Tinubu Must Go” procession. It reminded me that this dilemma has a public dimension I can no longer keep to myself.

Let me begin with context. Sowore and I have maintained a cordial relationship despite our different orientations — his rooted in activist journalism, mine in strategic communication. When I was removed from federal public service after my well-documented altercation with then Finance Minister Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Sowore used his platform, energy, and resources to defend me at a time when few were willing to be publicly associated with the controversy. That kind of solidarity is hard to forget.

When I later served as a communications consultant to a sensitive office and our media placements appeared on Sahara Reporters, which he still publishes, a misunderstanding followed. During my transit in New York on my way to Las Vegas, he declined to see me, suspecting, I believe, that I had come to compromise his editorial independence on behalf of the then National Security Adviser, Colonel Sambo Dasuki. He treated the man the same way.

Ironically, he and Dasuki later found common ground in a DSS detention cell, and were released the same day. I have never sought a favour from Sowore that he refused, except for one occasion when he confronted me over an article supporting Okonjo Iweala’s WTO aspiration. I respected his candour then, as I do now.

I offer this context not to demonstrate proximity to power on either side, but because the dilemma I am about to describe only makes sense against this background.

A few weeks ago, Kashifu Inuwa — a highly respected technocrat from the North and a strong supporter of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the First Lady, Remi Tinubu — invited me to his office. Known nationwide for championing digital literacy and transformation that has empowered training centres and young people, Kashifu came straight to the point: he wanted my professional guidance in building a movement.

Before I could respond, he named it: “Tinubu Must Stay — for Continuity, Stability and Prosperity.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

I asked why the framing was not simply “Tinubu Should Stay.” His explanation was strategic, not sentimental. The movement was intended as a counter-narrative to the “Tinubu Must Go” campaign, which he believed had gained momentum from northern opposition quarters aligned with former Vice President Atiku Abubakar. He needed a response that matched the opposition’s framing without conceding its terms.

He asked me to commit within 24 hours. I requested more time, but he held firm. I told him I would return with an assessment. The question was not whether I supported the President. The question was whether I could support a campaign on terms that were professionally defensible.

I asked my team to run a perception index and sentiment analysis on recent campaigns around the President. Using PRrev — PRNigeria’s cross-platform media monitoring software supported by NITDA — the findings were sobering. Negative sentiment, especially on social media, was not just high; it showed a level of public disaffection that no honest communicator could mask with slogans or rallies.

I then consulted a cohort of young communicators — professionals in their late twenties and early thirties, from different regions and with no political affiliations. I asked if they would support the Tinubu Must Stay campaign. Their initial response was lukewarm. But I pressed further. I asked them to independently assess the administration’s verifiable achievements against the weight of public grievance. What they brought back was more instructive than I anticipated.

They found that Tinubu facilitated the takeoff of new medical universities — not only in the South, but also in Tsafe and Funtua in the North — institutions many Nigerians hardly know exist. They noted hundreds of housing units commissioned across northern states and a marked rise in federation account allocations to states and local governments, funds that previous administrations often diverted into federal intervention schemes like PTF, DFRRI and SURE P. Security improvements were equally notable: new military divisions, acquisition of sophisticated armaments, and better personnel remuneration.

These were concrete, documented, verifiable facts that had not penetrated public consciousness because communication around them had been, to put it mildly, inadequate — buried in technical statistics and figures that ordinary citizens rarely engage with.

Three of the young communicators who had been most reluctant became the most thorough in their research. By the end of the exercise, they joined the movement voluntarily, without inducement. To me, that was more significant than any polling data. It suggested that the deficit was not in the administration’s record — it was in the communication of that record.

When I returned to Kashifu, I recommended that the campaign be strictly evidence-based: facts, data, documented outcomes, and verifiable comparisons. I also cautioned against attacks on opposition personalities and confrontational posturing toward anti-government movements. No hired crowds. No orchestrated demonstrations. No manufactured street energy. No faking.

The forum would contribute intellectual rigour to the national conversation, not spectacle. A communication campaign built on verifiable facts does not need to shout down its critics. It simply needs to be heard.

Then, as I finalised my position, Sowore’s video emerged. My brotherly friend — the man who stood with me when others did not — was now supporting the very movement my professional guidance was retained to counter. I do not know whether he will formally align with the Atiku Abubakar camp, based on endorsements from initial conveners in the North.

As a student and practitioner of public relations, I believe the battle for public opinion in the months ahead will not be won by the side that shouts loudest, marches furthest, or commands the most digital noise. It will be won by the side that builds the most credible narrative around verifiable reality.

If the administration’s achievements are as substantial as the data suggest, then failing to communicate them is a failure of professional execution—not a failure of governance. And that failure can be corrected.

Yushau A. Shuaib is the author of “An Encounter with the Spymaster” and “NIPSS: MNI Versus MNIPR- Tackling Institutional Bullying.” [email protected]

World.title: PDP speaks on candidates’ omission from INEC’s list, says it will be addressed
World.content:
The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) says it is engaging with the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to resolve the omission of some of its candidates from the commission’s final list for the 2027 governorship elections.

The party said its leadership, led by Abdulrahman Mohammed, was treating the development seriously and seeking an amicable resolution in line with the law and established electoral guidelines.

The PDP’s National Publicity Secretary, Jungudo Mohammed, stated this in a statement on Sunday.

“The party wishes to assure all affected candidates, members and supporters that it is already engaging with INEC to address the issues responsible for the omissions, with a view to securing an amicable resolution in accordance with the law and established electoral guidelines,” he said.

Mr Mohammed urged the affected candidates, members and supporters to remain calm and exercise patience while the party engages with the electoral commission.

He also cautioned them against actions or statements that could undermine the ongoing discussions.

The PDP reiterated its commitment to ensuring that all legitimate concerns arising from the omissions were addressed.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Consequently, the party calls on all affected candidates, members and supporters to remain calm, exercise patience and refrain from actions or statements capable of undermining the ongoing engagements with the commission,” the statement added.

INEC’s final list of candidates for the 2027 governorship elections, published on Saturday, did not include PDP candidates in Ogun and Gombe states.

The commission omitted the party’s governorship candidates in the two states, Oladipupo Adebutu and Isa Pantami, respectively, as well as their running mates. INEC listed 13 candidates for Ogun and 16 for Gombe, but neither list included a PDP candidate.

The omissions come amid disputes over the candidates’ nomination processes and questions about compliance with the Electoral Act 2026 provisions governing political party membership registers and participation in primaries.

On 24 September, the Supreme Court restored the Electoral Act provision requiring political parties to use membership registers submitted to INEC within the stipulated period when conducting primaries. The provisions also restrict participation in party primaries to members whose names appear on the relevant registers.

Mr Pantami’s omission followed a separate legal dispute over his nomination. The Federal High Court in Gombe had nullified his initial emergence as the PDP governorship candidate and ordered a fresh primary, which he won on 29 September.

In Ogun, Mr Adebutu’s omission came amid questions raised by groups over whether his name appeared on the PDP membership register submitted to INEC. The Ogun PDP rejected the concerns, insisting that Mr Adebutu had completed the required membership registration procedures.

INEC has not explained the omissions in the published lists. The affected candidates’ camps have, however, expressed confidence that the issues can be resolved through engagements with the electoral commission and the relevant legal processes.

World.title: Sanwo-Olu targets 3,000MW electricity supply for Lagos by March 2027
World.content:
Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu says his administration plans to increase electricity supply to the state to more than 3,000 megawatts (MW) by March 2027, from the current level of less than 1,000 megawatts.

In a post on X on Sunday, Mr Sanwo-Olu announced the target on Saturday at the fourth Lagos Business School Africa Energy Conference 2026 in Lekki, Lagos. He was represented by his deputy, Obafemi Hamzat.

He said the state planned to add about 2,000MW through a combination of electricity from the national grid, independent power projects, energy hubs, power barges, energy traders and embedded generation.

Mr Sanwo-Olu stated that the target would depend on improvements in generation, transmission and distribution, as well as a reliable supply of gas to power plants and wider access to electricity meters.

The government also plans to upgrade substations and distribution networks, expand metering and use digital technology to monitor electricity supply and improve accountability in the market.

The proposed expansion comes as Lagos assumes greater responsibility for regulating its electricity market following reforms introduced by the federal government.

In December 2024, the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC) transferred regulatory oversight of intrastate electricity activities in Lagos to the Lagos State Electricity Regulatory Commission (LASERC), in line with the Electricity Act 2023.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Lagos State Electricity Law 2024 provides the legal framework for electricity generation, transmission, distribution, supply and trading within the state.

LASERC is responsible for regulating the market and licensing operators.

Mr Sanwo-Olu said the state was also working to establish clearer contractual obligations and improve coordination among electricity market operators and regulators to attract private investment.

On technology, he spotlighted plans to deploy Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems, Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) and the Lagos Electricity Intelligence Platform. The systems are expected to improve monitoring, transparency and accountability across the electricity market.

The governor also cited progress in the state’s renewable energy programme, saying about 42,000 of the 50,000 streetlights earmarked for solarisation had been completed.

He noted that solar installations had also been carried out in 175 public schools, with work ongoing in another 100.

He urged investors, financial institutions, energy companies and development partners to support the plan, describing reliable electricity as essential to industrial growth, job creation and business competitiveness.

Mr Sanwo-Olu said the priority was to turn the plan into measurable results and build a sustainable electricity market in Lagos.

The conference was held under the theme, “Securing Nigeria’s Energy Future: Policy Reform, Capital Mobilisation, and Pathways to a Sustainable Power and Energy Market.”

World.title: NCDMB, Renaissance train 60 Nigerians in critical oil and gas technical skills
World.content:
The Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB), in collaboration with Renaissance Africa Energy Company Limited, has launched a 12-month training programme at Nigeria Machine Tools Limited, Osogbo, Osun State. The initiative will equip 60 young Nigerians with specialised expertise in oil and gas engineering as well as other critical technical skills, fostering a new generation of industry-ready professionals.

The programme is on the back of the Nigerian Content Human Capacity Development (NC HCD) Training Programme for Renaissance Africa Energy Company Limited’s EPU Phase 2 Gas Development Project. It is designed to equip participants with advanced technical expertise. The curriculum spans engineering design, fitter machining, conventional machine tool operations, programming, computer-aided design (CAD), computer-aided manufacturing (CAM), electrical and mechanical maintenance, and document control.

Structured over 12 months, the programme combines six months of intensive classroom instruction with six months of supervised on-the-job training in reputable companies. Graduates are expected to earn internationally recognised certifications upon completion.

At the official launch held at Nigeria Machine Tools Limited, Osogbo, Osun State, NCDMB’s Director of Capacity Building, Abayomi Bamidele, an engineer, reaffirmed the Board’s commitment to bridging critical technical skills gaps in Nigeria’s oil and gas industry.

Represented by Mr Tare Bufazi, Assistant Manager, Human Capacity Development, Bamidele described the initiative as a strategic intervention to address manpower shortages and prepare Nigerians for meaningful participation across the oil and gas value chain.

“The importance of this programme cannot be overstated,” he noted, revealing that the 60 trainees—comprising 33 graduates and 27 vocational trainees—would undergo specialised training tailored to industry needs. He emphasised that NCDMB’s mission extends beyond promoting local participation to building the technical capabilities required to sustain the sector.

Human capacity development, he stressed, is central to strengthening local content, creating opportunities, and advancing the Federal Government’s industrialization agenda. Bamidele urged participants to approach the programme with discipline and commitment, highlighting that it offers more than certificates—it builds practical competence and professional experience for long-term careers. He also acknowledged the contributions of Renaissance Africa Energy Company Limited, Seflam SGL, and Nigeria Machine Tools, whose collaboration made the initiative possible.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Speaking on behalf of Renaissance Africa Energy Company Limited, Mr Richard Oyiborhor, Interface and Integration Manager for the NLNG Supply Project, reiterated the company’s dedication to nurturing Nigerian talent and strengthening local capabilities. He commended NCDMB’s leadership in advancing Nigerian content and praised the partnership with Seflam SGL and Nigeria Machine Tools as a vital step in developing the nation’s industrial workforce.

Mrs Bisola Agboluaje, Senior Manager, Business Interface at Seflam SGL, congratulated the trainees and traced the programme’s origins to 2024, when NCDMB approved the training plans. She described the initiative as a forward-looking investment in Nigeria’s technical talent pool.

Nigeria Machine Tools’ Chief Operating Officer, Ms Obehi Ojeagha, welcomed the participants and lauded the collaboration. She emphasised the institution’s 46-year legacy in supporting Nigeria’s industrial development and expressed confidence that the trainees would acquire the skills, discipline, and experience needed to contribute meaningfully to the oil and gas sector.

World.title: LAWMA seals over 25 buildings in Lagos waste crackdown
World.content:
The Lagos Waste Management Authority (LAWMA) has sealed more than 25 buildings, including a Mobil filling station, along Ago Palace Way, Okota, Lagos, over alleged environmental violations.

The operation on Sunday involved clearing accumulated refuse from road medians and areas around bridge abutments, where the authority said illegal dumping had become a recurring problem.

LAWMA’s Managing Director, Muyiwa Gbadegesin, led the exercise, which involved compactor trucks, a payloader, tipper trucks and street sweepers.

In a statement posted on X, the authority said some of the sealed premises had illegal stalls on road setbacks or accommodated street traders whose activities contributed to littering and indiscriminate waste disposal.

Some cart pushers were also arrested for alleged illegal dumping. One of them, identified as Shamusi Muritala, reportedly admitted dumping refuse on road medians and told officials he collected up to N5,000 from customers to dispose of their waste.

LAWMA stated that Mr Muritala, who identified himself as being from Katsina State, pleaded for leniency when questioned.

The authority also used the exercise to educate residents and traders on proper waste disposal, urging them to use approved collection channels.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Gbadegesin said LAWMA would enforce the law against illegal street trading and those who patronised traders operating in prohibited locations.

He warned that the activities obstructed movement, undermined public order and contributed to environmental degradation.

Operatives of the Lagos State Environmental and Special Offences Unit, known as the Taskforce, and the Kick Against Indiscipline team supported the operation.

READ ALSO: LAWMA withdraws licences of six waste operators in Lagos

The exercise comes amid complaints about waste collection in the area. In August, The Guardian reported that residents of Ago Palace Way complained of overflowing refuse and delays in evacuation despite paying for collection services.

LAWMA said it would continue waste evacuation and enforcement operations to curb illegal dumping and protect public infrastructure across Lagos.

World.title: ‘We must stick together’ — Haaland after Man City’s win amid financial charges
World.content:
Manchester City’s players celebrate on the pitch after the English Premier League football match between Liverpool and Manchester City at Anfield in Liverpool, north west England on October 11, 2026.
