World.title: From the archive: The songs that all Mexicans magically know
World.content:
I’ve been living in Mexico for a very long time. When I first came, I was barely an adult, and I’ve “grown up” here in the sense that I grew into an adult here. In lots of ways, I feel like Mexico has raised me from the age of 21 on, which I think most of us can agree is the age of just a baby.

I also love karaoke. A lot. I have a pretty average voice but can mostly hit the notes, and that’s enough for me. Really, there are few things more fun than pretending to be a rockstar, and Mexico is where I first honed my rockstar-pretending skills.

It’s at these parties, though, that I remember: actually, I’m not Mexican.

What makes this obvious? Song choices, mostly. And also this sad fact: Everyone seems to know every single word to lots of songs I’ve never heard in my life. They belt them out with the passion and pain of recently jilted lovers while I stand awkwardly by.

How and when did they learn them? Is there a secret Mexican kids club where they learn all the mariachi classics in elementary school?

Basically, the answer is yes, there is. Really, though, it’s mostly just from them listening to the music their parents listened to growing up. Remember too that children are included at parties here just as much as adults. They might be running around and playing, but Juan Gabriel’s music is subliminally making its way to their memory centers while they do.

I did not grow up with Mexican parents, so I’m still playing catch-up. It’s hard not to feel second-rate at these moments. I mean, what are the songs that Americans universally know? “She’ll Be Comin’ Round the Mountain?” Give me a break.

I know plenty of songs in Spanish, but I really just want to sing “I Want to Break Free” and other favorites at karaoke that fall within my limited voice range. If only I could comfortably hit Shakira’s high notes!

At least I can do fellow Tejana Selena’s Como la Flor, right? Alas, I am still far behind. Luckily, I am surrounded by Mexicans who can help me learn them, or at the very least what they are.

Some are ballads, and some are pop hits. But they all seem to have a magical effect on all Mexicans’ party time. They’re keys that unlock something inside the Mexican psyche, making them close their eyes, tilt their heads back, and position their hands in a way that can only be described as a gesture of anguish born from a deep well of heartbreak and passion.

So I have gone on a deep well expedition for you all, my friends, and have returned! Here are some of the songs that Mexicans know — completely, by heart — and love.

‘El Rey’ by Vicente Fernández

Vicente Fernández - El Rey (En Vivo)

Watch this video on YouTube

You might actually recognize this song, or at least some parts.

“Con dinero y sin dinero, hago siempre lo que quiero…” and “Llorar, y llorar…” are two of its most recognizable lines.



Vicente Fernández, like many of the great Mexican acts of the 20th century, had a real rags to riches story. Born in Jalisco, he spent his teenage years doing odd jobs, including working as a cashier at an uncle’s restaurant. Eventually, he started singing at restaurants and weddings, and the rest is history.

‘ Rata de Dos Patas’ by Paquita la del Barrio

Paquita la del Barrio - Rata De Dos Patas (En Vivo)

Watch this video on YouTube





Now, this song has some seriously sick burns. Here’s the chorus: “Rata de dos patas / Te estoy hablando a ti / Porque un bicho rastrero / Aún siendo el más maldito / Comparado contigo / Se queda muy chiquito.”

“Two-legged rat / I’m talking to you / Because a creeping bug / Even the worst kind, Compared to you / Is nothing.”

As you might guess, Paquita is known for her fearless teasing of, and anger at, Mexican misogyny. “¿Me estás oyendo, inútil?” — “Do you hear me, you good-for-nothing? — often makes its way into her live performances, and honestly, who can get enough of it? Someone’s got to stand up to all those cheating machistas!

‘Bésame Mucho’ by Consuelo Velázquez

Consuelo Velazquez — Besame Mucho

Watch this video on YouTube

You’ve probably heard this song before — it seems every artist has a version of it.

This is a recording of the original composer, who, if Wikipedia is to be believed, had never been kissed when she wrote this song at the age of 16. Check out this video to see her chops on the piano. Wow!

‘Amor Eterno’ by Juan Gabriel

Juan Gabriel - Amor Eterno (En Vivo [Desde el Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes])

Watch this video on YouTube

Juan Gabriel, like many of the artists mentioned, is a Mexican institution. He sang passionately and often, accompanied by a full orchestra and mariachi singers.

I’m almost certain that most Mexicans know every single word to every one of his songs, but have not proved this scientifically.

‘El Triste’ by José José

José José - El Triste en vivo

Watch this video on YouTube

This is another one of those singers whose every song has essentially been memorized by a sizable portion of the population. Rumor has it that his singing voice completely left him after years of drinking.

Thankfully, he recorded quite a bit before that point.

‘Mis Ojos Lloran por Ti’ by Big Boy

Mis Ojos Lloran Por Ti

Watch this video on YouTube

This is a more contemporary song than the ones above, and it is a fun one! Whoever can sing this one at karaoke, in fact, pretty much wins the night.

Why? There’s a lot of really fast rapping woven throughout the song, and it is a major challenge.

‘Que Bello’ by Sonora Dinamita

La Sonora Dinamita - Que Bello (letra)

Watch this video on YouTube

This song cracks me up, and it’s one that I actually know! Sometimes I try to sing it at karaoke, but usually start laughing when I hear a line like “Pero me arrepiento, en el piso o donde sea y tómame” — “But I change my mind, on the floor or wherever, take me.”

Um, I’m sorry, a cold, hard floor? When there’s a nice, comfy bed available? Who are these people? In any case, it’s a fun little cumbia and a major classic.

‘Si No Te Hubieras Ido’ by Marco Antonio Solís

Marco Antonio Solís - Si No Te Hubieras Ido | Lyric Video

Watch this video on YouTube

This is the newest song on the list, having come out in 1999, the year I graduated high school. It’s a beautiful and heartbreaking ballad, with one of my favorite lines of any song: “El frío de mi cuerpo pregunta por ti.” “The cold of my body asks for you.”

See? Super romantic.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: An unauthorized police academy stirs a security row with US as triple storm threat keeps coasts on alert
World.content:
Listen to this article

Storms swirled around and within Mexico this week as a political misstep by Governor Mauricio Kuri in Querétaro became a national controversy.

Simon, currently located off the Pacific coast of Jalisco and Colima, is now a Category 4 hurricane and will make landfall this weekend. Hurricane Isaias swept past the Yucatán Peninsula and landed near Destin, Florida, on Friday evening. Far out in the Pacific, Tropical Storm Rachel, which briefly reached hurricane strength, stayed clear of the Mexican coastline on Saturday but was expected to weaken and send its remnants toward Baja California and the U.S. Southwest.

On land, President Claudia Sheinbaum reacted swiftly to the surprise inauguration in Querétaro of a binational security institution that received direct support from the United States. According to the federal government, the project was never disclosed to or authorized by the corresponding Mexican authorities.

In Nayarit, searching mothers helped authorities uncover an alleged “extermination center” near Tepic, where investigators found a makeshift burner and a pit containing the remains of recently cremated bodies. Officials haven’t said how many people died or tied the site to a criminal group. The discovery underscored Mexico’s disappearance crisis, with more than 130,000 people registered as missing.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Police academy controversy

Sheinbaum opened the week by questioning an “International Police Training Academy” in central Mexico, whose cornerstone Gov. Mauricio Kuri and U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson laid Oct. 2. She said such a project can’t exist without federal authorization and asked why the military, the Security Cabinet and the Foreign Ministry weren’t invited.

A leaked letter then showed Kuri had told Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco only that Johnson would visit Querétaro, calling the interactions ceremonial and never mentioning the academy. The Foreign Affairs Ministry replied that any security training project with a foreign government needs prior approval from the High-Level Security Group (GANSEG), which hadn’t been granted. It also offered to help Querétaro seek it.

On Tuesday, Sheinbaum said federal officials had approved nine Querétaro–U.S. cooperation projects since December 2021, but not this one. She cited the state’s security minister, who said the facility would bring specialized training from U.S. agencies. Johnson had called it a “State Interdiction Academy” and noted more than US $10 million in U.S. support for Querétaro police over the past decade. The episode drew parallels to April’s alleged CIA involvement in a Chihuahua drug lab raid. Both states are governed by the opposition National Action Party (PAN).

On Thursday, Sheinbaum met with U.S. business leaders at the National Palace, with Johnson in attendance, but said security would be handled separately. She said Johnson had agreed to meet Velasco soon, and Security Minister Omar García Harfuch told legislators that bilateral cooperation is subject to Mexican law.

Hurricane Simon threatens Jalisco and Colima

Simon strengthened into a Category 4 hurricane on Saturday morning, with sustained winds of 230 km/h (145 mph). The U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC) said the eye could pass near or over Mexico’s west-central coast late Saturday or Sunday, though its track remained uncertain. Civil Protection chief Laura Velázquez said the impact zone could be Cihuatlán, La Huerta, Tomatlán, Cabo Corrientes or Puerto Vallarta in Jalisco, or Manzanillo, Colima.

A hurricane warning covers Punta San Telmo, Michoacán, to Punta Mita, Nayarit. Rainfall could reach 20 to 38 centimeters, with isolated totals of 64 centimeters. Authorities set up command centers in Puerto Vallarta, Cihuatlán and Manzanillo, began evacuations in the flood-prone Jalisco community of El Rebalse and suspended classes in 22 Jalisco municipalities Friday and Monday. Simon could be the second hurricane to make landfall in Mexico this Pacific season, after Polo.

On the Atlantic side, Isaias became the season’s first hurricane Wednesday night, the latest first hurricane in the 60-year modern era. It was forecast to make U.S. landfall Friday evening, with no Mexico landfall expected, though it dumped heavy rain on the Gulf coast and Yucatán Peninsula states. It followed Mexico’s first hurricane-free Atlantic September since 1994, a contrast with a Pacific that had produced nine hurricanes by Wednesday. Experts point to a “super” El Niño, which warms Pacific waters and raises wind shear in the Atlantic.

Sheinbaum presents presidential decrees regarding nationality and social media

On Wednesday, Sheinbaum signed a decree formalizing a constitutional reform that requires exclusive Mexican nationality for presidential, gubernatorial and Mexico City mayoral candidates. The ban takes effect from 2028, after gubernatorial elections in 17 states next June. Citizens Movement (MC) Sen. Luis Donaldo Colosio Riojas criticized the reform for creating “two categories of Mexicans.”

On Friday, after a fatal machete attack at a Torreón school, the government presented a decree on “safe digital environments” for minors. It bars platforms from showing or recommending content that promotes hate speech, violent extremism, sexual exploitation, suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, cyberbullying and illegal conduct. Sheinbaum said it would be published in the official gazette next Tuesday or Wednesday after legal review to ensure it doesn’t exceed the executive branch’s authority.

Border deployment and gunfire incident

Mexico sent 500 Army and National Guard troops to the Tamaulipas border after U.S. Coast Guard personnel were fired upon from the Mexican side Sept. 26 and returned fire. The U.S. ordered 500 soldiers to the Texas side.

The Foreign Affairs and Defense ministries described the twin deployments as part of a “Concurrent Operation,” backed by two UH-60 helicopters, drones and anti-drone equipment in five Tamaulipas municipalities. The Navy is also participating through “Operation Saber.” No injuries or damage were reported in the shooting.

Mazatlán gets elite reinforcements as violence persists

The federal government formed a Special Operations Group of 29 Defense Ministry soldiers to work within Mazatlán’s municipal police after repeated troop deployments failed to stem the violence. The unit follows a wave of homicides, armed attacks and explosive assaults that led officials to urge caution between 3 and 10 p.m. The city also bought 50 bicycles for soldiers and National Guard members.

Then came Thursday’s shooting at El Castillo prison, which killed nine inmates and a 2-year-old boy and injured 16 prisoners. Alleged Sinaloa Cartel figure “El Owen” was reportedly among the dead. Sheinbaum said the Security Cabinet is working with interim Sinaloa Governor Graciela Domínguez to strengthen the state’s prisons.

Inflation edges up

Annual headline inflation rose to 3.45% in September from 3.26%, the highest since May but well below March’s 4.59% peak. Core inflation eased to 3.75% from 3.88%. Fruit and vegetable prices jumped 8.78% annually, while meat prices fell 4.46%. The Bank of Mexico held its benchmark rate at 6.50% two weeks ago and meets again Nov. 5.

Investment news

Fixed capital investment grew 6% annually in July, the fastest pace in two years, driven by construction. Private sector investment growth hit a 30-month high, though the total remains 2.35% below its July 2024 record. Spending on Mexican-made machinery and equipment fell 8% from January to July, while imported equipment rose 3.5%.

In Nuevo León, Gov. Samuel García announced US $600 million for industrial infrastructure, mainly data centers in Apodaca and Pesquería. That brings 2026 foreign investment in the state to $136.6 billion by his count.

Bárcena says ‘not yet’ to fracking in Mexico

On Tuesday, Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena told lawmakers the conditions for fracking “do not exist” and that Sheinbaum hasn’t authorized pilot tests. Only testing for deep saline water has been approved. Government scientists identified the Sabinas-Burro-Picachos basin as the only viable site, but nonprofit CartoCrítica says all the fresh water needed there would come from basins lacking available supply.

4 economy headlines to know

Mexico’s trade surplus with the U.S. rose 21.2% to US $155.87 billion from January to August, as exports hit a record $419.34 billion. Only Vietnam posted a larger surplus. The government faces a tough negotiating backdrop, with the U.S. having declined to renew the USMCA trade agreement in its current form, in part due to its deficit with Mexico, which the Trump administration views as an unacceptable imbalance.

The International Monetary Fund raised its growth forecasts to 1.5% for 2026 and 1.8% for 2027, citing a strong second quarter, but urged fiscal consolidation.

Auto parts output hit a record US $10.85 billion in July, up 7.15%. Vehicle production, however, fell 15.1% in September, its steepest drop since 2021, and car exports declined 11.85%.

Finally, a Citi survey of Mexico-based analysts sees the peso at 18 per dollar at the end of 2026 and 18.50 at the end of 2027, after the currency fell 6% in September.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Say cheese: A guide to 5 iconic Mexican quesos and the regions that produce them
World.content:
In Mexico, an endless debate spills across social media and enlists everyone from linguists and historians to cooks and passionate eaters: What belongs in a quesadilla? While cheese is an optional topping for many Mexican dishes — from tacos and tortas to chilaquiles and sopes — there is one contentious item that, depending on who you ask, is non-negotiable.

Now, we are not here to solve the great quesadilla debate, but unveiling the passion behind it shows just how central cheese is to Mexican gastronomy. From north to south, every region has crafted its own variety of queso tailored to its local heritage. Here are five of Mexico’s most iconic cheeses:

Queso Oaxaca (or quesillo)

The cheese at the very heart of the debate — and a cornerstone of Mexican street food — is queso Oaxaca, locally known as quesillo. It is celebrated for its soft, buttery texture and its exceptional meltability over high heat, whether tucked into a sope, folded inside a quesadilla or pressed into a torta.

What differentiates quesillo from other cheeses is its distinct curdling method: It is hand-stretched into long, milky strands and wound into a ribboned ball. Achieving this pliable texture relies on warm preparation techniques that keep the cheese flexible enough to stretch and interlace without breaking.

Quesillo is indispensable in Mexican households as it can turn a simple tortilla (corn or flour) into a quick homemade quesadilla for dinner, transform refried beans and bread into crispy, freshly baked molletes, or serve as a quick, savory snack eaten straight from the fridge.

Originally from: Oaxaca

Queso de cincho

Loosely translated as “cinch cheese,” queso de cincho originates in the central state of Morelos and the southwestern state of Guerrero. Its name refers to the rigid mold used during pressing, which is bound tightly with woven ixtle palm fibers (the same durable rope material used in traditional horse tack and saddlery).

Also known as queso prensado estilo Guerrero, this firm, aged cheese carries a strong aroma and is typically rubbed with a paste of dried guajillo chiles. While frequently crumbled over enchiladas or chilaquiles, one of its most traditional preparations is simmered directly in salsa as a guisado. Thanks to its dense consistency and high protein content, it serves as a substantial centerpiece. Better yet, its low moisture content allows it to age naturally at room temperature for up to a year without spoiling.

Originally from: Guerrero and Morelos

Queso asadero

Just like quesillo, queso asadero is popular due to its creamy, melty texture and the gastronomic possibilities it offers. This type of cheese has similar uses to queso Oaxaca; it can be used in quesadillas, and it is common at northern cookouts, paired with a great steak. If you’ve been to one of those, the name “asadero” might sound familiar — it comes from the word asado (grilled), a clue on how to enjoy this cheese.

Originally from: Chihuahua

Queso fresco

View this post on Instagram A post shared by 𝑪𝒂𝒔𝒂𝒏𝒅𝒓𝒂 𝑺𝒂𝒍𝒊𝒏𝒂𝒔 🤠🌵 (@yo_soy_casandra)

Queso fresco is a crumbly, soft cheese that is high in moisture and protein. Due to its short aging process (which is where the name fresco — or fresh — comes from), it is difficult to keep for long periods. It must always be kept refrigerated and consumed within approximately two weeks.

Regarding its preparation and curdling, queso fresco is quite versatile, as it can be made with cow’s milk, goat’s milk or a blend of both. In contrast to meltable cheeses, queso fresco does not work as a quesadilla filling, but it is the perfect topping for side dishes, whether sprinkled over a salad, street corn or refried beans.

Originally from: Chihuahua

Queso Menonita

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ¡ah Chihuahua! (@ahchihuahua)

Last but not least is Mennonite cheese, a famous variety that also comes from the northern region of the country. As its name reveals, it originates from a specific community: the Mennonites. Groups of Mennonite immigrants arrived in Mexico during the 1920s, and their cattle-ranching techniques thrived in the north.

Mennonite communities settled mainly in the drylands of Chihuahua and relied on dairy products, especially cheese, for sustenance. Nowadays — although the name remains — this smooth, buttery cheese is no longer exclusively made by Mennonite communities. You can find it melting inside chiles rellenos, on Mennonite-style pizzas or in choriqueso (a dish of melted cheese combined with seasoned chorizo).

Originally from: Chihuahua

Cheese has been a companion to Mexican cuisine for centuries. One key to understanding its strong northern presence is the geographic distribution of agriculture and livestock in Mexico. As you travel from south to north, the climate becomes drier, making the land better suited for cattle ranching than crop cultivation.

It is no surprise, then, that cheese became a fundamental pillar of northern Mexico’s economy and gastronomy.

After all, what would a northern carne asada be without quesadillas (con queso)?

Lydia Leija is a linguist, journalist and visual storyteller. She has directed three feature films, and her audiovisual work has been featured in national and international media. She’s been part of National Geographic, Muy Interesante and Cosmopolitan.

World.title: Does having dual citizenship have any downsides?
World.content:
In 2016, my wife and I embarked on a road trip together across central Mexico — starting on Jalisco’s Pacific Coast and, over a month later, ending up on the Gulf Coast of Veracruz with innumerable side quests along the way in Michoacán, Guanajuato, Querétaro, Hidalgo, Mexico City, Estado de México and Puebla.

It wasn’t our first time in Mexico. We had, after all, spent our lifetimes visiting our extended families in Mexico as the children of immigrants.

But now we were able to see it on our own terms, as independent adults with our own incomes to spend and itineraries to plan. We rediscovered the country through our own eyes.

That summer, we had a revelation: We wanted to live in Mexico.

Three years later, in 2019, we prepared a similar trek around the southern part of the country, beginning in Oaxaca’s capital, then winding our way through mountain towns en route to the coast on a colectivo. Months prior, we had left our jobs as high school teachers with the intent to live in Mexico long term. Then, COVID-19 happened while we were staying in Mexico City’s central Narvarte Poniente neighborhood.

It was an uncertain and frightening time to be traveling. We ultimately decided, as U.S. citizens with a travel visa, to return to California after nearly half a year away. As tourists, we would have violated our 180-day limit and didn’t want to risk overstaying; had we been dual citizens, we would have had less pressure to return so suddenly.

Navigating the consulate and paperwork

But we hadn’t given up on our ambitions to live in Mexico as Mexican Americans. Shortly after returning to the San Francisco region, I began my application process to become a dual Mexican citizen.

In my case, I had a major advantage: My mom never rescinded her Mexican citizenship, despite having lived in the United States for more than 30 years after immigrating as a young woman. When she eventually moved back to Mexico, it inspired me to follow her southward. Through her, my direct path to citizenship had already been laid out.

The process took me a couple of years, though it could have been completed much more swiftly. I took my time and wasn’t in a rush during the pandemic. I visited different consulates in California, and after waiting in many lines and talking to many people, I gathered all of the documents — most importantly, proof of my mother’s citizenship and birth certificate — and approvals.

Then, it happened: I had become a Mexican citizen, and I had my Mexican passport. (I would eventually get my INE, but I opted to do it in Mexico, rather than at any Mexican consulate in the U.S.).

My wife had a trickier path. Her Mexican-born father’s documents had a typo. Therefore, some of his documents didn’t exactly match. If you aren’t yet familiar with the distress an aberrant punctuation mark can trigger in the imperfect machinery of Mexican bureaucracy, I pray you never have to.

Ultimately, my wife was forced to hire a specialist who helps Mexican descendants obtain their Mexican citizenship — it was frictionless and worth the price. To date, we highly recommend it for anyone who has the funding or has experienced any complications with the process.

A historic surge in binational applicants

During that time, we weren’t alone in our journeys toward Mexican citizenship. Many of our Mexican American friends had expressed a desire to do the same, and in some cases, a few had already started their processes as well. In fact, dual citizenship applications — particularly for the U.S.-born descendants of Mexican immigrants — are reaching a historic apex. De Los, a Latino-focused branch of the Los Angeles Times, recently reported that “Between 2024 and 2025, registrations for Mexican citizenship skyrocketed by 161% at the Los Angeles consulate.”

The trend is universal throughout the U.S. In Boise, Idaho, reports indicate a rise in applicants due to Mexico’s law change in 2023, which simplified the route to dual citizenship for anyone with at least one Mexican-born parent. Combined with the ongoing pressures of xenophobic turmoil, immigration raids and other sociopolitical factors, more people are looking to gain a sense of security and connection on both sides of the border through binational citizenship.

The benefits of dual citizenship are certainly ample: Traveling as a dual citizen offers financial breaks and accessibility perks (there are fewer foreign fees to be paid at Mexican airports and museums, for example); purchasing property in Mexico involves fewer legal hurdles; and at large, it grants unrestricted freedoms on both sides of the border, which is an ultimate privilege.

The unexpected costs of double bureaucracy

But that’s where things can get a little complicated, depending on your plans and lifestyle. In my case, I don’t use my Mexican passport solely for a beach getaway once a year; I live and work in Mexico as a dual citizen, with employers and responsibilities in both countries, and the implications are different.

Vehicle registration in California expired and needs to be updated in person? Guess who’s flying back for a visit to the California Department of Motor Vehicles? Navigating Mexico’s monthly tax payments? Might require a tax accountant. Of course, each scenario comes with a cost, and many life lessons.

When I applied for dual citizenship, I wasn’t necessarily thinking about those realities, or how I would have to pay and renew double the amount of things as someone fully integrated into two federal systems. Of course, in retrospect it makes complete sense. But it’s not the sort of thing that a bright-eyed applicant has at the forefront of their mind while pursuing dual citizenship — nor is it the kind of thing that parents or friends who are encouraging dual citizenship are thinking about, either.

Political debates and balancing two worlds

The issue of dual citizenship has even caused some political strife. Just weeks ago, President Claudia Sheinbaum proposed a ban on dual citizens being able to reach the highest levels of office within Mexico’s borders. “Why have dual nationality if you’re going to represent the people of Mexico?” she rhetorically posed. The bill has been criticized by the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) as a discriminatory human rights violation.

However, for the average person who doesn’t intend to run for the Mexican presidency, dual citizens generally don’t have much to shy away from. If you plan to work in both countries as a dual citizen, be prepared to pay the taxes (literally and metaphorically). If you don’t plan to work in Mexico for Mexican-based companies, you can simply declare your non-working status in Mexico when registering for your INE, and your biggest potential taxation headaches will disappear — at least in one of the two countries.

The benefits

For all of its potential downsides, there are double the benefits. On days when I enter the U.S. through California airports and switch over to using English with my U.S. passport, it feels like I’m home. I’m just as happy and relieved as soon as I arrive back in Mexico, activate my Spanish mode, and show my Mexican passport.

As someone who grew up around many undocumented Mexican immigrants in California, I don’t take that lightly. And I use it to constantly toggle my way between both worlds, as my fullest self.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

The US bond market shuts for Columbus Day; US stocks trade normally. —Brazil data Brazil’s Focus survey on Tuesday, retail sales on Thursday and the IBC-BR activity index on Friday give the most complete domestic pulse of the week. —Argentina CPI Argentina’s inflation rate on Tuesday is the region’s most market-moving single print for the peso and local assets. —US CPI Wednesday’s US inflation rate will set the tone for the dollar and global yields that dominate LatAm financing conditions. —Mexico industry Mexico’s industrial production opens the week with a test of whether oil-linked strength is feeding the real economy. —Peru GDP Peru’s GDP and unemployment data on Thursday anchor the Andean commodity-export story. —Colombia data Colombia’s retail sales and industrial production on Friday show how oil revenue is reaching domestic demand.

The week turns on whether commodity support for Latin American exporters can outweigh the squeeze from a firm dollar and US yields near 5.2%.

Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Peru and Colombia all release data that will test the region’s resilience to expensive global capital. The most market-moving items for Latin American investors are Argentina’s inflation rate on Tuesday, the US inflation rate on Wednesday, and Brazil’s activity and retail figures later in the week.

A strong dollar remains the main transmission channel from global markets into the region. Any sustained fall in Treasury yields would support carry trades and regional equities, while renewed yield pressure would favour a defensive stance.

Three Themes for the Week

Brent above US$100 benefits Mexico, Colombia and selected Brazilian energy exposure but raises imported-fuel and inflation risks across the region. Net oil importers such as Chile, Peru and most of Central America feel that cost first.

High US yields raise the opportunity cost of local-currency exposure and limit room for central-bank easing, favouring country selection over broad regional beta. With the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.24% on Friday, Wednesday’s US inflation print is the week’s main test of that pressure.

World.title: Dominican Actress Yamilé Scheker Dies
World.content:
Obituary: Dominican Republic

Key Facts —Who. Yamilé Scheker (also spelled Schecker), a Dominican actress of theatre and cinema and a member of the Compañía Nacional de Teatro, the National Theatre Company. —What. She died after a career of more than 50 stage productions; her screen credits include Veneno (2018), Candela (2021) and Freddy (2023). —Where. Santo Domingo, according to El Día; no official statement on the place of death had been published. —When. The morning of Sunday, 11 October 2026. —As of 11 October 2026, 17:30 GMT.

Dominican actress Yamilé Scheker died on the morning of Sunday, 11 October 2026, according to Dominican media. Her death matters to Dominican theatre audiences and to Dominican-American readers who follow culture from home.

What We Know

Yamilé Scheker was a Dominican actress of theatre and cinema. Her death was reported on Sunday by Diario Libre, Listín Diario, Hoy, El Nacional and El Día, all Dominican outlets.

El Nacional spells her surname Schecker, and one colleague’s tribute uses the same spelling. We use Scheker, the spelling that appears in the Diario Libre and Hoy web addresses.

Diario Libre called her an outstanding actress of Dominican theatre and cinema. She was a member of the Compañía Nacional de Teatro, the National Theatre Company.

The Dominican flag flies over the Ozama Fortress in Santo Domingo. (File photo)

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Dominican Republic Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Her Career on Stage and Screen

Scheker took part in more than 50 stage productions, according to the Dominican coverage. Diario Libre and El Nacional name Mi tía La Jamona, El cepillo de dientes, El viaje chino and Las mariposas son libres among her works.

Listín Diario adds that she performed Los monólogos de la vagina, the Spanish title of The Vagina Monologues, for four years. The same paper reports that she debuted on stage in 1982 in Sabor a miel, which means “flavour of honey”, directed by Onix Báez.

On screen, El Nacional and Hoy name Veneno in 2018, Candela in 2021 and Freddy in 2023. Listín Diario lists other films too, so this is not her full filmography, and we have not confirmed her roles.

Actor Phillip Rodríguez called her a “teacher of generations”, according to El Nacional. The coverage we reviewed does not say whom she taught or where.

Tributes From Colleagues

News of her death spread when Cuban actor Orestes Amador, who lives in the Dominican Republic, posted on Instagram. According to Hoy, he wrote that he regretted the passing of his “dear and admired actress, friend Yamile Scheker”.

Actor Phillip Rodríguez said: “Peace and resignation for all of us who cared for her. Farewell always, dear Yamilé Schecker.”

Comedian Manolo Ozuna said: “Another great sadness that this 2026 gives us… My friend and former work colleague.” Listín Diario also quotes actor Johnnié Mercedes, who shared an emotional post.

What Is Not Known

Listín Diario reports that she died after a battle with cancer, based on colleagues and friends rather than an official statement. Her age had not been published, and El Día said funeral honours would be announced in the coming hours.

We found no statement from the Ministry of Culture or the government as of 17:30 GMT. We will not go beyond what the named outlets have published.

If Dominican outlets or official bodies confirm more details, we will update this article. Until then, we report only what the named outlets have published.

What It Means for Readers in the US

Dominican-American readers often follow home news through Dominican outlets like these. For them, the death of a veteran stage actress is part of following Dominican culture.

Readers who want to know her work can look for the films Veneno, Candela and Freddy, named in the reports. We have not confirmed where those films can be streamed.

Those interested in Dominican theatre can follow the Compañía Nacional de Teatro and the culture pages of Diario Libre and Listín Diario. We will report any official tribute or funeral details if they are published.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Yamilé Scheker?

Yamilé Scheker was a Dominican actress of theatre and cinema who took part in more than 50 stage productions. She was a member of the Compañía Nacional de Teatro, the National Theatre Company.

When did Yamilé Scheker die?

She died on the morning of Sunday, 11 October 2026, according to Dominican media. El Día places her death in Santo Domingo, and Listín Diario reports cancer as the cause, citing colleagues; neither was an official statement as of 17:30 GMT.

Which films did Yamilé Scheker appear in?

El Nacional and Hoy name Veneno (2018), Candela (2021) and Freddy (2023). This is not her full filmography, and we have not confirmed her roles.

How did colleagues react to her death?

Actors Orestes Amador and Phillip Rodríguez and comedian Manolo Ozuna paid tribute to her. Amador’s Instagram post, reported by Hoy, helped spread the news.

World.title: Chile’s Kast Approval Falls to 27%, Disapproval 64%
World.content:
CHILE · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country Chile, the top copper miner, governed by José Antonio Kast since March.

— What happened Kast approval fell to 27% in Criteria poll, from 30%.

— Disapproval 64%, up four points; 9% did not know.

— Expectations 82% say the government has fallen below their expectations.

— The sample 802 adults, online panel, Thursday 8 and Friday 9 October.

— US link Chile supplied 68% of US refined copper imports, 2021–2024.

Seven months into his term, the conservative president of the world’s largest copper producer has lost more ground in a weekly poll.

Kast approval in Chile fell three points to 27% in the weekly Criteria poll published on Sunday, 11 October 2026. Disapproval of President José Antonio Kast rose four points to 64%, the pollster said.

Chile is the world’s largest copper miner and supplied 68% of US refined copper imports in 2021–2024, US data show. Weaker support at home can slow the reforms Kast needs Congress to pass.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Chile ranks 3rd of 14 with 63.6 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (86); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (38). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Criteria Poll Shows

Criteria is a Chilean research firm that publishes a weekly political survey called Agenda Criteria. This edition polled 802 adults through a certified online panel on Thursday, 8 and Friday, 9 October.

One week earlier, Criteria had Kast at 30% approval and 60% disapproval. The week before that, he stood at 31% and 58%.

The share who did not know fell one point to 9%. In a single week, the gap between disapproval and approval widened from 30 to 37 points.

Criteria also pooled its weekly samples to show the longer trend. Across the government’s first four weeks, 3,208 interviews gave Kast 44% approval, against 29% in the last four weeks.

La Tercera, a leading Santiago daily, reported that Kast’s disapproval had topped former president Gabriel Boric’s for the first time. Boric, a leftist, governed from March 2022 to March 2026.

Last week’s reading is covered in Chile’s Kast Approval Slips to 30%, Disapproval 60%.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Is Turning Away From Kast

Kast founded Chile’s conservative Republican Party and took office on 11 March 2026. He won the December 2025 runoff against Jeannette Jara, the candidate of the governing left.

Criteria said the largest relative drops in Kast approval came among first-round voters of Franco Parisi and Evelyn Matthei. Parisi is a populist economist who leads the Party of the People (PDG).

Matthei is a centre-right former mayor of Providencia, a Santiago district, and was the traditional right’s candidate.

Only 18% said the government had exceeded their expectations, while 82% said it had fallen short. Even among Kast’s own first-round voters, more chose “below my expectations” than the alternative.

Spending Cuts and the Bachelet Question

The poll also tested the government’s push to trim the state. A majority of 58% said the state spends its money in a rather inefficient way, down from 66% in February under Boric.

Some 52% backed cutting the number of public employees to reduce spending. Only 19% were open to cutting social programmes, and 8% to trimming cash bonuses or subsidies.

Criteria also asked about Michelle Bachelet, the Socialist former president who governed twice. Some 43% opposed a third presidential bid by her, while 38% supported one.

Asked about the 2029 election, 51% said they were unlikely to vote for her. Another 44% said they were likely to, and 5% were unsure.

What It Means for You

For US investors, the poll lands just before a holiday. Chilean markets close on Monday, 12 October, while US stock exchanges stay open.

Chilean exposure trades in New York through the iShares MSCI Chile ETF and NYSE-listed shares such as SQM and Banco Santander-Chile. Falling Kast approval can weigh on expectations for his reform agenda in Congress.

The US Geological Survey estimates Chile mined about 5.3 million tonnes of copper in 2025, the most of any country.

The numbers do not change policy on their own. Kast’s term runs until March 2030, and the next presidential election is due in 2029.

What Is Not Known

Criteria’s online panel is not a probability sample, so the firm publishes no margin of error. It weights results by region, sex, age and socioeconomic group.

The poll does not say why approval fell this week. It is also unclear which Boric reading La Tercera used for its comparison, or whether other pollsters will show the same drop.

What Comes Next

If Criteria keeps its weekly rhythm, the next reading is due on Sunday, 18 October.

The government also faces a decision on Codelco, the state copper company. Economy and Mining Minister Daniel Mas told 24 Horas the state would decide early next week whether to join a criminal probe.

A weekly poll does not threaten Kast’s term. It does measure how much political capital he has left for Congress.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Kast’s approval rating now?

Criteria’s poll published on 11 October puts Kast’s approval at 27% and disapproval at 64%. Another 9% said they did not know.

Who is President Kast?

Kast is a conservative who founded Chile’s Republican Party and took office on 11 March 2026. He won the December 2025 runoff against Jeannette Jara.

How was the Criteria poll conducted?

Criteria surveyed 802 adults through an online panel on 8 and 9 October. It is not a probability sample, so no margin of error is published.

Why does Chilean politics matter to Americans?

Chile is the world’s largest copper miner and supplied 68% of US refined copper imports in 2021-2024. Its politics can affect copper supply and US-listed Chilean stocks.

World.title: Brazil Gives WhatsApp 3 Hours to Shut Pro-Lula Channel
World.content:
BRAZIL · COURTS

Key Facts — What happened Brazil’s electoral court told WhatsApp to suspend a pro-Lula channel.

— Deadline WhatsApp got three hours to comply, SBT News reported on Sunday.

— The channel “Exército do Lula,” run by deputy André Janones, had 2.09 million followers.

— US company Meta must keep the channel’s records for at least one year.

— Prediction markets Kalshi gives Flávio Bolsonaro 87% and Lula 13% (11 October, 11:07 a.m. ET). Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 88% and Kalshi at 88% (Lula: 13% and 12% ), as of 11 October, 2:20 pm ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

Brazil’s top electoral judge has ordered a US-owned messaging app to switch off a major runoff campaign channel.

Kassio Nunes Marques, president of Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE), gave WhatsApp three hours to suspend the pro-Lula channel “Exército do Lula.” SBT News reported the injunction on Sunday, 11 October, at 3:46 p.m. Brasília time.

WhatsApp belongs to Meta Platforms, the California company listed on the Nasdaq. The order puts a US platform at the centre of a fight over disinformation two weeks before the 25 October runoff.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 75.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Court Ordered

The channel is run by federal deputy André Janones, a Lula ally from the small Avante party in Minas Gerais. The suspension lasts until the runoff result is certified, SBT News reported.

The decision also sets a fine for non-compliance. It orders Meta to preserve the channel’s records and messages for at least one year.

According to the documents cited in the ruling, the channel had about 55,000 followers on the morning of 5 October. By 7 October it reached 2,090,796; SBT News now puts it above 3.2 million.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Brazil politics Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why the Judge Acted

Nunes Marques wrote that the channel worked as a “command centre” for mass sharing of claims he called “knowingly untrue.” He added that digital mobilisation itself “is lawful and is not the subject of this decision.”

The ruling cites instructions to get around WhatsApp’s safeguards, such as copying links by hand. It also cites deleted messages meant to avoid tracing, which made removing posts one by one ineffective.

SBT News did not include any response from Janones or WhatsApp.

Who Asked for It

The request came from Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign. He is a senator for the conservative Liberal Party (PL) and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

He faces President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the left-wing Workers’ Party.

On Saturday, 10 October, the TSE said Flávio’s side had filed an abuse case against Lula, running mate Geraldo Alckmin and Janones. The court’s inspector-general, Ricardo Villas Bôas Cueva, admitted the case but asked for more evidence.

The filing seeks to strip Lula and Alckmin of their registration and suspend the channel and the profile @janones.apoio. It alleges Janones coordinated disinformation against Flávio and used public campaign funds to boost negative ads.

The TSE stressed that admitting the case does not mean the allegations are accepted as true. Cueva gave Flávio 72 hours for more detail and the defendants five days to answer.

Nunes Marques is a Supreme Court justice appointed by Jair Bolsonaro in 2020. He now presides over the electoral court.

What It Means for You

For US investors in Meta, Brazil is again testing how far courts can direct a US platform during an election. The same court gave Meta 48 hours to explain Lula’s reach on its networks, SBT News reported.

For holders of Brazilian assets, the runoff shapes policy from January 2027. Court fights over online campaigning add noise to a race that betting markets already favour Flávio to win.

What Prediction Markets Say

Prediction markets · who wins the runoff Implied chance of winning Brazil’s presidency on 25 October, from traders’ prices. Polymarket Flávio Bolsonaro 87.9% · Lula 12.5% (US$180 million traded) Kalshi (regulated in the US by the CFTC) Flávio Bolsonaro 88% · Lula 12% As of 11 October, 2:20 pm ET (19:20 Lisbon), updated every 20 minutes. Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

On Kalshi, which US regulators at the CFTC oversee, bets gave Flávio 87% and Lula 13% at 11:07 a.m. ET on Sunday. On Polymarket, with about US$180 million traded on the election, Lula stood at 12.5% at 12:44 p.m. ET.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether WhatsApp had complied by Sunday evening. The amount of the fine has not been reported.

The full text of the decision was not yet on the TSE website when this article was written. It is also unclear whether Janones will appeal.

What Comes Next

The electoral abuse case continues on its own track, with deadlines running this week. Monday, 12 October, is a national holiday in Brazil.

Brazilians choose between Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula on Sunday, 25 October. The order runs until that result is certified.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Brazil’s electoral court order?

It ordered WhatsApp to suspend the pro-Lula channel “Exército do Lula” within three hours. Meta must also keep the channel’s records for at least one year.

Who runs the channel?

Federal deputy André Janones of the Avante party, an ally of President Lula, created and runs it. It had 2.09 million followers by 7 October, according to the ruling.

Why was the channel suspended?

Justice Nunes Marques found it coordinated mass sharing of claims he called knowingly untrue. He said digital mobilisation itself is lawful.

When is Brazil’s presidential runoff?

The runoff between Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula is on Sunday, 25 October. The suspension lasts until the result is certified.

Sources: Superior Electoral Court (TSE), 10 October 2026; SBT News, 11 October 2026; Metrópoles; SBT News on Meta (all accessed 11 October 2026).

World.title: Bolivia Reserves Rise 8.7% to US$3.93 Billion on Gold
World.content:
BOLIVIA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Bolivia’s central bank says net reserves rose 8.7% last quarter.

— The numbers US$3.93 billion on 30 September, up US$315.5 million since June.

— Gold share Gold makes up 87% of reserves, up from 80% in June.

— Liquid dollars Foreign-currency reserves fell 28.4% to US$474.2 million after debt payments.

— US link US exposures make up 68% of the foreign-currency reserves.

— Credit rating Moody’s raised Bolivia to Caa2 in early October, the bank says.

Bolivia’s reserves are growing again, but the gain is mostly gold while spendable cash shrinks.

Bolivia reserves rose 8.7% in the third quarter to US$3.93 billion, the Banco Central de Bolivia (BCB) reported. The gain came mainly from gold the bank bought on the domestic market, El Deber reported on Saturday, 10 October.

The figure matters for US investors who hold Bolivia’s dollar bonds and track its ability to pay. The same report shows the most liquid reserves, held mainly in US Treasury bills, fell by over a quarter.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 with 28.4 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (13). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (CCC+); economy contracting (-1.2%); inflation of 20%. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Central Bank Reported

The BCB is Bolivia’s central bank, based in La Paz, and it manages the country’s gold and foreign-currency holdings. Its report covers the quarter from July to September 2026.

Net international reserves reached US$3.93 billion on Wednesday, 30 September. That was US$315.5 million more than at the end of June, when they stood at about US$3.62 billion.

Gross reserves, a slightly different measure, reached US$3.88 billion, up 8.8%. The bank says the gap between the two comes mainly from Bolivia’s position at the International Monetary Fund and currency valuations.

The BCB says its foreign-exchange operations with local banks added more than US$400 million during the quarter. It calls this a “genuine accumulation” of reserves.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Bolivia economy Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Gold Now Makes Up 87% of Bolivia Reserves

The bank bought 4.1 tonnes of gold on the domestic market in the quarter, under Law 1503. Its gold holdings rose from 22.3 to 25.3 tonnes, valued at US$3.38 billion.

Of that gold, 14.7 tonnes sit with foreign banks, 8.9 tonnes are in BCB vaults and 1.7 tonnes are in transit. Among foreign banks, Toronto Dominion Bank holds the most, 6.0 tonnes, while JPMorgan Chase Bank holds 1.4 tonnes.

The BCB itself flags a risk. Gold now accounts for 87% of all reserves, up from 80% three months earlier, a level the bank calls “not recommendable.”

Its gold rose by one tonne in September, yet the market value fell by US$78 million. The bank recommends greater diversification.

Why Dollars Remain Scarce

Foreign-currency reserves, the cash Bolivia uses for import bills and debt service, fell by US$187.7 million to US$474.2 million. The BCB says this was due to payments of foreign obligations.

At the end of June, that cash buffer stood at US$661.9 million. El Deber noted that the headline total does not, on its own, show how many dollars are immediately available.

The bank keeps this cash in short-term instruments, mainly US Treasury securities. It says US exposures account for 68% of these holdings and supranational lenders for 24%.

The BCB set the official exchange rate at 11.73 bolivianos per US dollar for Saturday to Monday, 10 to 12 October. That is the basis for any local-currency conversion in this story.

What It Means for You

For bond investors, rising reserves support Bolivia’s recent credit upgrades. The BCB says Moody’s raised Bolivia from Caa3 to Caa2 with a positive outlook in early October, still deep in speculative grade.

The report says Fitch and S&P Global also upgraded Bolivia earlier this year. Yet the drop in liquid dollars means debt payments still compete with fuel and import needs.

For US companies and travellers, dollars inside Bolivia are likely to stay tight. Most of the reserve gain is gold, which cannot be spent at once.

What Is Not Known

The report gives no release date, though its PDF file is dated Thursday, 8 October. It names neither the foreign obligations paid nor a reserves forecast for end-2026.

It is not known how quickly the BCB will act on its own advice to diversify away from gold. No official comment beyond the report was available on Sunday.

What Comes Next

The next quarterly report will cover October to December. The BCB expects an uncertain global backdrop, with inflation pressure and geopolitical tension.

The rise does not mean Bolivia’s dollar shortage is over. The liquid part of the reserves is smaller than it was in June.

Frequently Asked Questions

How large are Bolivia’s reserves now?

Net international reserves stood at US$3.93 billion on 30 September 2026. That is 8.7% more than at the end of June.

Why did the reserves rise?

The central bank bought 4.1 tonnes of gold on the domestic market in the quarter. It also gained more than US$400 million through foreign-exchange operations with local banks.

Why are dollars still scarce in Bolivia?

Gold makes up 87% of the reserves and cannot be spent quickly. Liquid foreign currency fell to US$474.2 million after foreign debt payments.

Where does Bolivia keep its gold?

About 14.7 tonnes sit with foreign banks, including JPMorgan Chase Bank, and 8.9 tonnes are in the central bank’s vaults. Another 1.7 tonnes were in transit on 30 September.

Sources: Banco Central de Bolivia, quarterly reserves report, third quarter 2026; Banco Central de Bolivia, official exchange rate; El Deber (all accessed 11 October 2026).

World.title: Honduras Fuel Prices Rise Again From 12 October
World.content:
HONDURAS · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country Honduras imports its fuel and sets pump prices every week.

— What happened Gasoline, kerosene and vehicle LPG prices rise from Monday, 12 October.

— Regular gasoline L139.96 (US$5.22) a gallon in Tegucigalpa, up L2.04 (US$0.08).

— Diesel Unchanged at L153.53 (US$5.73) a gallon for a second week.

— Biggest rise Kerosene, up L2.50 (US$0.09) to L145.92 (US$5.44) a gallon.

Gasoline goes up again at Honduran pumps on Monday, while a government tax measure keeps diesel flat.

Honduras will raise the price of gasoline, kerosene and vehicle gas from Monday, 12 October. The Secretaría de Energía, the energy ministry, published the new weekly price table on Saturday, 10 October.

Diesel stays unchanged for a second straight week under a temporary government measure that began on 5 October.

What the Energy Ministry Announced

In Tegucigalpa, super gasoline rises L1.23 (US$0.05) to L157.84 (US$5.89) a gallon. Regular gasoline rises L2.04 (US$0.08) to L139.96 (US$5.22).

Kerosene posts the biggest increase, up L2.50 (US$0.09) to L145.92 (US$5.44) a gallon. Vehicle LPG rises L1.14 (US$0.04) to L54.93 (US$2.05).

In San Pedro Sula, the northern business hub, super reaches L153.13 (US$5.71) and regular L135.49 (US$5.05). Kerosene there costs L141.17 (US$5.27) and vehicle LPG L50.92 (US$1.90).

The ministry’s table cites a rise in international fuel prices as the reason. All dollar values use 26.81 lempiras per US dollar, the market rate on 11 October 2026.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Honduras economy Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Second Weekly Rise for Gasoline

A week earlier, super had already jumped L3.44 (US$0.13) in Tegucigalpa, according to the Honduran daily La Tribuna. Regular rose L2.66 (US$0.10) and kerosene L5.03 (US$0.19) that week.

The increases this week are smaller, but they come on top of those. Super in the capital has gained L4.67 (US$0.17) a gallon in two weeks.

The ministry keeps a temporary subsidy on regular gasoline, which it describes as 70% support. Its table lists L4.82 (US$0.18) a gallon in Tegucigalpa and L4.59 (US$0.17) in San Pedro Sula.

How Diesel Is Being Held Down

Diesel stays at L153.53 (US$5.73) a gallon in Tegucigalpa and L149.20 (US$5.57) in San Pedro Sula. The ministry says the price is stabilised through the fuel tax.

The government is absorbing about L12 (US$0.45) a gallon of diesel for 30 days from 5 October, La Tribuna reported. The aim is to shield transport, farming and food prices.

Domestic cooking gas also stays at L249.62 (US$9.31) in Tegucigalpa, with continued state support. In San Pedro Sula, the price remains L228.47 (US$8.52).

What It Means for You

For US businesses, the ministry links higher Honduran pump prices to rising international fuel costs. Weekly price tables show how fast those costs reach Central American consumers.

For US companies that buy goods made or grown in Honduras, transport costs matter. The diesel freeze limits the impact on trucking, at least until early November.

For US travellers driving in Honduras, a full 12-gallon tank of regular now costs about L1,680 (US$63) in Tegucigalpa. Prices are slightly lower in San Pedro Sula.

What Is Not Known

The ministry does not explain how its 70% support for regular gasoline is calculated. La Tribuna put that support at L6.31 (US$0.24) a gallon last week, above this week’s listed amount.

It is also unclear what happens to diesel prices when the 30-day measure ends. The government has not said whether it will extend the tax relief.

What Comes Next

The energy ministry usually publishes the next price table on Saturday, effective the following Monday. The next change is therefore due on Monday, 19 October.

The diesel measure runs until early November. Any decision to extend or end it will show in the weekly tables.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the new fuel prices in Honduras from 12 October?

In Tegucigalpa, super costs L157.84 (US$5.89) a gallon and regular L139.96 (US$5.22). Diesel stays at L153.53 (US$5.73).

Why did fuel prices rise in Honduras?

The energy ministry cites higher international fuel prices. Honduras imports its fuel, so world price moves reach local pumps within weeks.

Is diesel cheaper this week?

No, diesel is unchanged for a second week. The government absorbs about L12 (US$0.45) a gallon for 30 days from 5 October.

How often do fuel prices change in Honduras?

The energy ministry sets a new price table every week. It usually publishes it on Saturday, effective on Monday.

Sources: Secretaría de Energía de Honduras, price structure from 12 October 2026; Secretaría de Energía, fuel price history; El Heraldo; La Tribuna, prices from 5 October (all accessed 11 October 2026).

World.title: Paraguay Judge Jails 4 Over Miami Cannabis Jet
World.content:
PARAGUAY · JUSTICE

Key Facts — The ruling A judge ordered pretrial detention for four suspects on Saturday.

— The case A private jet from Miami carried 261.6 kilos of cannabis.

— The suspects Two aviation officials, a paperwork agent and an operations supervisor.

— The charges International drug trafficking, criminal association, coercion and aggravated bribery.

— The US link Three US passport holders were ordered into pretrial detention in June.

— Next step Transfer to the former Tacumbú prison once the ruling is final.

Paraguay’s investigation into a jet that flew high-potency cannabis from Florida has moved from the passengers to the airport itself.

A judge in Paraguay has ordered four airport-linked suspects held in pretrial detention in the Miami cannabis jet case. Judge Lici Teresita Sánchez issued the order on Saturday, 10 October, after a hearing in Asunción, the capital.

The private jet flew in from Miami in May with 261.6 kilos of high-potency cannabis on board. For US readers, the case shows American cannabis moving south, allegedly with help from inside a national airport.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 with 36.0 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (55); weakest: future resources (13). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Judge Decided

Sánchez is a criminal guarantees judge who specialises in organised crime, according to the newspaper Hoy. In Paraguay, such judges supervise investigations and decide on detention before any trial.

The hearing was set for Saturday afternoon at the Palacio de Justicia, the main court building in Asunción. The newspaper Última Hora reported the outcome on Sunday, 11 October.

According to Última Hora, the four will stay at the headquarters of the national anti-drug agency for five days. If no appeal changes the ruling in that time, they will move to the former Tacumbú prison in Asunción.

Pretrial detention is not a conviction, and all four are presumed innocent.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Paraguay Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who the Four Suspects Are

The Secretaría Nacional Antidrogas (SENAD), Paraguay’s national anti-drug agency, named three of the men in a statement on Friday, 9 October. They are flight controller Herman Melgarejo Morales and José María Fernández Vera, an agent handling airport paperwork.

The third is Víctor Fernández Arce, an operations supervisor at Munser S.A., an airport company. Local reports identify the fourth as an official at Dinac, the civil aviation authority.

SENAD and the Ministerio Público, the public prosecutor’s office, carried out four raids in the operation. Three targeted homes in Luque, the city that hosts the airport, and one targeted a company inside Silvio Pettirossi International Airport.

How the Miami Cannabis Jet Was Caught

SENAD intercepted the private jet at Silvio Pettirossi International Airport on 30 May 2026. The agency said the plane came from Miami with 261.6 kilos of cannabis high in THC.

The newspaper ABC Color reported in June that the aircraft was a US-registered Bombardier Challenger business jet. It said the plane stopped in Panama City before landing near Asunción, and that the bags were described as musical instruments.

On 1 June, a judge ordered pretrial detention for three passengers travelling on US passports, ABC Color reported. The pilot left Paraguay soon after landing, and the co-pilot was dropped from the case after cooperating with prosecutors.

What Prosecutors Allege

Prosecutor Ingrid Cubilla charged the four airport-linked suspects on Friday, Última Hora reported. The charges include international drug trafficking, criminal association, coercion and aggravated bribery.

According to the prosecution, one suspect coordinated the flight and the unloading. Another allegedly pressed control staff to release the seized cargo.

A third suspect allegedly helped move the bags from the plane to a nearby vehicle. The fourth, a Dinac official, allegedly discussed releasing the cargo in exchange for a reward, prosecutors said.

A Growing Flow of US Cannabis

The jet is part of a wider pattern, according to SENAD. On 7 October, it reported over 1,200 kilos of high-potency cannabis seized under the current government.

Most came from the United States, and part was bound for Brazil. Earlier cases included 311 kilos hidden in two pickup trucks from Miami.

What It Means for You

For US readers, the case links American cannabis supply with smuggling routes into South America. Three people travelling on US passports were ordered into Paraguayan pretrial detention in June.

The charges also point to alleged weak spots inside the country’s main international airport. No new rules for commercial passengers have been announced in connection with the case.

What Is Not Known

Neither the courts nor the prosecutor’s office had published the detention order by Sunday evening. The ruling is known from Última Hora’s report, and the suspects’ defence arguments have not been made public.

It is also not known who paid for the flight or who was meant to receive the cannabis. Local reports give different job titles for the fourth suspect.

What Comes Next

The defence can appeal the detention order before it becomes final. If the ruling stands, the four will be moved from SENAD headquarters to the former Tacumbú prison.

Prosecutors must then build a formal indictment against the airport-linked suspects. The detention ruling does not decide guilt, and no trial date has been set.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Miami cannabis jet case?

It is a Paraguayan drug case over a private jet from Miami seized on 30 May 2026. The plane carried 261.6 kilos of high-potency cannabis, according to the anti-drug agency SENAD.

Who was jailed on Saturday?

Four people linked to the airport were ordered into pretrial detention on Saturday, 10 October. They include a flight controller, a civil aviation official, a paperwork agent and an operations supervisor.

Are any Americans involved?

Three passengers travelling on US passports were ordered into pretrial detention on 1 June, local media reported. The four suspects jailed on Saturday are airport workers and aviation officials in Paraguay.

Does pretrial detention mean they are guilty?

No, pretrial detention only keeps suspects in custody while the investigation continues. All four are presumed innocent until a court rules otherwise.

Sources: SENAD, raids in the narcojet case; SENAD, cannabis seizures from the United States; Última Hora; Hoy; ABC Color (all accessed 11 October 2026).

World.title: Ecuador Army Seizes 54 Guns and 30,700 Rounds in Quito
World.content:
ECUADOR · SECURITY

Key Facts — What happened Ecuador’s army raided an unlicensed weapons warehouse in north Quito.

— When Saturday, 10 October, during a holiday weekend in Ecuador.

— The haul 54 firearms, 770 cartridges and 30,700 further rounds of ammunition.

— Detained One man, reportedly linked to a 2024 seizure of 108 guns.

— Still open The guns’ origin, buyers and any gang link are not known.

Soldiers found dozens of shotguns, pistols and submachine guns in a warehouse that had no permit to store weapons.

Ecuador’s army seized 54 firearms and more than 30,000 rounds of ammunition from a warehouse in north Quito on Saturday, 10 October. The Defence Ministry announced the Quito arsenal on its official X account that afternoon.

The raid matters to Washington because Ecuador is a front-line US partner against cocaine gangs. Two of those gangs, Los Choneros and Los Lobos, are designated by the US State Department as foreign terrorist organisations.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Ecuador ranks 8th of 14 with 38.2 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (14). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B); 51 homicides per 100,000. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Army Found in the Quito Arsenal

The Defence Ministry said soldiers seized “54 firearms, 770 cartridges and munitions of different calibres, as well as 30,700 munitions.” It said the Ecuadorian Army carried out the operation in the Monteserrín neighbourhood as part of the government’s security bloc.

The ministry posted the statement at 1:25 p.m. Quito time, under the headline “Arsenal of more than 30,000 munitions seized.” Monteserrín is a residential district in the north of the capital.

The Quito news site Primicias, citing the armed forces, listed 44 carbines of 12 calibre, the bore used in most shotguns. It also listed seven 9mm pistols, two submachine guns and one air rifle.

Primicias added four magazines, two telescopic sights and a spare carbine barrel. For scale, 30,700 rounds would fill more than 600 standard boxes of 50 cartridges.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Ecuador Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A Warehouse Without a Permit

According to the armed forces, the property “did not have authorisation from the arms control body to store this type of material.” In Ecuador, the military oversees the licensing of firearms and ammunition stocks.

One man was detained at the site, Primicias and the Guayaquil daily Expreso reported. The authorities did not release his name or say which offence he will face.

The army told Primicias the same man was linked to a January 2024 seizure in Cumbayá, a suburb east of Quito. Police then found 108 firearms, 4,689 rounds and equipment for reloading cartridges.

That earlier case was known as “Operation Arsenal.” It is not known how it ended in court or why the man was free.

Ecuador’s Security Campaign

The raid took place under a 60-day state of exception that President Daniel Noboa declared on 15 September, Expreso reported. Executive Decree 498 covers eight provinces, including Pichincha, where Quito lies, and runs until 14 November.

Noboa, a conservative businessman, has made the fight against drug gangs the centre of his presidency. He uses states of exception to deploy soldiers alongside the police in city streets.

Quito has seen a run of gun seizures this year. Primicias reported that authorities confiscated more than 70 firearms in the capital during August alone.

What It Means for You

For US policymakers, Ecuador is a test of whether a military-led crackdown can weaken gangs that move cocaine north. Illegal weapons stocks are the fuel of that violence, so seizures are one yardstick of progress.

For investors in Ecuador’s dollar bonds, security is a core part of the country risk. Ecuador uses the US dollar as its currency, so its economy is closely tied to US financial conditions.

For travellers, Quito remains a major gateway to the Galápagos Islands and the Andes. US visitors should check the State Department’s Ecuador advisory before booking and follow local authorities.

What Is Not Known

The authorities have not said where the weapons came from or whom they were meant for. They have not linked the Quito arsenal to any criminal group.

The detained man’s identity, nationality and possible charges are unknown. It is also unclear whether any of the weapons had been legally registered at some point.

What Comes Next

Under Ecuadorian law, a detained suspect must appear before a judge within 24 hours for a so-called flagrancy hearing. At that hearing, prosecutors can bring charges such as illegal possession of weapons.

The seizure does not mean the cache belonged to a known gang. Officials have made no such claim so far.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Ecuador’s army seize in Quito?

The army seized 54 firearms, 770 cartridges and 30,700 further rounds of ammunition. The Defence Ministry announced it on Saturday, 10 October.

Where was the Quito arsenal found?

It was found in a warehouse in Monteserrín, a district in the north of Quito. The armed forces said the site had no permit to store weapons.

Was anyone arrested?

One man was detained, according to Ecuadorian media citing the armed forces. His name and possible charges have not been released.

Why does Ecuador matter to the United States?

Ecuador is a key transit country for cocaine bound for the United States and Europe. Washington lists two Ecuadorian gangs, Los Choneros and Los Lobos, as terrorist organisations.

Sources: Ministry of National Defence of Ecuador, statement on X; Primicias; Expreso (all accessed 11 October 2026).

World.title: Francisco Cerúndolo Falls in Shanghai as Breakthrough 2026 Season Faces Another Test
World.content:
Francisco Cerúndolo’s run at the Shanghai Masters ended Sunday with a 6-3, 3-6, 6-2 loss to Czech player Jakub Menšík, bringing another early finish at a major tournament in what has otherwise been one of the Argentine’s most successful seasons. The defeat was especially frustrating for Cerúndolo, who had beaten Menšík in straight sets at the China Open in Beijing just eight days earlier. Entering Sunday’s match, the Argentine had won all three of their previous meetings.

This time, Menšík found a way through. The 21-year-old Czech controlled the opening set, breaking Cerúndolo in the fourth game and using his powerful groundstrokes to keep the Argentine on the defensive. Cerúndolo responded in the second set, saving a crucial break point before finally breaking Menšík’s serve late to force a decider.

But the momentum did not last. Menšík broke early in the third set, raced to a 3-0 lead and closed out the match in approximately two hours. The victory sends Menšík into the fourth round against France’s Arthur Gea, who produced one of Sunday’s biggest surprises by defeating third seed Ben Shelton in straight sets.

For Cerúndolo, the loss ends his Asian hard-court swing with a quarterfinal appearance in Beijing and a third-round exit in Shanghai. He remains Argentina’s highest-ranked men’s singles player, sitting at No. 20 in the ATP rankings entering the tournament. Yet judging his season by those two results would overlook how much the 28-year-old has accomplished in 2026.

Cerúndolo began the year by winning the Argentina Open in February, finally claiming his hometown title after falling short in the 2021 and 2025 finals. He defeated Luciano Darderi 6-4, 6-2 in the championship match, winning his fourth career ATP title in front of a home crowd in Buenos Aires.

Four months later came an even bigger breakthrough. At London’s Queen’s Club, Cerúndolo defeated American Tommy Paul 6-7(4), 6-4, 6-3 in a three-hour final to become the first Argentine to win the prestigious grass-court tournament. It was his first ATP 500 title and fifth career singles championship, strengthening his reputation as a player capable of winning well beyond the clay courts where he initially established himself.

His success on different surfaces has been a recurring theme throughout his career. Cerúndolo first attracted international attention by reaching the Miami Open semifinals in 2022, and his 2026 performances have further demonstrated that his best tennis can trouble leading opponents on hard courts.

In March, he reached the Miami Open quarterfinals after defeating former world No. 1 Daniil Medvedev. His run ended against Alexander Zverev, who won their quarterfinal 6-1, 6-2. The pattern continued during the Grand Slam season, where Cerúndolo produced promising results but could not quite turn them into a breakthrough appearance in the final eight.

He reached the fourth round of the Australian Open in January and the third round at Roland Garros in May. His Queen’s Club title raised expectations ahead of Wimbledon, but that momentum disappeared quickly when he lost his opening match to Spain’s Jaume Munar. At the US Open in September, Cerúndolo delivered one of his most impressive victories of the year, recovering from two sets down to defeat American Taylor Fritz in the third round.

His New York campaign ended one match later against Belgium’s Alexander Blockx, who won their fourth-round encounter 6-3, 4-6, 7-5, 7-5. Taken together, those performances show both the progress Cerúndolo has made and the challenge still facing him. He has established himself as one of Latin America’s leading players, won titles on clay and grass in the same season, and demonstrated that he can compete with highly ranked opponents on hard courts.

What remains missing is a Grand Slam quarterfinal appearance or another deep run at the Masters 1000 level. Sunday’s defeat in Shanghai does not erase his accomplishments. Menšík, ranked No. 15, is one of the ATP Tour’s strongest young competitors, and Cerúndolo had beaten him only a week earlier.

But with the season approaching its final stretch, the Argentine faces a familiar challenge: turning the high points of an already successful year into more consistent results against the game’s strongest opponents. After five ATP titles and repeated appearances in the world’s top 20, the next step is no longer proving he belongs among the best. It is finding a way to stay in contention deeper into tennis’s biggest tournaments.

World.title: Costa Rica’s OIJ Warns of Motorcycle Groups Blocking Roads and Attacking Drivers
World.content:
Groups of motorcyclists performing stunts on public roads, blocking traffic and, in some cases, attacking drivers who confront them have become a serious problem in Costa Rica, a senior official with the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) warned. Víctor Moreno, head of the Investigation Unit within the OIJ section responsible for crimes against physical integrity and traffic offenses, said during a press conference that the newest trend on our roads involves riders moving in packs. He described groups that perform tricks while they ride and obstruct the free flow of other vehicles.
