"The extreme heat we experienced this summer is something everyone was aware of. Politicians shouldn't be afraid of electoral repercussions if they take courageous measures on environmental issues."

Aurore Schreiber, who works for a development cooperation NGO, said she had attended with her family "so that politicians wake up and hear the citizens' message".

"We need to listen to the demands of young people and the most vulnerable", she said. "We need greener, fairer supply chains that take into account workers' issues and wages".

EU's low expectations for COP31

After having its hopes dashed for a more ambitious deal last year in Brazil, the European Union is setting its sights low for next month's COP31.

With climate sceptic Trump withdrawing the United States from the negotiations, international efforts to combat global warming had already taken a battering.

But now the situation looks even less promising as surging energy prices have put major oil and gas producers in a position of strength that makes them less likely to want to discuss phasing out fossil fuels.

Students march in Brussels, Belgium urging for action against climate change. Sunday Oct. 10, 2026. Evelyn Dom / Euronews

The EU insists it remains the global leader on climate action and is the principal international donor in the field.

But the bloc arrives at the COP having recently watered down its own environmental legislation.

As it struggles to compete with China and the United States, Brussels has been on an increasingly business-friendly push.

The most recent example last month was the commission proposing to postpone the implementation of a law targeting methane — an extremely polluting greenhouse gas — by one year, from 2027 to 2028.

World.title: Police clear Guano beach camp in Ceuta days before royal visit
World.content:
The eviction operations carried out by the state security forces began shortly after 8:00 am on the Guano beach in Ceuta, where around 400 migrants were still present following the wave of illegal immigration from Morocco that brought more than 70,000 people at the end of July.

 

The operation was made up largely of officers from the National Police, the Spanish riot units, immigration staff and members of the Civil Guard and local police. The procedure was similar to the two previous clearances on Tarajal and Trampolín beaches.

The migrants were grouped together and taken by bus to the Centro de Atención Temporal de Extranjeros (CATE), where their details will begin to be registered. Afterwards, they will be housed in one of the camps set up by the government, such as the one at the port.

On the two previous occasions, not all the migrants cooperated with the procedure, and many fled into the hills, only coming down when food was distributed. This morning, many gathered up their belongings and left the area before the police arrived.

Minors separated from adults

During the eviction, officers found numerous minors. They were assembled separately and will be transferred apart from the adults.

Several of them were carrying signs asking to be taken to a centre for minors. According to local media, many of the children on this beach had already tried to be registered previously but ran away.

On 20 August, the transfer of migrants from Trampolín beach to temporary reception centres in Loma Margarita and El Embolsamiento began. Some migrants later returned to the beach, as happened when the camp at the port of Ceuta was opened.

Clean-up and assessment of the settlement

Once the site had been emptied, cleaning crews moved in to remove tents, rubbish and all kinds of debris. The work will continue throughout the day, as there is still much to do in a place that has served as a camp for a long time. The ecological damage is significant and will have to be assessed by environmental experts in contact with the Ministry of the Environment.

The camp has left behind serious incidents, including the deaths of two people, as well as brawls, thefts and fights. A parallel life also developed there, with street markets and a way of life of its own.

The eviction comes ahead of the visit by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, scheduled for 13 October. The royal couple will preside in Ceuta over a tribute to those who died at sea during the mass crossing at the Tarajal border. After spending the night in the autonomous city, they will travel on to Melilla. It will be the first time a Spanish monarch has spent the night in Ceuta since the visits by Alfonso XIII in 1904 and 1927.

World.title: Paris motor show: Macron calls for European preference against China
World.content:
Emmanuel Macron is bidding farewell to the Paris Motor Show. The French President will head to the Paris event this Monday, a biennial gathering he has never missed, for his final visit as head of state. It will be an opportunity for the man who declared in 2023 that he "loved" cars to take stock of his record in this strategic sector.

 

Macron insists that the car industry is "at the heart" of French manufacturing, providing 400,000 direct jobs nationwide. The presidency particularly points to ramping up electric vehicle production and the emergence of a national battery industry.

Before 2017, electric car production in France was still marginal and relied almost entirely on a single flagship model: the Renault Zoe. At the start of Emmanuel Macron's term, a presidential source recalls, the country had "no battery factories at all, obviously".

Electrification and "Made in France"

Since then, output has taken off, but it is still not enough to meet domestic demand. In 2025, according to Insee (source in French), 331,000 new electric passenger cars were registered in France, compared with 216,000 produced in French factories.

But six out of ten electric cars made in France are exported, notably to the United Kingdom and other European markets. In the end, only 26% of new electric vehicles bought in France are manufactured on national soil. Car makers, therefore, have to rely heavily on imports to supply the French market.

France remains far off the target (source in French) set by the government of producing two million electric vehicles a year by 2030. The Élysée nonetheless highlights progress in the electrification of the car fleet and welcomes the opening of four battery plants in the north of the country.

As for every edition, the presidential trip to the show will be preceded, on Sunday evening, by a dinner at the Élysée bringing together representatives of the automotive sector, the presidency has confirmed. Around 60 stakeholders are expected, including carmakers, equipment suppliers, battery manufacturers and companies specialising in rare earths, both French and European.

The presidency notes that no brand boss or Chinese exhibitor will attend the dinner. The show itself, however, will host numerous Chinese manufacturers.

The following day, Emmanuel Macron will stroll through the aisles of the Motor Show, with stops scheduled at the stands of Stellantis, Renault and equipment supplier Valeo. The visit will end with a roundtable devoted to autonomous cars.

Related Stellantis to halt four French plants for several days over supply shortage

A strict European preference

While China has an export capacity of 55 million vehicles of all types, compared with 12 million for Europe, Paris wants the EU to "finally support what it produces" in the face of the wave that is coming.

When it comes to electric cars, France argues that European public subsidies should more strongly favour vehicles produced within the 27 member states. The aim is to establish a "genuine" European preference that covers the entire value chain, from batteries to spare parts.

Even though Paris remains open to "high-quality" Chinese investment in Europe, notably including technology transfers, France wants to avoid the creation of "screwdriver factories", where only "the last bolt is tightened in Europe" while all the other components are made elsewhere.

This is a position Paris needs to align with Berlin, which "is not easy", as France and Germany have "very different" models, the Élysée points out.

"Germany is a country that exports far more vehicles than France, so the interests are inevitably not entirely the same," says a source at the presidency of the Republic.

In practice, Berlin fears retaliatory measures against its own manufacturers, which are highly dependent on Chinese customers, if access to the European market were to be restricted for Beijing, whether through a strict European preference or environmental criteria.

Talks with Germany still ongoing

German business and finance daily Handelsblatt reported on Wednesday that an agreement had been reached between France and Germany: Paris would agree to further relax the European target for cutting CO2 emissions from new cars by 2035, lowering it from 90%, as proposed by the European Commission, to 80% compared with 2021. In return, Berlin would back stricter "Made in Europe" rules.

The Élysée has denied this ahead of the Motor Show: "There is no agreement", but "talks" are indeed under way over European preference.

After a day reserved for the press, featuring the president's visit, the Paris Motor Show, one of the oldest and best-attended in the world, will open its doors to the public from 13 to 18 October at the Porte de Versailles exhibition centre.

World.title: Nepal flash floods sweep away houses, five people missing
World.content:
Flash floods hit central Nepal on Sunday, sweeping away houses and leaving at least five people missing, officials said, weeks after devastating flooding that killed hundreds.

 

Videos circulating online showed a dark, debris-filled river surging through the hills in Gorkha district.

"What we know is that a dry landslide had blocked the river and then it burst to cause the flood", said national disaster agency chief Dharam Raj Uprety.

Some 45 houses were swept away, with the flood also damaging three hydropower projects and four bridges.

According to the disaster agency, at least 82 people, including nine foreigners, have been rescued from the affected areas.

"Five people are unaccounted for", Uprety said.

In this photo provided by the Nepal Army, Budhi Gandaki river in north central Nepal is seen in spate, Sunday, 11 October 2026. Nepal Army via AP/Nepal Army

Four helicopters were deployed to support rescue and evacuation efforts as water levels in the Budhi Gandaki continued to rise.

Authorities earlier issued an alert, urging residents to move away from the river to safer areas.

Nepal still recovering from latest flooding

The latest flooding comes with Nepal still recovering from devastating floods, triggered by a mountain glacial collapse on August 26, which killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing.

"The flood looked similar... It was very scary, and it still feels like a nightmare for us," said local official Laxmi Gurung of Chumnubri rural municipality.

"Our house is gone, we have no electricity... but there have been no casualties."

The Kathmandu‑based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) said the floods highlight the "range of hazards capable of generating destructive floods in Himalayan river systems".

"While response efforts must remain the immediate priority, understanding what triggered this flood, will be critical for reducing future risks and strengthening resilience," ICIMOD's director general Pema Gyamtsho said in a statement.

Heavy rainfall in late September also triggered floods and landslides, killing at least 21 people, according to the disaster agency.

World.title: Houthi war risks dragging Israel and Turkey into Horn of Africa standoff
World.content:
The escalating clash between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia now threatens to ignite the already tense rivalry between Israel and Turkey in the Horn of Africa. This week, Turkey threw its military weight behind Saudi Arabia, while Somaliland – a self-declared state recognised only by Israel – is urgently seeking Israeli military support.

Advertising

Somaliland, a breakaway state from Somalia, is calling on Israel to provide military hardware. “We need air defence systems,” Mohamed Osman Fadal, a senior foreign affairs adviser to Somaliland’s president, said in a Middle East Eye interview this month.

Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi made a similar request last month for Israeli military support.

Last December, Israel became the first nation to recognise Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991. Because of its close ties to Israel, Somaliland now fears it could become a target for the Houthis, who operate from Yemen just across the Gulf of Aden and have previously targeted Israel.

“The Houthi threat is growing; it’s a major issue,” said Gallia Lindenstrauss of the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University.

“Access to the Red Sea and Somaliland’s location just across from Yemen are very important, and I think this is where Israel recognises that it’s difficult to deal with the threat only from afar, and it’s important to have allies in the Horn of Africa,” she added.

Israel, which is in the midst of an election campaign ahead of the 27 October vote, has not commented on the request. But Lindenstrauss predicts a favourable response. “Obviously, if you look at the location, there should be some military support," she said.

Turkey’s backing for Somalia

Yet Somaliland’s call for military aid is fuelled by more than just anxiety over the Houthis. Somalia’s government is still intent on reclaiming Somaliland, branding it a rogue state. At the same time, Turkey has stepped up its military support for Somalia, deploying F-16s and advanced drones in January, and running its largest overseas military base to train Somali troops.

Somaliland president makes 'historic' visit to Israel

“Turkey has strong defence cooperation with Somalia; Somaliland sees that as an issue for them. It sees them as a potential future threat down the road. And so that’s why they’re calling for Israeli security support,” explained Horn of Africa analyst Omar Mahmood of the International Crisis Group.

“I think what’s happening is both sides, Somalia and Somaliland, are drawing external actors into their local dispute,” added Mahmood. “So it’s elevating what has been an unresolved but a local dispute for quite some time into something broader, something more regional.”

Tensions between Turkey and Israel have also been mounting, fuelled by Israel’s ongoing wars in Gaza and Lebanon and Ankara’s vocal support for Hamas. Both nations now see each other as an increasing threat.

“There is a security dilemma evolving between Turkey and Israel,” warns Lindenstrauss. “What Turkey does for its security, Israel sees as threatening. What Israel does for its defences in [Syria] is seen as threatening.”

Soli Ozel, an expert on Turkey at the Institut Montaigne in France, warns that because Somalia holds such strategic value for Turkey, any Israeli military involvement in Somaliland could dangerously escalate the situation.

“They may consider the deployment of Israeli missiles in Somaliland another destabilising factor,” said Ozel. “But I don’t think that the F-16s or the drones would be used against Somaliland, honestly; at least for the moment, I wouldn’t expect that to happen.”

Lebanon becomes latest battleground in Turkish-Israeli tensions

Containment, not conflict

Ozel argues that while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan are trading increasingly bellicose rhetoric, both countries are engaged in a high-stakes battle of containment rather than conflict.

“The theatrics and the realities of Turkish-Israeli relations may not be exactly the same,” explained Ozel. “I don’t think they will fight, but they are both showing their colours, right? Israel sent missiles to Somaliland; the Turks send F-16s and drones in order to set limits to what the other party will do.”

Turkey is preparing to expand its military footprint in the region. This week, Turkey and Pakistan pledged armed support to Saudi Arabia against the Houthis under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed in August, a pact binding the three nations to mutual defence.

While the specifics remain unclear, Lindenstrauss notes that despite rising friction between Turkey and Israel, both countries may still find common cause in confronting the Houthis.

“I think the recognition that the Houthis are not something that is seen as only Israel’s problem, and it’s not just a minor proxy of Iran, but it’s a major problem that many states have to join together to deal with. I think that’s actually good news,” said Lindenstrauss.

Turkey warns it could be Israel's 'next enemy' as tensions escalate

Yet Mahmood cautions that as clashes in the Red Sea escalate, Israel’s possible deployment of military hardware to Somaliland points to a worrying new trend.

“Horn actors need to realise that while they’re inviting external actors in to support their own ambitions locally, to get one step over their political adversaries, they risk turning their theatre into a wider proxy battleground. And so certainly, I think there’s a risk that those types of tensions can spill over,” he warned.

World.title: Saudi Arabia: Second strike hits Riyadh airport
World.content:
Sunday's strike came as the King Khalid International Airport remained closed after a deadly attack on Saturday, and after a warning from Houthi rebels in Yemen that "worse is yet to come." Dammam airport was also hit.

King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was struck by an "unidentified projectile" for the second time in two days on Sunday, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.

"King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was subjected to a new attack on Sunday afternoon," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement, adding that it "resulted in injuries, and the assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities are still under way."

Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki also said that a cruise missile had been intercepted by air defense systems in the vicinity of the airport, but no further details were immediately available.

The Houthis later claimed responsibility for the strikes, saying they had "carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones."

A spokesman said the group targeted the Riyadh airport multiple times, as well as the Dammam airport in the east of the country and two facilities belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco.

Later on Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed an attack on Dammam airport.

Sunday's strikes came as Riyadh airport remained closed following an attack on Saturday which killed 12 people and injured over 300 more — the deadliest such strike on the kingdom in over a decade.

On Sunday, the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia confirmed that one of its citizens died after being wounded in Saturday's attack.

"It is learnt that one Indian national injured in the Riyadh attack has unfortunately lost his life today," read a statement posted on social media. "We convey our heartfelt condolences to the family of the deceased."

Houthis warn airlines after deadly Riyadh airport strike To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Houthis warn airlines to avoid Saudi Arabia

The latest Houthi strikes also came just hours after the rebel group warned airlines and travelers to avoid Saudi airports.

"We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces," read a statement released by the group on social media. It added that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina would not be targeted.

"We ‌urge everyone to take our warnings seriously," the statement continued, stating: "Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions."

What now for Saudi Arabia after Riyadh airport attack? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why are Saudi airports being targeted?

Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the rebels seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, including around the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The Houthi-run health authority claimed this weekend that 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in the last five weeks, 60% of them women and children. Earlier on Sunday, it said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa.

The Houthi-run Al Masirah TV also reported that Saudi Arabia had struck the international airport in Sanaa on Sunday afternoon.

There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims.

"Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the Houthi-run Foreign Ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah TV on Sunday, adding that its ​actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.

What has Saudi Arabia said about the Riyadh airport attacks?

The Saudi-led coalition, which supports the internationally recognized Yemeni government in its conflict against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, vowed a tough response to the attack, which it labeled a "full-fledged war crime."

The Houthi strikes on Riyadh come amid a surge in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia this week, which have targeted other airports, military sites and oil infrastructure.

The spike in attacks has followed a major military offensive by the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis.

The rebels, one of Tehran's regional proxies, have been fighting Yemen's government, which is recognized by the international community, since the outbreak of a civil war over a decade ago.

While a truce in 2022 froze the conflict, it failed to secure a lasting peace deal. The US-Israeli war with Iran has seen fighting flare up again in Yemen, worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis.

Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How has the international community reacted to the Riyadh strikes?

US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he would be speaking to Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in the wake of the attack, which he said was "not acceptable."

Trump also said that the US was "going to look" at potentially joining Saudi strikes against the rebels.

On Sunday, European leaders expressed their "shock" at the attack on Riyadh airport.

The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia" as she condemned the "dangerous escalation."

"These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shock waves sent through the world," von der Leyen said.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul "firmly" condemned what he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation".

"Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he said on X.

UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting slammed the attacks as "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation," while the French Foreign Ministry condemned the "heinous attack" and stressed its "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia.

Russia, which is a strategic partner of Iran, also condemned the Houthis' attack and called for the hostilities to end "through political and diplomatic means."

Australia, meanwhile, has urged its citizens in the Saudi capital to "shelter in place" amid the escalating attacks.

World.title: German 'lawfare': When lawsuits become a political weapon
World.content:
The Left Party is suing two government ministers for accusing them of antisemitism, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz has been sued several times by various parties. Is German politics descending into "lawfare?"

A verbal slip, an attempted quip, a lawsuit: Things can move fast in the rancorous atmosphere that currently rules German politics.

The brief exchange happened on a political TV talk show shortly after the Berlin election on September 20, won by the socialist Left Party. The show's host, Maybrit Illner, quickly corrected herself after accidentally saying of the Left Party's Berlin mayoral candidate, "Elif Eralp says she is an antisemite…. She is not an antisemite."

One of her guests, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), responded immediately: "Na doch" (or, "well, yes she is"). In the angry fallout, the Left Party's lawyers jumped on these two words, and have filed a lawsuit, arguing that this amounted to defamation of Eralp, as it falsely suggested that the Left Party politician did indeed consider herself antisemitic.

Not only that, the suit stated, Dobrindt's remark would "undermine her integrity as a political officeholder" and hinder her attempts to form a government in Berlin.

It was not the first time the Left Party has got its lawyers involved following its election victory, as it gets bombarded by accusations of antisemitism from the center right, especially over an incident at an election campaign event in Berlin when a rapper chanted "Death to the IDF" — the Israel Defense Forces, or the Israeli army.

Economy Minister Katherina Reiche also angered the socialist party by giving a speech in which she said that the party was now "openly embracing antisemitism." A video of the speech was posted on the Economy Ministry's Instagram account.

Power of the lawsuit

The lawsuit has become an increasingly popular weapon in German politics in recent years, usually by deploying sections 185, 186 and 187 of the German Criminal Code , which cover offenses including insult, defamation and "intentional defamation," which means knowingly asserting or disseminating untrue facts about others. Theoretically, the punishment can be a fine or up to a year in prison.

In September 2025, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) pressed defamation charges against ChancellorFriedrich Merz after he said that the far-right party's policy of remigration amounted to "ethnic cleansing."

Similarly, the Green Party in Berlin brought hate speech charges against Merz last year, when he said "we still have this problem in the cityscape" when describing the presence of immigrants.

In another case, the Green Party's own Robert Habeck was sued in 2024 by the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason(BSW) for claiming that the new upstart party was "buying votes" on the internet by building up "troll armies." Prosecutors dropped the case after Habeck agreed to pay €12,000 ($13,500) to three charities without admitting any wrongdoing, on the grounds that there was only limited public interest in a criminal procedure.

What's behind the rising polarization in German politics? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But charges like these, especially when politicians claim defamation, have little chance of success. "Prosecutors usually dismiss such cases very quickly due to a lack of sufficient grounds for suspicion," media lawyer Christian Solmecke, of the firm WBS Legal, told DW in an email.

"The Federal Constitutional Court has consistently held that, in the political arena, the boundaries of what is permissible are significantly wider than in the private sphere," Solmecke added. "Anyone who voluntarily enters the political arena must also be prepared to endure sharp, polemical, exaggerated and hurtful criticism."

Felix Zimmermann, editor-in-chief of the legal affairs outletLegal Tribune Online (LTO) , agrees, because German law makes a careful distinction between an opinion and a false statement. "'Antisemitic' or 'not antisemitic' is an opinion, especially at the moment, when people have very different definitions of it," Zimmermann told DW.

Lawsuits as PR

That hasn't deterred politicians from trying it more and more often. "We are undoubtedly observing a new level of intensity and scale of this practice," said Solmecke. "Political culture has become harsher and more polarized. The threshold for no longer merely engaging political opponents through debate, but instead outright criminalizing them, has dropped dramatically."

The danger, Solmecke argues, is that this often amounts to the "misuse" of law enforcement agencies as political instruments.

But lawfare appears to be effective as a political tactic, not least because it's a guaranteed headline. "From the point of view of the parties filing the complaints, they are highly effective as a PR strategy," said Solmecke. "The political benefit arises entirely independently of the legal outcome."

Elif Eralp: From daughter of refugees to Berlin mayor? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the Left Party's case, Zimmermann thinks it certainly pays to show you won't stand to be called antisemitic — not least because Eralp has repeatedly underlined her commitment to the Jewish community in Berlin.

"I think it's mainly about the fact that the Left Party wants to form a coalition in Berlin and Ms. Eralp wants to become mayor," Zimmermann said. "So of course it's good if you're insulted to challenge it, as a signal."

When lawsuits have a constitutional point

The motion against Katherina Reiche, on the other hand, may have much better chances — because she chose to post her inflammatory speech on the Economy Ministry's official social media channels. This could, Zimmermann said, well be seen as a violation of the "principle of neutrality," a constitutional rule that forbids the state from vilifying any particular political party.

"That is of course difficult for a politician, because if they say it on their own account they're allowed, but if they say it on the ministry's account they're not allowed," said Zimmermann. "It's a little absurd, because you're effectively splitting one person into two."

But even though the Left Party filed the complaint against Reiche as an urgent motion, the Constitutional Court may take several weeks, if not months, to actually decide the case — by which time the coalition negotiations in Berlin may have long since finished and Reiche's speech has had its effect.

The consequences for Reiche, in other words, will be limited — even if her ministry is forced to take down the post and the Left Party can eventually claim a victory.

Edited by: Rina Goldenberg

World.title: Trump announces 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine
World.content:
US President Donald Trump says both sides have agreed to stop targeting oil refineries, power plants and other energy infrastructure immediately.

US President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure.

"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," the president wrote on his Truth Social network.

Trump continued: "Both parties have agreed," before urging restraint from both Kyiv and Moscow: "Do not break it!"

Zelenskyy: Energy ceasefire 'news for me'

There was ‌no immediate ​confirmation ⁠from Moscow, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the news site Axios within minutes of Trump's post that the ceasefire was "news for me."

"The ceasefire announcement was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree. If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins; we are ready and we will accept it," he told Axios.

How Russia turned sanctions into a diesel deal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Earlier Sunday, Zelenskyy repeated his stance that Ukraine would stop hitting Russian oil refineries if the Kremlin curbed its energy attacks.

Trump and Zelenskyy have argued this week over Ukraine's attacks on Russian diesel facilities, which the US president said have contributed to a global diesel shortage, rather than the Iran war.

Trump needs lower fuel prices before midterms

Trump said Friday he had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia.

The controversial move was an attempt to bring down high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections next month.

However, this move undercuts fresh US sanctions Trump signed just weeks ago to further hurt Russian energy revenues funding the war.

Backing Zelenskyy in the Trump row, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that she "fully supported" the call for a "ceasefire that protects global food supplies and energy infrastructure in Ukraine and Russia."

"And my full support for President Zelenskyy as he leads the fight for his people's freedom," she wrote online.

French President Emmanuel Macron said his country backs a "real energy ceasefire," but lamented that "Russia continues to refuse that."

War abroad, soaring prices at home: is Trump in trouble? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Blackouts and refinery strikes

Russia has repeatedly struck Ukraine's power plants and transmission lines around Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa and elsewhere, to lower civilian morale, especially during the winter months.

Recently, Ukraine has stepped up long-range strikes deep inside Russian territory, targeting major oil refineries and other facilities to curb Moscow's refining capacity and fuel supplies.

Kyiv on Sunday pressed on its campaign against Russian infrastructure, hitting a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex.

It was the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV to undergo surgery to remove lump on lung
World.content:
The pontiff said he would be operated on "in the coming days" to remove a lung nodule, which he said was found at "a very early stage."

Pope Leo XIV said Sunday that he will undergo surgery this week to remove a lump on his lung.

"During recent medical checks, a nodule on my lung was found. It has been detected at a very early stage and is very localized," the 71-year-old said during his weekly address in St Peter's Square in the Vatican.

"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene and so, following their advice, I have decided to have the operation to remove it. The operation is already planned in the coming days," he added.

Pope Leo to undergo lung nodule surgery To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do we know about the pope's condition?

This is his first major health scare since the 71-year-old American became pope in 2025.

A lung nodule is a small, contained lesion that is smaller than 3 centimeters (1 inch) and can be benign.

According to the American Thoracic Society, fewer than 5% of lung nodules turn out to be cancerous.

The American Cancer Society says the nodules sometimes appear on CT scans of the chest or abdomen during searches for trauma or lung infections that are unrelated to cancer screenings.

Leo is younger than most popes. His predecessor, Francis, was five years older when he assumed the role, while Francis' predecessor, Benedict XVI, was 78 at the start of his tenure.

Leo is not known to have had any previous health issues, and leads a relatively active lifestyle.

World.title: A migrant boat sank off the coast of Djibouti with the UN reporting over 200 people dead or missing
World.content:
The UN migration agency has reported that at least 139 people were killed and 84 remain missing after a migrant boat sank overnight on its way to Yemen. At least 80 Ethiopians survived the incident but 15 children died.

The United Nations International Organization for Migration (IOM) on Sunday said that at least 139 people were killed when a migrant boat carrying an estimated 305 people capsized off the coast of Djibouti in northeastern Africa.

At least 84 people remained missing in what is thought to be one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations.

In a statement, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac called the loss of life "devastating," adding, "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities" by trying to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen and reach Gulf countries.

"Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East," according to the IOM.

IOM representatives said, "Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations as fears grow for those still missing."

Djibouti to Yemen a dangerous crossing

The IOM says it has detected more than 20,000 crossings from Djibouti to Yemen — which is currently in the middle of a raging civil war — in the past month. More than 900 migrants were killed attempting the passage in 2025.

The IOM says most of those attempting to cross are from Ethiopia and Somalia. The 80 survivors from Saturday night's capsizing were all Ethiopian nationals.

The IOM on Sunday urged "donors and partners to strengthen support for Djibouti's response, including search and rescue operations and life-saving assistance."

Of the bodies so far recovered, 52 were men, 42 were women and 15 were children.

World.title: Poland arrests man over plot to kill PM Donald Tusk
World.content:
Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed the arrest hours after police received information about a possible assassination plot. Poland is still reeling from a wave of school violence this week.

Poland on Sunday detained a man accused of plotting to assassinate Prime Minister Donald Tusk and the country's defense minister, the PM wrote on X.

"The man threatening an attack has been detained," Tusk wrote on X, praising the police for their "swift and decisive action."

The Interior Minister also confirmed the arrest. No details about the man's identity were made public.

Security chiefs convene urgent talks

Tusk's tweet followed an emergency meeting by Poland's security services to discuss what officials said was a potential attack against both the prime minister and Defense ‌Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz.

The meeting was convened at short notice after police received a tip-off about a possible assassination attempt, a spokesperson for the Interior Ministry wrote in a post on X.

While the nature of the apparent threat was not immediately clear, Poland remains on high alert after a wave of violent attacks at schools in the country this week.

Poland, which borders Ukraine, has also been facing growing security threats from hybrid attacks by Russia in recent months.

What do we know about the school attacks in Poland?

Poland is reeling from three knife attacks at schools in just four days this week, which have left at least one person dead and injured many others, including children.

The first incident was on Wednesday, when a 19-year-old student at a vocational school in the central Mazovian province injured nine people when he attacked his fellow students and teachers with a sharp object.

A day later, a 15-year-old killed a school caretaker and injured two others at his former school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, also in the same province. Tusk said the suspect had worn a camera mounted to his helmet to film the attack.

On Saturday, a 21-year-old woman attacked an adult education school in Warsaw, wounding three other women.

Polish police have detained 117 people across the country for carrying knives or dangerous weapons, as well as for threatening to attack schools or students. Police checked 64,000 schools, most of them in central Mazovian province.

Police said Friday that cybercrime investigators have found no evidence that a social media challenge is fueling the wave of youth violence, or that the attacks were coordinated.

What did Tusk say about the school attacks?

On Sunday morning, Donald Tusk said the attacks were "spontaneous actions" that were fueled by rising "glorification of violence" online.

"We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said during the government crisis meeting.

"In the past years and months, we have noted — globally and in Poland — a rise in the fascination with violence," Tusk continued.

The prime minister blamed "nihilistic violence" for the wave of attacks, rather than a specific political ideology. However, he did acknowledge that "some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment."

Tusk added that authorities have observed an increase in online searches for Nazi or far-right content and for "mass killers who have become idols online."

The prime minister pointed to a "civilizational phenomenon" of children becoming more exposed to violence online through video games or crime stories.

Tusk added that police checks would continue at schools across the country next week to make sure children who have been exposed to these stories of knife attacks do not "get stupid and unsafe thoughts" of perpetrating copycat attacks.

World.title: Pakistan: President puts Khan stronghold province under emergency rule
World.content:
President Asif Ali Zardari has effectively suspended the provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The northwestern state is an epicenter of support for former PM Imran Khan and run by his PTI party.

Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari on Sunday announced that the northwestern Pakistani province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had been put under emergency rule, effectively removing power from former Prime Minster Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.

The imposition of emergency rule comes as thousands of Khan supporters continue to stage anti-government protests and demand the former leader be released from jail.

Current Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif proposed the move, which Zardari signed into order on Sunday.

The suspension of regional government was justified under constitutional articles that allow the central government to confront security threats and give it sweeping powers in emergency situations.

Sharif's government claims regional authorities have not done enough to curb Islamist violence in the province.

Authorities have set up massive roadblocks across Pakistan to keep Khan supporters at bay Image: Abdul Majeed/AFP

Why is Pakistan's government taking control of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa?

Last Sunday, thousands of Khan's supporters began to make their way from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to the Pakistani capital, Islamabad.

Organizers had declared their intent to rally hundreds of thousands more along the way in hopes of bringing about Khan's release from prison.

Despite being jailed since 2023, Khan, a popular former cricket star, maintains great influence in Pakistan, with he and his followers convinced that his imprisonment is the result of political persecution.

Khan, who began his term as prime minister in August 2018, was ousted from office in April 2022 after losing a no-confidence vote.

Khan's supporters want him released from jail Image: Faridullah Khan/DW

He has been in prison since August 2023.

Beyond corruption and treason charges, he was also accused of inciting violence after widespread anti-government protests in May 2023. Khan rejects the charges as a politically motivated plot to keep him away from power. He remains a popular political figure in Pakistan.

Khan's supporters claim that the 2024 election that brought Shehbaz Sharif back to power was rigged — an accusation the government denies.

Pakistan has seen a resurgence of terror attacks over the past several months and the Sharif government accuses Khan's PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, which is largely thought to be behind the attacks.

The PTI rejects these accusations as a baseless smear campaign.

World.title: Germany rejects Trump demand, 'fully supports' Zelenskyy
World.content:
10/11/2026 October 11, 2026 Deutsche Bank CEO: Political extremism putting off foreign investors

Christian Sewing, CEO of Deutsche Bank, Germany's biggest, warned that the growing strength of both the far right and the far left is spooking foreign investors.

Sewing told the tabloid Bild that recent election victories for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and post-communist Left Party "pose a significant risk for Germany and should not be downplayed."

The Deutsche Bank boss said it mattered little that the elections were on the state and local level. "You can't expect a foreign investor to immediately draw a distinction ‌between a state government and Germany as a whole," he ‌said.

"It's ​seen as Germany as a whole and I think that from an investor's point of view, that's understandable."

Some economists say the AfD is creating an atmosphere that will drive away much needed skilled labor as well as foreign investors.

The Left Party, meanwhile, won victory in Berlin promising to expropriate residential property companies' holdings to lower housing costs in the German capital.

"Whether ​it's Saxony-Anhalt with ⁠the AfD or what's happening here in Berlin," said Sewing, "it's anything but conducive to economic growth. ⁠And it's anything ​but investment-friendly."

Sewing said Chancellor Friedrich Merz must get on with carrying out reforms and reviving the economy, saying, "That is the only response we have to the far-right and far-left extremists in this country."

World.title: Gabriel Rufián será candidato por Esquerra Republicana el 29-N
World.content:
Gabriel Rufián se queda en Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya (ERC). El actual portavoz en el Congreso repetirá como cabeza de cartel este 29-N, ha explicado el partido independentista en un comunicado este domingo. Se le designará con el visto bueno de un tercio de la ejecutiva, no por avales de los militantes, y la nota no revela las condiciones específicas que han permitido el acuerdo casi in extremis. Sobre la mesa está un una vía de “cooperación” con Podemos para que, por ejemplo, Rufián pueda hacer algún acto de campaña fuera de Cataluña y así poder poner su tirón electoral al servicio de la movilización en el resto del Estado pero que está condicionado a que los morados no se presenten en Cataluña o acepten un puesto en la lista republicana como independientes.

La decisión pone fin a días de incertidumbre, en los que incluso desde las filas de Esquerra se planteaban escenarios alternativos en el caso de que Rufián optara finalmente por dar el salto a la arena estatal. Hasta ayer mismo, voces de diferentes sectores le pedían al republicano que se atreviera, dando a entender que aún había margen para negociar el encaje en el Frente Amplio. “Hay espacio para todos, se necesita mucha gente, no solo una cara, sino muchas”, dijo la exalcaldesa Ada Colau el pasado viernes, interpelándole de manera directa. Todo parece indicar que ahora ambos pugnarán por los votos en un espacio con muchas fronteras en Barcelona. En 2023, la marca Sumar fue segunda tras el PSC y ERC la cuarta, tras el PP.

La apuesta de Rufián por una suma amplia de las izquierdas para hacer frente a un posible Gobierno de PP y Vox, con Esquerra incluso teniendo un papel central en la operación, chocó desde un principio con la cúpula de su partido, que descarta diluir sus siglas. Formaciones como Bildu o BNG tampoco la recibieron con mucho entusiasmo. Con todo, el republicano no tiró la toalla e intentó hasta el final lograr algún tipo de suma y que aún sigue a la espera de si hay encaje entre el actual Frente Amplio y Podemos.

El portavoz republicano en las Cortes no se ha presentado de manera oficial a la carrera por encabezar la lista de Barcelona de ERC, por lo cual no ha tenido que recoger los casi 400 avales fijados por el reglamento. Nadie más ha optado por ocupar el número uno de esa candidatura y, para estos casos, se contemplan otras vías de proclamación. Aquí se usará el visto bueno de un tercio de los miembros de la ejecutiva.

Los de Junqueras anunciarán también esta tarde qué otros candidatos han pasado el corte para aspirar a ser cabeza de cartel en Lleida, Girona y Tarragona. La competencia solo estaba abierta en la segunda provincia, pues allí compiten las dos diputadas Teresa Jordà y Etna Estrems. Esta semana, además, continuará el proceso de los congresos territoriales y las reuniones sectoriales que han de nutrir de otros nombres las listas y que el día 20 han de estar ya aprobadas por la ejecutiva y el Consell Nacional, el máximo órgano entre congresos. El plazo límite para presentarlas ante la Junta Electoral es el día 26.

Las negociaciones entre la cúpula de ERC y Rufián han sido especialmente discretas, pero no por ello han estado exentas de momentos de tensión. Una de las incógnitas que sigue sobre la mesa es cuáles son las cesiones hechas por Junqueras para lograr que el portavoz aceptara quedarse, incluso con encuestas de todo tipo que le auguraban un gran desempeño si se decantaba por dar el salto a nivel estatal. Rufián, en otros momentos, había puesto sobre la mesa poder contar con más interlocución política en Madrid, tener influencia en la confección de las listas y en la futura bancada y conservar su equipo.

De momento, los nombres que han trascendido para liderar las listas de las otras tres provincias o que serán propuestos por federaciones de peso como la de Barcelona están más cerca de Junqueras que del flamante candidato. La pérdida de sintonía de Rufián con el resto de la bancada fue uno de los grandes dolores de cabeza del partido esta legislatura y de momento se impone cierto continuismo. El exvicepresident tiene un comodín y es que el 25% de los nombres de independientes que van a las listas son de elección suya y, ahí, podría darle margen a Rufián para poner su toque.

Esos puestos también serían claves dentro del acuerdo de cara a darle un encaje a Podem en la lista. ERC espera que los morados reconozcan a ERC como la fuerza de referencia en Cataluña y por tanto no concurran a las elecciones. Así se evitaría una coalición que implique diluir las siglas y darle representación. Si ese marco queda claro, Rufián, con previa autorización, podrá participar en algún acto de campaña de Podemos en otras ciudades españolas, algo inédito. “Ya hemos dicho que si podemos ayudar de alguna manera a que la izquierda española le vaya bien, lo haríamos”, ahondan desde la dirección. ERC ha hecho mítines fuera de Cataluña para las elecciones europeas, donde ha concurrido con Bildu y BNG, y la secretaria general Elisenda Alamany dejó la puerta abierta, el pasado lunes, a que se pudieran hacer actos similares en el camino al 29-N.

ERC logró siete escaños en las pasadas elecciones generales: cuatro por Barcelona, uno por Girona, otro por Lleida y el último por Tarragona. Obtuvo entonces 466.020 votos, perdiendo casi la mitad de los que había obtenido en 2019. Entonces había cosechado 17 diputados.

World.title: “Si un alumno no entrena la capacidad de frustración, entre lo bueno y lo fácil elegirá lo fácil”
World.content:
Horizontes laborales en un futuro dominado por la IA. Conversaciones sobre la educación que queremos | Pensemos el mañana (Episodio 5)

Miguel Antón, profesor del IESE Business School, y su alumna Ana Jara charlan sobre qué habilidades deben desarrollar las futuras generaciones tras la irrupción de la IA en el mundo laboral: dominar la comunicación oral y el trabajo en equipo, preservar la capacidad de concentración y desarrollar el pensamiento crítico

Miguel Antón PROFESOR DE FINANZAS Y DIRECTOR DEL MIM Y DEL MIF EN IESE BUSINESS SCHOOL Es licenciado y máster en Economía por la Universidad de Navarra y doctor en Finanzas por la London School of Economics. En el IESE Business School su misión es guiar y formar a aquellos jóvenes que quieren convertirse en los ejecutivos del mañana en grandes compañías Ana Jara ALUMNA DEL MÁSTER EN MANAGEMENT EN IESE BUSINESS SCHOOL Después de estudiar Humanidades se matriculó en una escuela de negocios para dar un giro a su carrera y buscar mejores salidas laborales. Su objetivo al finalizar esta formación es incursionar en el universo de las grandes consultoras

¿Qué vamos a hacer cuando las máquinas hagan nuestro trabajo? La pregunta que abre esta nueva entrega de Pensemos el mañana, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja y EL PAÍS para responder a los desafíos que presenta la educación, es la que articula la conversación entre dos perfiles muy concernidos, cada uno a su manera, por el futuro del mundo del trabajo: por un lado, el profesor del IESE Miguel Antón, cuya misión es analizar en profundidad los cambios en el mercado para ofrecer a los futuros ejecutivos las herramientas con las que puedan hacerse un hueco en una gran compañía; y por otro Ana Jara, una de sus alumnas, que observa con cierta inquietud cómo la irrupción de la inteligencia artificial (IA) puede cambiar por completo la estructura de las empresas.

“¿Un consejo para los jóvenes que quieran ser exitosos en el trabajo? Que comuniquen bien”

En este entorno volátil, Antón ofrece una receta en la que destacan varios pilares: dominar a la perfección la comunicación oral y saber trabajar en equipo; preservar la capacidad de concentración en un mundo inundado de estímulos; desarrollar el pensamiento crítico para manejar y cuestionar grandes volúmenes de información; entrenar la capacidad de frustración y buscar conocerse a uno mismo: las fortalezas, los deseos y los sueños más profundos, pero también las debilidades.

“Los alumnos tenemos miedo porque todo está evolucionando tan rápido que no sabemos si en dos años vamos a tener trabajo”

Un consejo, este último, que lleva al profesor a vaticinar que las nuevas generaciones, representadas en alumnos como Ana, deberán volver a plantearse a aquellas preguntas esenciales que en la Antigua Grecia dieron origen a la Filosofía, no solo para encontrar su sitio no solo en el mercado de trabajo sino en el mundo: ¿Quiénes somos?, ¿de dónde venimos?, ¿hacia dónde vamos?

Pensemos la educación del futuro ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja, busca fomentar el conocimiento, los valores de la educación, un aprendizaje sostenible y responsable y dar respuestas a los grandes desafíos de la educación del futuro. El proyecto pivota sobre seis ejes: 1 Aprendizaje y sentido vital 2 Bienestar y salud mental 3 Futuro y empleabilidad 4 Sostenibilidad y sentido colectivo 5 Tecnología y ética 6 Carácter y ciudadanía ¿Qué está ocurriendo en estos tiempos de cambios profundos y transversales? ¿Cuáles son los grandes retos para afrontar la transformación que viene? ¿Qué educación necesitamos? Diferentes personalidades de todos los ámbitos nos ayudarán a responder a estas y otras preguntas destinadas a impulsar cambios, dinamizar ideas y apoyar propuestas con impacto pedagógico y social. ‘Pensemos el mañana’ es un proyecto inspirador para las futuras generaciones llamadas a conquistar nuevas cotas del saber en un mundo complejo y cambiante.

World.title: Las cajas de ahorro islámicas están de moda en Turquía
World.content:
Sus sucursales se han multiplicado en los últimos años, especialmente en las capitales de provincia del interior de Turquía, donde ocupan los puestos de honor de las principales avenidas. Sus lustrosos y modernos escaparates prometen hacer realidad los sueños de sus clientes: adquirir una casa, un automóvil o una tienda “sin necesidad de créditos” o “sin pagar intereses”. Son las Empresas de Financiación mediante Ahorro (TFS, en turco), una suerte de cajas de ahorro islámicas basadas en los principios de las finanzas islámicas, como el rechazo a los intereses —aunque esto, como mucho en las finanzas islámicas, tiene truco— y la mutualización del riesgo: un grupo de ahorradores aporta cuotas mensuales a un fondo común y, por turnos o por sorteo, cada miembro recibe el capital solicitado para adquirir la propiedad elegida.

Algunas, como Eminevim o Fuzul, se han convertido en grandes grupos empresariales. Comenzaron su existencia como sociedades de ahorro colectivo creadas durante los años noventa por empresarios del entorno del islamismo político deseosos de financiarse fuera de unos bancos controlados por la —entonces dominante— élite laica del país. Otras quebraron o fueron liquidadas, pues operaban en un vacío legal. Su historia cambió en 2021, cuando el Gobierno del conservador Recep Tayyip Erdogan endureció los requisitos de solvencia, profesionalizándolas y poniéndolas bajo el control de la Agencia de Regulación y Supervisión Bancaria. Pero sobre todo, su verdadera explosión se ha dado desde que, en 2023, Mehmet Simsek fue nombrado ministro de Finanzas con el mandato de reducir una tasa de inflación que había llegado a superar el 100% interanual. Aplicó el manual más ortodoxo e instó al Banco Central a elevar el precio del dinero, lo que ha supuesto que los bancos restrinjan los créditos y eleven los intereses de sus préstamos hipotecarios por encima del 40% anual (la inflación sigue sin bajar del 30%). “Debido a las medidas de macroprudencia financiera, se ha hecho muy difícil acceder a créditos bancarios. Aunque, al inicio, las TFS se dirigían a personas de bajos ingresos, ahora les interesan a trabajadores de cuello blanco e incluso a gente de ingresos altos que no puede acceder a créditos bancarios”, explica Ahmet Büyükduman, analista financiero.

Una comisión fija por adelantado

Frente a los elevados intereses que demandan los bancos —y que implican que se termine pagando casi cuatro veces el capital inicial en préstamos a diez años—, las TFS cobran una comisión fija por adelantado, equivalente a entre el 7% y el 10% del capital solicitado. La pega es que solo se puede acceder a la casa, el automóvil o el negocio que se va a adquirir cuando se ha aportado al fondo el 45% de su valor, lo cual puede ocurrir pronto —si se adelanta parte del capital o se eligen cuotas de pago mensuales elevadas— o tardar varios años. La TFS, luego, hipoteca el bien hasta que el cliente ha terminado de pagar los plazos, pero entretanto puede hacer uso de él. Otro de los problemas es la protección de los ahorros contra la inflación galopante, ya que la cantidad solicitada por un cliente al inicio del programa puede haberse convertido en insignificante cuando llega a ejecutarla. Así que las TFS han tenido que establecer programas de inversión de estos ahorros en oro, bonos del Estado acordes con las finanzas islámicas (sukuk) o fondos.

De los apenas 370.000 usuarios que las TFS tenían hace tres años en Turquía se ha pasado a más de 1,5 millones en la actualidad, y su tamaño en activos se ha multiplicado por diez hasta superar los 9.000 millones de euros. Aun así, apenas suponen una fracción de la banca tradicional, y es que muchos turcos mantienen cierta suspicacia: por el carácter islámico de este sistema y porque algunos lo acusan de ser un esquema piramidal, debido a la necesidad de que lleguen nuevos ahorradores para mantenerse. Pero Büyükduman atribuye estas críticas a falta de información: “También los bancos pueden quebrar si los depositantes se retiran”. Para este experto, lo más importante es que estas entidades “promueven el ahorro antes de ofrecer un préstamo” y permiten a personas que trabajan en sectores informales acceder a financiación.

World.title: Inburgering with DN: 10 Dutch words every foreigner in NL uses
World.content:
There are some Dutch words which all foreigners in the Netherlands seem to adopt as soon as they get off the plane, train or ferry. So here’s a list of some of them.

Lesson 63: First words

Lekker: means tasty and is the first Dutch word everyone learns. Lekker describes just about everything which is positive: from a lekker broodje with lekker weer and lekkere sex.

Borrel: For some reason, we don’t go for drinks; we always have a borrel. And if you work in an office you may well have a vrijmibo (vrijdagmiddagborrel) on Friday afternoon.

Btw: Always pronounced bay-tay-vay in the Dutch way and meaning sales tax, not “by the way”.

Belasting: Closely associated with btw is, of course, tax in general. Given that we pay so much of it in NL, it is hardly surprising everyone gets to know the word very quickly.

Gemeente: Perhaps it is because internationals have so much to do with the good folks at the town hall, but everyone talks about the gemeente, never the council or city hall.

Apotheek: Another word that just sneaks in, even though there are plenty of respectable foreign-language equivalents for pharmacy.

Makelaar: Those other good folk who find houses for extortionate fees.

Bel: When you have been in the Netherlands a few weeks, everyone seems to stop phoning. We bel, as in “I’ll bel you tonight”. NB: when the Dutch say “we bellen” it means they will ring you sometime, or never.

Horeca: As in working in the horeca. A terrifically handy term derived from hotel, restaurant, cafe – and one which the rest of the world could easily adopt.

Agenda: Almost instantly, the English diary becomes an agenda – there is no escaping it. You will make appointments in your agenda and you will consult your agenda to see if you can have a meeting in three weeks’ time at 2.30pm.

Wintersport: Once you are settled in the Netherlands you will stop going on skiing holidays. You will go on wintersport instead – even if you spend more time on the après-ski than on the slopes.

Storing: If your train does not arrive, your tram is late, the internet is down and you can’t pay for your groceries with your phone, this is probably due to a storing. If you are a frequent rail user, you will probably get to know it very well.

Gezellig: Cosy, fun, warm, inviting… one of those words which are so crucial to understanding the Dutch that we wrote an entire lesson around it.

World.title: Trump administration sanctions International Criminal Court
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The United States has announced sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), escalating Trump’s war on the international tribunal.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” US secretary of state Marco Rubio said in an announcement.

The Trump administration has previously pledged to dismantle the court “brick by brick” and has sanctioned 13 current and former staff members, but this is the first time it has levied sanctions against the institution itself.

Ahead of the announcement, prime minister Rob Jetten said the Netherlands will protect the ICC “stone by stone”.

Foreign minister Tom Berendsen said the country would stand behind the court. “The announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court are an undesirable new escalation,” Berendsen said in a statement. “I deeply regret this new step.”

The sanctions will cut the court off from any US company or organisation, including providers of financial and technology services.

The announcement came hours after South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the ICC and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

Trump has long coveted the prize, telling reporters earlier this week that he deserved the award for what he said was ending eight wars.

World.title: Russia wants NL to hand over ICC judges
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Russia has asked the Netherlands to hand over nine International Criminal Court (ICC) officials who were convicted in absentia last year.

The prosecutor’s office in Moscow requested the extradition of the court’s president, Tomoko Akane, and other staff members for their involvement in the arrest warrant of Russian president Vladimir Putin.

The ICC issued the warrant for Putin’s alleged involvement in “the war crime of unlawful deportation of children” from occupied Ukraine.

The ICC has also issued an arrest warrant against Maria Alekseyevna Lvova-Belova, Russia’s commissioner for children’s rights.

In December, a court in Moscow convicted Akane and others in absentia, sentencing them to prison terms ranging from 3.5 to 15 years.

Japan, Akane’s home country, said the request was regrettable. “Measures targeting individuals connected to the ICC are unjust and unacceptable,” Masanao Ozaki, the country’s deputy chief cabinet secretary, said.

The United States has also sanctioned 13 staff members, including Akane, over the investigation into alleged Israeli war crimes in Gaza.

World.title: Unions call regional transport strike, threaten weekly walkout
World.content:
Regional bus services across the Netherlands will be heavily disrupted on Wednesday, after the FNV and CNV unions called a nationwide 24-hour strike in a dispute over a new pay and conditions deal.

If Wednesday’s strike does not shift the employers, the unions say they will hold an action day every week, and will only announce the dates shortly beforehand. Earlier this month they said they were considering weekly strikes in the run-up to Christmas.

Some 13,000 workers, mainly bus drivers, are covered by the public transport collective agreement, which expired on July 1. Staff at Arriva, EBS, Qbuzz, Keolis, Transdev and RET’s regional services are involved. City transport in Amsterdam, Rotterdam and The Hague is not affected.

Talks broke down after eight rounds of negotiations. This week an ultimatum to the employers’ organisation VWOV expired without a response.

“Employers are holding on to drastic cuts in working conditions,” FNV negotiator Marijn van der Gaag said in a statement. “In doing so, they are forcing their staff to take action.”

The unions say employers want to reduce sick pay, add more unpaid breaks to shifts and give staff less say over their rosters. Rosters are currently fixed about eight days in advance, and employers want to cut that to four days or less, Van der Gaag said.

The FNV wants a 6% pay rise. The CNV is calling for 9.5% over two years, as well as better arrangements for older workers and faster access to permanent contracts.

“We will not let employers sabotage the action by drawing up emergency rosters at the last minute,” CNV negotiator Niels Rook said, explaining why dates will not be announced in advance.

World.title: Former ICC judge Navi Pillay awarded Nobel Peace Prize
World.content:
South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

Most recently, the 85-year-old chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel had committed genocide.

Announcing the prize in Oslo, Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said it was going to someone who “held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict”.

Reacting to the news in Nuremberg, Pillay said “if you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”

The award comes as the system of international justice is under attack. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has threatened to dismantle the International Criminal Court “brick by brick, if necessary”, and the US has sanctioned several of its staff.

Pillay played a significant role in the anti-apartheid movement in her homeland as a defence lawyer for Nelson Mandela and other activists. She went on to serve as a judge on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, spending the last four of her eight years there as its president.

She was one of the ICC’s first judges, sitting in the appeals chamber from 2003 until 2008, when she stepped down to become UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

In 2019, she was appointed as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice by the Gambia, which had filed genocide proceedings against Myanmar over its treatment of the Rohingya minority.

Last year, as chair of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, she said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

In a post on social media, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Pillay. “Few have devoted their lives to justice, peace and human dignity like she did,” she said.

The prize is administered by the Nobel Foundation and comes with 12 million Swedish kronor (around €1.07 million).

World.title: Museums, festivals and clubs in Groningen ban smart glasses
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

In a joint statement on Friday some 30 cultural organisations in Groningen announced they were banning the use of smart glasses from their buildings and events.

The devices, the most popular version is sold by Meta, look like normal glasses but allow users to film and take photos covertly.

“This technology compromises the privacy and safety of visitors, staff, and artists, and undermines trust in an open, respectful environment,” the statement says.

Backers including the Groninger Archieven, the Groninger Museum, Noorderlicht, Stichting Kunst & Cultuur and the Grand Theatre Groningen.

Last week, eyewear chain Hans Anders announced it would stop selling Meta camera glasses following demands from privacy advocates concerned about the so-called “pervert glasses”.

Dutch privacy watchdog AP has warned that sharing images made with camera glasses violates GDPR laws unless permission is given by everyone in the images.

The consumer watchdog Consumentenbond has also issued a warning about the glasses, noting that it was possible to manipulate or cover the indicator light to make it even harder to tell images were being captured.

MPs have called for a full ban on the glasses but the cabinet is opposed to a blanket measure and wants to see other restrictions put into place.

Utrecht music venue Tivoli Vredenburg banned smart glasses at its events in 2025 and has since refused entry to one man who would not take them off.

World.title: NL’s only legal medicinal cannabis grower goes bust
World.content:
Patients who use medicinal cannabis face having to switch to imported products after the only licensed grower in the Netherlands was declared bankrupt on Thursday.

A court in Groningen declared Veendam-based Bedrocan bankrupt two weeks after the company had applied for protection from its creditors. The firm, whose main growing site is in Emmeloord, employs around 70 people.

Bedrocan ran into trouble after the health ministry ended its contract at the start of this year. All medicinal cannabis sold in Dutch pharmacies is bought and distributed by the state-run Bureau for Medicinal Cannabis (BMC).

The ministry ended the deal in anticipation of a change in the law that will let growers sell directly to pharmacies. But health minister Sophie Hermans (VVD) told MPs in July that the change is not expected to take effect until July 1, 2028.

That left Bedrocan unable to supply the BMC and not allowed to sell to pharmacies itself, the Volkskrant reported. The state was by far its largest customer.

Limited stockpile

The BMC built up a stockpile of Bedrocan cannabis before the contract ended, but the minister said it was limited and had a finite shelf life. The BMC will switch to imported cannabis during 2027, with products matching current THC and CBD levels as closely as possible.

Around 7,000 people in the Netherlands are prescribed medicinal cannabis, according to the Volkskrant. They include people with multiple sclerosis (MS), severe pain, certain forms of epilepsy, and patients in palliative care.

Patients fear a different variety will not work as well for them. Cannabis contains many compounds that together determine its effect, and the mix depends on the plant and how it is grown.

The MS association has written to Hermans warning that some long-term patients depend on a specific variety.

Bedrocan also supplied patients in other European countries through the BMC. The BMC is due to stop exporting at the end of 2026. In September, Bedrocan told foreign pharmacies and wholesalers to order from it directly.

Poland’s security services have held an urgent meeting after receiving “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. At the time of writing, no details have been released regarding where and how the alleged attacks were expected to take place, who might be behind them, nor what the source of the information was. W związku z informacją, która wpłynęła do @PolskaPolicja i dotyczy możliwego zamachu na premiera @donaldtusk oraz wicepremiera, ministra obrony narodowej @KosiniakKamysz, minister koordynator służb specjalnych @TomaszSiemoniak oraz minister spraw wewnętrznych i administracji… — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 11, 2026 On Sunday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for the security services, first announced that the police had received “information…regarding a possible assassination attempt” on Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz, who, as well as serving as defence minister, is also a deputy prime minister. Dobrzyński revealed that the Internal Security Agency (ABW), police and State Protection Service (SOP), which provides security for high-ranking officials, would meet to discuss the potential threat. Speaking after that meeting, interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka confirmed that the threat had first been identified by SOP, which passed the information on to the police. “We are taking this matter extremely seriously,” added Dobrzyński, speaking alongside her. He criticised “pseudo-experts” in the media who had expressed doubt about the announcement of a possible assassination attempt. “We’re talking about threats directed at the most important people in the country,” he added. “This information is so serious and credible that we’ve decided to share it with you now…We are talking about a high probability that these threats will be carried out.” Dobrzyński did not divulge any details about the nature of the attack nor where the warnings had come from, but said that he would be able to provide further information once the police and security services had carried out further investigation. "Sprawę traktujemy śmiertelnie poważnie. Mówimy o dużym prawdopodobieństwie spełnienia tych gróźb" Rzecznik prasowy ministra koordynatora służb specjalnych o możliwym zamachu na premiera i szefa MON. pic.twitter.com/2xoWrZJT2w — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 11, 2026 Government spokesman Adam Szłapka, speaking to broadcaster TVN, acknowledged that the authorities constantly receive a “cascade of indications” regarding potential threats. However, “this signal was more disturbing than previous” ones, he added. Szłapka also indicated that one element of the warning had come via email, but added that “it was not just an email” that had raised concern. Like Dobrzyński, he said that further information would be released in due course. Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading daily, reports that an unnamed “official close to the prime minister” had said that the threat came from “right-wing extremists” and that the perpetrators were Poles. Another source within the intelligence services told the newspaper that the threat was treated more seriously than others because it contained information about addresses linked to Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz. Poland has charged a 17-year-old with planning neo-Nazi terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school. Two other Polish teenagers who were part of the same online community promoting neo-Nazism and violence have also been detained https://t.co/86AnIHWFe8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 22, 2026 Last month, police detained a 56-year-old man in the city of Przemyśl after he posted a video on social media threatening Tusk. Earlier in September, a 52-year-old man in the town of Oława was likewise arrested for making criminal threats against the prime minister online. Also in September, the security services detained three teenagers who were accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One of them was additionally charged with planning terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school. This week has also seen Poland facing an unprecedented security challenge after three knife attacks took place on schools, leaving one person dead and many injured. In response, the police have since Friday carried out checks at over 64,000 locations, including many schools, and detained over 100 people, most of them teenagers found to have made threats or been in possession of weapons. World.title: Polish prosecutors seek to drop case against South Asian men who slaughtered goat in kebab bar
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
