Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar. They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time. 🔴Ubili kozę na zapleczu. Wkrótce decyzja sądu, zastanawia ruch prokuratury Sąd Rejonowy w Wałbrzychu w najbliższym czasie zdecyduje o losie trójki obcokrajowców, którzy pod koniec zeszłego roku niezgodnie z polskim prawem ubili kozę. Oskarżająca Hindusa i dwójkę Bengalczyków… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 7, 2026 The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar. After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time. The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”. However, “the harmfulness of the act is relatively low, although I know that what these people did shocks many people”, he continued. “We must be realistic about the fact that the court proceedings will take some time, thus blocking the docket for other cases. A trial also entails costs for the state.” Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska. The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 Not all cases involving illegal animal slaughter have been treated as causing low social harm. Last month, a court in the town of Limanowa convicted three men for carrying out illegal halal ritual slaughter and selling unapproved meat. The main suspect, a Polish man, was found guilty of overseeing the operation, while two Azerbaijani nationals were convicted of helping distribute the illegal meat. The verdicts can still be appealed. Although it has relatively small Muslim and Jewish populations, Poland is one of Europe’s biggest producers and exporters of kosher and halal meat. Almost a third of Poland's meat exports are halal and kosher, making it one of Europe's leading producers. Having fought off attempts by the ruling party to ban ritual slaughter, the industry is now hoping to expand further to cater to a growing market https://t.co/duOJTfHoLT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2022 However, the country has itself been experiencing growing levels of migration in recent years. Most of the new arrivals are from neighbouring Ukraine and Belarus, but there are also growing numbers from outside Europe, too. Indians are now Poland’s third-largest immigrant group, numbering around 25,500, according to recent data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Among first residence permits issued by Poland last year, Indians (9,230) and Turks (7,533) were the fourth and fifth largest recipients. Poland’s current government has blamed some immigrant groups for a rise in crime and has stepped up deportations of those found to have broken the law. However, data show that, overall, immigrants are less likely to commit crimes than Poles themselves. World.title: Polish police detain more teens following school knife attacks amid fears of further incidents
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Following this week’s two knife attacks on schools in Poland, police have today carried out security checks on over 10,000 schools and detained at least 10 more people, many of them teenagers found to have made online threats or been in possession of weapons. Meanwhile, many parents decided not to send their children to school today, as rumours swirled online that this week’s attacks were somehow coordinated and that further incidents were planned on Friday. The issue has also sparked a political dispute, with the government criticising opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for previously vetoing laws intended to improve children’s safety. The opposition in turn accuses the government of failing to protect schools properly. 🚨 Ponad 10 tysięcy skontrolowanych placówek i 10 osób zatrzymanych w całym kraju. Bezpieczeństwo w szkołach priorytetem Policji ⬇️ Tragiczne zdarzenia, do których doszło w ciągu ostatnich dni na Mazowszu, wywołały w przestrzeni medialnej falę nieprawdziwych informacji,… pic.twitter.com/WVkYUdVO9C — Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) October 9, 2026 On Thursday, a 39-year-old school caretaker was killed in an attack by a 15-year-old former pupil on a primary school. Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that the assailant had been wearing a head-mounted camera intended to broadcast the attack. That came a day after a 19-year-old student carried out a knife attack on another school, leaving eight people injured. Two other teens were also detained on suspicion of planning attacks in other locations. In response, Tusk announced on Thursday that police would carry out regular checks on schools. However, on Friday, many parents in the Masovia province around Warsaw, where both of this week’s attacks took place, decided to keep their children at home. Some districts closed schools entirely. One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school by a 15-year-old former pupil. Yesterday, a knife attack by a 19-year-old at another school left eight people injured. The assailant also had a homemade explosive that failed to detonate https://t.co/xJAzhT6u3U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026 Concern was stoked by claims circulating on social media that this week’s school attacks were part of a coordinated action by a group of teenagers, who were planning further incidents on what they were calling “Bloody Friday”. Two schools in the town of Legionowo, just north of Warsaw, were closed on Friday after local authorities said they received “unconfirmed information that they were on a list” relating to the alleged group. Poland’s national police headquarters issued a statement on Friday morning saying that they were aware of the rumours but that “so far nothing indicates such an event is actually happening”. They urged people to remain calm, not share unverified information, and rely only on credible sources. At the same time, police and local authorities stepped up security in schools. At 9 a.m. on Friday, the national police headquarters announced that checks had been conducted at over 10,000 schools around the country and that ten people had been detained. Among those to be arrested was a 17-year-old in the town of Ełk, who had reportedly made online threats to attack other students, and a 13-year-old in Sochaczew who wrote in a chat that he would bring a machete to school. The boy later said it was a “silly joke”. In Bartoszyce, a school principal saw that an 11-year-old student had posted a photo of a knife alongside a statement indicating a threat. Police detained the boy and found an “imitation knife” in his backpack. In Ostrów Mazowiecka, police announced they had arrested a 15-year-old boy who had sent out images of himself in a Guy Fawkes-style mask, saying that he planned to take people’s lives. In Warsaw, police detained a 14-year-old who was found to be in possession of a concealed blade and 11 firecrackers. 🚨 Policjanci z Mokotowa niezwłocznie po otrzymaniu informacji o zagrożeniu bezpieczeństwa zatrzymali na terenie szkoły 14-latka, który posiadał nóż z ukrytym ostrzem. Nastolatek miał przy sobie także 11 petard hukowych. W sprawie prowadzone są dalsze czynności. Dokumenty… pic.twitter.com/lbQrqe2pgl — Policja Warszawa (@Policja_KSP) October 9, 2026 The situation has also taken on a political dimension. On Thursday, Tusk criticised Nawrocki for earlier this year vetoing a government bill intended to improve online safety by blocking harmful content. The president had argued that the measures were an “Orwellian” threat to free speech. In a hastily called vote in the lower-house Sejm on Thursday evening, Tusk’s ruling coalition passed a new version of the bill that will now be sent to the upper-house Senate. Once it receives final parliamentary approval, the legislation will return to Nawrocki for his signature or veto. Meanwhile, education minister Barbara Nowacka also noted that Nawrocki had vetoed a bill introducing new rights and responsibilities for school pupils, including greater powers to confiscate dangerous items. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Mieliśmy jedną z najmocniejszych propozycji zmiany prawa w Europie, która miała chronić w internecie przede wszystkim dzieci i młodzież. pic.twitter.com/dyxY6prGzB — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 8, 2026 In response, presidential spokesman Rafał Leśkiewicz criticised those who were “exploiting this issue for political purposes”, saying that “a political argument is the last thing we need right now”. Meanwhile, Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, accused the government of focusing on “political warfare” instead of ensuring security in schools. “There is no coordination or top-down directives on what to do, where it is safe, and where there is risk or threat,” he wrote on social media, calling the situation “chaos”. World.title: Polish parliament approves ban on nighttime alcohol sales in shops
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. An overwhelming majority of MPs in the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, have voted in favour of a bill that would introduce tough new anti-alcohol measures, including a ban on all forms of advertising and on sales in shops during nighttime hours. The legislation must still pass through the upper-house Senate and will then require the signature of President Karol Nawrocki. However, given the level of support – with only two small far-right groups voting against the bill – it appears likely the measures will be approved. #PILNE | Sejm uchwalił ustawę wprowadzającą na terenie całego kraju nocną prohibicję, zakazującą reklamy alkoholu i podnoszącą opłatę za sprzedaż alkoholu. https://t.co/OawNUdtqM6 — tvn24 (@tvn24) October 8, 2026 The new restrictions were initially proposed in separate bills submitted by two junior members of Poland’s ruling coalition, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), which were combined into a single package. The measures include a ban on the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., with local authorities able to extend those hours up to 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. if they wish. Bars, clubs and restaurants would still be allowed to sell alcohol for on-premises consumption as presently. Almost 200 Polish municipalities, including large cities such as Warsaw and Kraków, have already introduced their own local bans on nighttime alcohol sales. In the first six months following the implementation of its restrictions in 2023, Kraków saw a nearly 50% decrease in nighttime police interventions, with other cities reporting similar improvements. The newly approved bill also includes a complete ban on advertising and promoting alcoholic drinks. Those who violate the prohibition can be fined up to 1 million zloty (€228,400). Packaging for alcoholic drinks will be required to include warnings about their harmful effect on pregnant women and minors. The legislation also toughens requirements for shop staff to check the age of buyers if they suspect they may be underage. The cost of licences to sell alcohol will be increased from 525 to 1,050 zloty for drinks with up to 18% alcohol content and from 2,100 to 4,200 zloty for stronger drinks. Warsaw has announced a ban on nighttime sales of alcohol in shops. The new measure will come into force on 1 June 2026 and will apply from 10 p.m to 6 a.m. across the entire city https://t.co/A7xVvJMpvU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 12, 2026 In a vote on Thursday night, the bill won support from 400 of the 433 MPs present in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. The only groups that did not vote in favour were the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). The legislation now passes to the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but only delay, not block, a bill’s passage. Once finally approved by parliament, it will reach the desk of President Karol Nawrocki, who can sign the bill, veto it, or send it to the constitutional court for assessment. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of bills. However, given the level of support for the alcohol bill in the Sejm, including from the largest opposition groups, Law and Justice (PiS) and Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), it appears likely he will sign it. Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, new data show. The average person in Poland ate 82kg of meat last year, up 7.5% from 2024 and 22.7% since 2005. They also drank 82 litres of beer, down 18.7% since 2018 https://t.co/FxFMupWLRv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 1, 2026 In June, an IBRiS poll for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 55% of Poles support some form of ban on nighttime alcohol sales while 43% are opposed. A survey by IBP for Super Express published today showed even stronger support, with 67% in favour of a ban and only 26% opposed. Recent data released by Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, showed that alcohol consumption among Poles is continuing its recent decline. In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019. However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005. World.title: Polish man suspected of helping Russian plot to assassinate Zelensky sentenced to 5.5 years
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. The sentence was handed down by the court of appeal in Lublin on Thursday, increasing by two years a jail term issued by a lower court earlier this year. The ruling is now final and binding. The 51-year-old former Polish soldier, who has been named only as Paweł K. under privacy law, was detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) in April 2024. Investigators found that the suspect had declared his willingness to collaborate with Russian intelligence and, between December 2022 and March 2024, had established contact via email and instant messaging with Russians involved in military operations against Ukraine, including army officers. Prosecutors determined that Paweł K. had been assigned tasks including gathering and transmitting information regarding security at Rzeszów airport, which is the main hub for goods and people being transported in and out of Ukraine. “These activities could have been used by Russian intelligence services, including in the context of planning a possible assassination attempt on the head of a foreign state, that is, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky,” wrote Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office earlier this year. Poland and Ukraine have revealed further details of a foiled plan to assassinate @ZelenskyyUa at Poland's Rzeszów airport. A Polish man was last month indicted in relation to the incident, which he is accused of seeking to carry out on behalf of Russia https://t.co/Lrp99vH4s2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 23, 2025 Last year, the head of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said that Paweł K. had been “recruited decades ago and firmly believed in the Soviet cause”. Polish prosecutors have not commented on that claim. However, they did find that the suspect had declared his willingness to join Russian “sabotage structures”, including the Wagner mercenary group and Unit 29155 of the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency, which is tasked with carrying out destabilisation activities. Paweł G. denied the accusations against him and claimed that he had actually been trying to help capture Russian war criminals by deceiving them into trusting him, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). His defence attorney argued that the information Paweł G. had transmitted regarding Rzeszów airport was “trivial and publicly available”, according to news website Onet. In January this year, Paweł K. was found guilty of espionage and illegal possession of ammunition by the district court in the city of Zamość, which sentenced him to three and a half years in prison. However, prosecutors appealed against that ruling, arguing that the suspect deserved a longer jail term of seven and a half years. In a judgement issued on Thursday, the Lublin appeals court agreed that Paweł G’s initial sentence had been “grossly lenient” and increased it by two years, reports PAP. “Submitting an offer to work for…the intelligence service of a country that is at war with a country directly neighboring Poland, a country that is making quite extensive unfriendly gestures towards Poland, cannot be treated leniently,” said judge Artur Achrymowicz. Poland has charged three of its own citizens with working on behalf of Russian intelligence. They are accused of spreading disinformation, conducting reconnaissance of NATO troops, and undergoing firearms training in preparation for acts of sabotage https://t.co/maYd0kb9HW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 20, 2026 Poland has become a primary target for acts of espionage, sabotage and disinformation conducted by operatives working on behalf of Russia. In many cases, they are so-called “disposable agents”: individuals already on the ground, often amateurs hired and paid through messaging apps such as Telegram, rather than professional spies or soldiers. The AWB last year launched 48 investigations related to espionage, more than twice as many as in 2024. Over those two years, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined A report published earlier this year by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026 In January, Polish prosecutors indicted five people – four Ukrainian citizens and one Russian – accused of carrying out a plot on behalf of Russia to plant explosives in packages that were then dispatched by courier services across Europe. In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops. In July this year, a Russian married couple who had been studying in Poland were jailed for spying on behalf of Moscow and involvement in a plot to send a parcel bomb. World.title: Beavers destroy sign warning about beavers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it. The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack. “We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters. “So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.” Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000. Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP. However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down. World.title: One person killed in second school knife attack in Poland in two days
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school carried out today by a 15-year-old former pupil. It comes just a day after another knife attack by a 19-year-old on a different school in Poland, which left eight people injured. The assailant was also carrying a homemade explosive device that failed to detonate. Meanwhile, police also announced today the arrest of a 17-year-old who had reportedly threatened to attack a school and was found to be in possession of knives. The developments have caused shock in Poland, a country where such violent incidents are normally rare. “We are seeing a radicalisation of young people,” warns the education minister, who has called for tougher controls on online content. W rękach Policji jest już 15-latek, który około godziny 9 wszedł do szkoły w miejscowości Leszczydół-Nowiny, w powiecie wyszkowskim i ostrym narzędziem ranił 3 pracowników placówki. Wśród rannych jest dyrektor, który ujął 15-latka. Policja była na miejscu już po kilku minutach od… pic.twitter.com/EV1RPP7LA5 — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 8, 2026 The latest attack took place in a primary school in the village of Leszczydół-Nowiny, around 60 km (37 miles) northeast of Warsaw, on Thursday morning. A 15-year-old former pupil of the school entered the facility and stabbed three members of staff, including the principal, who managed to subdue him. One of the victims, a 37-year-old female caretaker, died from her injuries. The other victim, a teacher, was hospitalised. The attacker was detained and will appear before a family court, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. The incident comes just a day after another similar tragedy only 50 km away, in the town of Ostrołęka. On Wednesday morning, a 19-year-old attacked a vocational high school, leaving four students, two teachers and two bystanders injured before being captured. The assailant, who has been named only as Jakub Z. under Polish privacy law, is a student at the school. On Wednesday evening, national prosecutor Dariusz Korneluk told broadcaster TVN that the attacker had a homemade explosive in his backpack “that almost detonated”. “The backpack was already in the computer room and, only due to the responsible actions of the teacher and the students, was it thrown out of the window” after smoke had begun to billow out of it, he said. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek pledged that “prosecutors will ensure that the perpetrator answers for every blow inflicted and faces the legal consequences…There is no tolerance for violence in Polish schools”. Policjanci z Ostrołęki w pobliżu plaży miejskiej zatrzymali 19-letniego mężczyznę podejrzewanego o zaatakowanie ostrym narzędziem osób w pobliżu i na terenie szkoły w Ostrołęce. Ze wstępnych informacji wynika, że mogło dojść do zranienia 7 osób. Policjanci na miejscu wykonują… pic.twitter.com/cRzqMs36rD — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 7, 2026 On Thursday morning, around the same time as the attack in Leszczydół-Nowiny was unfolding, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński announced that a 17-year-old boy had been detained by police after threatening to attack another school. The suspect, who resides in the same Masovia province where Wednesday and Thursday’s attacks took place, “was found with two knives”, said Kierwiński, quoted by news website Interia. His internet history also showed that “he was looking for information on how to carry out this type of bloody act”, added the minister. The potential incident was prevented after fellow pupils reported to teachers that the suspect announced he wanted to “do something bad at school”. Last week, a 13-year-old was detained by police after telling a fellow online gamer that he was planning an attack on his school in the village of Książki, north-central Poland. He reportedly confessed to having killed cats and said that he wanted to attack random people with a cleaver in the school halls. Dzięki przytomnej reakcji uczniów, nauczyciela oraz błyskawicznej akcji policjantów z Sierpca powstrzymano 17-latka, który zapowiadał, że „zrobi coś złego w szkole”. Policjanci zatrzymali nastolatka i zabezpieczyli należące do niego noże, a w jego telefonie natrafiono na historię… pic.twitter.com/oUkwKbHmNr — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 8, 2026 The Polish authorities have recently warned of growing concern over radical ideas spreading among young people. Last month, the security services detained three teenagers accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One was charged with planning an attack on a school and a mosque. Last year, a 19-year-old student was detained after it was determined he was planning an Islamic State-inspired attack on a Christmas market. In August, he was indicted to stand trial. In February, an 18-year-old was indicted over claims he planned to attack a school, also inspired by the Islamic State. Speaking on Wednesday, after the Ostrołęka incident but before today’s events, education minister Barbara Nowacka warned that “we are seeing a radicalisation of young people”, reports the Onet news website. She called for “much greater control over what happens on the internet”. Earlier this year, Poland introduced a new law banning online content depicting illegal acts or other forms of abusive and degrading behaviour. The government is also working on measures to block children from social media and has banned the use of smartphones in schools. Poland’s state-owned National Development Bank (BGK) has announced the launch of the country’s first fund to support companies developing space technologies. Vinci Space Tech Fund will be worth 500 million zloty (€114 million), investing up to 100 million zloty each in 15-20 firms in the sector. The brainchild of finance minister Andrzej Domański, the fund aims to foster the growth of Polish space technologies and bolster the country’s technological independence. Kosmos to nie tylko gospodarka i innowacje. Kosmos to także bezpieczeństwo Polski. 🇵🇱 Dziś w Krakowie uruchamiamy pierwszy w Polsce fundusz dla sektora kosmicznego – Vinci Space Tech Fund. 500 mln zł na rozwój sektora @BGK_pl Vinci. Mamy ambitne spółki, znakomitych naukowców i… pic.twitter.com/NQBy8HYOcY — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) October 6, 2026 According to the growth and technology ministry, one of the fund’s strategic partners, BGK will invest between 10 and 100 million zloty in companies with a potential for rapid growth and expansion into international markets through its Vinci investment vehicle. The fund’s other partners are the Polish Space Agency and Kraków Technology Park (KTP), where the launch took place, along with ICEYE, a world-leading Finnish microsatellite manufacturer and operator co-founded by Pole Rafał Modrzewski. Announcing the fund, Domański highlighted the space sector’s role in responding to threats, protecting critical infrastructure, strengthening energy security and monitoring Poland and its surroundings. “The money from the Vinci fund is an investment in Poland’s capacity to build its own strong companies and develop competences that will be strategically significant for our economy and security,” he said. Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Mirosław Czekaj, president of the BGK management board, also noted that the development of the space industry would help “to build Poland’s technological sovereignty”, as one of the projects that are “vital to the Polish economy”. The fund is expected to invest in 15 to 20 companies, mainly Polish, although companies from elsewhere in Europe may also qualify if they have their main business operations in Poland, the ministry said. Its key investment areas include satellites, optics and Earth observation, satellite communications, electronics and photonics, rockets and propulsion systems, and artificial intelligence. In addition to funding, companies will benefit from advice and support from the fund’s partners. KPT, the city of Kraków and the Faculty of Space Technologies at AGH University are expected to provide much of the initiative’s academic, research and technical expertise. ICEYE, meanwhile, will share its experience of growing a space company and expanding into global markets. Last month, the company opened a satellite technology centre in Warsaw, and it plans to invest more than 120 million zloty in Poland by 2028, reports industry website Space News. Modrzewski said that raising capital in Poland was difficult when the company was founded 12 years ago, but that it has become easier as space has emerged as one of the country’s “strategic domains”. “The availability of capital in Poland will allow our companies to build their position on the global market without needing to leave the country at an early stage,” Modrzewski said, quoted by financial news site Bankier.pl. Vinci has previously invested in ICEYE as part of its private equity fund. Astronaut @astro_slawosz's recent trip to the International Space Station highlighted the Polish space industry's growing importance. Once limited to making components for others, Poland is now building its own spacecraft and participating in missions https://t.co/TmQiD91IzZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 6, 2025 Poland’s space sector has expanded rapidly since the country joined the European Space Agency in 2012, moving from supplying components for foreign missions to developing its own satellites and space systems. A key milestone came in 2024 with the launch of EagleEye, Poland’s largest satellite, which was designed and built by a consortium of Polish companies and research institutions. In 2025, a Pole went to space for the second time in history, 50 years after the first Polish astronaut’s flight. The sector is now taking on larger international projects, while Russia’s war in Ukraine has highlighted the importance of domestic space capabilities for national security. In July this year, Warsaw was chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency centre focusing on civil security and resilience. World.title: The Story Society Is Bringing an English-Language Book Community to Prague
World.content:
Meet Julia and Ioana, the founders behind The Story Society, a new English-language bookstore and community project in Prague.

Their idea combines a selection of books with a space for reading, book clubs, events and meeting other people.

The project is still in development, with the founders currently looking for a location and working towards opening the bookstore in early 2027.

Why a bookstore?

For Julia, the idea started from a personal need. “I wanted to create a place where introverted people like myself could spend time comfortably, discover books at their own pace and potentially meet others with similar interests,” she says.

But there was also a practical reason behind the idea. According to the founders, finding a wider selection of English-language books in Prague can be difficult, particularly when it comes to special editions. Ordering books from abroad can also mean higher shipping costs, taxes and waiting several weeks for delivery.

“I wanted to solve two problems. One is community, and the other one is buying books in English here,” Julia says.

The Story Society plans to source books from the UK and offer a selection that the founders feel is currently difficult to find locally.

What they hope The Story Society to be

The Story Society is intended to be more than a place to buy books, although the physical bookstore remains an important part of the idea. Julia and Ioana imagine a colorful, cozy space with areas for reading, book clubs and other events.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Story Society (@thestorysociety.prague)

They are also considering collaborations with authors and artists, pop-ups and other activities connected to books and the community around them. “We want to make a third place in Prague,” Ioana says.

The idea is that people could come not only to buy a book, but also to stay for a while, read, meet friends or take part in an event.

The expat/local divide

The Story Society was initially imagined largely with Prague’s expat community in mind. But “when the project took shape, we got a huge response from locals, and we learned that they are also interested in it,” Julia says. The attraction is the chance to have an English-language space where they can read books, meet people and be part of a bookish community.

That response has broadened the founders’ idea of who The Story Society is for. Rather than separating Prague’s expat and local communities, they hope the project can help mend the gap between them.

“If you like English, if you can speak English, and if you like books, we don’t care where you’re from,” Julia says. “Just be there and enjoy it with us.”

Where the project stands now

The Story Society doesn’t have a physical location yet. Julia and Ioana are currently exploring the market and looking for a suitable space in Prague’s city centre, while also working on the book supply and other practical foundations of the project.

In the meantime, they plan to take The Story Society to pop-ups and other events. These will give them an opportunity to introduce the project to more people, build a community around it and raise visibility for their crowdfunding campaign.

Everyone can help

For now, support can take different forms. Sharing the crowdfunding campaign, introducing the project to someone who might be interested or simply helping spread the word can help The Story Society reach more people as Julia and Ioana work towards opening their first space.

They also want people to feel that contributing does not necessarily mean making a financial donation. Ideas, feedback and suggestions can help shape the project as it develops. As the founders put it, “any thought counts.”

World.title: Which Stores Will Be Open in the Czech Republic on October 28
World.content:
Most large supermarkets and retail chains in the Czech Republic will close on Wednesday, October 28, as the country marks the Day of the Establishment of an Independent Czechoslovak State.

Under Czech law, shops with a sales area exceeding 200 square meters must close on the public holiday. The restriction covers most major supermarkets as well as large retailers selling clothing, electronics, furniture and other goods.



Major chains including Lidl, Kaufland, Albert, Billa, Penny Market and Tesco are expected to close their large stores for the day.

The restrictions apply nationwide and are based on Act No. 223/2016 Coll., which regulates retail opening hours on selected public holidays.

October 28 commemorates the establishment of an independent Czechoslovak state in 1918, following the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire at the end of World War I.

Which shops can remain open

Not all retailers are subject to the closure requirement. The law provides several exceptions, allowing certain businesses to operate as usual.

These include:

Small grocery stores and convenience shops with a sales area of up to 200 square meters

Pharmacies

Shops at petrol stations

Retail outlets at airports

Shops located at railway and bus stations

Shops within medical facilities

Smaller shops are not required to open, however. Their owners can decide whether to operate on the holiday and may introduce shorter opening hours.

Customers are therefore advised to check the opening times of individual stores before setting out to shop.

What about shopping centres in Prague

Shopping centres may continue operating on October 28, even though their largest retail outlets must remain closed.

Smaller shops that fall below the 200-square-meter threshold may open, while restaurants, cafés, cinemas and other leisure businesses can continue serving customers.

Opening arrangements may differ between individual shopping centres, so visitors should check the holiday schedules published on their official websites before travelling.

World.title: Mayors and Independents Come First in Prague Elections as Pirates Fall Back
World.content:
The opposition Mayors and Independents (STAN) party came first in municipal elections in Prague, with 23 percent of the vote.

Led by Prague Deputy Mayor Petr Hlaváček, secured more than 23 percent of the vote, up sharply from 7.8 percent four years ago. The party recorded the largest increase among the main political groups contesting the capital’s city council.



The Spolu coalition, comprising the Civic Democratic Party (ODS) and TOP 09, finished second with approximately 22 percent. Its result was around three percentage points lower than in the previous election.

Praha Sobě, another group led by a serving deputy mayor, also improved its position. Under Adam Scheinherr’s leadership, it won nearly 18 percent of the vote.

The ANO movement, the strongest party in the Czech national parliament, finished fourth in Prague after losing support.

In 2022, ANO won 19.3 percent of the vote in the capital. This time, it failed to reach 15 percent.

The Pirate Party suffered an even steeper decline. After finishing third with 17.7 percent of the vote in 2022, it received just over 9 percent this time, narrowly securing representation on the Prague City Council.

The election results set the stage for negotiations over Prague’s next city government.

World.title: Police Car Ends Up in Vltava River, Three People Treated for Hypothermia
World.content:
A police car plunged into the Vltava River in Prague on Saturday morning after crashing through the guardrails of Hlávkův Bridge.

The vehicle’s two occupants and a man who jumped into the water to help them were treated by emergency crews for hypothermia.

The accident was reported to police at around 8 a.m. on October 10. A man and a woman, both approximately 30 years old, were inside the car when it went into the river.



A witness jumped into the water after the vehicle fell from the bridge and helped the occupants. Emergency services subsequently treated all three people at the scene.

Prague Emergency Medical Service dispatched three ambulances, a medical inspector and a rapid response vehicle to the incident.

All three were suffering from hypothermia but were not in life-threatening condition, according to emergency responders.

“We are very grateful to the rescuer for their help,” Prague Emergency Medical Service said in a statement, confirming that all three people were in its care.

Police are investigating the circumstances of the crash, including what caused the vehicle to break through the bridge’s guardrails and fall into the Vltava.

World.title: Prague Outperforms Vienna and Berlin in Visitor Ratings
World.content:
Prague has received higher visitor satisfaction ratings than Vienna and Berlin, according to the latest Global Tourist Perception Index by Data Appeal Mabrian Intelligence.

The Czech capital scored 92.7 out of 100, compared with 85.6 for Vienna and 78.4 for Berlin, Prague City Tourism (PCT) announced on Thursday.

The results reflect six years of efforts to improve tourism services, visitor experiences and the city’s destination branding, the organization said during International Customer Service Week, held from October 5 to 9.

The Global Tourist Perception Index assesses several aspects of the visitor experience, including hotel satisfaction, safety and tourism products. Prague scored highest among the three capitals, according to PCT.



Visitor spending rises as tourism shifts upmarket

Data from Mastercard transactions indicate that spending by visitors from key foreign markets increased by 18% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, while the number of visitors rose by approximately 1%.

Social media analysis also points to Prague’s growing association with culture. More than a third of social media posts shared by visitors about the city focused on art and culture, an increase of around five percentage points year-on-year. Nightlife accounted for just 4.5% of reported reasons for visiting, according to PCT.

The Data Appeal Mabrian Intelligence Platform also gave Prague a score of 80 out of 100 for hotel service satisfaction, ahead of Vienna at 75.8 and Berlin at 71.8.

Figures from hotel data provider STR point to further growth in the market. Between January and August 2026, hotel occupancy in Prague increased by 4.9% year-on-year, while the average room rate rose by 5.1%.

Occupancy reached 84.7% in August. According to a recent overview of Prague’s tourism sector by the Czech Institute of Tourism, the average room rate was approximately €123, rising to €170 in the city center and €241 in the luxury segment.

Prague attracts hotel investors

The city is also gaining ground among hotel investors. According to the Cushman & Wakefield Hotel Investor Compass 2026, published in March, Prague ranks among the 15 most attractive European cities for hotel investment, ahead of Vienna, Zurich and Budapest.

Investor interest in Prague’s hotel market has increased for two consecutive years. In the previous edition of the study, the city recorded the largest year-on-year increase in investor interest among the markets surveyed, at 14%. The latest edition showed a further increase of 7%.

World.title: Prague 7 Turns Streets Into Outdoor Art With Designs by Local Children
World.content:
Prague 7 has transformed several streets around local schools with large-scale colorful paintings created with the help of local schoolchildren.

The new artwork can be seen on Rajská, Plynární, Jablonského and Antonínská streets, as well as part of Bubenská Street. The municipality placed the designs mainly near schools and along busy pedestrian routes.



On Antonínská Street, students from grades five through eight at Strossmayerovo Square Elementary School helped create the artwork. They produced the original drawings, which artist Jakub Karlík then combined into the final design.

Several other educational institutions are located close to the painted streets, including Bratrská Elementary School, the Holešovice Business Academy, the Higher Vocational School of Fashion Design and the Secondary Industrial School of Fashion Design.

The new designs have received mostly positive reactions from local residents. Comments on Prague 7’s Facebook page described the streets as more cheerful and said the artwork had made the area more interesting.

There has also been criticism, particularly over the cost and the practical impact of painting the asphalt. Some residents questioned whether the project was necessary and raised concerns about the roughness of the surface, pedestrian movement and whether the paint could become slippery.

Prague 7 said anti-slip paint was used, similar to materials applied to cycle paths and sports surfaces.

The project cost 755,000 CZK, covering the designs, preparation, materials and application. According to Prague 7 spokesperson Martin Vokuš, each of the two phases took around 20 days.

The municipality awarded the contract directly to Karlík. Before selecting his proposal for the Antonínská and Bubenská sections, Prague 7 compared three offers and chose his as the most advantageous.

World.title: Beer Consumption in Czech Republic Falls to Lowest Level on Record
World.content:
Czech beer consumption fell to its lowest level on record in 2025, with the average resident drinking 121 liters during the year, according to data from the Czech Association of Breweries and Malt Houses (ČSPS).

Total domestic consumption reached 14.86 million hectoliters, down 3.2% from 2024. The figure is the lowest recorded since nationwide beer consumption statistics began.

Overall beer production in the Czech Republic also declined last year. Breweries produced 19.96 million hectoliters of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beer, 4.3% less than in 2024.



The decline affected nearly every category, with non-alcoholic beer the main exception. Production of non-alcoholic and flavored non-alcoholic beer increased by 4% to 1.68 million hectoliters.

Demand for non-alcoholic beer has been rising steadily for more than a decade. Between 2019 and 2024 alone, production increased by around 50%.

Pubs lose ground as more Czechs drink at home

The shift in drinking habits is particularly visible in restaurants and pubs. Draft beer accounted for 28% of beer sold on the Czech market in 2025, down one percentage point from the previous year.

The longer-term decline is more significant. Draft beer represented 35% of sales in 2019 and 51% in 2008.

The ČSPS said the figures reflect changes in consumer behavior, including greater interest in moderation and healthier lifestyles. When Czechs do go out for beer, they are increasingly looking for quality and variety rather than simply drinking larger quantities.

Czech beer exports also decline

Exports followed the domestic market downward. Czech breweries exported 5.48 million hectoliters of beer in 2025, an 8.2% decrease compared with the previous year.

European Union countries accounted for around 90% of Czech beer exports, with Germany and Slovakia among the largest buyers.

Imports also declined, falling by 18.3% year on year. Foreign beer accounted for only 2.5% of total beer consumption in the Czech Republic, down 0.5 percentage points from 2024.

World.title: Nearly Half of Czechs Spend More Than 30% of Their Income on Housing
World.content:
Nearly half of people in the Czech Republic spend more than 30% of their net income on housing, while around one in 10 spends more than half.

Housing is generally considered financially burdensome when rent, utilities and other related costs exceed 30–40% of household income. The EU average is around 24%.



The findings come from a survey by Česká spořitelna and Evropa v datech, conducted with Ipsos among 1,000 respondents in February.

Housing affordability remains particularly difficult for young Czechs. Among people aged 18 to 29, 58% live with their parents at least part of the time, while 29% live with friends or a partner.

The survey found that 60% of people under 30 who are dissatisfied with their housing situation have postponed a major life decision because of it. For around one-third, this has happened repeatedly. Starting a family is among the decisions affected by housing conditions.

Homeowners were considerably more likely to be very satisfied than renters, with 41% of owners describing themselves as very satisfied compared with 18% of renters.

Czechia still has the least affordable housing in the EU

The Czech Republic improved by six places in this year’s housing conditions ranking, reaching 17th among the 27 EU member states. The improvement was linked to increased investment in residential construction, fewer households facing excessive housing costs or difficulties paying for heating, and relatively favorable rental conditions.

Buying a home, however, remains more difficult than elsewhere in the EU.

An average-sized Czech apartment costs 13.3 average annual gross salaries, compared with 13.6 a year earlier. The figure has improved only slightly, while other countries have made faster progress. In Hungary, the ratio fell from 13.6 to 11.9 annual salaries, while Slovakia improved from 13.2 to 11.7 and Slovenia from 13.4 to 11.4.

Ireland has the most affordable housing by this measure, with an average home costing 6.2 annual salaries, followed by Belgium and Finland.

An average apartment in Czechia costs roughly the equivalent of 29 years of average rent. In city centers, the figure is close to 31 years, compared with less than 13 years in Ireland.

High housing costs are changing household decisions

Housing expenses are also forcing some households to reduce other spending. Last year, 40% cut their budgets because of housing costs. Nearly one-quarter reduced spending on holidays, hobbies and entertainment, while 16% cut spending on essentials such as food, clothing and personal-care products.

Around 38% of Czechs see living with parents as an economic necessity caused by high property prices. Another 26% consider it a reasonable temporary solution, while 9.4% see multigenerational living as a viable long-term model.

At the same time, 46% of young people expect to inherit property from their families.

World.title: US-Hungary Relations: exercise in patience and self-interest
World.content:
When Donald J Trump walked down the gold-plated elevator at his New York Trump Tower in June 2016 to announce his candidacy for presidency of the United States, hardly any European leader –not to mention many in his own country—took him seriously.

Written by Peyman Pejman

Except one: Hungary’s former strongman and long-time Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.

“Prime Minister Orbán used to say we were Trump before Trump,” reminisced Márton Ugrosdy, who served as Deputy State Secretary at Orbán’s office from 2022 to 2026. When Trump ran for office, Orbán was all in supporting the candidate.

Orbán and his administration were already upset by what they saw as the Obama administration’s constant pro-democracy push in Hungary. Relations worsened during Joe Biden’s presidency after Trump’s first time in office.

“Under the Biden administration, relations were stormy. US ambassador (David Pressman) tried to interfere in Hungarian internal affairs every day. You can do it but not every day and on that scale. At the end of the day, you are a guest of the host country. It was very harmful,”

adds Dávid Nagy, a political analyst, security and defense policy expert at Oeconomus Economic Research Foundation, which was partially funded through pro-Orbán organizations and networks.

Since coming to office, much has been written about the Orbán-Trump relationship.

Photo: Facebook/OrbánViktor

The US-Hungary relationship changed “in the last 10 years mainly because the relationship was not a classical diplomatic line but more ideological because Orban’s foreign policy was personalized and served power interest rather than national interest,” Zsuzsanna Szelényi, director of the Democracy Institute Leadership Academy for Central and Eastern Europe at the Central European University (CEU).

“The relations became more Orbán-Trump, not Hungary-US.”

Szelényi spoke to Daily News Hungary on the sidelines of the Budapest Forum, organized by CEU on October 1.

But Orbán is no longer the prime minister and Trump will constitutionally have to leave office on Jan 20, 2029. So, what’s next? What will the relationship look like under Péter Magyar premiership? What will each side want from the other partner?

The answer is not clear cut and depends on with whom you talk but there are commonalities regardless of political ideology. Short answer: expect neither a miracle nor a tragedy. But the longer answer is more nuanced.

If you missed it: Have Orbán’s former allies abandoned him? He may be seeking international posts that offer protection

Diplomatic and economic relations between Hungary and the United States go back to 1921. To judge the relations, or predict their future, based on Trump-Orbán relations might not pass historical scrutiny.

“Hungary was interesting in the 90s because of the Balkan war. At the time Hungary was not even a NATO member but it was interesting because the US could use Hungarian (military) bases for bombings in the Balkans. That’s how Hungary got on the US map,” adds Nagy. During the 2003 US-led operation to topple the regime of Saddam Hussein, Hungary contributed non-combat support.

Europe –including Hungary—have so far stayed out of the US-Iran war, despite Trump having complained on multiple occasions about Europe not “helping.”

Military cooperation aside, at least for now, prospects for warm and fuzzy diplomatic relations also seem to be farfetched.

“What I see is that if there is nothing special in Hungary, we just don’t matter because we are a small country in the middle of Europe with no strategic importance,” says Ugrosdy. What could that special thing be? “Aside from ideology, not much!”

There is disagreement on whether Prime Minister Magyar’s stated goal of wanting to mend relations with the European Commission after years of friction with Orbán could prove an obstacle in the US-Hungary relations.

Ugrosdy thinks Magyar will likely bow to pressure from the Commission leadership and several anti-Trump EU presidents by keeping his distance from Washington unless needed otherwise. CEU’s Szelényi disagrees.

Zsuzsanna Szelényi, director of the Democracy Institute Leadership Academy for Central and Eastern Europe at the Central European University (CEU)

“Every European country has some relations with the United States, especially NATO countries so that is not unique to the Hungarian foreign ministry. It is very important for the Hungarian administration to convey that Hungary will be a faithful partner in NATO and the EU and NATO is also the US. I don’t see any special conflict,” says Szelényi.

Economics and trade relations might be the wild card in the US-Hungary relations.

The exact amount of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) by the US government and US companies in Hungary is not clear because of accounting method differences between organizations such as the Magyar National Bank, the US Department of State, and the US Bureau of Economic Analysis.

Roughly speaking, the US has invested about $9.5 billion in Hungary since 1989, with 2025 reportedly seeing the largest amount. According to the Hungarian Investment Promotion Agency (HIPA), 16 major US companies announced $480 million new investments in 2025, potentially creating 800 high-value-added jobs. According to figures by the International Trade Administration, a US government entity, US wholly owned and “affiliate” companies, employ 110,000 Hungarians.

Will the Magyar government be able, or be interested, to maintain high-level US investments?

“American companies did not come here because they like us politically. They came here because the business environment was good for them. Energy prices were low, low corporate income tax, cheap and available labor. As long as those factors are here, they might be interested in keeping their projects but if the energy prices go up or the corporate taxes go up, they will leave,” says Ugrosdy.

Szelényi also points out that the two countries still have a chance to renegotiate the abrogation of the double taxation treaty between the two countries which went into effect in on January 1, 2024, and canceled the 1979 agreement which benefitted many American companies because of low corporate tax rate in Hungary.

Under current rules imposed by the European Union, companies with group revenue above €750 million are already subject to a global minimum tax of 15 percent. Should the Magyar government try to tweak Hungary’s rates, it could adversely affect American and multinational companies.

Few, whether in Hungary or the United States, think Magyar will compensate for Orbán’s close relationship with the Trump administration and his extreme conservative, right-wing MAGA supporters by reaching out particularly to the Democratic establishment and the progressive wing of Democrats in America.

“The new government recognizes that it has different geopolitical views than the White House but I don’t think Magyar is going to champion progressive causes. He is essentially conservative. He came from the Fidesz political group. So I don’t see too much turbulence in the Washington-Budapest relationship,” says Robert Benson from the left-leaning Center for American Progress in the United States.

If you missed it: Watch here: Hungarian foreign minister Anita Orbán speaks to CNN about changes under new government

Hungarians concur.

“He (Magyar) claims to be a conservative politician so for me it would be strange if he reached out to the AOC progressives or donors like (Hungarian-born US billionaire philanthropist) George Soros,” says Ugrosdy, referring to progressive US Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Soros has been a major donor to Democrat-supported and liberal-progressive causes, institutions and civil society organizations, including the CEU. “I don’t think any further outreach is necessary.”

While Magyar’s inclination would likely be stabilizing relations with Washington and not revolutionizing it, Orbán’s shadow could still loom large, maybe even with help from the Trump administration.

Orbán and his allies established, funded, and nurtured numerous conservative organizations and think tanks in Europe and maintained solid ties with similar groups in the United States. Much of his financial support was financed with Hungarian taxpayer money, although his affluent business and ideological allies also contributed. It remains to be seen how viable those funding mechanisms will be.

Benson, from the Center for American Progress, says the US Department of State’s Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor has a $5 million grants budget from which European organizations and think tanks allied with the Trump administration can benefit. He questions whether Orbán can be influential in funneling some of that money into organizations he supported before.

“I think it would be important for Orbán to nurture these international illiberal networks which he was building so carefully over 10 years and he probably hopes that if he can maintain it might help him to come back to power again, but that is my personal evaluation,” says Szelényi.

As we wrote earlier, Hungary seeks US exemption from Russian energy sanctions during transition

World.title: A connected energy asset should never have more authority than it needs
World.content:
A wind turbine on a distant ridge still looks like old-fashioned physical infrastructure. So does a field of solar panels beside a highway. But increasingly, each is also part of a digital system that can be reached, monitored and sometimes controlled from somewhere else. That quiet change matters because the green transition is not only adding generation capacity. It is adding doors.

Written by Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi (A.S. Alhebsi) – Author and Researcher specializing in Security, Heritage, Risk Management, and Control Room Operations.

Dutch researchers working with the Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre reported this week that 8,547 wind and solar systems across 35 European countries were improperly exposed to the internet. Reuters reported that around 181 sites appeared to offer interfaces capable of operational control, including actions such as turning turbines on or off. The immediate lesson is obvious: exposed administrative interfaces should not be sitting openly on the internet. The larger lesson is less comfortable. We are building critical infrastructure faster than we are learning to count all the ways it can be reached.

I do not see this as an argument against renewable energy or against connected infrastructure. Connectivity is one of the reasons modern energy systems can be monitored, maintained and balanced efficiently. Remote access can reduce downtime and allow specialists to diagnose equipment without travelling to every site. The problem begins when convenience and authority travel through the same digital doorway without enough separation between them.

Hungary sits inside an increasingly interconnected European energy environment, where domestic assets, regional grids and digital services depend on one another. That makes a remotely reachable renewable asset more than a local IT issue.

This is where I think the usual cybersecurity question is too narrow. We often ask whether a device is secure. Operators should also ask three simpler operational questions: Who can reach it? What authority does that access provide? What physical consequence can follow? I think of this as a Reach–Authority–Consequence test. A public dashboard, a maintenance portal and a command interface may all be connected to the same asset, but they should never be treated as if they carry the same risk.

If you missed it – Hungarian State Treasury hacking scandal: Is the Russian connection merely a cover story?

The distinction becomes important in distributed energy. A traditional power station concentrates equipment, people and security controls in a relatively bounded place. Renewable systems distribute assets across rooftops, farms, industrial sites and remote terrain. That is a strength for generation, but it also distributes the security problem. Energy decentralisation creates security decentralisation. Every new inverter, turbine controller, gateway, vendor account and remote-maintenance path can become part of the operational perimeter.

For operators, the practical priority is least privilege translated into physical terms. A maintenance account should have exactly the authority required for maintenance, for exactly as long as it is needed, and no more.

There is a useful connection here with what the UAE announced on 6 October. The UAE Cyber Security Council and SCC Middle East said they plan to establish a Centre of Excellence for Cyber Resilience and Trusted Technology where government, industry and specialists can test real use cases and examine how technologies can be adopted securely at scale. What interests me is not the existence of another technology centre. It is the emphasis on proving how technology behaves in the environment where it will actually be used. That is exactly the habit critical infrastructure needs.

A procurement checklist can tell an organisation that a product supports encryption, authentication or logging. It cannot by itself tell an operator what happens when a contractor account is compromised at 2 a.m., whether a remote command can bypass a local safeguard, or how quickly a control room can isolate a connection without taking down the service it is trying to protect. Those questions need exercises, test environments and people from operations, engineering and cybersecurity sitting at the same table.

The practical response does not have to begin with an expensive new platform. Asset owners can start by identifying every internet-reachable operational interface, removing public exposure that is not necessary, separating monitoring from command authority, tightening vendor access and testing whether operators can revoke remote privileges quickly. Most importantly, they can map digital access to physical consequence. A credential that can only read performance data is not the same as a credential that can stop equipment. Security architecture should make that difference visible.

I would also resist the instinct to turn every discovery into a story about an inevitable cyber catastrophe. The researchers found exposure and potential control paths; that is serious enough without exaggeration. Good security culture is built on precision. If we overstate every weakness, operators eventually stop listening. If we understate reachability, we discover too late that a digital convenience had become operational authority.

Hungary and the UAE both have strong reasons to treat energy resilience as an operational discipline. The most useful question is not whether an asset is online, but what being online allows someone to do.

The green transition will put more intelligence at the edge of the energy system. That is not something to fear. It is something to design for. The next generation of resilient infrastructure will not be defined by how few devices are connected, but by whether every connection has a reason, a boundary and a consequence the operator understands.

World.title: Hungarian dishes that seemed strange to me at first as a foreigner, but eventually won me over
World.content:
Cold fruit soup, sweet pasta, “bird’s milk” and meat served in jelly are among the Hungarian specialities that initially left me puzzled. What seemed unusual at first eventually became surprisingly enjoyable, turning culinary confusion into genuine appreciation.

Written by Fabiola Sosa

Meggyleves – Sour cherry soup

Picture this: a creamy pink soup with small, deep-red spheres. Floating in the centre is what looks like a dollop of white cream. Let’s be honest, it is a strikingly unusual composition, yet incredibly Instagrammable. If I am not mistaken, this is the only food I know with a colour quite like that.

Where do I even begin? This was the dish that taught me that cold soups actually exist, and I have to say, what a brilliant invention for those hot days when all you want to do is jump into Lake Balaton. I also had no idea that you could make a meal based on fruit without it being considered a dessert.

Then came the real adventure for my taste buds. I have a sweet tooth, so I love all sorts of combinations involving sweet flavours. For that reason, I sometimes wonder what it must have been like on the day a Hungarian woke up and said: “I know! I’m going to mix sour cherries with sour cream.” I will probably never find out, but I am quite sure I would have liked to be their friend.

Madártej – Hungarian floating islands

If you were expecting to read about an exotic ingredient, an unusual texture or a peculiar colour, I am sorry to say that will not be the case. I chose this dessert because its name has always caught my attention so much that I believe it actually shaped my experience the first time I tried it.

Madártej literally means “bird’s milk”. Yes, you read that correctly. When I was told what it means, I was so confused that for a few seconds I thought: “Wait, do birds produce milk?” But once I remembered that this could not be further from reality, I became slightly worried about trying it, as my intuition told me there might be some unexpected surprise involved.

As soon as I cautiously started eating it, I kept it in my mouth for quite a while because I wanted to figure out where such an expression came from. However, in the end, all I could sense was something soft and delicious that made me feel as though I were levitating among clouds of cotton. Although I ended up enjoying it, I still need someone to explain that name to me so I can sleep peacefully at night.

If you missed the article about the top restaurants in Hungary: Biggest restaurant awards 2026 announced – here are the Dining Guide winners

Mákos tészta – Poppy seed pasta

During my initial visit to Budapest, before officially moving to Hungary, I remember it was a summer day and I was walking around looking for a restaurant where I could have some traditional food. At one point, I came across a buffet that caught my attention. When I went inside and started looking at the variety of options on offer, there was one in particular that stood out for its eccentricity.

From my point of view, the only normal thing about it was the pasta, but what really caught my attention was the black colour of an unfamiliar powder it was mixed with. My immediate thought when I saw it was rat poison and, because of that, my curiosity only grew stronger. When I served myself some and finally tasted it, I did so blindly, with no idea what to expect.

Once I took a bite, it felt so strange to sense the texture and flavour of that mysterious powder, which turned out to be nothing more and nothing less than ground poppy seeds. I had never encountered this ingredient before, and I found it both fascinating and highly unusual that this kind of seed could be part of a pasta dish.

It was definitely unlike anything my palate was accustomed to, but my experience with mákos tészta did not end there. And there was still another surprise: a peculiar sweetness. The moment I noticed it, I briefly wondered whether someone in the kitchen was deliberately trying to get fired so they could collect their severance pay.

Nevertheless, I continued my investigation and, when I discovered that it was icing sugar, I simply could not believe it. How was it possible for something like that to be mixed with pasta? And, more importantly, how was it possible for something to taste so different and yet so good?

Kocsonya – Jellied meat

It is night, you are hungry and visiting someone else’s home when a jelly filled with pieces of pork and vegetables appears in front of you: R.I.P. Seriously, I think I lost around 30% of my brain cells as I struggled to understand what exactly I was looking at.

The nearest window to jump out of was quite far away, so I stayed there examining it carefully while wondering: “Do astronauts eat anything like this in space?” At that point, finding out did not really matter because there was no graceful way out of this one, and I had to face whatever was sitting on my plate, seemingly staring back at me through its two slices of carrot as though it had a life of its own.

The texture was familiar to me to some extent, as I had grown up with fruit jellies, but what I had to mentally digest was the fact that, this time, it was savoury. At first, it was also interesting to chew something gelatinous combined with pieces of solid food. Finally, after swallowing my last bite, I concluded that I could, in fact, be an astronaut.

World.title: Flight diversion plans need a passenger plan too
World.content:
Most travellers prepare for a delayed flight by allowing extra time or keeping a charger in their hand luggage. Few can prepare for an airport security emergency that suddenly changes where an aircraft can land. Yet the consequences may reach a passenger travelling far from the location of the original incident.

Written by A.S. Alhebsi (Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi)

Recent attacks on civilian airports in Saudi Arabia, followed by a statement of condemnation from the United Arab Emirates, offer a timely reason to examine the less visible side of aviation resilience. The first responsibility is the protection of life. The next is ensuring that operational decisions do not leave passengers without understandable information or practical assistance.

For travellers in Hungary and across Central Europe, this matters even when the incident occurs outside Europe. Routes to destinations in Asia and the Gulf rely on international connections, and disrupted itineraries can affect the rest of a journey. It would be wrong to suggest that every incident produces a direct disruption at Budapest Airport. The point is that travellers and airlines should not discover their responsibilities only after a route changes.

A diversion is a technical success when a flight lands safely at an alternate airport. For the person on board, however, a different set of problems may just be beginning. Is onward transport available? Is immigration clearance needed? What happens to checked baggage, medication, a connecting flight or an unaccompanied traveller? Who explains the next step if the airline, airport and booking company provide different information?

If you missed it: Record-breaking investments are pouring into Europe – here’s where the billions are going

These questions suggest three simple standards. First, airlines should have a single source of verified updates that can be shared consistently with passengers and airport service desks. Second, airports expecting diverted flights should test reception plans that include accessible information, basic welfare support and coordination with border authorities. Third, operators should evaluate recovery by more than the time of the first resumed flight: people who have been diverted or stranded must also have a workable route forward.

Hungary can draw a useful lesson here without pretending that its aviation system is identical to those in the Gulf. Budapest sits within a wider European transport network, giving passengers alternative routes by road and rail as well as air. That potential flexibility is an advantage only when travellers receive timely, accurate guidance and different providers cooperate. An alternative that nobody can explain is not yet a practical solution.

The UAE offers another relevant perspective as an international aviation crossroads. Its interest in regional stability reflects the reality that passenger safety and operational continuity depend on cooperation across national systems. The recent Saudi incidents are therefore not merely a security headline; they are a prompt to rehearse how aviation authorities and commercial operators communicate when normal assumptions fail.

Emergency communication does not have to promise certainty. A message that clearly states what is known, what remains unknown and when the next update will arrive is often better than an optimistic announcement that soon proves inaccurate. Passenger confidence is not built by removing every inconvenience. It is built by treating people as capable of understanding a difficult situation when institutions communicate with care.

The right time to design these arrangements is before the airport becomes crowded and the phones begin ringing. Aviation resilience should be judged not only by whether an aircraft lands safely, but by whether the people on board can continue their journey with dignity and reliable support.

Author: A.S. Alhebsi | Author and Researcher specializing in Security, Heritage, Risk Management, and Control Room Operations
