World.title: McLarens, Mar-a-Lago and machine guns: Introducing Gina Rinehart’s controversial  new frontier point man
World.content:
Ricardo Lopez Tugendhat believed he was going to die and wanted the world to know who he thought was going to kill him.

The former manager at a mining company linked to Australian billionaire Gina Rinehart spelled out his fears in a chilling letter to an Ecuadorian news outlet.

“Being familiar with the character and temperament of Mr Carlos de Miguel III, I am deeply concerned that the threats I have received from him … are carried out,” read the letter, published by the outlet.

“I hereby publicly hold the aforementioned Carlos de Miguel III responsible for any attack against the life or physical integrity of my family or myself.”

Carlos de Miguel is Rinehart’s man on the ground in Ecuador – the chief executive of Hanrine Ecuadorian Exploration and Mining, a subsidiary of Hancock Prospecting.

He is a former US serviceman who instilled fear in some workers. Some former workers claim de Miguel would saunter around Hanrine’s sites in northern Ecuador with an assault rifle and flanked by menacing-looking dogs.

He loomed as a central character when this masthead spent a month in Ecuador tracking Hanrine’s controversial activities in the Latin American country.

The investigation examined hundreds of pages of government documents, company records, court files and research papers, and spoke to dozens of villagers, environmental activists and experts, who detailed allegations of human rights breaches, irregularities in the concessioning process and a pattern of violence and harassment towards local villagers.

Former Hanrine workers detailed allegations of exploitation and abuses at the company’s site in La Merced de Buenos Aires, including hiding workers without contracts from authorities conducting compliance checks, serving raw meat to labourers, forcing employees to work while sick and a culture of threats and intimidation.

Most workers this masthead spoke to were too scared to be quoted on the record, fearing retaliation from Hanrine, which categorically denies any wrongdoing and maintains it complies with “relevant laws and regulations”.

The claims raise serious questions about the company’s operations, which have been a subject of sustained controversy, and which critics say highlight the lack of accountability and oversight for Australian subsidiaries operating overseas.

A member of the Awa Indigenous community wears a Hanrine T-shirt during a communal labour meet-up known as a “minga” in Palmira de Toctemí, a community in the Awa’s ancestral land in La Merced de Buenos Aires parish. James Ross

Julien Vincent, an experienced climate change governance campaigner and former winner of the Goldman Environmental Prize, which recognises grassroots activists, says there should be an expectation that Australian companies and their subsidiaries operate to a higher standard overseas than they would at home.

“That’s because they’re not just doing business, they are representing Australia in another part of the world,” Vincent says.

Local media have chronicled de Miguel’s career from working as a security contractor for former Ecuadorian president Rafael Correa to handling security for WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange at the Ecuadorian embassy in London in 2012.

Gabriela Chiriboga and Carlos de Miguel attend the Hispanic Prosperity Gala at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, in February. Getty Images for Latino Wall Street

The mining executive said in interviews with local media outlets that he has had a decade-long association with Hancock Prospecting, beginning in 2015 when the company became interested in diversifying its portfolio into Latin America.

De Miguel shares Rinehart’s conservative political views and her support for US President Donald Trump. He made a US$250,000 donation to the Trump-Vance inaugural committee and attended the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), where Rinehart is a regular attendee.

De Miguel was among several Hancock Prospecting executives who toured the US with Rinehart in early 2025. He later attended the Starlight Ball in Washington to mark Trump’s inauguration, where Rinehart was photographed talking to Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa and his wife, Lavinia Valbonesi.

Hanrine chief executive Carlos de Miguel oversees Gina Rinehart’s operations in Ecuador.

De Miguel posed on a red carpet while wearing a velvet suit and aviator sunglasses at the Hispanic Prosperity Gala in Florida, where the mining executive owns a $US1.4 million home. The event, held at Mar-a-Lago in February, was sponsored by Hanrine, Trump Vodka and the Gina Rinehart Foundation.

De Miguel is also a car aficionado and the owner of a silver McLaren GT that he occasionally races. The car is nicknamed Maverick in a reference to the Top Gun movies.

‘THREATS, WEAPONS AND RAW MEAT’

Luis Fausto de la Cruz remembers when he fell out of love with working for Hanrine. It was 2022 and the farmer turned labourer was at the company’s camp on the edge of La Merced de Buenos Aires when, he says, a ute pulled up.

De Miguel, surrounded by security guards and flanked by two menacing-looking dogs, had walked out of the vehicle armed with a sophisticated assault-style rifle, de la Cruz says.

“He spoke about having been to war; I don’t know how many wars,” de la Cruz says. “It hurt my soul.”

De la Cruz, a father of six, believes this was an attempt to intimidate staff. It made him furious but he felt helpless.

“There was nothing one could do; if you spoke up, you were treated like a criminal,” he says. “So much for the claim that they are trained, educated people … you don’t come to [deal with] humble folk with weapons.”

De Miguel did not address questions about this alleged conduct directly but “categorically rejects” any allegation workers were mistreated.

De la Cruz says he worked carrying building materials and doing manual labour for Hanrine for about eight months, before staff were fired en masse and the company withdrew from the area. He claims the working conditions were brutal.

Workers would be sent to the mountains around La Merced de Buenos Aires for 20 days at a time, and left incommunicado from their family, he says. No phones were allowed on site, which also meant workers could not take photographs of their living conditions.

Staff slept in bunk beds in large tents, and the food served, he claims, often arrived cold, spoiled or raw. De la Cruz remembers one occasion when staff were given a special Christmas meal of roast pork that made several people sick.

“We aren’t dogs that eat raw meat,” he says.

He says staff who became ill were denied leave and made to work.

La Merced de Buenos Aires local government president Lucia Chicaiza says Hanrine staff often referred to her as “Lucifer” because of her anti-mining advocacy. James Ross

Lucia Chicaiza, the president of La Merced de Buenos Aires parish, says many workers were too scared to report their working conditions to authorities.

As previously reported by this masthead, several villagers in the parish claim, including in a judicial council report, to have been assaulted, stabbed and harassed by Hanrine staff for their anti-mining views. The company is also accused of hiring illegal miners as security guards, who were often armed.

Another former Hanrine employee, who spoke anonymously because of safety concerns, claims de Miguel was permanently armed and kept weapons inside company premises.

“He told us he had a permit to carry a weapon and that the police couldn’t even touch this gun,” the former employee alleges.

Local anti-mining protesters who had blocked the company from accessing its concessions in the parish would often be referred to by Hanrine staff as “chunchos” – a derogatory term that roughly translates to “savages”. Chicaiza was often called Lucifer.

Chicaiza says reports about Hanrine’s camps were so concerning she asked authorities to carry out a compliance visit.

“That’s when they hid us,” de la Cruz claims. “I was there.”

One morning, de la Cruz says, casual workers were told to leave the camp and head “for a walk” in the mountains. Staff were made to “hide” away from the camp while officials from the department of employment inspected the site.

Another Hanrine employee also claimed staff were told to leave the company’s facilities whenever authorities conducted compliance checks.

Manuel de la Cruz, a potato farmer who also worked as a manual labourer for Hanrine, says staff would be hidden from officials “because they weren’t paying the daily wages legally as they should”.

Former Ecuadorian employment minister Patricio Donoso told a human rights committee of non-government MPs in Ecuador’s national assembly in 2023 that the company was twice sanctioned for blocking department officials conducting compliance checks, and failing to present employment contracts for its workers.

It is unclear how many locals were employed by Hanrine. De Miguel has previously claimed in the media to have hired up to 200 people, many from the local community. Donoso placed the figure close to 300, although 169 contracts had been terminated at the time he spoke to the committee in 2023.

Hancock Prospecting has publicly acknowledged in its annual reporting on its modern slavery obligations that its operations in Ecuador are its highest risk jurisdiction.

This masthead is not accusing the company of breaching those obligations, only noting that it has stated repeatedly its awareness of potential labour issues in the country.

In a statement, de Miguel denied all claims workers were treated poorly. He said he had received “numerous messages from staff expressing their appreciation for Hanrine, its workplace culture and the opportunities the company has provided” and shared two undated messages from unnamed employees praising the company.

“In countries like Australia it can be easy to underestimate just how significant the opportunity of employment can be for people living in poor areas,” de Miguel said.

The average annual GDP per person in Ecuador is estimated at $10,000, according to anti-modern-slavery organisation Walk Free.

THE STASH OF WEAPONS AND 9500 BULLETS

The letter Ricardo Lopez Tugendhat penned to news outfit La Fuente: Periodismo de Investigacion in 2020 highlights just how feared de Miguel was by some who had crossed paths with him.

Lopez Tugendhat had previously worked closely with de Miguel as assistant manager, handling security for Hanrine, until their relationship soured early that year.

Hanrine and Lopez Tugendhat were caught in a messy dispute that led to both parties taking each other to court, and Lopez Tugendhat reporting de Miguel to authorities for alleged intimidation.

Part of the dispute involved claims by Hanrine that Lopez Tugendhat had used a fake disability card to claim benefits he was not entitled to. Lopez Tugendhat claimed he had been unfairly dismissed by the company.

Hanrine later dropped the disability card case after signing an agreement with Lopez Tugendhat, and the court found him not guilty this year. The unfair dismissal claim was settled and Hanrine paid $US20,000 to Lopez Tugendhat in 2022, according to court documents.

At the time he sent the letter, Lopez Tugendhat was worried an article published by the news outlet would draw the ire of his former boss.

The article suggested Lopez Tugendhat, a three-time shooting world champion, could have tipped off the police to a stash of firearms and ammunition hidden in de Miguel’s home gym.

Police had raided de Miguel’s property and arrested the businessman the previous month on the basis he did not hold valid permits for three of four firearms found, which included a high-powered rifle used by elite police and military officers. Investigators also found 9500 rounds of ammunition, several magazines, an air rifle and a training gun, according to court documents and local media reports.

In the letter, Lopez Tugendhat claimed de Miguel had threatened to kill him and his family, and he provided a case number to track his report of the alleged threat through the prosecutor’s office.

This masthead was able to find a record of the original report Lopez Tugendhat filed against de Miguel for alleged intimidation in January 2020, but it did not contain any findings.

“The only report I’ve made against Mr Carlos de Miguel III is for intimidation and death threats, of which me and my family were the victims of,” Lopez Tugendhat pleaded in his letter.

“I expressly request that your prestigious media outlet clarify and correct the record.”

The weapons case against de Miguel was dropped 10 months after the raid, after it was determined the businessman was in the process of renewing the expired permits.

The decision was partly informed by Lopez Tugendhat’s evidence that de Miguel was a member of his recreational shooting club and the ammunition found in his home had been bought through the club.

De Miguel later said the raid was part of a plot to discredit him as a mining executive and derail Hanrine’s bid to obtain a lucrative copper project near its concessions in La Merced de Buenos Aires called Llurimagua that the company was offering to acquire for US$400 million.

When contacted by this masthead, de Miguel said it was not uncommon in Ecuador for allegations to arise in the context of employment disputes.

“The unfounded workplace allegations against myself that you reference were categorically dismissed and did not result in any charges or adverse findings against me,” de Miguel said.

Lopez Tugendhat declined to comment when contacted by this masthead.

BROKEN PROMISES

On a clear morning, you can see the Colombian border from the top of Luis Fausto de la Cruz’s land.

Motilon trees – a high-altitude Andean species that produces a deep purple berry used to make “colada morada”, a thick smoothie-style drink used to commemorate the Day of the Dead festivities – grow in the small valleys that form between the hills undulating through his land.

Bears and guans, a large chicken-like bird native to the Andes, are regular visitors to the property, which is also home to a waterfall and walking trails.

De la Cruz, yellow shin-high rubber boots on his feet, walks through the overgrown paths with a machete in his hand. He wants to turn part of his land into an ecotourism venture with huts, bird lookouts, a zipline and horseriding routes.

“There’s a lot of birds here,” he says. “I am going to fight little by little to do something.”

De la Cruz says he doesn’t regret working for Hanrine. It was an eye-opening experience. But he feels locals were taken advantage of and promises of new homes, roads and services that lured locals like himself to work with the company were never fulfilled.

He says he isn’t afraid that speaking out will make him a target.

“The only thing I fear is God, no one else.”

World.title: Enjoyed your weekend? You have a resident of this UK city to thank for it
World.content:
InspirationEurope Enjoyed your weekend? You have a resident of this UK city to thank for it Steve McKenna October 12, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Overshadowed by Manchester, its rival just across the River Irwell, Salford marks its 100th birthday as a city in 2026 (it was officially granted city status by King George V in 1926). But its story stretches back much further – think neolithic tribes, ancient Roman troops – and it’s bursting with surprising firsts, claims and feats. A big one is that a Salfordian invented the weekend. In 1843, activist Robert Lowes (actor Sir Ian McKellen’s great-great-grandfather) successfully campaigned for workers at a Salford mill to have Saturday afternoons off. Salford Quays, near the Manchester Ship Canal, is the setting for the annual We Invented the Weekend festival. iStock This trailblazing trend spread around the UK, sowing the seeds for a two-day weekend and ultimately sparking more freedom for the joys of life, from sports and travelling to lie-ins to read the papers. Many visitors attending soccer matches, arena concerts and arts festivals in Manchester stay in Salford without realising it. Manchester and Salford essentially share the same city centre – or “town” as it’s known locally – and several hotels rise on Salford’s side of the river, including CitySuites, an aparthotel in whose lobby I once bumped into soccer legend Pep Guardiola. He lived here during his decade-long stint as Manchester City boss and was often seen riding his bike on Chapel Street, Salford’s historic thoroughfare.



Touted, in 1806, as the UK’s first street to be lit by gas, it’s backdropped by towering modern offices and apartments with traditional pubs, tapas bars and cafes alongside attractive older buildings. 



There’s a recreation of a typical Victorian cobbled street, lined with authentic reclaimed shopfronts, at Salford Museum & Art Gallery. It’s by the university campus overlooking the riverside Peel Park, one of the most idyllic spots in a city usually associated with grit and industry. Rugby pioneer William Webb Ellis and brewer-cum-scientist James Prescott Joule were also born in Salford, which local folk musician Ewan MacColl immortalised in Dirty Old Town, a 1949 tune later covered by the Dubliners, The Pogues and Rod Stewart. MacColl also wrote The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face, which was a massive hit for Roberta Flack in 1972. Regeneration, however, is a Salford forte. A 62-hectare botanical retreat, RHS Garden Bridgewater, has revived an overgrown country estate at Worsley, a canal-hugging Salfordian village with pretty timber-beamed houses and woodland walks. Ordsall Hall is a beautifully preserved Tudor manor house near Salford Quays. iStock Close to Ordsall Hall, a beautifully preserved Tudor manor house, Salford Quays is another alluring waterside draw. This district is the setting for the annual We Invented the Weekend festival and is located near the end of the Manchester Ship Canal, which once brought ocean-going cargo vessels 60 kilometres inland from the Irish Sea.



Derelict by the 1980s, Salford’s rejuvenated docks are anchored around MediaCity, a glossy TV and tech hub where the BBC’s studios soar opposite Lowry, a theatre and gallery complex honouring L.S. Lowry (1887-1976), a revered artist who also worked as a debt collector in Salford. It stages everything from original local plays to Broadway and West End productions and displays Lowry’s idiosyncratic paintings, peopled with “matchstick men”. There’s a giant audiovisual exhibit of his 1953 piece Going to the Match. The BBC’s studios are housed in Salford’s MediaCity, a creative and tech hub. iStock Incidentally, you’ll see Old Trafford, Manchester United’s stadium, from the terrace of Central Bay, a cosmopolitan food hall by Lowry (which often is, but shouldn’t be, confused with the similarly named hotel in “town”). Another MediaCity favourite is the Coronation Street Experience, showcasing the sets of the world’s longest-running TV soap opera, which creator Tony Warren modelled on working-class life in Salford. There’s actually a real Coronation Street.



Located between the Quays and Chapel Street, it’s a magnet for lovers of “Corrie” and The Smiths, as the street’s community space, Salford Lads’ Club, graced the sleeve of the Manchester band’s 1986 album The Queen is Dead. Inside, there’s a room jammed with The Smiths memorabilia. The soap opera Coronation Street is filmed in the ITV Trafford Wharf Studios backlot at MediaCity. iStock Related Article Newcastle England England’s most northern city is heaving with unexpected delights One repeat visitor to the club is British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. You’ll find his flagship mayoral project, the Bee Network, and its yellow-branded trams, bikes and double-decker buses, a handy way to buzz between Manchester and Salford. THE DETAILS



FLY

Emirates flies to Manchester from Sydney and Melbourne via Dubai. STAY

CitySuites has studios from around £110 ($211). See citysuites.com MORE

visitsalford.info; visitmanchester.com; visitbritain.com The writer travelled at his own expense. For more on travel in the UK, watch Getaway on 9now.

World.title: No, eggs don’t actually increase cholesterol levels (plus four more common myths)
World.content:
Sponsored Tips & adviceDietitian’s guide No, eggs don’t actually increase cholesterol levels (plus four more common myths) Is it okay to eat eggs every day and how many is too many? A dietitian separates the facts from the fiction (and not the yolk from the white). Produced in partnership with Australian Eggs. Sponsored by Australian Eggs Susie Burrell October 12, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Whether you enjoy your eggs poached to perfection, hard-boiled for a quick protein hit or scrambled on sourdough every Sunday morning, eggs are a nutrient powerhouse. Scrambled eggs. Getty Images/iStockphoto Offering 17 different vitamins and nutrients, along with high-quality protein, eggs are versatile, and can be enjoyed in a number of ways. Many of us also hold certain beliefs about eggs, which can affect how many eggs we eat, or how frequently we eat them. Here are some of the most common beliefs about eggs, and why, in many cases, they are complete myths. Eggs increase cholesterol levels



Perhaps the most common food myth of all time is that eggs increase blood cholesterol and as such should be avoided by anyone who has elevated lipid levels. While eggs, like all animal foods, do contain cholesterol, it does not mean that blood cholesterol levels are affected after eating eggs. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Rather, the saturated fat content of foods is more likely to affect cholesterol levels, and even then, blood cholesterol levels are usually dependent on a number of other variables including genetics, diet quality overall and the balance of fat types consumed. For this reason, even if you have elevated cholesterol levels, including up to seven eggs in your diet each week is the number suggested by the Heart Foundation. Are egg yolks all right? You bet they are. iStock Egg whites are healthier than the yolks



While gym bros may load up on the egg whites as a concentrated protein source, not enjoying the nutrient-rich yolks would be a real shame nutritionally. While egg whites contain little to no fat, ultimately the key nutrients eggs offer are all found in the egg yolk. With just over four grams of fat per yolk, all of the fat-soluble vitamins including vitamins A, D and E are found there, along with iron, selenium, choline as well as the antioxidants lutein and zeaxanthin, which support eye health. The yolk also contains almost three grams of protein. This is compared to the egg white, which contains almost four grams of protein. This means if you are looking to increase your protein intake, you can certainly use extra whites, but you’ll be missing out on plenty of goodness the yolks have to offer. Related Recipe collection Eggs for dinner? Give it a crack with these easy protein-packed dishes Raw eggs are a good source of protein



Whether you have seen it in the movies, or even at the gym, buffed individuals downing raw eggs is something we have been taught is a great thing to do if building muscle mass is the goal. While consuming egg whites is an easy way to consume relatively large amounts of high-quality protein in a small volume of food, or a protein-rich ingredient to add to dishes to increase the protein content, the protein in eggs actually becomes more bioavailable when the eggs are consumed cooked. Specifically, cooking eggs helps to increase how much protein from eggs the body can absorb, from just 50 per cent when the egg is consumed raw to more than 90 per cent. The reason is that when the egg protein is exposed to heat, the dense protein structures are denatured, making it easier for the digestive enzymes to break the proteins down into absorbable amino acids. This means that if maximising your protein intake is the goal, cooking your eggs is a no-brainer. A couple of eggs a day can help keep the doctor away. William Meppem



Eating “too many” eggs is bad for you It is not uncommon to hear recommendations to limit egg intake both to control fat consumption and support heart health, but public health organisations support the consumption of a couple of eggs every day, noting them as a nutrient-dense, protein-rich food addition that is relatively low in saturated fat. Related Article EASY Adam Liaw’s Florentine egg muffins < 30 mins While it is entirely possible to eat too much of any one food, moderate, daily egg consumption is completely safe for the average person, only likely to improve overall nutrient intake given the natural presence of a number of more obscure nutrients, including choline and selenium, few Aussies get optimal amounts of. In practical terms this means that for the average person a couple of eggs can be enjoyed daily with no cause for concern.



Hard boiled eggs are better for weight loss. Marina Oliphant You should not eat eggs if you want to lose weight On many a low-fat diet, eggs as a key breakfast option have been ditched in favour of low-fat yoghurt and cereal breakfast options, but if anything, the science shows eggs are a superior breakfast option when it comes to weight loss. One key study that demonstrates this was published in the International Journal of Obesity. Researchers found that when compared to a bagel-based breakfast as part of a diet with a calorie deficit to support fat loss, egg-based breakfasts that offered a similar calorie load to the bagel-based breakfast resulted in a 65 per cent greater weight loss and 34 per cent greater reduction in waist circumference over an eight-week period. It is thought that as eggs are typically more satisfying, an egg-based breakfast also positively affects calorie consumption for the remainder of the day.

World.title: Top food talents bring two exciting new dining concepts to surprising Sydney suburb
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outJust open Top food talents bring two exciting new dining concepts to surprising Sydney suburb A former Soul Dining chef launches a 35-seater that specialises in Korean broth dishes, while cult Darlinghurst restaurant Joe’s Table is opening a new modern Thai venture. Scott Bolles October 12, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Two of Sydney’s seasoned hospitality pros are turning their attention to an unexpected suburban pocket, with cult Darlinghurst restaurant Joe’s Table opening a new dining concept at Macquarie Park next year, and the former head chef at recently closed CBD fine diner Soul Dining launching the broth-focused Jin Guk in the suburb this week. Why the sudden interest from the city’s food talent in the northside commercial and residential hub? Jin Guk caters to the growing appetite for Korean food. Daniel Choi “The Korean community in Eastwood is just a 10-minute drive away,” said Kenny Lee, chief operating officer at JS Hospitality, the group backing Jin Guk. The appetite for Korean food at Macquarie Park is evident in last month’s launch of the sprawling S-Mart, a Korean specialty food store. Lee and Joe’s Table owner, Joe Kitsana, both rate Macquarie Park – with its tech industry and university – as already possessing a strong, captive dining market, and a location with potential as a wider-catchment food destination. The close proximity of the food-savvy residents of Ryde and Lane Cove was an attraction. “I see us building a whole new clientele there,” Kitsana said.



Kitsana started as a one-man band chef, waiter and sommelier at the well-reviewed, no-frills Joe’s Table in Darlinghurst. Skills he picked up working at Sydney restaurants Longrain, Sailor’s Thai and Phamish helped make Joe’s Table a chef and foodie haunt. But he’s teaming up at the new northside venue with restaurateur Darase Kraykaew, from Haymarket restaurant At Bangkok. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Spicy sogigi yukgaejang. Daniel Choi “It’ll be called Song Wat,” Kitsana said, referring to the vibrant Song Wat neighbourhood in Bangkok, which mixes old shopfronts, spice houses and restaurants. “We’ll do modern Thai – the Chinese-Thai thing is hot in Thailand now,” Kitsana said. Song Wat will be located on Mahogany Avenue near the new Macquarie Park Public School, which opens next year. The restaurant is aiming for a mid-2027 launch. The wait won’t be as long for Jin Guk, with the 35-seater opening from lunch on Monday, October 12. Jin Guk takes its name from the Korean broth of pork, beef or seafood, and the restaurant’s specialty, gomtang, which is served with rice.



“Jin guk is similar to ramen, but we don’t use the bones, only meat,” chef Jay Lee explained. Lee skips bones in his version with an eye to producing a clearer soup. Joe Kitsana. Edwina Pickles Lee, the long-time head chef at Soul Dining, said he is enjoying the switch from an exacting chef’s hatted restaurant kitchen to the simpler yet still precise preparation of the soupy cornerstone of Korean cooking. “[Jin guk] is a deep, comforting broth, you can have it any time. For me, twice a week,” he said He admits to early trial and error with the cooking time of the different cuts of meat in the broth, and the rice proved equally challenging. They trialled rice from around the world, but couldn’t match the high moisture content and “sweetness” of Korean rice. So the broth at Jin Guk is served with rice from Cheorwon, a region near the demilitarised zone. Lee said the amount of rice added to the broth in Korea is up to the individual taste, similar to the way some Australians love lots of Vegemite and some a light smattering.

World.title: My suburb was sold to me as a bush paradise. Too bad about the heavy construction vehicles
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

My first experience of Brisbane was World Expo 88. Visiting from Sydney with my Dad, we zipped around on the monorail, watched the nightly laser light shows, and marvelled at the bright future of a rapidly changing “BrisVegas” – entirely unaware that I would, eventually, be calling this city home. The following year, when I was just 22, I bought a modest, one-bedroom flat in Kedron. No New South Wales bank would give me a mortgage at that age, but a Queensland bank backed me, and I became what would later be known as a “rentvester”, owning in Brisbane but living in a rented unit in Harbord – now Freshwater – on Sydney’s Northern Beaches. Roadworks and development along Canvey Road, Upper Kedron. Markus Ravik More homes are on the way. Markus Ravik Back then, there was no way I could afford to buy anything on that expensive slice of the coast, and I kept my Kedron unit for 13 years, finally selling it to buy my first home in Belrose. But Brisbane wasn’t done with me. Decades later, I needed to escape a volatile situation on those same Northern Beaches. I fled to Queensland, initially looking at new townhomes in Norman Park. Then I realised I could buy a brand-new house-and-land package in a masterplanned community called Ellendale, Upper Kedron, for the same price. Sold. So it’s a tale of two Kedrons, in fact.



The common misconception is that Upper Kedron must be right next door to Kedron. But the two suburbs are some 15 kilometres apart, separated west to east by Keperra, Mitchelton, Everton Park, Stafford Heights and Stafford. The explanation? We get our name from Kedron Brook, not Kedron proper. D’Aguilar National Park is, to be fair, a lovely bit of bushland. Markus Ravik Bushwalking here is a fabulous stress reliever. Markus Ravik The waterway notwithstanding, Kedron is highly urbanised, powered by the pumping artery of Gympie Road. Upper Kedron, by contrast, is surrounded on three sides by D’Aguilar National Park. Back in 2019, Canvey Road was a remarkably quiet place. Not so today. The masterplanned reality has manifested as a dense sea of massive, two-storey family homes increasingly crammed onto microplots. Despite having worked as a fact-checker in print and broadcast media, focused on truth-seeking, I managed to buy a suburban display home based on a developer’s glossy brochure that singularly failed to mention they were situated right on what would become the primary arterial road through the expanding estate. Ellendale at Upper Kedron is “a thriving community where the city meets nature”. Markus Ravik



Family homes here are large. Markus Ravik I should have realised I was buying into an expanding estate. Markus Ravik Instead of quiet bushland bliss, I have heavy dump trucks rattling my windows six days a week, pounding past until 6.30pm. This endless line of heavy construction vehicles treats my “peaceful haven” like a major highway. I’ve been forced to install a double-glazed uPVC entryway just to keep the din out. The Pensar water reservoir project is providing important infrastructure to the estate and while “every effort will be made to minimise impacts to the community”, the official masterplans tell me the work will continue until late 2027. Despite the noise, I am grateful to be in my own home, far away from the turmoil of the Northern Beaches. I am an outlier here – a self-proclaimed spinster librarian living with my cat Chloe in a heavily family-centric suburban estate. Conveniently, the Arana Hills library is just around the corner from the pool, allowing me to borrow books and converse with like-minded librarians.



As an avid animal lover, pet-sitting has become my passion, giving me a wonderful sense of productivity and purpose. Bushwalking on nearby trails is a fabulous stress reliever, and being so close to the native bush brings back pleasant memories of my childhood in Beacon Hill. When Ellendale Village finally opened we could hardly believe it. Markus Ravik Indi and Lily working the deli counter at IGA Upper Kedron. Markus Ravik Pharmacist Tony Yan from Terry White Chemmart, Upper Kedron. Markus Ravik Honeyeaters dart frantically through the canopy, and scrub turkeys prowl the ground level, completely indifferent to the changing landscape. They offer a fleeting escape from the suburban sprawl. In 2024, when Ellendale Village shops finally opened, we could hardly believe it. It was a long time coming. The car park is always full, but I prefer the walk as it’s so close to home. I seem to be in the IGA every other day. Their friendly staff always greet customers with a smile. We have a chemist right next to our Upper Kedron Medical Centre. Now I can walk down to see my new GP, too. When I need it most, kind neighbours often step in to help me.

World.title: Brisbane school stalls iPad program as cloud hangs over classroom tech
World.content:
NationalQueenslandSchools Brisbane school stalls iPad program as cloud hangs over classroom tech Catherine Strohfeldt October 12, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A Brisbane school has halted plans to make parents shell out for laptops for student use from year 4 following concerns they were buying into an expensive program with an uncertain future. Although the Queensland government favours a “balance” between traditional and digital teaching, other eastern states plan to pare back screen use in classrooms next year. Corinda State School, in south-west Brisbane, has announced it will delay a plan to overhaul its one-for-one iPad program – running from years 4 to 6 – after a vote by parents and school leaders last year. Individual schools in Queensland control how devices are used in classrooms, but state and national curriculums require them to be used across all subject areas. iStock Instead, it will offer school-owned devices shared between two students for a year, until families buy their own laptops for years 5 and 6.



Principal Carmel Herbert revealed the delay in a school newsletter, blaming “a recent escalation in the price of laptops, along with increased cost-of-living expenses”. Corinda parents told this masthead school officials and families had felt wary about buying into a potentially costly device program while the role of technology in classrooms was being debated. Corinda State School parent Doireann McPhee (centre) says the two-to-one iPad program is “so much better”. Corinda parent Doireann McPhee said she agreed with the postponement, adding: “The cost [of an iPad] was a concern for us.” The delay also reduced the amount of time children in early primary spent with screens, which McPhee said had resolved friction around setting boundaries for her older child.



“We had to get firm and put it away for most of the week ... the two-to-one iPad program is so much better, with limited use at school,” the mother-of-two said. Related Article Education Why Queensland hasn’t followed interstate crackdown on screens in classes “[It was] also great we didn’t have to bring another screen into the house.” A newsletter from Herbert in June last year estimated that participating in the one-for-two program could save families up to $600 on computers and tablets across a child’s 13 years of schooling. Mother-of-three Chloe Lowe said a similar shared program operated at Rainworth State School in Brisbane’s west, which her children attend. Students begin working with devices from year 3, then follow a one-to-one laptop program from year 5.



“I’m actually really happy with how they do technology at our school because I know [at other schools] they do iPad one-to-one devices from prep, or some version of that,” she said. “I prefer not to because they can pick up things so quickly with the technology … even my littlest will pick up my phone and she knows how to swipe across to get into the photos and open the photos. “I see a lot of merit in the pen-and-paper approach and developing fine motor [skills] and using your hands for learning – a mix of both, that’s pretty important.” The Education Department said schools managed their own device programs, with the department helping “as required”.

World.title: Profits prompt Wilson’s departure from VRC as he downplays talk of board rift
World.content:
SportRacingVictorian racing Profits prompt Wilson’s departure from VRC as he downplays talk of board rift Danny Russell and Bridget McArthur October 12, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Outgoing Victoria Racing Club chairman Neil Wilson has pointed to a $12.6 million year-on-year turnaround and a $5.4 million profit as one of the key reasons behind his surprise decision to step down, while dismissing claims his board was split by a move to appoint his successor. In a wide-ranging interview, Wilson told this masthead on Friday he decided to call time after 14 years at the club and the past six years as chairman because he was satisfied the organisation had emerged from the lingering financial pain of COVID-19, having lost $78 million across five years between 2020 and 2025. Victoria Racing Club chairman Neil Wilson with chief executive Kylie Rogers. Luis Enrique Ascui “I’m leaving with the view that this momentum and this growth and this strong performance will continue,” he said. But Wilson, who will relinquish his post after the annual general meeting (AGM) in December, said he was disappointed to have to confront allegations of a board rift on the eve of the Melbourne Cup carnival.



It comes after a source, speaking on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of club business, told The Age a decision to appoint Wilson’s replacement before the coming AGM had split the VRC board. The prestigious club announced Vin Cox as chair elect last week after a secret vote. Numbers were not released. But the source said they understood the 11 directors voted 6-5. The source told this masthead three candidates initially put their hands up for the chair role. Votes were reportedly split between Cox and vice chair Michael Ramsden, prompting a re-vote just between the two of them. Ramsden’s late father, Andrew, was a former VRC board member and chairman. Wilson and club CEO Kylie Rogers, who is also a director, took part in the vote.



But the decision to anoint the Queensland-based Cox raised eyebrows because he is up for re-election next month, meaning there was a possibility he could be voted off the board before taking over as chairman in December. The source also noted that Wilson had voted on his successor despite never intending to serve under their leadership – his seat will be filled in the coming elections and announced at the AGM. Vin Cox has been elected chair of the VRC and will take up the post later this year. Luke Marsden But Wilson dismissed the concerns, saying the same process had been followed during his entire time at the VRC and was “completely aligned with the governance processes across our constitution, bylaws, code of conduct and board charter”. “We felt the right decision was to be clear and to not have a period of unknown, and in fact, use the period between now and the 15th of December for me to work with the new chairman in a transition phase so that we could then reach that date, and things would just then move forward as expected.”



Wilson joined the VRC board in 2012 and became the only person in the club’s history to serve as both chief executive – from 2017 to 2020 – and chair. He said there was nothing in the club’s constitution preventing the CEO from voting. “The CEO in our club is a director, so they’re entitled to vote,” Wilson said. “When I was the CEO, I voted [on board matters], and there was never an issue.” Wilson said the board wanted to be clear and transparent with members, partners and the broader racing industry that the announcement of his retirement also included the name of the incoming chair. “It’s how good businesses operate from a succession point of view, and that was the decision we made,” he said. Wilson said Cox would be available in Melbourne whenever needed.



He said the former Godolphin managing director and Yulong general manager had not been part of any long-term succession plan. Related Article Blinkers On

Victorian racing Racing’s big gambling problem, and why it’s hurting punters “I think the term ‘succession’ has actually created a bit of noise because it was more, ‘who’s going to succeed me?’, and so we need a plan to actually make that happen,” Wilson said. “So it was a succession plan based on me announcing my retirement, and the plan was to go through the process to have people nominate, and then for the board to vote on who they wanted.” The source said dissenting directors believed the incoming board should have been allowed to determine who served as chair.



But Wilson said: “Each of the board directors made a choice based on their view of who the best person is to be the next chairman to succeed me. So, board members individually made the determination on that.” Club members will vote on four board positions at the coming elections, including the vacancy created by Wilson’s retirement. Cox, Carmody and Michael Saadie are up for re-election after serving three-year terms. The nomination process is expected to open in late October or early November before closing on Oaks Day and then would go to the members’ vote. It was possible several VRC members would nominate to join the board, but they would need to front a subcommittee to be ruled eligible to stand. Wilson refused to comment on any changes to the board after the AGM because it was purely speculation.



“I’m focused entirely on what’s best for the club,” he said. “And right now, what’s best for the club is to manage this transition to the new chairman, deliver an outstanding Melbourne Cup carnival, and make sure that we’re meeting all of our members’ expectations.” Wilson said he had known “personally for some time” he was going to step down. Outgoing VRC chairman Neil Wilson. Eddie Jim “I’ve been there 14 years, I’ve turned 65 this year, and I am at a stage in my life now where I have my other world in the tech and data and AI business world, and that’s really exciting,” he said. “And I’ve got some opportunities that are emerging, and I just felt all of that combined, as long as the VRC was in good shape … it was the right time for me to move on.”



Wilson, who recently played a part in opposing key changes to a state government racing bill on behalf of the VRC, said he was most proud of having helped his organisation navigate COVID and the ensuing years. “I was the CEO for 2020, and I was the chairman for 2021, and it completely consumed my life seven days a week, 14 to 16 hours a day, trying to work out how we were going to get through that period,” he said. The club lost millions in Cup-week crowd revenue and had to manage considerable debt following the construction of the new $128 million Club Stand. “There were some very difficult decisions and difficult scenarios,” Wilson said. “One of those decisions was to keep investing because we knew that we were going to go backwards, and we knew that we’d cop it, but we had to actually preserve the asset that was going to get us out of the position that COVID had put us in, and I’m proud that is what happened.



“We could have cut costs, we could have not had a Birdcage, we could have not had entertainment, we could have really scaled down the nature of the Melbourne Cup carnival event. But what we decided to do was the opposite, and continue to invest in the carnival and the platform.” Related Article Updated

Spring racing carnival VRC chairman to stand down after Melbourne Cup carnival, and his replacement has already been picked As a result, he said, the club had done new deals, including the biggest racing media rights deal in the world, which involves Nine (the owner of this masthead) as well as increasing its membership to record levels. The VRC finished the past financial year with a record $23.9 million EBITDA – “which is a proxy for cash” – a net profit of $5.4 million, which is a $12.6 million turnaround year-on-year, and has increasing investment “from a capital point of view” by more than 200 per cent. “Our debt levels, including the Racing Victoria debt ($10 million), is at $52 million, and that’s down from $67.5 million,” Wilson said.



“What I’ve also really instilled heavily to the board and to the team, and I’m not in an exclusive position pushing this, is that the history and heritage of this club is so important, and that the combination of being progressive and innovative and contemporary is really important and a unique asset for us. “I’m very proud of how we’ve thought about that and look forward to that continuing.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: ASX eyes gains after Wall Street rises; Oil market in focus
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX eyes gains after Wall Street rises; Oil market in focus Stan Choe October 12, 2026 — 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The Australian sharemarket is set for gains after a positive session on Wall Street, while eyes will be on oil markets this morning after developments over the weekend. The S&P 500 climbed 0.6 per cent for its first gain since setting its all-time high three days earlier. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 423 points, or 0.8 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 0.6 per cent. The Australian sharemarket is set to 37 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. Investors will also have to digest developments in the oil market, after Donald Trump struck a controversial deal with Russia on Moscow’s exports of diesel. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.78¢. Wall Street closed a positive week with more gains. AP Trump announced on Sunday (US time) that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an “energy ceasefire” effective immediately. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on his Truth Social platform. He didn’t provide further details.



Treasury yields flipped up and down in the bond market following their own sharp moves earlier in the week. The yield on the 10-year Treasury eventually climbed to 5.24 per cent from 5.22 per cent late Thursday. Related Article Updated

Russia-Ukraine war Ukraine backs energy ceasefire after Trump declares surprise deal is done It recently touched its highest level since 2002 because of worries about high inflation, the US government’s massive debt load, signals that the US economy is continuing to grow and other factors. High yields threaten to slow the economy by making borrowing money more expensive for everyone, and the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage has already leaped to its highest level in nearly three years. Yields are also shooting higher in other bond markets around the world, which makes investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other investments. But the high yields have attracted investors to recent auctions of Treasurys, and that demand is helping to limit further increases for yields. On Wall Street, Humana rallied 11.6 per cent and helped lift the US stock market despite the swings in the oil and bond markets. The insurer said it received encouraging data about its quality ratings versus its competitors for Medicare Advantage plans.



Companies that own cell towers were also at the front of the market, including leaps of 15.6 per cent for Crown Castle and 9.3 per cent for American Tower. They rallied after SpaceX announced a purchase that could help it become a major mobile carrier in the United States. It still needs to get approval from US regulators, but SpaceX said the purchase of low-band spectrum would allow its Starlink Mobile business to have a signal that can penetrate walls and connect customers inside buildings who may not be able to access its satellites. SpaceX’s stock added 1.2 per cent. The threat of another big competitor sent stocks lower across the wireless industry, including drops of 13.3 per cent for T-Mobile US, 9.8 per cent for AT&T and 8.7 per cent for Verizon. Delta Air Lines erased an early loss and eked out a tiny gain of less than 0.1 per cent after reporting profit and revenue for the summer that was slightly weaker than analysts expected. CEO Ed Bastian said demand remains strong and customers want to fly, but the airline is also having to absorb a $6 billion increase in fuel costs this year. The pressure is on companies broadly to deliver strong growth in profits after their stock prices ran toward records despite the downward push from high bond yields. Next week will bring high-profile profit reports from the country’s biggest banks, including Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo all on Tuesday.



Related Article Exclusive

Insolvency ‘Totally Vile Shambles Network’: TVSN faces legal demands after $40m rescue bid fails Expectations are high for corporate profits, even as Americans say they’re feeling more squeezed by high inflation. A preliminary report from the University of Michigan said Friday that US consumers are raising their own forecasts for how bad inflation will be over the coming year. They’re expecting inflation of 4.7 per cent, up from their forecast of 4.6 per cent a month ago and just 3.4 per cent in February before the war with Iran began. Sentiment among consumers is falling sharply for Americans with lower incomes and smaller investments in stocks, who can least afford the fast increases in the cost of living. All told, the S&P 500 rose 46.18 points to 7,811.54. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 423.31 to 51,654.95, and the Nasdaq composite gained 172.83 to 27,366.17. In stock markets abroad, indexes rallied in Europe with gains of at least 1 per cent in France, Germany and the United Kingdom.



Asian markets were more mixed. Japan’s Nikkei 225 finished nearly unchanged, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng jumped 1.8 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: McLarens, Mar-a-Lago and machine guns: Introducing Gina Rinehart’s controversial  new frontier point man
World.content:
Ricardo Lopez Tugendhat believed he was going to die and wanted the world to know who he thought was going to kill him.

The former manager at a mining company linked to Australian billionaire Gina Rinehart spelled out his fears in a chilling letter to an Ecuadorian news outlet.

“Being familiar with the character and temperament of Mr Carlos de Miguel III, I am deeply concerned that the threats I have received from him … are carried out,” read the letter, published by the outlet.

“I hereby publicly hold the aforementioned Carlos de Miguel III responsible for any attack against the life or physical integrity of my family or myself.”

Carlos de Miguel is Rinehart’s man on the ground in Ecuador – the chief executive of Hanrine Ecuadorian Exploration and Mining, a subsidiary of Hancock Prospecting.

He is a former US serviceman who instilled fear in some workers. Some former workers claim de Miguel would saunter around Hanrine’s sites in northern Ecuador with an assault rifle and flanked by menacing-looking dogs.

He loomed as a central character when this masthead spent a month in Ecuador tracking Hanrine’s controversial activities in the Latin American country.

The investigation examined hundreds of pages of government documents, company records, court files and research papers, and spoke to dozens of villagers, environmental activists and experts, who detailed allegations of human rights breaches, irregularities in the concessioning process and a pattern of violence and harassment towards local villagers.

Former Hanrine workers detailed allegations of exploitation and abuses at the company’s site in La Merced de Buenos Aires, including hiding workers without contracts from authorities conducting compliance checks, serving raw meat to labourers, forcing employees to work while sick and a culture of threats and intimidation.

Most workers this masthead spoke to were too scared to be quoted on the record, fearing retaliation from Hanrine, which categorically denies any wrongdoing and maintains it complies with “relevant laws and regulations”.

The claims raise serious questions about the company’s operations, which have been a subject of sustained controversy, and which critics say highlight the lack of accountability and oversight for Australian subsidiaries operating overseas.

A member of the Awa Indigenous community wears a Hanrine T-shirt during a communal labour meet-up known as a “minga” in Palmira de Toctemí, a community in the Awa’s ancestral land in La Merced de Buenos Aires parish. James Ross

Julien Vincent, an experienced climate change governance campaigner and former winner of the Goldman Environmental Prize, which recognises grassroots activists, says there should be an expectation that Australian companies and their subsidiaries operate to a higher standard overseas than they would at home.

“That’s because they’re not just doing business, they are representing Australia in another part of the world,” Vincent says.

Local media have chronicled de Miguel’s career from working as a security contractor for former Ecuadorian president Rafael Correa to handling security for WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange at the Ecuadorian embassy in London in 2012.

Gabriela Chiriboga and Carlos de Miguel attend the Hispanic Prosperity Gala at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, in February. Getty Images for Latino Wall Street

The mining executive said in interviews with local media outlets that he has had a decade-long association with Hancock Prospecting, beginning in 2015 when the company became interested in diversifying its portfolio into Latin America.

De Miguel shares Rinehart’s conservative political views and her support for US President Donald Trump. He made a US$250,000 donation to the Trump-Vance inaugural committee and attended the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), where Rinehart is a regular attendee.

De Miguel was among several Hancock Prospecting executives who toured the US with Rinehart in early 2025. He later attended the Starlight Ball in Washington to mark Trump’s inauguration, where Rinehart was photographed talking to Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa and his wife, Lavinia Valbonesi.

Hanrine chief executive Carlos de Miguel oversees Gina Rinehart’s operations in Ecuador.

De Miguel posed on a red carpet while wearing a velvet suit and aviator sunglasses at the Hispanic Prosperity Gala in Florida, where the mining executive owns a $US1.4 million home. The event, held at Mar-a-Lago in February, was sponsored by Hanrine, Trump Vodka and the Gina Rinehart Foundation.

De Miguel is also a car aficionado and the owner of a silver McLaren GT that he occasionally races. The car is nicknamed Maverick in a reference to the Top Gun movies.

‘THREATS, WEAPONS AND RAW MEAT’

Luis Fausto de la Cruz remembers when he fell out of love with working for Hanrine. It was 2022 and the farmer turned labourer was at the company’s camp on the edge of La Merced de Buenos Aires when, he says, a ute pulled up.

De Miguel, surrounded by security guards and flanked by two menacing-looking dogs, had walked out of the vehicle armed with a sophisticated assault-style rifle, de la Cruz says.

“He spoke about having been to war; I don’t know how many wars,” de la Cruz says. “It hurt my soul.”

De la Cruz, a father of six, believes this was an attempt to intimidate staff. It made him furious but he felt helpless.

“There was nothing one could do; if you spoke up, you were treated like a criminal,” he says. “So much for the claim that they are trained, educated people … you don’t come to [deal with] humble folk with weapons.”

De Miguel did not address questions about this alleged conduct directly but “categorically rejects” any allegation workers were mistreated.

De la Cruz says he worked carrying building materials and doing manual labour for Hanrine for about eight months, before staff were fired en masse and the company withdrew from the area. He claims the working conditions were brutal.

Workers would be sent to the mountains around La Merced de Buenos Aires for 20 days at a time, and left incommunicado from their family, he says. No phones were allowed on site, which also meant workers could not take photographs of their living conditions.

Staff slept in bunk beds in large tents, and the food served, he claims, often arrived cold, spoiled or raw. De la Cruz remembers one occasion when staff were given a special Christmas meal of roast pork that made several people sick.

“We aren’t dogs that eat raw meat,” he says.

He says staff who became ill were denied leave and made to work.

La Merced de Buenos Aires local government president Lucia Chicaiza says Hanrine staff often referred to her as “Lucifer” because of her anti-mining advocacy. James Ross

Lucia Chicaiza, the president of La Merced de Buenos Aires parish, says many workers were too scared to report their working conditions to authorities.

As previously reported by this masthead, several villagers in the parish claim, including in a judicial council report, to have been assaulted, stabbed and harassed by Hanrine staff for their anti-mining views. The company is also accused of hiring illegal miners as security guards, who were often armed.

Another former Hanrine employee, who spoke anonymously because of safety concerns, claims de Miguel was permanently armed and kept weapons inside company premises.

“He told us he had a permit to carry a weapon and that the police couldn’t even touch this gun,” the former employee alleges.

Local anti-mining protesters who had blocked the company from accessing its concessions in the parish would often be referred to by Hanrine staff as “chunchos” – a derogatory term that roughly translates to “savages”. Chicaiza was often called Lucifer.

Chicaiza says reports about Hanrine’s camps were so concerning she asked authorities to carry out a compliance visit.

“That’s when they hid us,” de la Cruz claims. “I was there.”

One morning, de la Cruz says, casual workers were told to leave the camp and head “for a walk” in the mountains. Staff were made to “hide” away from the camp while officials from the department of employment inspected the site.

Another Hanrine employee also claimed staff were told to leave the company’s facilities whenever authorities conducted compliance checks.

Manuel de la Cruz, a potato farmer who also worked as a manual labourer for Hanrine, says staff would be hidden from officials “because they weren’t paying the daily wages legally as they should”.

Former Ecuadorian employment minister Patricio Donoso told a human rights committee of non-government MPs in Ecuador’s national assembly in 2023 that the company was twice sanctioned for blocking department officials conducting compliance checks, and failing to present employment contracts for its workers.

It is unclear how many locals were employed by Hanrine. De Miguel has previously claimed in the media to have hired up to 200 people, many from the local community. Donoso placed the figure close to 300, although 169 contracts had been terminated at the time he spoke to the committee in 2023.

Hancock Prospecting has publicly acknowledged in its annual reporting on its modern slavery obligations that its operations in Ecuador are its highest risk jurisdiction.

This masthead is not accusing the company of breaching those obligations, only noting that it has stated repeatedly its awareness of potential labour issues in the country.

In a statement, de Miguel denied all claims workers were treated poorly. He said he had received “numerous messages from staff expressing their appreciation for Hanrine, its workplace culture and the opportunities the company has provided” and shared two undated messages from unnamed employees praising the company.

“In countries like Australia it can be easy to underestimate just how significant the opportunity of employment can be for people living in poor areas,” de Miguel said.

The average annual GDP per person in Ecuador is estimated at $10,000, according to anti-modern-slavery organisation Walk Free.

THE STASH OF WEAPONS AND 9500 BULLETS

The letter Ricardo Lopez Tugendhat penned to news outfit La Fuente: Periodismo de Investigacion in 2020 highlights just how feared de Miguel was by some who had crossed paths with him.

Lopez Tugendhat had previously worked closely with de Miguel as assistant manager, handling security for Hanrine, until their relationship soured early that year.

Hanrine and Lopez Tugendhat were caught in a messy dispute that led to both parties taking each other to court, and Lopez Tugendhat reporting de Miguel to authorities for alleged intimidation.

Part of the dispute involved claims by Hanrine that Lopez Tugendhat had used a fake disability card to claim benefits he was not entitled to. Lopez Tugendhat claimed he had been unfairly dismissed by the company.

Hanrine later dropped the disability card case after signing an agreement with Lopez Tugendhat, and the court found him not guilty this year. The unfair dismissal claim was settled and Hanrine paid $US20,000 to Lopez Tugendhat in 2022, according to court documents.

At the time he sent the letter, Lopez Tugendhat was worried an article published by the news outlet would draw the ire of his former boss.

The article suggested Lopez Tugendhat, a three-time shooting world champion, could have tipped off the police to a stash of firearms and ammunition hidden in de Miguel’s home gym.

Police had raided de Miguel’s property and arrested the businessman the previous month on the basis he did not hold valid permits for three of four firearms found, which included a high-powered rifle used by elite police and military officers. Investigators also found 9500 rounds of ammunition, several magazines, an air rifle and a training gun, according to court documents and local media reports.

In the letter, Lopez Tugendhat claimed de Miguel had threatened to kill him and his family, and he provided a case number to track his report of the alleged threat through the prosecutor’s office.

This masthead was able to find a record of the original report Lopez Tugendhat filed against de Miguel for alleged intimidation in January 2020, but it did not contain any findings.

“The only report I’ve made against Mr Carlos de Miguel III is for intimidation and death threats, of which me and my family were the victims of,” Lopez Tugendhat pleaded in his letter.

“I expressly request that your prestigious media outlet clarify and correct the record.”

The weapons case against de Miguel was dropped 10 months after the raid, after it was determined the businessman was in the process of renewing the expired permits.

The decision was partly informed by Lopez Tugendhat’s evidence that de Miguel was a member of his recreational shooting club and the ammunition found in his home had been bought through the club.

De Miguel later said the raid was part of a plot to discredit him as a mining executive and derail Hanrine’s bid to obtain a lucrative copper project near its concessions in La Merced de Buenos Aires called Llurimagua that the company was offering to acquire for US$400 million.

When contacted by this masthead, de Miguel said it was not uncommon in Ecuador for allegations to arise in the context of employment disputes.

“The unfounded workplace allegations against myself that you reference were categorically dismissed and did not result in any charges or adverse findings against me,” de Miguel said.

Lopez Tugendhat declined to comment when contacted by this masthead.

BROKEN PROMISES

On a clear morning, you can see the Colombian border from the top of Luis Fausto de la Cruz’s land.

Motilon trees – a high-altitude Andean species that produces a deep purple berry used to make “colada morada”, a thick smoothie-style drink used to commemorate the Day of the Dead festivities – grow in the small valleys that form between the hills undulating through his land.

Bears and guans, a large chicken-like bird native to the Andes, are regular visitors to the property, which is also home to a waterfall and walking trails.

De la Cruz, yellow shin-high rubber boots on his feet, walks through the overgrown paths with a machete in his hand. He wants to turn part of his land into an ecotourism venture with huts, bird lookouts, a zipline and horseriding routes.

“There’s a lot of birds here,” he says. “I am going to fight little by little to do something.”

De la Cruz says he doesn’t regret working for Hanrine. It was an eye-opening experience. But he feels locals were taken advantage of and promises of new homes, roads and services that lured locals like himself to work with the company were never fulfilled.

He says he isn’t afraid that speaking out will make him a target.

“The only thing I fear is God, no one else.”

World.title: Enjoyed your weekend? You have a resident of this UK city to thank for it
World.content:
InspirationEurope Enjoyed your weekend? You have a resident of this UK city to thank for it Steve McKenna October 12, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Overshadowed by Manchester, its rival just across the River Irwell, Salford marks its 100th birthday as a city in 2026 (it was officially granted city status by King George V in 1926). But its story stretches back much further – think neolithic tribes, ancient Roman troops – and it’s bursting with surprising firsts, claims and feats. A big one is that a Salfordian invented the weekend. In 1843, activist Robert Lowes (actor Sir Ian McKellen’s great-great-grandfather) successfully campaigned for workers at a Salford mill to have Saturday afternoons off. Salford Quays, near the Manchester Ship Canal, is the setting for the annual We Invented the Weekend festival. iStock This trailblazing trend spread around the UK, sowing the seeds for a two-day weekend and ultimately sparking more freedom for the joys of life, from sports and travelling to lie-ins to read the papers. Many visitors attending soccer matches, arena concerts and arts festivals in Manchester stay in Salford without realising it. Manchester and Salford essentially share the same city centre – or “town” as it’s known locally – and several hotels rise on Salford’s side of the river, including CitySuites, an aparthotel in whose lobby I once bumped into soccer legend Pep Guardiola. He lived here during his decade-long stint as Manchester City boss and was often seen riding his bike on Chapel Street, Salford’s historic thoroughfare.



Touted, in 1806, as the UK’s first street to be lit by gas, it’s backdropped by towering modern offices and apartments with traditional pubs, tapas bars and cafes alongside attractive older buildings. 



There’s a recreation of a typical Victorian cobbled street, lined with authentic reclaimed shopfronts, at Salford Museum & Art Gallery. It’s by the university campus overlooking the riverside Peel Park, one of the most idyllic spots in a city usually associated with grit and industry. Rugby pioneer William Webb Ellis and brewer-cum-scientist James Prescott Joule were also born in Salford, which local folk musician Ewan MacColl immortalised in Dirty Old Town, a 1949 tune later covered by the Dubliners, The Pogues and Rod Stewart. MacColl also wrote The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face, which was a massive hit for Roberta Flack in 1972. Regeneration, however, is a Salford forte. A 62-hectare botanical retreat, RHS Garden Bridgewater, has revived an overgrown country estate at Worsley, a canal-hugging Salfordian village with pretty timber-beamed houses and woodland walks. Ordsall Hall is a beautifully preserved Tudor manor house near Salford Quays. iStock Close to Ordsall Hall, a beautifully preserved Tudor manor house, Salford Quays is another alluring waterside draw. This district is the setting for the annual We Invented the Weekend festival and is located near the end of the Manchester Ship Canal, which once brought ocean-going cargo vessels 60 kilometres inland from the Irish Sea.



Derelict by the 1980s, Salford’s rejuvenated docks are anchored around MediaCity, a glossy TV and tech hub where the BBC’s studios soar opposite Lowry, a theatre and gallery complex honouring L.S. Lowry (1887-1976), a revered artist who also worked as a debt collector in Salford. It stages everything from original local plays to Broadway and West End productions and displays Lowry’s idiosyncratic paintings, peopled with “matchstick men”. There’s a giant audiovisual exhibit of his 1953 piece Going to the Match. The BBC’s studios are housed in Salford’s MediaCity, a creative and tech hub. iStock Incidentally, you’ll see Old Trafford, Manchester United’s stadium, from the terrace of Central Bay, a cosmopolitan food hall by Lowry (which often is, but shouldn’t be, confused with the similarly named hotel in “town”). Another MediaCity favourite is the Coronation Street Experience, showcasing the sets of the world’s longest-running TV soap opera, which creator Tony Warren modelled on working-class life in Salford. There’s actually a real Coronation Street.



Located between the Quays and Chapel Street, it’s a magnet for lovers of “Corrie” and The Smiths, as the street’s community space, Salford Lads’ Club, graced the sleeve of the Manchester band’s 1986 album The Queen is Dead. Inside, there’s a room jammed with The Smiths memorabilia. The soap opera Coronation Street is filmed in the ITV Trafford Wharf Studios backlot at MediaCity. iStock Related Article Newcastle England England’s most northern city is heaving with unexpected delights One repeat visitor to the club is British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. You’ll find his flagship mayoral project, the Bee Network, and its yellow-branded trams, bikes and double-decker buses, a handy way to buzz between Manchester and Salford. THE DETAILS



FLY

Emirates flies to Manchester from Sydney and Melbourne via Dubai. STAY

CitySuites has studios from around £110 ($211). See citysuites.com MORE

visitsalford.info; visitmanchester.com; visitbritain.com The writer travelled at his own expense. For more on travel in the UK, watch Getaway on 9now.
