World.title: No, eggs don’t actually increase cholesterol levels (plus four more common myths)
World.content:
Sponsored Tips & adviceDietitian’s guide No, eggs don’t actually increase cholesterol levels (plus four more common myths) Is it okay to eat eggs every day and how many is too many? A dietitian separates the facts from the fiction (and not the yolk from the white). Produced in partnership with Australian Eggs. Sponsored by Australian Eggs Susie Burrell October 12, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Whether you enjoy your eggs poached to perfection, hard-boiled for a quick protein hit or scrambled on sourdough every Sunday morning, eggs are a nutrient powerhouse. Scrambled eggs. Getty Images/iStockphoto Offering 17 different vitamins and nutrients, along with high-quality protein, eggs are versatile, and can be enjoyed in a number of ways. Many of us also hold certain beliefs about eggs, which can affect how many eggs we eat, or how frequently we eat them. Here are some of the most common beliefs about eggs, and why, in many cases, they are complete myths. Eggs increase cholesterol levels



Perhaps the most common food myth of all time is that eggs increase blood cholesterol and as such should be avoided by anyone who has elevated lipid levels. While eggs, like all animal foods, do contain cholesterol, it does not mean that blood cholesterol levels are affected after eating eggs. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Rather, the saturated fat content of foods is more likely to affect cholesterol levels, and even then, blood cholesterol levels are usually dependent on a number of other variables including genetics, diet quality overall and the balance of fat types consumed. For this reason, even if you have elevated cholesterol levels, including up to seven eggs in your diet each week is the number suggested by the Heart Foundation. Are egg yolks all right? You bet they are. iStock Egg whites are healthier than the yolks



While gym bros may load up on the egg whites as a concentrated protein source, not enjoying the nutrient-rich yolks would be a real shame nutritionally. While egg whites contain little to no fat, ultimately the key nutrients eggs offer are all found in the egg yolk. With just over four grams of fat per yolk, all of the fat-soluble vitamins including vitamins A, D and E are found there, along with iron, selenium, choline as well as the antioxidants lutein and zeaxanthin, which support eye health. The yolk also contains almost three grams of protein. This is compared to the egg white, which contains almost four grams of protein. This means if you are looking to increase your protein intake, you can certainly use extra whites, but you’ll be missing out on plenty of goodness the yolks have to offer. Related Recipe collection Eggs for dinner? Give it a crack with these easy protein-packed dishes Raw eggs are a good source of protein



Whether you have seen it in the movies, or even at the gym, buffed individuals downing raw eggs is something we have been taught is a great thing to do if building muscle mass is the goal. While consuming egg whites is an easy way to consume relatively large amounts of high-quality protein in a small volume of food, or a protein-rich ingredient to add to dishes to increase the protein content, the protein in eggs actually becomes more bioavailable when the eggs are consumed cooked. Specifically, cooking eggs helps to increase how much protein from eggs the body can absorb, from just 50 per cent when the egg is consumed raw to more than 90 per cent. The reason is that when the egg protein is exposed to heat, the dense protein structures are denatured, making it easier for the digestive enzymes to break the proteins down into absorbable amino acids. This means that if maximising your protein intake is the goal, cooking your eggs is a no-brainer. A couple of eggs a day can help keep the doctor away. William Meppem



Eating “too many” eggs is bad for you It is not uncommon to hear recommendations to limit egg intake both to control fat consumption and support heart health, but public health organisations support the consumption of a couple of eggs every day, noting them as a nutrient-dense, protein-rich food addition that is relatively low in saturated fat. Related Article EASY Adam Liaw’s Florentine egg muffins < 30 mins While it is entirely possible to eat too much of any one food, moderate, daily egg consumption is completely safe for the average person, only likely to improve overall nutrient intake given the natural presence of a number of more obscure nutrients, including choline and selenium, few Aussies get optimal amounts of. In practical terms this means that for the average person a couple of eggs can be enjoyed daily with no cause for concern.



Hard boiled eggs are better for weight loss. Marina Oliphant You should not eat eggs if you want to lose weight On many a low-fat diet, eggs as a key breakfast option have been ditched in favour of low-fat yoghurt and cereal breakfast options, but if anything, the science shows eggs are a superior breakfast option when it comes to weight loss. One key study that demonstrates this was published in the International Journal of Obesity. Researchers found that when compared to a bagel-based breakfast as part of a diet with a calorie deficit to support fat loss, egg-based breakfasts that offered a similar calorie load to the bagel-based breakfast resulted in a 65 per cent greater weight loss and 34 per cent greater reduction in waist circumference over an eight-week period. It is thought that as eggs are typically more satisfying, an egg-based breakfast also positively affects calorie consumption for the remainder of the day.

World.content:

Two of Sydney’s seasoned hospitality pros are turning their attention to an unexpected suburban pocket, with cult Darlinghurst restaurant Joe’s Table opening a new dining concept at Macquarie Park next year, and the former head chef at recently closed CBD fine diner Soul Dining launching the broth-focused Jin Guk in the suburb this week. Why the sudden interest from the city’s food talent in the northside commercial and residential hub? Jin Guk caters to the growing appetite for Korean food. Daniel Choi “The Korean community in Eastwood is just a 10-minute drive away,” said Kenny Lee, chief operating officer at JS Hospitality, the group backing Jin Guk. The appetite for Korean food at Macquarie Park is evident in last month’s launch of the sprawling S-Mart, a Korean specialty food store. Lee and Joe’s Table owner, Joe Kitsana, both rate Macquarie Park – with its tech industry and university – as already possessing a strong, captive dining market, and a location with potential as a wider-catchment food destination. The close proximity of the food-savvy residents of Ryde and Lane Cove was an attraction. “I see us building a whole new clientele there,” Kitsana said.



Kitsana started as a one-man band chef, waiter and sommelier at the well-reviewed, no-frills Joe’s Table in Darlinghurst. Skills he picked up working at Sydney restaurants Longrain, Sailor’s Thai and Phamish helped make Joe’s Table a chef and foodie haunt. But he’s teaming up at the new northside venue with restaurateur Darase Kraykaew, from Haymarket restaurant At Bangkok. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Spicy sogigi yukgaejang. Daniel Choi “It’ll be called Song Wat,” Kitsana said, referring to the vibrant Song Wat neighbourhood in Bangkok, which mixes old shopfronts, spice houses and restaurants. “We’ll do modern Thai – the Chinese-Thai thing is hot in Thailand now,” Kitsana said. Song Wat will be located on Mahogany Avenue near the new Macquarie Park Public School, which opens next year. The restaurant is aiming for a mid-2027 launch. The wait won’t be as long for Jin Guk, with the 35-seater opening from lunch on Monday, October 12. Jin Guk takes its name from the Korean broth of pork, beef or seafood, and the restaurant’s specialty, gomtang, which is served with rice.



“Jin guk is similar to ramen, but we don’t use the bones, only meat,” chef Jay Lee explained. Lee skips bones in his version with an eye to producing a clearer soup. Joe Kitsana. Edwina Pickles Lee, the long-time head chef at Soul Dining, said he is enjoying the switch from an exacting chef’s hatted restaurant kitchen to the simpler yet still precise preparation of the soupy cornerstone of Korean cooking. “[Jin guk] is a deep, comforting broth, you can have it any time. For me, twice a week,” he said He admits to early trial and error with the cooking time of the different cuts of meat in the broth, and the rice proved equally challenging. They trialled rice from around the world, but couldn’t match the high moisture content and “sweetness” of Korean rice. So the broth at Jin Guk is served with rice from Cheorwon, a region near the demilitarised zone. Lee said the amount of rice added to the broth in Korea is up to the individual taste, similar to the way some Australians love lots of Vegemite and some a light smattering.

World.title: 'Not as attractive as it used to be' - Winston Peters on living in NZ today
World.content:
Audio player for " Election campaign weekend brings fresh policy announcements " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics/1852240%2Fnot-as-attractive-as-it-used-to-be-winston-peters-on-living-in-nz-today

Election campaign weekend brings fresh policy announcements Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Analysis: Winston Peters is on a mission and says the idea that either Chris will be calling the shots once the votes are counted is a nonsense.

With just 26 days of the election campaign to go, the New Zealand First leader is by far the most experienced political leader, having first entered Parliament with the National Party in 1978 before breaking off and setting up his own party in 1993.

In the first MMP election held in 1996, New Zealand First won 17 seats and Peters took on his first stint as deputy prime minister and treasurer.

Heading into the November election, 30 years after the birth of MMP, Peters is convinced stability will return to the increasingly fragmented political landscape this year.

Asked about the evolution of MMP and the potential for three or four parties being needed to form a government based on current polling, Peters said that was a suspicion he did not agree with.

"I think that things are going to be stabilised at the end of this event," he says with confidence.

RNZ / Nick Monro

Asked to explain whether he thought a two-party governing arrangement was still possible, he replied, "I'm not going to tell you what the permutations are, but there are variations on the thing, which go to the core of your question."

"Let's just say the composition of the government," he added.

Last week National's Christopher Luxon and Labour's Chris Hipkins sparred in the first televised leaders' debate - something Peters is miffed about.

"Why have we seen these two leaders going head-to-head when they will not be deciding the outcome come election day, of that I can guarantee you.

"The first person gets up and says 'the National government's going to do this'. The other person says the 'Labour government's going to do that'.

"Neither such things exist anymore; they just don't exist," he exclaimed.

"But they're allowed to get away with that sort of language, and in so many ways, the tragedy is - deliberate or not - that the mainstream media are allowing a conversation to happen as though it's first-past-the-post when it was no longer the case for 33 years."

RNZ / Nick Monro

Labour and ACT have both released fiscal plans already this campaign and National is due to do the same on Monday, but Peters pushes back on questions about whether his party will do the same.

"Well, we have got a fiscal plan, and we've outlaid it for two years. We talked about having a future sovereign fund, what it would cost, and how much would be put into it.

"We laid out that plan two years ago, and we're going to keep on developing that in more detail in the next few weeks," he said.

As for other parties, Peters doesn't believe anything is adding up.

"When you talk about costings, see nobody's costings are working.

"They're just lying when they say they are working."

Peters says that is because the country's growth rate is nowhere near high enough to afford what is being promised.

"If the economy goes on the way that it is, then all these promises that are being made are worthless because they won't have the money to do it."

So after nearly 50 years in and around politics is the octogenarian, who has held some of the most senior roles in government multiple times, enjoying being back in the thick of another campaign for re-election?

"Well, I'm still getting inspirations, yes, I get serious inspirations from it, but I never understood why people say, "are you enjoying it? Because it's not a matter of enjoyment.

"When you're on a mission, you're there to make sure something happens and you believe in the national interest.

"So whether you get an enjoyment out of it, it's not the point, whether you, like as any decent servant does, feel rewarded by the outcome, that's probably more important," he concluded.

Peters still firmly believes New Zealand is an attractive place to live, work, and raise a family - "but it's not as attractive as it used to be".

"Our job is to restore it, make it an attractive place again for people to come here who we need, not who need us."

New Zealand First released its party list last week with well-known new candidates getting prime spots near the top.

While Peters and his fellow current ministers Shane Jones, Casey Costello and Mark Patterson took the top four spots, the next five rankings went to fresh candidates over sitting MPs.

Former National Party minister Alfred Ngaro, former National MP and Whanganui Mayor Michael Laws, former National MP Harete Hipango-Brownlie, former chair of the Financial Markets Authority Craig Stobo, and former All Black captain Taine Randell rounded out the top nine.

In a surprise move, former Defence Minister and New Zealand First MP Ron Mark - who left politics in 2020 - was given the low ranking of 16 on the list despite the party talking up his chances of reclaiming his old ministerial posting if back in government.

Mark had approached the party about a return some time ago, but then dragged the chain confirming whether he would actually run.

Not helping his prospects were comments to media he had other opportunities abroad he could pursue, and making clear he wasn't excited by the idea of returning to Parliament.

The party has also been keen to present as a rejuvenated version of itself that is attracting candidates from the old National guard.

Ngaro would have secured a decent list ranking before committing to joining the party, while Laws' high spot lines up with the party being keen for him to hold local government minister in any future government.

Hipango-Brownlie has political experience but also brings a background in law, and a similar te ao Māori view of the world to Peters and Jones.

Stobo has credibility in finance and the economy while Randell is arguably more of a household name than Peters himself, and will be getting primed for a leadership role down the line.

Peters believes the list is the "best set of candidates we've ever had".

"We've got a real team, make no bones about it, and that's what's giving us the confidence in our present circumstance that we're going to do well.

"But our job is to ensure we get the maximum number of those people into Parliament."

It's all still on the table according to Peters who is convinced nothing is set in stone yet.

World.title: Dozens strand as ferry loses power and left drifting at sea
World.content:
Authorities in Solomon Islands are assessing how to rescue dozens of people stranded on the vessel MV Awka, that has lost power and is drifting at sea.

The Temotu Provincial Government on Sunday provided an update on the ongoing search and rescue operation involving the vessel.

The vessel issued a distress signal on Friday when its engine stopped working while travelling from Anuta to Vanikoro in Temotu Province, with more than 70 passengers, crew members, and officers on board.

The government said significant progress has made in delivering emergency supplies to the vessel via vessels and aircraft belonging to other countries.

A French military aircraft arrived at the location of the MV Akwa on Saturday evening, dropping essential relief supplies into the sea near the vessel with the help of pilot chutes-small parachutes used to deliver supplies from aircraft.

An Australian Challenger aircraft is also reported to have delivered essential supplies, including drinking water, food and medicine, to those on board.

The Temotu government said further maritime assistance is being mobilised to support the safe rescue of all passengers.

It said a "final operational plan is to be determined by the rescue operators at the scene after assessing the situation, including the prevailing swells, rough seas, weather conditions, vessel positions, and the safety of the passengers and rescue personnel".

World.title: International student fired on the spot wins payout for unjustified dismissal
World.content:
An international student fired on the spot at an Auckland jewellery store says students need more protection.

Yucen Xi was awarded $27,890 after the Employment Relations Authority (ERA) found her employer Silvertime Trading Limited (STL) unjustifiably dismissed her on 19 July 2025.

Xi said the legal process was challenging, but she was determined to pursue justice.

"I need to prove that even [if] I'm holding a student visa, I can still go for justice."

Xi was employed by STL as a client advisor to work at Qeelin, a fine jewellery store in Newmarket.

The jewellery brand is owned by publicly listed company Kering - a global luxury group which also owns brands including Gucci, Balenciaga, Alexander McQueen and Bottega Veneta.

On 19 July 2025, Xi was asked to attend a 6pm meeting with area manager Edwin Wu.

She was not informed what the meeting was about, but decided to record the meeting.

According to a transcript viewed by ERA, Wu asked Xi to resign.

In the recording, Wu said as store manager, he was "the decision-maker".

"Two warnings, including this warning I'll give you," he said.

"I give you two choices, first amicable separation - you resign yourself - second, two warnings are termination.

Today you directly hand over the key," Wu told her. "If you resign, you give me the key…if you want termination, it will be done quite ugly."

The transcript showed Wu told Xi she will not receive compensation because she was fired, and he called mall security after Xi allegedly refused to leave.

Xi did not complete her shift and was escorted out by security in front of employees from other stores.

The Qeelin store in Auckland's Newmarket. Ke-Xin Li/RNZ

ERA member Simon Greening noted in the transcript, Wu referred obliquely to STL's grooming policy and an allegation that Xi had not complied with the policy previously - but there was no evidential basis to establish Wu's concern.

The ERA found STL acted egregiously towards Xi, and its failure to act in good faith during the meeting was "deliberate, serious and sustained".

Xi, a chemistry master's student at the University of Auckland, said her mental health was severely impacted by her employer's conduct.

She said it left her depressed and anxious.

The humiliation, financial pressure, and risk of being unable to complete her studies due to the stress, made her unable to speak to anyone for a week.

But what frustrated her more was the lack of care shown by the brand and parent company.

"I feel like Qeelin doesn't really care about this because every time we have [issues], we need to directly report it to [the manager]," she said.

"So if Edwin (the manager) is bullying us, we need to report it to him - that basically means nothing."

Xi said she was never informed on how to raise official complaints, never met their HR, and had no contact with Qeelin head office other than when ordering stock.

Both Qeelin and Kering have policies around cultivating a respectful work environment.

First Up asked whether they were aware of Silvertime Trading Limited's conduct, and whether any actions will be taken.

Neither company has responded.

First Up also approached Wu and Silvertime Trading Limited director Haixiang Alex Zhang.

The company's representative before the ERA, employment advocate Aimee Cai, said they would not be responding to queries.

Student workers 'may not be aware of rights'

Anu Kaloti from the Migrant Workers Association (MWA) said to come study in New Zealand, international students often go through long and rigourous processes before they even arrive.

The opportunity is precious to these students, and many of them do not come from well-off families.

"These are vulnerable members of our society here in Aotearoa and they may not necessarily be aware of their rights as employees," Kaloti said.

World.title: Apprenticeships should be offered at same level as degrees - training provider
World.content:
Audio player for " Training provider wants degree-equivalent apprenticeships " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/education/1852769%2Fapprenticeships-should-be-offered-at-same-level-as-degrees-training-provider

Training provider wants degree-equivalent apprenticeships Morning Report Download MP3 3m

One of the country's biggest training providers wants apprenticeships offered at the same qualification level as a Bachelor's degree.

In a white paper published today, the Skills Group also called for incentives for employers to take on apprentices, a greater focus on achieving specific skills rather than serving time in an industry, and access to student loans and allowances for trainees.

Head of consulting Josh Williams told RNZ successive governments had made changes to the organisations that offered vocational education and training, and now it was time to change the offering itself.

"We think there's been enough restructuring of the vocational education system in terms of who does what," he said.

"What we really need to do is modernise what it offers, make sure it's responsive, get rid of a few old things and old habits and really expand both where apprentices can go and where apprenticeships can work."

Williams said one of the first changes should be a review of rules that limited apprenticeships to level 4 of the Qualifications Framework.

"It's a mystery to me why the funding rule says that all of our apprenticeships have to point at level four," he said.

"Level 4 is one level above a school-leaver and it's three levels below the holder of a degree. In terms of the real skills, knowledge, attributes of licensed, professional, qualified tradespeople, we'd argue in the paper many of them are actually sitting more like level 6 or level 7."

Williams said it should be possible for Bachelor's degrees to be offered by way of an apprenticeship as already happened in Scotland.

"So if you imagine an engineering degree, at the lecture on Monday morning, half the lecture theatre is full-time students, but the other half is people that have been released from the companies," he said.

"They're actually achieving the same degree level qualifications it's simply that they are doing applied learning and doing part of their study through their work itself."

Williams said removing the level 4 limitation would allow industries to develop and offer work-based, higher-level qualifications that people could pursue after they completed an initial apprenticeship.

He said apprenticeships could also change to ensure apprentices got more credit for skills they already had.

"Over half of the apprentices in the construction area are coming in from another part of the industry. They're not green as grass. They've already got relevant skills that we can build on," he said.

"But at the moment, the apprenticeship system sort of asks everybody to begin at the beginning and do a big box qualification rather than just add the skill sets that make sense in terms of helping them to go forward."

Williams said countries including Singapore and increasingly Australia were already focusing on skills as the "currency" of their workplace training.

He said the group's proposed changes would help resolve some of the country's employment and skills problems.

"We know from the OECD data that New Zealand has a terrible problem of skills mismatch. That means people are working in a different area from the one they actually studied in.

"That's why apprenticeships are the natural solution. You resolve youth employment, you are training up in the industry that needs the skills and just supporting a person to progress in the industry that they are seeking to make their future in."

On the money

Seven Electrical general manager Peter Couchman told RNZ the Skills Group recommendations were "on the money".

He said giving apprentices the option of receiving a student loan would be "huge" for some.

"Some employers will pay them a training allowance. We don't. We pay above the minimum adult wage because it's hard to live in Wellington. They've still got tools to buy. They've got all this other stuff going on. So I think a student loan would be huge for them," he said.

Couchman also backed the call for a rethink of the qualification level of apprenticeships and the ability to provide higher-level qualifications by way of an apprenticeship.

"It also shifts the conversation at home about doing a trade. Because at the moment it's a struggle, mum and dad would like to see them get a degree," he said.

"They get a higher qualification through this pathway and one of the things in our advantage at the moment is a lot of young people are worried about 'will AI or super intelligence take away their career in the future'. In a trade, highly unlikely, and we're going to see some better quality, more intelligent people coming through [so] we need to be going to this."

Fourth-year apprentice Mikyla Brown said a student loan or allowance would have been useful while she was studying for her pre-trade certificate.

She was not sure whether level 4 was the right level for her qualification but the knowledge and skills it provided were critical.

"People's lives depend on our jobs. If we make mistakes or forget to do things I could be in prison or someone else could be dead," she said.

Riki Blundell completed his electrical apprenticeship three months ago.

He said the ability to complete further study via an apprenticeship would make a big difference.

"Basically what it is at the moment is you get qualified and then that's all you need to do. There's no way to really move yourself up without doing a different course or getting qualified for a different version of an electrician," he said.

Blundell said clear, work-based progression would encourage more newly-qualified tradespeople to stay in New Zealand, rather than go to Australia for work.

"I reckon that would be ideal. It's something I would have definitely looked at," he said.

Blundell also backed the notion of access to student loans.

"The apprentice wage, although it is better than a benefit or something like that, it's still not a massive amount of money and I know a lot of the guys that I work with are struggling week-to-week with their expenses," he said.

"So some sort of assistance while you're doing your apprenticeship would definitely be something I think would help."

At the other end of the apprenticeship journey, Ethan Sheddan told RNZ he quit his accountancy career to pursue a pre-trade qualification this year and was now looking for an electrical apprenticeship.

He agreed student loans would be useful for many apprentices, but he believed employers also needed help to take on apprentices.

"I think the bigger incentive would be to help the employers," he said.

World.title: Auckland Central: Boundary changes, move-on orders shake up the race
World.content:
Audio player for " Auckland Central set for another close election race " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1853109%2Fauckland-central-boundary-changes-move-on-orders-shake-up-the-race

Auckland Central set for another close election race Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Auckland's city centre, several of its swanky inner-city suburbs, and the Hauraki Gulf Islands all make up the Auckland Central electorate.

But with new challengers for the electorate seat and a history of close races, Auckland Central is set to be hotly contested once again.

What happened at the last election?

At the last election in 2023, National won the most party votes in the electorate. Just under a third (33.13 percent) of the electorate voted for them.

The Green Party came in second, earning 23.97 percent of the electorate's party votes.

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick was elected for a second time as the area's MP. She beat the National Party candidate, Mahesh Muralidhar, by almost 4000 votes.

Why is it interesting?

This year, many Western Springs, Grey Lynn, and Westmere residents are in the Auckland Central electorate for the first time.

Boundary changes mean the electorate has absorbed part of Mount Albert, while Grafton and Newmarket have moved under the Epsom Electorate.

The electorate has also been at the centre of the Government's move-on orders legislation, which was passed under urgency before Parliament was dissolved.

Soon, Police will have the power to move people on from the city centre if they are being disorderly, begging, or rough sleeping.

Chlöe Swarbrick is hoping for a third term as the electorate's MP. RNZ/Jessica Hopkins

Who's standing?

Chlöe Swarbrick is hoping for a third term as the electorate's MP.

If this election is a repeat of the three-horse race of 2020, where Swarbrick won by just over 1000 votes, the contenders to take the seat are newcomer Candice Kinser for National and former MP Naisi Chen for Labour.

These candidates and their volunteers have been out in force door-knocking, hosting line-dancing events, and posting TikToks to attract prospective voters.

ACT's Antonia Modkova and Opportunity's Johan Chang, both first-time candidates, are also standing.

There are also some fringe candidates who have thrown their hat in the ring.

What do the locals say?

Move-on orders had been on the mind of one Auckland Central voter.

"The move-on policy, I just reckon it's not fair," he said.

"They're picking on them, targeting them, and making people who are already drowning in their own misery worse.

"It's personal as well. I've been there. I've lived out there most of my life."

He wanted a night shelter in the city and for people sleeping rough to be safe.

The electorate has been at the centre of the debate surrounding the Government's move-on orders legislation. RNZ / Nick Monro

"Get some money together, find a building they can turn into a night shelter because there are a lot of them (rough sleepers) out there getting robbed at night."

Another voter thought the city centre was safer than it was three years ago.

"The violence has decreased in the past three years, at least from my observation. I'm really all about getting the CBD area in order and making it safe. In terms of who I'm voting for, I'm leaning towards ACT at the moment."

One voter at the Grey Lynn shops was pleased to have new choices for representation.

"I've been a Labour person, but I think I might vote for Chlöe because she has integrity, common sense and speaks her mind on things, and stick to Labour for the party vote."

She was hoping for a change in government.

"I've always been interested in education, health and housing, and I think the National government is more interested in money. I'd do anything to get rid of this government. I think the National government has done a lot of harm. However, I'm a bit disillusioned with Labour as well."

Another voter said she would probably go with National for her local candidate and party vote.

But she urged them to do more to bring down the cost of living.

"Labour, I just can't see policies, plans, or anything that particularly does anything for me. That's my feeling at the moment. I need to do a bit more homework; it has been a while since we've had an election. But a lot has changed, and things are costing so much."

Another voter was still considering her options.

"I'm sort of weighing up. I'm reasonably left-wing. I feel like many people have lost faith in the status quo, partly because there are so many big problems in the world. I think we need a paradigm shift."

World.title: The ‘disgusting creep’ who raped his daughter, step-grandaughter, sisters and former partners
World.content:
This story discusses details of long-term sexual and physical abuse.

For about four decades a South Island predator carried out the most horrific offending against those close to him, including raping his daughter, step-granddaughter, sisters, and former partners. National Crime Correspondent Sam Sherwood reports.

Standing inside the dock at the High Court, the man stood quietly in his prison clothes as his lawyer formalised the guilty pleas and discussed arrangements for sentencing.

There was no mention in the brief hearing of the extent of his offending before he walked back out of the dock to be sent back to prison where he will stay until he is sentenced later this year.

Inside a court document released to RNZ is the full story of the man's offending, detailing 20 charges he has pleaded guilty to, with offending that began in the 1980s through to the 2020s.

It includes eight charges of sexual violation by rape (seven of which are representative), a representative charge of rape, and eight charges of sexual violation by unlawful sexual connection (six of which are representative).

He also pleaded guilty to a representative charge of making objectionable material, a representative charge of doing an indecent act on a young person and one charge of wounding with intent to injure.

His offending includes raping his daughter, his step-granddaughter, two of his sisters, and two ex-partners. He also committed indecent acts on a distant relative.

The man now in his 50s has interim name suppression. RNZ is not reporting the locations of his offending or the court in which he is being sentenced, to avoid the victims being identified.

Twenty years of violence

The court document begins by discussing the man's offending against an ex-partner who he began dating in the early 1990s when she was 17. It did not take long before he became violent, "physically, emotionally and sexually".

The woman, who had four children with the man, left in about 2015.

"During the relationship, which lasted around 20 years, the defendant offered violence towards the victim by hitting, pushing, and kicking her. On one occasion he smacked her in the face over making a coffee."

In one incident, while pregnant with her first child, the man punched her in the eye and kicked her in the stomach, telling her he hoped her baby died.

The woman thought she was going die during one assault when he put his hands around around her neck, squeezing so it was difficult for her to breathe.

The summary of facts says by the mid 2000s the man raped her multiple times.

The man also pleaded guilty to a representative charge of sexual violation by rape in relation to another former partner.

The woman was 15 when she began a sexual relationship in 1990 with the man, who was then 21.

"The victim recalls feeling controlled by the defendant. She recalls the defendant being a jealous person. He didn't like her joking or laughing with anyone of the opposite sex.

The summary of facts refers to three occasions where the man raped her.

The relationship ended when she turned 16.

Man raped daughter 'whenever he had the opportunity'

The man also offended against one of his children.

The summary of facts says his daughter lived with him in several different houses from when she was born until she was about 16 and left home.

The offending started in about 2006/2007 when she was five and lasted until she was 15.

"While [she] was around 5 to 6 years old, she recalls her father raping her whenever he had the opportunity."

After the first attack he told her what happened was "secret between them, and she wasn't allowed to tell her mother".

The court document refers to one incident when her father was driving down a gravel road.

"Knowing what was going to happen, she jumped out of the car and ran off. He then drove away leaving her there frightened in the pitch black."

The man started letting his daughter go out drinking alcohol with friends between the ages of 13-15.

"She recalls getting home drunk on several occasions, where he would proceed to rape her while she was intoxicated. [She] described him as thriving off any situation she was intoxicated."

In the early 2020s, the man also offended against his step granddaughter.

The girl was two when her mother began dating the man's son.

The relationship lasted about five years before she and her mother moved to another city.

Since then, the girl travelled once a month to stay with her stepfather and the man who lived in the same house.

She would often sleep in the man's bedroom, which had a second mattress prepared.

When the girl was aged between 6 and 8, he raped her for the first time. He also took multiple photos of the victim being raped as well as other photos of her.

'Disgusting creep'

The man also raped two of his sisters.

One of his sisters recalled living with the family at a property when she was about 13 in the 80s.

"It was here the defendant carried out the sexual activities he wanted with her on a frequent basis until she was around 18 years old."

He started assaulting another sister when she was about 11 up until she was 17.

"The victim recalls the defendant often saying disgusting comments to her including 'old enough to bleed, old enough to butcher'."

When the victim, then in her mid 20s, was about eight months pregnant with her first daughter, the man drove her to deliver something [firewood] after a family gathering. The woman reluctantly went with him after her father insisted.

On their way, he took her to an area he had previously raped her when she was a child and asked to have sex with her.

"The victim told him to 'f.. off' and that he was a 'disgusting creep'. The defendant replied that 'the other girls still let me do it'."

She again told him to "f... off" and said he was "sick in the head".

"To which the defendant replied 'I know I am' while smiling."

The man also admitted a representative charge of indecent act on a young person under 16 in relation to a distant relative.

In response to questions from RNZ, police confirmed the investigation into the man began following an in-person report on 18 January 2024.

"The defendant was arrested and charged with sexual violation offences related to that report on 7 May 2024.

"Further investigations uncovered additional victims and resulted in 94 charges laid in total."

Where to get help:

If it is an emergency and you feel like you or someone else is at risk, call 111.
